Discovered contamination is one of the three abandonment triggers — the affected containers are discarded regardless of how clean the material looks. Washing and cooking are hygiene steps, not decontamination guarantees, and the trigger exists so that risk is never carried home.

Labeling before filling and never refilling a container with a second species are what make one-species-per-container real — an unlabeled bag is an unidentifiable bag, and sorting at home is exactly the failure mode the rule prevents. Container size and post-fill labels leave identity to memory, which is where it goes wrong.

Cornell's weed science profile documents that nightshade berries and foliage can be poisonous to humans, and immature berries are particularly toxic — while black and eastern black nightshade berries are dull blue-black and shiny purple-black, the color family of sought-after dark berries. Color and resemblance are not identification. Tasting to "test" a berry is never a documented safety method; the correct action is positive identification of the whole plant, or rejection.

The core test is the decisive documented field character: when a raspberry is picked, the receptacle stays on the plant, leaving a cup-shaped cavity in the fruit; when a blackberry is picked, the receptacle stays with the fruit, leaving a spongy white center. The stem side confirms it — after a raspberry is picked, the core remains on the plant. The other options reverse the test or invent a rule.

Ohio State University Extension documents reports of toxicities from unripe fruits or even uncooked ripe elderberry fruits, and its explicit guidance is to avoid eating unripe elderberries and cook ripe elderberries before consumption. The deep-purple color is the documented ripeness cue, but ripeness does not remove the cooking requirement — and "toxic at every stage" overstates the documented facts for fully ripened fruit.

Purdue University Extension documents that unripe persimmons have a high tannin content that makes the fruit very astringent, and that collectors wait for the fruit to become soft and fall from the tree — while, contrary to popular belief, the fruit does not have to experience a frost to ripen. Unripe fruit is also the documented source of the tannin-related phytobezoar risk, so firm attached fruit is not a harvest signal; it is a wait signal.

Identification is a whole-plant exercise, not a fruit-only one. Penn State Extension documents the serviceberry as a shrub or small tree with five-petalled white flowers that emerge before or at the same time as the leaves and small edible fruit that darkens to deep reddish-purple to black when ripe — and the fruit is a pome, not a berry. Color, size, and season are supporting clues at most; the other options treat single clues as proof.

Cornell documents that nightshade berries and foliage can be poisonous to humans and livestock, immature berries are particularly toxic, and toxicity varies greatly (it is reduced, not removed, in ripe berries). The fact that some people use some nightshades for jam elsewhere is precisely why guessing is unsafe — no reliable rule of thumb exists across species, so an unidentified nightshade is rejected. The other options assert blanket rules the documentation does not support.

Site evaluation comes after plant identification and is its own gate: brambles are documented as thriving in disturbed areas such as roadsides, and roadside fruit may carry exhaust deposits, spray residue, or polluted runoff. No amount of appearance or washing at home reliably reverses a contaminated harvest site — the site is rejected in the field. The other options trade safety for convenience.

Poison Control documents that apple seeds contain amygdalin, which the body converts into cyanide, and that the seeds release only a small amount of hydrogen cyanide per gram — you would need to chew or grind hundreds of seeds to cause toxicity, and swallowing seeds in a whole core is safe. The proportional rule is not fear but practice: do not chew or eat fruit seeds, remove them before serving children, and discard cores. The other options misstate the documented dose.

NC State's plant database documents the wild strawberry's five round white petals and lists the mock strawberry as a plant it is "often confused with" — a look-alike with similar leaves and fruit but yellow flowers. Whole-plant characters, including flowers, separate the two; fruit appearance alone does not. The other options either invent a variety or dismiss the documented character.

No authoritative source documents a rule connecting wildlife feeding to human safety, and documented facts cut against it: birds and other wildlife are heavy competitors for serviceberries, while nightshade berries are documented poisonous to humans. Edibility for a bird never establishes edibility for a person — the identification and ripeness sequence is the only documented path. The other options promote the shortcut the lesson exists to remove.

Penn State Extension documents both traps in one sentence set: blackberries are red when unripe, and black raspberries are easily confused with blackberries — so color cannot decide either ripeness or species. The documented characters are the core test (hollow cavity = raspberry; spongy white center = blackberry), fruit shape, and cane appearance. Options A and B guess by color; option C abandons identification entirely.

Extension sources document fiddleheads (ostrich fern) in a narrow window, late April through May, with tightly coiled heads picked and several left per plant. Dandelion's tender young leaves belong to early spring, while lamb's-quarters and purslane are summer greens. Timing is part of identification: harvest the right stage in the right week.

Positive identification means multiple characters, all of them confirmed. For fiddleheads, extension sources name three features — brown papery scale covering, smooth stem, and a deep "U"-shaped groove — and identification rests on all of them. Resemblance, single characters, or "cook longer" reasoning do not convert an unconfirmed plant into a safe one.

Extension guidance is explicit: harvest only from areas you know have not been treated with chemicals, fertilizers, or herbicides, and avoid pathways, roadsides, animal/pet areas, and high-traffic areas. Washing is a required step, but it is not documented as a substitute for a clean harvest site — the site is part of the food's safety.

The documented method is scale removal, multiple washes in potable water, then a full rolling boil of at least 15 minutes or steaming for 10–12 minutes. Raw, lightly sautéed, and briefly parboiled fiddleheads are exactly the preparation associated with documented foodborne illness — cooking is a safety step, not a preference.

NC State Extension documents the sequence: soak young shoots in warm water to remove dirt and debris (no dish detergent or sanitizer), then boil in salted water for five minutes; the stinging quality disappears after cooking. Rinsing, sun-drying, and freezing are not documented ways to make nettles edible.

Extension sources document that several foodborne illness outbreaks have occurred as a result of consuming raw or undercooked fiddleheads. Washing reduces grit; it does not make raw fiddleheads safe. The documented method is a full rolling boil of at least 15 minutes or steaming 10–12 minutes.

The documented step is boiling — the stinging quality disappears after cooking. Young shoots are the edible stage, but they are not edible raw; the sting is a property of the plant, not of age. Soap and detergent are explicitly excluded from the documented cleaning method.

The rule is rejection: no plant in this module should be consumed without positive identification and its documented preparation steps. Guessing by resemblance, taste-testing, and assuming "similar greens prepare the same way" all replace documented method with improvisation — and improvisation is not a preparation requirement.

Extension sources document picking young, tender dandelion leaves before the plant begins to flower; older leaves become bitter, and boiling with a water change is the documented way to mellow that tang. The flower stem is documented as inedible because the milky sap is bitter — the opposite of tender.

Extension sources document freezing and pickling as the preservation options for fiddleheads, with tested recipes. Preservation does not change the preparation requirement — frozen fiddleheads still must be boiled at least 15 minutes or steamed 10–12 minutes before serving. Air-drying, room-temperature storage, and salting are not documented methods, and serving any preserved batch raw repeats the documented illness risk.

Extension guidance documents refrigerating dandelion leaves not used right away, and food storage fundamentals ([[FOD-food-storage-K01]]) govern shelf life: label, date, rotate, and know how long food lasts. Room-temperature storage and indefinite airtight storage ignore documented shelf-life limits, and freezing without documented preparation does not preserve a food that was never documented as freezable.

The method is a comparison process: list the observable features, compare each against a documented source, and check every diagnostic feature — not one, not "most of them." Confirming from one feature, a remembered photo, or a companion's impression is exactly the shortcut that produces look-alike mistakes.

Identification is confirmed only when every diagnostic feature matches. Hairless, blotched stems are a documented poison hemlock feature, and the plant cannot simultaneously be wild carrot. The abandonment rule applies — treat the plant as the dangerous option. No combination of "verified" parts or a smell test can override a failed diagnostic feature.

The entire danger of a look-alike pair is that the toxic member matches most features of the edible one — that is how the confusion happens. The features that separate the pair (stem hairiness and blotches, odor, hollow interior) are precisely the ones the "90% right" rule skips. Any single mismatch means the identification fails.

The full feature set — smooth hairless stems, purplish blotches, height well above the two feet wild carrot rarely exceeds, and no carrot scent — matches the documented poison hemlock description across every diagnostic feature. White umbel flowers are shared by both plants and separate nothing. The smell test is only one row of the check, not a shortcut on its own.

The documented death camas feature list is an onion-shaped, scaly bulb that lacks onion odor, with V-creased grass-like leaves, poisonous at all growth stages. Every observed feature matches death camas, so the identification of "wild onion" fails and the abandonment rule applies. Shape alone, cooking, and single-feature flower color are not identification.

The diagnostic set for true morels is pitted cap, cap attached at the base, and a hollow stem — and the extension guidance is to slice every morel lengthwise to verify. A filled interior is a documented false-morel feature, so one diagnostic feature fails and the identification is not confirmed. Checking only the two features you like, or assuming a season, skips the check that the slice is designed to make.

The comparison process is what makes an identification traceable: every feature maps to a documented description, and a mismatch becomes visible. Memory and folklore silently merge features from different plants, which is precisely how a toxic member gets "confirmed" — and there is no legal or species-specific reason to skip the check; the method applies to every pair and every plant.

The documented pairs exist precisely because the toxic member shares habitat and appearance with the harmless one. Similarity is the reason to run the full feature check, never evidence that the check can be skipped. Plants do not become toxic from proximity or crowding; the risk is mistaken identity, which only the feature-by-feature comparison resolves.

The documented features for water parsnip — leaf veins ending at the tips and flowers with bracts — fail on both counts, and the observed features match the water hemlock side of the pair. Under the abandonment rule, a failing diagnostic feature means the plant is treated as the dangerous option. Habitat, regional assumptions, and eating only "verified" parts do not override a failed identification.

A common name cannot be checked against a source the way a feature can. Names like "wild onion" are applied inconsistently across regions and people, and the death camas pair exists because the onion-shaped bulb without onion odor looks like the thing people call an onion. The feature list — odor, bulb structure, leaf shape — is what a source documents, and it is the only safe basis for identification.

Every feature on the list — scaly onion-shaped bulb, V-creased leaves, no onion odor — matches the documented death camas description across the board, so the "wild onion" candidate is not confirmed and the plant is treated as death camas. Shape alone is not identification, cooking is not documented as making this plant safe, and "eat only the leaves" contradicts the source's warning that all parts are poisonous at all growth stages.

Poison Control's documented answer is that unless you are very experienced in mushroom identification, you cannot tell a safe wild mushroom from a poisonous one; the Ohio State fact sheet adds that there is no test or characteristic that distinguishes them, and poisonous kinds can resemble edible ones in the same habitat. Counting "a few species" or adding a photo does not create the expert-level examination that edibility decisions require.

Poison Control describes post-exposure identification as specialist work done with mycologists, and the documented principle is that there is no test or characteristic that separates edible from poisonous mushrooms — a photo cannot supply one. An app match, a second opinion, or good lighting does not change what was actually examined.

The documented amatoxin pattern is a 6–24 hour delay between ingestion and symptoms, with the toxins completely absorbed by the time symptoms show. NAMA's instruction is "DON'T WAIT for symptoms to appear!" Feeling fine hours after a wild-mushroom meal is exactly the situation that has preceded documented poisonings.

Poison Control states directly: "Cooking doesn't make a poisonous mushroom safe." The Ohio State fact sheet marks the idea that parboiling, drying, or pickling removes toxins as False. With false morels the hazard can even grow during cooking, since the toxin breaks down into a volatile compound and the fumes can be toxic.

Michigan State documents the false morel as "commonly mistaken for a true morel" with potentially deadly results, and Ohio State states that false morels "must be regarded as poisonous and not collected for eating" and can cause death or serious illness. Age, dryness, or who eats them does not change the documented hazard.

Poison Control's documented instruction is to call a poison center right away if you think someone has eaten a wild mushroom — 1-800-222-1222 — and NAMA warns "DON'T WAIT for symptoms to appear!" because amatoxin symptoms are delayed 6–24 hours. Preserving a sample (and noting what was eaten and when) supports identification, and severe symptoms would additionally require emergency assessment per [[MED-emergency-assessment-K01]].

The Ohio State fact sheet explicitly marks "silver-spoon tarnishing, peeling skin, mushrooms on wood, animal consumption, meadow safety, white color" as myths — each one False. No household or habitat test is a documented identification method; the only documented basis for an edibility decision is expert-level identification of the actual mushroom.

NAMA documents amatoxin onset at 6–24 hours, and Michigan State Extension documents *Amanita* symptoms at 6–36 hours — "too late for the only antidote – a stomach pump." Symptom timing varies by toxin class, and the most dangerous classes are the slow ones, which is precisely why waiting for symptoms is the documented failure mode.

Ohio State's documented rule is that no mushroom should be eaten unless edibility is absolutely certain — a standard that requires expert-level identification, not the picker's confidence or regional experience (Poison Control notes identification skill does not transfer between regions). "A small amount" of an unidentified mushroom is still an unidentified exposure, and cooking does not make a poisonous mushroom safe.

NAMA's amatoxin species list includes *Galerina marginata*, *Pholiotina (Conocybe) filaris*, and several *Lepiota* species — small, brown mushrooms with the same severe toxicity as the large *Amanitas*. Size and color do not indicate safety, which is why "little brown mushroom" is a documented category requiring expert identification.

GI distress beginning 6–24 hours after a wild-mushroom meal is the documented amatoxin pattern, so this is a Poison Control call and a medical evaluation, not a wait-and-see situation. Preserving an uneaten portion helps identify the species, and severe symptoms would trigger the emergency assessment in [[MED-emergency-assessment-K01]]. Waiting for more family members to fall ill wastes the window in which prompt treatment matters most.

Opposite arrangement means two leaves at each node, directly across from each other. Alternate is one leaf per node, staggered; whorled is three or more at one point. Arrangement is a first-order character — getting it right determines which branch of any key you follow.

A leaf that divides into leaflets along a central stalk is pinnately compound — the standard term for that structure. Whorled describes where leaves attach to a stem, not leaf division. Simple leaves are single blades; they do not have leaflets.

Positive identification requires all key characters to match, and leaf arrangement is a first-order character in every key. A mismatch means the resemblance is unresolved evidence, not confirmation. Ignoring it because the flower matches is exactly the pattern-matching this module teaches against.

Positive identification means every key character matches a verified reference, checked against more than one authoritative source. The margin difference is exactly the kind of character that separates look-alike species, so it must be resolved with the references — not ignored, guessed, or tested by taste.

The documentation set that supports later confirmation covers the whole plant in habitat, both leaf surfaces, reproductive parts, the stem, and a scale reference — the characters extension identification guidance requests. A single flower photo, leaves-only, or a location shot each leaves most of the evidence undocumented.

An entire margin is smooth and unbroken. Lobed and toothed describe indented or saw-like edges, and compound describes a leaf divided into leaflets, not an edge character. Margin is one of the standard leaf characters recorded on every specimen.

A photo match is a suggestion, not a confirmation — and this plant is missing reproductive parts and has not been verified in person, so a key part of the evidence is absent. Misidentified plants can be toxic or deadly; when an identification is not positive, the correct action is no consumption, not a cautious taste.

An annual completes its life cycle within one growing season. A biennial flowers in its second season, and a perennial lives across many seasons. Life cycle is a basic classification step that narrows the field before finer characters are examined.

Seasonal state is a real limit: flowers and fruit appear only part of the year, and juvenile leaves can look very different from the mature form in the guide. When the plant's current state matches no reference, the honest answer is "not identified yet" — record it and revisit when key parts appear.

Structural characters — leaf arrangement, shape, margin, underside surface, bark, buds, and stem features — remain available all year and carry the identification when flowers and fruit are absent. Leaf color, height, soil, or branch lean are weak or misleading evidence on their own.

The field record — habitat shot, both leaf surfaces, stem, reproductive parts, and a scale reference, plus location notes — is what makes later confirmation possible at all. A dug-up specimen, memory, or a taste test preserves none of the evidence and none of the safety.

A dug-up bulb carries almost no identifying information; many species produce onion-like bulbs, and not all are food. The rule is absolute: positive aboveground identification comes first — no identification, no digging, no tasting. Appearance, smell, and cooking are not identification.

The USDA cattail plant guide explicitly calls rhizomes "underground stems." Burdock's documented structure is the taproot — "slender, fleshy, gray-brown tap roots growing to depths of 3 feet." Sunchoke's edible part is its tuber, and ramps form bulbs. Each mis-pairing above swaps the documented structure for a different species.

Underground parts grow in the soil and hold what the soil holds. Ground beside an actively sprayed field is a contamination red flag, and no documented washing or cooking step removes that risk. The other options contradict documented facts: cattail parts are edible "when gathered at the appropriate stage of growth," and spring is the season for the young shoots, not for rhizomes in general.

The USDA guide documents rhizomes eaten raw, baked, roasted, or broiled, with the core ground into flour. Options A, B, and C describe restrictions that appear nowhere in the verified sources — a good reminder to follow documented steps rather than folklore.

NC State Extension documents that "harvests should be limited to 5% to 10% of the plants in each plot" and warns that "the annual intensive harvesting is seriously damaging the wild populations of ramps." Ramps take 5–7 years from seed to root harvest, so aggressive takes are not replaced quickly, and flower-stalk plants should be left to set seed.

The rejection rule is absolute: no identification, no digging, no tasting. Neither digging a sample nor cooking a portion performs identification, and taste-testing underground parts is never an acceptable test. Rejection is the decision that keeps you safe; the opportunity to forage returns with knowledge.

The NC State Extension page documents that sunchoke "spreads by rhizome" and that "any tiny piece of the plant left in the soil will sprout new plants." Excavating everything is not needed for regrowth and destroys more of the patch than a take matched to the documented season (fall, after the flowers fade).

The USDA arrowhead guide documents: "After roasting, some tubers were dried and stored for winter use. The Chippewa gathered the 'Indian potatoes' in the fall, strung them, and hung them overhead in the wigwam to dry." Drying, then keeping the harvest cool and dark, is the storage pattern that carries underground foods through the winter ([[FOD-food-storage-K01]]).

NC State Extension documents that cultivated first-year burdock roots "are harvested by late autumn before becoming too fibrous," and that young leaves and immature flower stalks are edible "before flowers appear." Edibility at a given stage does not transfer to other stages or other parts of the same plant.

Identification is a package deal — habitat, season, and aboveground characteristics together — and it always precedes digging. Ramps are spring ephemerals of rich, moist hardwood forest with broad leaves and onion-garlic aroma. Comparing a dug bulb to produce, smelling it, or tasting it are not identification.

A cattail dug shallowly leaves "enough plants and rhizomes to grow back during the growing season" (USDA); a ramp bulb dug whole is gone, and the species is slow to replace it. Because excavation removes the structures plants regrow from, documented collection limits exist — no more than one-quarter of the plants in an area, and 5–10% for ramps.

Life-threatening external bleeding is defined by volume and flow: blood flowing continuously (or spurting) and a volume around half a soda can — a soaked-through pant leg indicates high volume. Not every bleeding wound is life-threatening, and location alone does not make a wound life-threatening.

The tourniquet goes 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart, and never directly over the wound or on a joint. "High and tight" is outdated guidance. Placement on the wound or joint fails to compress the vessels and can damage tissue.

Never remove a blood-soaked dressing — removing it disturbs any clot forming. Add material on top and keep pressing. Do not peek at the wound, and a tourniquet only applies to life-threatening limb bleeding, not the torso.

Never remove an embedded object — removal can make the bleeding much worse. Apply pressure around the object and pad/bandage around it, then seek medical care. Pressing on the rod itself delivers no pressure to the wound and may shift the object.

A tourniquet cannot be used on the groin — it works only on limbs. Life-threatening bleeding from the scalp, neck, shoulder, groin, or back is controlled with wound packing (if trained) plus direct pressure. Elevation does not stop life-threatening bleeding, and loose cover does nothing.

Uncontrolled bleeding, a tourniquet applied, signs of shock, embedded objects, amputations, and serious injuries all require emergency services now. Minor, controlled, and stopped bleeding does not meet those thresholds — but when in doubt, call.

Pale, cool, clammy skin; a rapid weak pulse; and altered responsiveness are signs of shock — a progressive, life-threatening condition that can follow severe bleeding. Care: keep the person warm and lying flat with feet raised about 12 inches, reassure, and monitor breathing and responsiveness while emergency services are en route.

Continue twisting until the bleeding stops — or until you cannot twist further — even if the person complains of pain; the pain is expected and the bleeding must stop. Then clip or secure the rod so it cannot unwind. Loosening or removing a tourniquet can restart life-threatening bleeding.

For a life-threatening limb wound with no tourniquet available, wound packing (if trained) plus direct pressure is the correct intervention. A thin shoelace fails and cuts into tissue; elevation and cold do not stop life-threatening bleeding.

Once applied, a tourniquet must not be loosened or removed except by a medical professional. Loosening can restart life-threatening bleeding and release harmful toxins into circulation. Reassure the person, note the application time, and hand that information to EMS.

The first priority is stopping the burning process and cooling the tissue — heat in the skin keeps driving the injury deeper. Butter, breaking blisters, and airtight wraps all worsen the burn and are strictly avoided in first aid.

A red, dry, painful burn with no blisters damages only the outer layer of skin — a superficial (first-degree) burn. Partial-thickness burns blister and are moist; full-thickness burns are waxy or leathery and may be painless in the center.

Cool running water (not ice-cold) for at least 5–30 minutes is the standard — about 10–20 minutes is a common practical target. Ice and ice-cold water deepen the injury, a brief rinse does not cool deeply enough, and ointments are never applied to a burn.

Intact blisters protect the damaged skin beneath from infection — first aid leaves blistered and dead skin undisturbed. Leaving blisters intact, loose covering, and removing constricting items early are all correct actions.

For dry chemicals, brush off excess powder first, remove contaminated clothing, then flush with cool running water for at least 15 minutes. Adding water before brushing, neutralizing with household products, and applying oil can spread the chemical or worsen the injury — and some dry chemicals (lime, elemental metals) must not be flushed with water.

Touching a person still in contact with live current can electrocute the rescuer, so power must be turned off at the source first. Water conducts electricity — pouring water on wires or using wet objects creates exactly the hazard you are trying to avoid.

Soot in the nose or mouth, coughing, a hoarse voice, and breathing difficulty after a fire are classic airway-burn signs — an emergency, since the airway can swell closed. A small blister, red dry skin, or a waxy patch alone does not indicate inhalation injury.

A waxy or leathery burn with a painless center is a full-thickness burn — deep damage may have destroyed the nerve endings that report pain. Lack of pain is a danger sign, not reassurance, and full-thickness burns need emergency care regardless of size.
Spreading redness, increasing pain, drainage or pus, and fever are signs of infection and need medical attention. Mild itching, tenderness during dressing changes, and normal healing flaking are not.

A full-thickness burn on the hand combines two red flags — severe depth and a high-risk location — and an electrical cause requires medical evaluation because internal damage may be hidden. A small superficial burn, a small blister, and mild sunburn are the kinds of cases first aid alone can manage.

The scene is unsafe — a person in contact with high-voltage current can electrocute a rescuer. The rule is to stay at least 20 feet away until the power is turned off and never touch a person still in contact with the source. You do not become a second victim; you call for help and keep the scene clear.

Responsiveness comes first: tap the shoulder and shout "Are you okay?" No response means the person is unresponsive and the situation is an emergency. Positioning, compressions, and fluids all come after you know the person's responsiveness and breathing — and an unresponsive person must never be given anything to eat or drink.

The reliable move is to send a specific person to call the emergency number while you stay with the casualty — "send someone else to call while you begin CPR." A general shout to a crowd lets everyone assume someone else is doing it. Calling a specific, named direction closes that gap, and calling before the secondary check keeps the fastest threat first.

Gasping or gurgling is not normal breathing. It is a sign of a person in trouble, and waiting to "see if it becomes normal" spends the minutes that matter. Treat a person who is only gasping as not breathing normally: call (or send someone to call) the emergency number, then begin hands-only CPR.

For an unresponsive person who is breathing normally, the recovery position keeps the airway open while they cannot protect it themselves — and you keep checking, because breathing can stop and then the person needs to be rolled onto their back for CPR. Compressions are for the person not breathing normally; sitting an unresponsive person up can block the airway.

The person is not breathing normally, so the priority is chest compressions: hands-only CPR in the center of the chest, hard and fast, with minimal interruptions, until help arrives. The recovery position is for a person who is breathing; waiting, or trying to wake the person, spends the minutes in which compressions keep blood moving.

In a multiple-casualty scene, unresponsiveness and abnormal breathing are the fastest threats. The person who is shouting is awake and breathing; the silent, unresponsive person may not be. Prioritization means checking the unresponsive casualty first — do not let the loudest casualty monopolize the assessment.

The assessment loops, it does not end: breathing can stop and bleeding can worsen while you wait, so you check frequently and stay with the person until help arrives. If breathing stops, the person goes onto their back and compressions begin. "Help was called" and "looks stable" do not end the reassessment loop.

A fall from height makes spine injury a real possibility. The person stays still with the head and neck supported; movement can make a spine injury worse. Sitting them up, walking them, or having them move their head all violate that stillness. The only reason to move is a scene danger.

Assessment starts with activation, and activation starts with knowing the number and the plan. A household that knows the local emergency number, has decided who calls, and has practiced the plan makes the right calls under stress — a rehearsed plan is a decision already made. Equipment is a tool, not a substitute for the practiced plan, and waiting to learn until the emergency is the opposite of preparedness.

Official lists converge on a core wound-care set: adhesive bandages in assorted sizes, sterile gauze, adhesive tape, and antiseptic wipes, supported by tools like scissors and tweezers. Fire gear is preparedness, not first aid; medications are a separate layer; and bandages are not optional — they are the point of the layer.

PPE protects the person giving care first. Non-latex gloves shield the responder from blood and body fluids while avoiding latex allergies — which may affect the very person you are helping. No glove makes hands completely sterile, and latex is not banned; it is just the wrong choice when a non-latex option exists.

Kits include your own prescription medications — a 7-day supply minimum per preparedness practice — kept in original labeled containers, used per label instructions, and checked at every inspection. Antibiotics are not kit items, and medications are never shared or used outside their labels. When in doubt, a pharmacist or healthcare provider decides.

Organization is a safety feature: the most-used items — bandages, wipes, gloves — go on top, and transparent labeled pouches group items by function so nothing must be emptied to find one thing. Buried bandages convert a two-second response into a search, which is exactly what a kit must not be.

Kits decay silently, so the fix is a routine: a full check every six months anchored to daylight-saving changes, immediate restocking after any use, and a pre-trip check for the vehicle and personal kits. A single purchase-day check ignores expiration, and daily checks are not a sustainable schedule.

The tier pattern is home, vehicle, personal: each kit holds what that location realistically needs, and every tier stays compact enough to be carried. A full duplicate home kit is bulky and unnecessary, and a vehicle is where you most need the basics when you are away from the house.

Adaptation follows the household: ages (child sizes and extra dressing supplies where children live and visit), medical history (personal prescriptions, 7-day supply), and the household's non-human members (a small pet section). One generic kit ignores these needs, and medications belong in the kit stored out of reach, not removed from it.

Red Cross guidance is blunt: knowing how to use first-aid items is as important as having them, if not more. A manual is a backup for memory, not a replacement for training, and first aid is not definitive treatment — severe bleeding, chest pain, and trouble breathing are calls to your local emergency number.

Preparedness supplies decay — including stored water, which should be rotated on the same schedule logic as medications and food. Tying water rotation to the six-month inspection keeps the whole emergency supply healthy, rather than waiting for visible signs that may not appear before the water is needed.

Preparedness has three legs — plan, kit, knowledge — and a kit without a plan is a box of bandages. The written, rehearsed plan decides where supplies live, who uses them, and when the household escalates to emergency services. No kit, however complete, replaces calling for help in a true emergency.

Deformity, a snap heard at impact, and swelling are signs of a possible fracture, and a fracture may be present even when the limb can still move. The correct response is to keep the limb still and splint it as found. Testing the wrist, straightening it, or waiting to see if pain eases can all cause further damage.

Sprains (ligaments), strains (muscles/tendons), and fractures (bones) produce overlapping signs — pain, swelling, bruising, trouble moving the part — and only imaging can reliably tell them apart. The safe rule is to treat the worst case: immobilize and seek evaluation, never "walk it off."

A splint must immobilize the joints above and below the injury so the bone cannot be moved through them. A splint that covers only the injury site, or leaves the wrist and elbow free, allows movement that can cause more damage. Immobilizing the elbow to the shoulder adds nothing for a forearm injury.

Circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) are checked in the fingers or toes beyond the injury before and after splinting. Skin that blanches and pinks back within about two seconds, normal feeling, and voluntary movement indicate intact circulation. Pain scales and swelling comparisons do not detect a splint cutting off blood flow.

An injured limb is splinted in the position it was found; straightening or realigning a possible fracture can cause more damage to bone, blood vessels, and nerves. The only exception is a last-resort case where professional help is unavailable and the limb is abnormally bent AND pale from poor circulation — and even then it is done gently.

Coldness, paleness, or a bluish color below an injury are signs of compromised circulation and require immediate emergency care — the limb can be threatened within a narrow window. Wiggling, rubbing, or waiting to see if color returns delays that care and can make the outcome worse.

A suspected hip or pelvis injury — like a suspected spine injury — means the person is kept still and supported while EMS is called; moving them can cause further damage. Bearing weight on the hip, carrying her, or testing her ability to walk all risk making the injury worse.

A good improvised splint has three parts: a rigid support (rolled newspaper), padding to avoid extra pressure on the limb, and ties placed above and below the injury, snug but not tight. It must extend beyond the injury to immobilize the joint above it (the elbow) as well as the joint below it (the wrist). A rigid splint without padding, or ties directly over the injury, can cut off circulation or cause pressure damage.

A cold pack wrapped in a thin, dry towel, applied for no more than 20 minutes at a stretch with breaks between applications, reduces pain and swelling safely. Ice placed directly on the skin, or left on continuously, can damage tissue — and cold relieves symptoms without treating the injury, so it never replaces getting the person to care.

Movement does not rule out a fracture; an X-ray is usually required to diagnose a broken bone, so the injury is treated as a possible fracture regardless of what the person can do. Sending him off without care — or worse, testing the limb — risks turning a manageable injury into a worse one.

Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, rapid breathing, and a fast weak pulse with intact thinking describe heat exhaustion, which is treated on scene: cool place, loose clothing, sips of cool water, cooling, and monitoring. Heat stroke is distinguished by the mental state — confusion, irritability, slurred speech — which this hiker does not yet show. Continuing the hike or dismissing the signs risks progression to heat stroke.

Hot skin with confusion and collapse is heat stroke — a medical emergency, even though the skin is sweaty. The correct response is to call emergency services immediately and cool aggressively while waiting: shade, excess clothing removed, cold water immersion if possible, and cold packs on the neck, armpits, and groin. Resting in place, walking him out, or keeping him in the sun delays emergency care and cooling.

Confusion, drowsiness, slowed breathing, and shivering that has stopped are signs of severe hypothermia, not recovery — shivering stops when the body can no longer generate heat. This is an emergency: handle gently and keep her still because sudden movements can trigger cardiac arrest, warm gradually, and call EMS. Warming extremities first or treating this as fatigue would delay emergency care.

Heat exhaustion is treated by stopping and cooling: move to a cool place, loosen clothing, sip cool water, cool the body, and monitor — untreated, it can progress to heat stroke. Caffeine and fever-reducing medicines are not appropriate (caffeine makes it harder for the body to regulate temperature), and continuing to work in the sun increases risk.

Frostbitten tissue is rewarmed gently: warm (never hot) water for roughly 20–30 minutes when there is no refreezing risk, or body heat for small areas. Rubbing or massaging damages frozen tissue, and direct dry heat like a stove or radiator can burn numb skin that cannot feel it. Blowing warm breath and massaging combines friction with an unreliable heat source.

Severe hypothermia care is gentle and gradual: keep the person still because sudden movements can trigger cardiac arrest, warm the center of the body first with dry blankets, and call EMS. Alcohol and caffeine interfere with temperature regulation and must be avoided, and nothing is given by mouth to a person who is not fully alert. Hot showers, vigorous rubbing, and warming extremities first all risk driving cold blood toward the core.

Heat illness prevention centers on hydration, limiting time in the heat, scheduling exertion for cooler hours, resting in shade, and never leaving infants or children in parked cars. Midday heavy work, skipping breaks, and cracked-window parked cars all raise risk. Prevention is also where the preparedness plan in [[SUR-preparedness-K01]] pays off: the decisions are made before the heat arrives.

Stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, and grumbles — the "umbles" — are early hypothermia signs: cold is degrading coordination and judgment. The response is to stop and warm: out of the wind, wet clothing removed, insulated from the ground, and warmed with dry covering. Picking up the pace, treating it as dehydration, or focusing only on extremities ignores a whole-body cooling problem.

Frostbitten feet must not be walked on, and tissue should be thawed only where it can remain thawed — rewarming before a 20-minute walk risks refreezing, which causes more damage. Rubbing (with snow or hands) and popping blisters are both prohibited, and a heating pad can burn numb skin. Hard, white tissue suggests deep frostbite, which needs professional care.

Cold-weather prevention is planning plus gear: knowing the forecast and route, carrying dry layers and wind protection, covering the exposed areas (hands, feet, ears, nose, cheeks), and using buddy checks for shivering and behavior changes. Cotton holds moisture, "keep moving" fails when rest or a delay happens, and experience does not replace a forecast — all are gaps the preparedness plan in [[SUR-preparedness-K01]] is designed to close.

A deep, gaping wound — one whose edges do not meet, in this case roughly the size of a thumbnail — needs professional evaluation because wounds more than about a quarter inch deep may require stitches. Bleeding control still comes first, but self-care is not appropriate here. Calling 911 is reserved for severe or unstoppable bleeding, and taping a wound closed is closure, which is a professional procedure.

Bleeding control comes before everything else — bleeding is the number one cause of preventable death after injury. Cleaning, ointment, and debris removal all wait until bleeding is controlled. Direct pressure with a clean cloth and elevation is the standard first step.

Clean running water rinses the wound, and mild soap goes on the surrounding skin, not inside the wound. Hydrogen peroxide and rubbing alcohol can further irritate the wound and delay healing, so they are out. Scrubbing the wound interior or skipping cleaning both raise infection risk.

The dressing keeps the wound clean and maintains a moist environment that promotes healing, so it must be changed at least once a day and whenever it gets wet or dirty. Leaving a wet or soiled dressing in place invites infection; changing hourly is unnecessary.

Unknown tetanus vaccination status after a wound — especially a dirty or puncture-type injury — requires professional evaluation, and vaccination is a professional procedure, not a first-aid supply item. Whether a booster is needed is a decision for a healthcare professional, not a self-assessment.

Small, loose debris can be lifted out gently with tweezers that have been cleaned with alcohol. Digging with fingers or forcing an embedded object out can damage tissue or drive debris deeper. Long or deeply stuck objects are never removed at home — they are stabilized and handled professionally.

Increasing redness, warmth, and a red streak extending from the wound are classic infection warning signs, along with growing swelling, worsening pain, pus-like drainage, and fever. Normal healing redness fades and stays local; spreading warmth and streaks mean professional care now.

Wound closure — stitching or otherwise bringing wound edges together — is a professional procedure, and deep wounds that may need closure should go to a professional. Attempting closure without training risks trapping bacteria and producing poor healing. First aid stops at cleaning, dressing, and escalating.

Animal bites are always a professional-care trigger — saliva contamination and infection risk make them high-risk regardless of size. Minor scrapes, scratches, and paper cuts that are clean, shallow, and stop bleeding quickly are typical self-care wounds.

Pus-like drainage plus fever are infection signs that require professional care. A dry, intact dressing, stable pink edges with non-spreading redness, and bleeding that stopped promptly are all signs the wound is behaving normally. The monitoring routine exists to catch changes like the one in option A.

The orienting arrow and its parallel lines are the component that boxes the needle: you rotate the bezel until the needle sits inside them, then read the bearing at the index line. The needle points to magnetic north, not true north, and the bezel is designed to rotate freely — that rotation is what sets a bearing.

A compass needle aligns with the magnetic field and settles toward magnetic north, while maps are drawn to true north — the difference is the declination, and it varies by location and over time. The needle is doing exactly what it should; the instrument is not broken, and neither is the map.

The bearing procedure is fixed: aim the direction-of-travel arrow at the target, rotate the bezel until the needle is boxed by the orienting arrow, then read the dial at the index line. Setting the bezel before aiming, or reading from the baseplate itself, bypasses the needle-boxing step and produces a wrong or meaningless number.

Walking to intermediate objects keeps you on a straight line without watching the dial, and gives you checkpoints so drift is noticed early. Staring at the needle causes drift and stumbles; a single unverified reading cannot hold a long leg against terrain and obstacles.

The back bearing is the forward bearing plus or minus 180 degrees: 55° is less than 180°, so add 180° to get 235°. The other options are arithmetic errors — 125° is 180° minus 55°, and 305° is 360° minus 55° — and holding the original bearing would march you past your start point.

Converting a true bearing to a magnetic bearing with east declination means subtracting the declination: 290° − 10° = 280°. Leaving the bearing unconverted (290°) or adding instead of subtracting (300°) both send you 10° off line — about 175 meters per kilometer of travel.

Declination drifts year to year, so a map collar's printed value is only accurate for the year the map was made. USGS recommends getting a current value — NOAA's online calculator — for maps more than about 15 years old. Using a stale value is the same error as ignoring declination: the mistake is the size of the change, not of the printed number.

Erratic, jumping readings are the signature of magnetic interference: iron, vehicles, electronics, and magnets deflect the needle. The remedy is to sight away from metal and keep devices at arm's length. A compass is not re-magnetized by tapping, and the sun does not deflect a compass needle.

A 180-degree reversal — walking 280° instead of 100° — is the classic wrong-end error: the bezel was rotated so the white end of the needle sat in the box, so the dial read exactly opposite the true bearing. Declination errors shift readings by degrees, not by a half-turn, and a slipped bezel would not reverse the direction.

To reverse your line, compute the back bearing: 15° is less than 180°, so add 180° to get 195°. The reciprocal of a bearing near north is a bearing near south — 165° and 345° are arithmetic slips, and keeping 15° would march you farther from the vehicle.

The decimal degrees convert by multiplying the fractional degrees by 60 twice: 0.976331° is 58' 34.79", and 0.700936° is 42' 03.37". The converted minutes and seconds must stay below 60, so option C is an invalid conversion, and the hemispheres and the latitude/longitude order of the other options move the point to the wrong part of the world.

NOAA defines latitude as distance north or south of the equator, with parallels running east–west, and longitude as distance east or west of the prime meridian, with meridians running pole to pole. Option C describes meridians, not parallels, and option D gives latitude the wrong direction and range.

Grid references are always read right, then up: the easting (vertical line) comes first, then the northing (horizontal line), giving a reference that starts 16 and then 23. Reversing the order points at a different square, and neither rounding nor averaging produces a usable reference.

Per USGS, the UTM system is 60 zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide, and every zone contains the same easting and northing values — so a zone number (and hemisphere) is required to know which of 60 identical-numbered points the caller means. UTM is a complete coordinate system by itself; the issue is the dropped zone, not the system.

USGS states that most USGS topographic maps published through 2006 use NAD 27, while WGS 84 is the default datum on almost all GPS devices. The two frames can shift the same printed coordinate by tens to hundreds of meters (UTM values by roughly 200 m), which matches the error exactly. The fix is to check the map's margin datum and set the device — or the report — accordingly.

Four digits identify the whole 1,000-meter square; adding one digit to each half of the reference (six digits total) subdivides the square by ten, claiming about 100 meters of precision. Contour lines describe elevation, not position, and skipping interpolation gives you a kilometer of ambiguity.

A location is not complete until format and datum are stated, because the same digits mean different ground points under different frames; reading digit by digit protects against misheard numbers, and a terrain description lets a searcher verify the plotted point. A rushed single pass, a bare landmark, or zone-and-elevation alone all leave the plotted point ambiguous.

Each added digit pair subdivides the grid square by ten: 4 digits give about 1,000 meters, 6 give about 100, and 8 give about 10. Halving (option C) confuses precision with something else — the square divides by ten, not two — and the other options reverse the digit-to-precision relationship.

A pair of numbers written with decimal points, like 37.7749 and -122.4194, is decimal degrees — the format most phone and GPS displays output. DMS uses degree, minute, and second symbols; UTM and MGRS values are meters and include zone or letter identifiers, not plain signed decimals.

Per USGS, the military uses its own implementation of the UTM system, called MGRS, which packages the zone and 100,000-meter square into a compact prefix. That makes references short, unambiguous, and plot-ready for ground reporting. It is UTM-based, works with paper maps, and is measured in meters, so the other options describe something else.

A coordinate pair is complete only when its format and datum are stated — the same numbers point to different ground positions in different reference systems and written formats. Speaking slowly, digit by digit, and confirming the read-back ensures the numbers arrive exactly as displayed. Omitting the datum or rushing the numbers can shift your stated position.

The rescue message carries six parts — who, what, where, injuries, resources, and plan — because those facts decide where crews search, what they look for, and what they bring. A bare plea or a long narrative gives rescuers neither. Hanging up after coordinates loses the condition and route information that narrow the search.

A trip plan left with someone who is not on the trip is a message sent before the emergency: where you started, where you were heading, and when you were due back. Rescuers search the corridor you traveled, and the plan tells them where that corridor is. It supports the search but never replaces your own message, signals, or position report.

At night sound carries, and the documented pattern is three whistle blasts with a pause before repeating — a pattern a rescuer can distinguish from wind and random noise. Shouting burns energy and carries poorly in forest, a fire at night in dense brush risks becoming the emergency itself, and a steady light beam does not read as a distress pattern the way SOS sequences do.

A PLB transmits on 406 MHz, the distress frequency monitored by the satellite rescue system, and activates an alert to rescue authorities within minutes wherever you are — but it sends no texts and receives no replies. A phone is a two-way tool that ends at the edge of coverage. They are different tools: the PLB is a last-resort 911, not a text machine.

The documented guidance is to stay put: changing location makes you harder to find, and rescuers searching the corridor you reported will expect you near where you were last known. Moving on a guess risks injury and a lost position. Unless an immediate threat — floodwater, fire, unstable ground — is at your location, staying put is the findable choice.

A descriptive fallback works when it names features a map can find: named or distinctive landmarks — the lake, the ridge face, the junction, the creek crossing — plus your relationship to them. "Somewhere in the mountains" and "trees and rocks" describe every location in the region, and a half-remembered hill has no place a rescuer can pin to a map.

Airplane mode with scheduled, brief check-ins is the documented practice: the device transmits only when you choose, preserving battery for the moment there is actually something to transmit. Constant signal searching, screen use, and bright displays drain the battery with no rescue benefit — a dead phone cannot make the call that matters.

In daylight, visual contrast is what aircraft crews see: a mirror (or foil) flash aimed at the aircraft and a large bright ground shape — clothing, a shelter, rocks in a pattern — make your position visible from the air. Whistle sound competes poorly with an aircraft engine; a fire in dry season violates fire-safety rules; and texts need a tower that is not there.

The rescue message must reflect your honest condition: a twisted ankle that slows you changes how long your resources last, where you can move, and what the crew needs — extraction gear, more carriers, more time. Assessing yourself before you report, then reporting the truth, lets rescuers bring the right response instead of arriving unprepared for the real situation.

GPS is satellite-based: the receiver listens to one-way signals from satellites and computes a three-dimensional position and time from them. The cell network is not involved in the position fix at all. What does need a connection is the map display, which is why offline areas must be downloaded before the trip.

GNSS is the general term for any satellite constellation providing positioning, navigation, and timing; GPS is one of four global systems, with regional systems like QZSS and NavIC alongside. A receiver that draws on several constellations sees more satellites — better geometry and redundancy, which matters exactly where yours struggled: deep valleys and under cover.

The position fix comes from satellites, not towers, so it works with zero cell service. The map display, however, is data — if the offline area was not downloaded at home, there is nothing to render. Option C is the reverse of reality: nothing is cached automatically, and what is cached may be only what was downloaded deliberately.

Offline map areas are regions of map data stored on the device, so the download must happen while you have connectivity and power — at home, on Wi-Fi, covering the route plus a margin. Waiting for the trailhead gambles on signal you may not have. A static screenshot cannot give you a position overlay or pannable, zoomable map.

Airplane mode stops the cellular radio from hunting for signal, location stays on so GPS still works, and screen discipline plus closed background apps remove the biggest drains. Continuous tracking and a bright screen burn the battery far faster, and a phone that is always off is not a navigation aid during the day you actually need it.

The National Park Service documents that batteries for electronic devices often lose charge in the cold, and its guidance is to carry backup power and keep batteries in a pocket on an inside layer, where body heat keeps them warm. Satellite signal strength and software bugs do not drive the drop; the cold does.

The accuracy circle is the app's estimate of how far the fix could be off, not a boundary around your true position. GPS.gov gives typical smartphone accuracy as within a 4.9 m (16 ft) radius under open sky, worsening near buildings, bridges, and trees. The correct habit is to treat the circle as guidance and confirm your position against terrain and map features.

Reflected signals ("multipath") and blockage by buildings are documented causes of degraded GPS accuracy. Satellite orbits do not shift hour to hour, battery level does not change how the fix is computed, and the U.S. ended Selective Availability in 2000 with no intent to reintroduce it — the error is environmental, not policy.

The failure drill is: stop and take stock, mark the last known position on the paper map, switch to map and compass, and conserve the device — a dead battery is final. Gambling on a wet phone reviving, walking toward a fix, or retracing without the map all replace a practiced plan with hope.

Electronics fail in routine ways — water, impact, dead battery, app crash — so the primary navigation system must be the one that cannot run out of power: paper map and compass, practiced. GPS is a valuable convenience on top of that foundation. A phone-only setup, even with backup power, still hangs the whole plan on a single device.

Off-trail route planning requires relief — the shape and height of the land — which only a topographic map shows through contour lines. Road maps show transportation, recreation overviews generalize detail away, and satellite photos, however sharp, show no elevation contours at all.

At 1:24,000, one inch on the map equals 24,000 inches on the ground, which is 2,000 feet. Two and a half inches is 2.5 × 2,000 = 5,000 feet. The other options confuse units: A drops a factor of two, C treats 24,000 as feet per inch, and D applies the scale number to a single inch only.

The legend is the map's own dictionary: every symbol on that specific map is explained there, along with scale, contour interval, and date. Symbols vary between publishers and series, so context, memory, and other people's guesses all fail where the legend cannot.

Stream valleys make contour V's that point upstream, toward higher ground, with the stream in the middle — that is a valley or draw. Ridges and spurs point the V downhill, a saddle dips between two summits, and a depression is a closed ring with inward ticks.

Contour spacing shows slope: lines close together mean elevation is gained quickly over a short horizontal distance — steep ground — while wide spacing means gentle ground. Spacing does not tell elevation, wetness, or distance; those come from labels, blue lines, and the scale.

Index contours repeat every fifth contour line, so with a 20-foot interval the next index is 5 × 20 = 100 feet higher: 1,140. The 1,060 option is a single interval step — that is an intermediate contour, not an index — and the other values do not follow the map's interval pattern at all.

1:24,000 is the larger scale — the fraction 1/24,000 is bigger than 1/250,000 — and the larger-scale map shows fine detail: small streams, foot trails, and individual buildings. The small-scale map trades that detail for a wider view, so it cannot show the features this route depends on.

The inward-pointing ticks on a depression contour always point toward the lower ground, so the closed loop marks a hole or sink, not a hill. A hilltop's innermost ring is the highest ground; a saddle is an open dip between hills; a spur is an open V pointing downhill.

Index contours are labeled with their exact elevations, so moving from a 2,800 line to a 2,600 line means the ground dropped 200 feet. Index contours repeat every fifth line, but their labels give real elevations — reading the labels directly is the fastest way to check whether your route climbs or descends.

A map is a promise the terrain may not keep: trails close and land changes after the survey, so when the map and the terrain disagree, the terrain wins. Adjusting the route to the real ground is normal navigation, not failure — abandoning the trip and waiting for the map to be right are both overreactions to a routine discrepancy.

A checkpoint that fails to appear on schedule is data — you are not where you think you are, and the honest moment is when the correction is cheapest. Ten more minutes of hope, or trusting the look of the terrain, is denial by another name and compounds the error. Turning back in alarm without verifying skips the thinking step entirely.

Wrong turns happen at decision points, and the decision must be made with the map and compass, not by the look of the trail — two similar branches are precisely the situation where memory and appearance fail. Wear, sun position, and the assumption that forks rejoin are all guesswork compared to a bearing and contour check.

Parallel streams and ridges look alike, and a single matching feature is confirmation bias, not confirmation. The missing lake is the second check failing: distance, shape, and the sequence of features must all match. A dry lake is a guess, a scale misread would not remove a lake, and a compass that "matches" the wrong stream was never the problem.

The procedure's order is the procedure: the first thing is to stop — before the compass, before the high point, before any retracing. Every unplanned step moves you away from the last position searchers can anchor on. Bearing, observation, and backtracking are all later steps that depend on the stop.

The order is stop, think, observe, plan: reconstruct the last known position and the distance traveled since, then observe the terrain and map to narrow the possibilities, then plan. Planning before observing inverts the procedure, moving before thinking skips it, and signaling without assessing abandons the analysis that makes the signal useful.

Backtracking is the strongest recovery move when the distance is short, the route is clear, and daylight remains — all three hold here. Continuing forward from an unverified position compounds the error, sheltering ignores that the conditions do not say stop, and cutting cross-country from an unknown position is exactly how the search area grows.

A catching feature — a road, river, or summit — is prominent enough that reaching it re-establishes a known position, and this river leads to a road. Staying put is right when it is the plan, but it is not an absolute rule with daylight and a reliable feature within reach. Cliff bands are hazards, not catching features, and a random bearing just expands the search area.

Darkness approaching, weather deteriorating, and no known position are the conditions that say stop and shelter — all three apply at once. The backtrack is over an hour of rough terrain and will outrun the light, and pushing on without a plan moves you from the only position searchers can use. Drainages are a last resort, not a first move.

Exhaustion and injury are stop-moving conditions regardless of whether you know your position — judgment and coordination degrade, and 6 km of steep ground with a bad ankle is how a fixable problem becomes a rescue. Pushing on and descending steep ground with an injury both raise risk, and whistles are used in bursts — three blasts, then listen — not continuously.

The route plan's whole purpose is to give your contact and searchers the where and when — the trailhead, the route, and the expected return time — so the response starts from your last known position, not a guess. Reporting early, while stopped, is the plan working; waiting, hiding the situation, or moving to "make" the return time all discard the plan's advantage.

The navigation problem is built from four components — position, direction, distance, and destination. You have position ("where am I") and destination ("where am I going"); what is missing is direction (which way you have been moving) and distance (how far you have come). Until those two are re-established, the next leg cannot be planned honestly.

A bearing is a single number — the direction to the lake in degrees from north. A route is the actual path, chosen for the ground: the gentler slope, the open ridge, the safe crossing. The direct bearing up the talus slope is the correct direction but a poor route — you plan the bearing, then choose a route that may bend around the terrain, with a bearing for each leg.

The workflow opens with "know your starting point" — identifying it on the map before moving, because an unconfirmed start poisons every step after it. Position is fixed first; direction and distance tracking then build on that fix. Starting to walk and sorting it out later is how drift begins.

A checkpoint is the moment the plan meets reality: the map is the authority and the ground is the evidence. Before treating the creek as the mapped one, confirm the details — its position, the direction it flows, the shape of the surrounding ground. If they match, you are verified and continue; if not, the creek is a look-alike and your position is not what you believed.

Staying oriented is continuous — building a mental picture of what you have crossed, climbed, and noticed, and correcting it the moment the ground disagrees. Deliberate observation works without instruments and is exactly the situational awareness that catches errors before they compound. One sun check or a step count is a reading, not orientation.

Parallel ridges and spurs look alike from a distance, and a junction chosen in haste is followed for hours — the classic wrong-ridge mistake. The fix is checking the ridge's shape and trend against the map before committing at every junction. Blaming the compass, the terrain, or the map's age does not change the ground; confirming your position does.

Drifting off bearing is one of the silent errors: 15 degrees of drift puts you roughly 270 meters off line for every kilometer walked — invisible in a hundred meters, decisive at a valley. The fix is correction now and regular rechecks, because the error built without being noticed. Fifteen degrees is not "normal" and does not only matter at long range — it matters exactly as much as you walked.

Forest hides the landmarks terrain association needs, canopy can degrade GPS signal, and natural indicators give only coarse direction with no distance or position. Map and compass work in any visibility, so they lead; the GPS provides a precise cross-check on position while it has battery. The rule holds: map and compass are the baseline, and GPS is the check, not the whole system.

Featureless terrain removes the landmarks that terrain association relies on, so position checks must come from direction and distance — a disciplined bearing, tracked distance, and verification against the GPS while it works. Natural indicators give direction but no distance or position. Flat ground is not "nothing to hit"; it is where drift becomes invisible.

When position cannot be verified, the safe move is to stop, fix it carefully, and be prepared to turn back or wait — never out-walk your ability to navigate, because errors compound silently and the fastest person going the wrong way is merely lost sooner. Walking faster into unverified ground, gambling on the weather, or trusting a stream that may sink or turn are all navigation errors wearing an optimistic coat.

Night preserves large, high-contrast, linear features — a ridgeline against the sky is the most reliable night checkpoint there is. Contour reading, color contrast, and depth perception are precisely what darkness removes: slope, color, and distance judgment all fail without light.

Sound is one of the cues night preserves — the stream confirms you are where the map says the stream is. But audible confirmation is not depth or bank assessment; the crossing itself must be at a daylight-verified point, approached slowly with light on the footing.

Night routes follow handrails — linear features like roads and streams that guide you without needing to be located. The shortest cross-country route relies on contour reading and terrain association that darkness removes, and a route's familiarity never replaces its identifiability in the dark.

The test for a night checkpoint is whether you can confirm it at midnight: a road crossing and a lake edge are visible shapes or audible features you cannot miss. A knoll read from contours, a subtle junction, or a vague hillside point cannot be confirmed in the dark.

FM 3-25.26 calls determining distance "the most common source of error" in land navigation, and night shortens strides and adds fatigue error. A pace count is an estimate to be confirmed at checkpoints, never a measurement that overrides what the ground shows.

With no distant landmark, a bearing leg is broken into intermediate points picked in the light beam — walk to each, recheck, repeat. A long leg with no visible point is where holding error wanders; white light destroys night vision; spreading the group breaks cohesion and risks a lost person.

Night vision takes about 30 minutes to adapt and red light preserves it — even a second of white light resets it and costs another 30 minutes of adaptation. Red light is for reading and compass work; brief white light is justified only when foot placement or hazard assessment genuinely needs it.

Losing a person at night is easy even on familiar trails, so a headcount and position check at every checkpoint is the core group-cohesion procedure. Sending a scout ahead, letting members set their own pace, or counting gear instead of people all open the gap where someone goes missing.

Lost plus dark is the clearest stop condition: movement without position confirmation compounds the error, and a group that stops early and navigates at dawn is not failing — it is applying the rule that night is when lost people get hurt. Pushing on, splitting up, or walking downhill on faith all multiply the risk.

The stop rules name exhaustion, cold, and failed lighting — all three are present: the group is shivering, a light has failed, and the remaining route is exposed open ground. Half-charged batteries with a bright moon, a short overgrown stretch, or mere tiredness are manageable; the shivering group with one light down is the rule, not an exception.

Route planning begins with naming the objective and the destination — a specific, nameable point on the map — because every later decision (route, time, water, gear) is checked against them. Gear, start time, and trail reputation matter, but they cannot be planned correctly until the endpoint is defined. "The lake area" is not a destination; a named point on the map is.

Closely spaced contour lines mean steep ground; widely spaced lines mean gentle ground. Map distance is flat distance that ignores the rise and fall of the land, so the short ridge line may cost far more time than the longer valley trail. The route choice trades distance against climb — you compare both, not distance alone.

For a winding route, the string method is the standard technique: trace the route with string, mark the endpoints, and compare the length against the graphic scale, which FM 3-25.26 defines as the ruler printed on the map that converts map distance to ground distance. A straight ruler under-measures bends, the representative fraction must be converted by calculation, and bend-counting factors are invented, not documented.

Elevation gain is estimated by counting the contour lines the route crosses and multiplying by the contour interval printed in the map margin (12 × 40 = 480 feet). Because the count captures every line crossed but real gain adds the rise and fall of intermediate ground, the result is a floor, not an exact value — and cross-checking against spot elevations on the map is part of the procedure.

Contour spacing reads steepness directly — tight lines mean steep ground — and exposure follows from landforms: open ridges above treeline put the party in the wind and weather, which is also where the National Weather Service says to get off elevated ground when thunderstorms threaten. Water and vegetation are read from the map's symbols and legend, but they are separate factors, not the ones this stretch shows.

The route connects to water deliberately: crossings are planned in advance with the NPS hazard questions — currents, underwater hazards, cold water — and any water collected from natural sources is treated (filter, boil, or chemical), per NPS hiking guidance. A four-mile dry stretch means the party carries for the full leg, and that weight and time belong in the estimate. Improvising crossings or skipping treatment turns a planned leg into a gamble.

The turnaround rule exists precisely for this moment — fatigue, momentum, and a visible summit argue for continuing, which is why the decision is committed in advance while you are calm: "the decision you make calmly at the table is the one you can trust on the trail." Splitting the party spreads risk, and extending the rule on the spot turns the plan into a suggestion. The rule is the plan's guardrail, not its suggestion.

The backup logic applies on the map: the plan carries a primary route, an alternate route that still reaches the objective, and a bail-out — the shortest escape toward trailhead, road, or help. Deciding these at the table means a trail closure, injury, or weather change triggers a written response instead of a hasty improvisation. Day trips face closures and weather too, and the alternate and the bail-out serve different purposes: one continues the trip, the other ends it safely.

Conservative estimation fits the plan to the slowest member — the party moves at that pace — remembers that map distance is flat distance, adds margin, and records estimates per leg so the party can compare actual to plan at checkpoints. No formula substitutes for the party's own recorded pace, and planning to the fastest member builds the plan on hope. Leg-level times are what make decision rules executable.

The trusted contact is the planning-and-preparedness layer on the route: the written plan names where, what, and when back, and the contact acts if you are overdue — the return time is the plan's outer deadline, the last anchor of the turnaround rules. It does not guarantee rescue, does not replace the alternate route or bail-out, and is not a paperwork formality; it is a committed external check on the plan ([[SUR-preparedness-K01]]).

In a draw or valley, the contours bend up-slope, forming a V that points toward higher ground; the stream or drainage runs out through the open mouth of the V. A ridge or spur bulges downslope in a U instead, a saddle pinches between two highs, and a bench shows as a spread-out flat.

A spur is a tongue of high ground jutting out from a ridge, and it pushes the contours downslope in a U shape that opens toward low ground. A valley or draw draws its contours into a V pointing up-slope instead; a depression shows closed loops with hachures inside; a saddle pinches between two highs.

A saddle is the low dip in a ridge between two higher points, so the map shows two high areas as contour loops with a pinched waist of contours between them — the ground rises on all four sides. A peak is a single innermost loop, a draw V's up-slope, and a bench shows spread-apart contours on a slope.

The predict step comes before the look: naming what the map says you should see turns what you look at into evidence — every feature found confirms position, every feature missing is an alarm. Rotating the map or folding it prepares the map, but the association loop only works when you predict first, then confirm.

Confirmation feeds the loop: you update your position on the map from everything that matched, then schedule the next check at the next decision point — junctions, crossings, terrain changes. Confirmation is a step, not a destination; skipping the update is how small position errors become large ones.

A handrail is a linear feature you travel along — here, the stream that runs in your direction down the valley. A catching feature lies across your direction of travel beyond the objective, so the river crossing two kilometers past your start tells you when you have gone too far. Swapping them makes both useless: you would be catching on the feature you walk beside all day.

A good handrail runs close to your intended direction and is easy to identify in both map and ground; a handrail that meanders away pulls you off line, no matter how convenient it looks. "Water is always best" and "higher is always better" are both false — direction and identifiability decide.

A missing big landform — a whole saddle — is a position error, not a map error. The association loop only works from an honest anchor, so the response is to stop and re-establish: backtrack to the last confirmed feature, take a bearing and distance check, and relocate. Walking on converts a small error into a large one.

Deliberate observation means naming what you see: each named feature is a map comparison, and each direction of slope confirmed is a test of your position. Naming forces the comparison a glance does not. A photo, a feeling of familiarity, or a fatigue estimate gives you no confirmation against the map at all.

On USGS topographic maps, a solid blue line marks a perennial stream that flows all year, while a dashed blue line marks an intermittent stream that may be dry when you arrive. Knowing the difference matters for navigation: you can rely on the valley shape even when the dashed stream holds no water.

On topographic maps, solid blue lines mark perennial streams that flow year-round, and broken or dashed blue lines mark intermittent streams that flow seasonally or after rain. The symbol tells you what to expect before you arrive — and an intermittent stream can be a surprise hazard after upstream rain.
