Flat, unwooded ground beside a stream is the flood plain — the area the stream spreads over during high water. It tells you the water will expand during floods, so crossings and camps go elsewhere when water is high. It is neither a guaranteed ford nor always a swamp.

Contours pinching toward a stream mean the valley is closing into a gorge — banks become impassable and the river can box you in, and following it downstream can dead-end at falls or canyon walls. A river is a position handrail, not a trail: when the map shows the gorge, route on the terrain beside it.

The National Park Service's safe-crossing guidance is to select a route through the widest channels: as water disperses it flows slower and becomes shallower, and the straight section in the middle of the "S" between bends is the safest place to cross. Narrow channels concentrate depth and speed, so "narrowest is best" is exactly backwards.

Branches and debris that let water pass but block people and gear are strainers — among the most dangerous features downstream of a crossing. The safe pattern is to identify downstream hazards and plan a rescue and take-out point before entering, and never to treat a logjam as a bridge or a dry crossing.

Rivers always run downhill, so the direction of flow shows the direction of slope. Where the water is flowing tells you which way the drainage runs, which lets you match the stream on the ground to the blue line on the map and fix your position along it.

A mapped bridge is a guaranteed dry crossing and is often placed exactly where the terrain is worst; a ford is a candidate, not a certainty — flood conditions can make it unusable, and its depth and speed are unknown until you are in it. Walking upstream to the mapped bridge beats an unknown ford every time.

A stream running over the trail is flood water of unknown depth and speed, and the National Weather Service rule is absolute: it is never safe to drive or walk into flood waters — a mere 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock over an adult. The no-cross rule applies to the whole group, and testing the bottom in flood water is testing fate.

The no-cross rules are explicit: no crossing when you cannot see the bottom, when the water is cold enough to threaten hypothermia, when you are alone, or when darkness is near. A calm surface does not mean safe water, and a pack is ballast that can drag you down. The correct navigation decision is upstream, backward, or waiting.

The safe-crossing guidance is to avoid water deeper than the knees — except for the documented exception of a flat pool with little or no current. With the bottom visible, the current negligible, and the exit confirmed, the site meets the exception; every other option either ignores the rule or misreads the feature.

Terrain association runs on visible landmarks and on depth — the space that lets you judge distance and slope. Dense fog removes both, so the map stops matching what you can see. The nearby trail tells you nothing about where you are along it; the method must switch to bearing-and-distance and handrails while some landmarks remain, not after they are gone.

When features are invisible, navigation shifts from terrain association to the systematic methods — compass heading held deliberately, legs shortened so error cannot grow, and distance measured rather than felt. Memory of where the destination "should be" is exactly what fog removes. Wind direction shifts and cannot fix position.

The rule pairs two questions — can I confirm my position, and is visibility stable or deteriorating? Unconfirmed position plus deteriorating visibility is a stop, not a slowdown. Memory of a familiar trail is exactly what the condition removes, and reversing on an equally unconfirmed back-bearing buys nothing. Stop, and let the weather window decide the schedule.

The USGS documents that small-watershed streams can see a hundredfold increase in flow during a storm and rise and fall within hours, while the map shows yesterday's terrain. The crossing plan is re-decided at the water every time, never inherited from the morning. If the crossing cannot be fully assessed, find an alternative line or wait.

Snow is a layered thief: it buries the trail, then flat light erases the shadows and shading that reveal slope and distance, color contrast washes out so features stop separating from the ground, and in whiteout every directional cue disappears at once. Navigation shifts from reading the ground to pure compass discipline, with legs shortened drastically.

NPS guidance is explicit: with the AQI above 100, reduce outdoor activity — especially strenuous hikes or prolonged exposure — and consider delaying or adjusting plans, because risk grows with exertion and time outdoors. Smoke also removes the distant landmarks navigation uses, so the decision is both a health limit and a navigation downgrade.

Movement without a handrail in whiteout is random — and near edges it is how people walk off them. The documented response is to stop, shelter against wind and cold, communicate, and wait for visibility to return. In wind-driven snow and cold, disorientation comes quickly; the NWS winter guidance is the same doctrine at road scale: stop and wait for visibility.

Route choice in fog follows one test: which line can I verify? The valley floor is where fog collects and visibility collapses earliest, and its landmarks are the least distinct on the map. The ridge crest is a handrail — a physical line you cannot lose — at the cost of wind and exposure, and it is only the right choice if it has a safe line onward. If neither line verifies, you wait rather than improvise.

The forecast is the cheapest navigation decision you will make: knowing the weather window lets you time travel to the visible hours, and a shared trip plan means the person searching knows whether you are moving or waiting. Electronics fail in wet weather, and comfort does not fix position. Planning — from [[SUR-preparedness-K01]] — converts a forecast into an itinerary.

Smoke decisions are health limits plus navigation limits: when the AQI is unhealthy, strenuous outdoor activity should be reduced or stopped, and with a possible fire in the area the correct move is to leave and report rather than investigate — closures and rangers are not guaranteed to be between you and the fire. Thick smoke also removes the landmarks navigation needs, so leaving while you can still navigate is the professional call.

Breath produces moisture that condenses on the shelter's inner surface and drips. A small vent lets it escape; sealing the shelter makes it worse, and a fire inside a fabric shelter is a fire hazard. Wetting the sleeping bag destroys its loft.

Downward heat loss to the ground can dominate, and a sleeping bag compressed under body weight loses most of its loft at the contact point. The ground layer — a pad or debris bed — is the first priority, ahead of overhead insulation.

The debris bed needs elevation or a waterproof layer against damp ground, then dry, fluffed material thick enough to keep insulating under body weight — with extra depth where weight compresses it most (hips, shoulders). Wet material conducts heat instead of trapping air.

Wet clothing evaporates into the shelter air and condenses into the insulation; "drying by body heat" wets the whole sleep system. The dry set goes to bed; the damp set is stored outside the sleeping area or sealed in a waterproof bag.

A sleeping bag compressed under body weight loses most of its loft exactly where it touches the ground, and the ground conducts heat away. The fix is a ground layer — pad, raised bed, or deep debris — beneath the bag.

Wind strips the warm boundary layer and can dominate heat loss. Spot B trades a manageable issue (damp ground, fixed with boughs or a waterproof layer) for a hard one (constant wind). Wind protection multiplies the value of every insulation layer.

Exertion produces sweat that soaks clothing, and evaporation and conduction from wet clothing accelerate heat loss — a direct hypothermia risk. Strip layers before hard work, pace it, and shelter in place rather than sweat through a build.

Wet material conducts heat out of the body rather than trapping air. Only dry material insulates, so the bed is built from the dry stock, and the search for more dry material continues. Thick, dry, fluffed — not deep, wet, and compacted.

Insulation works by trapping still air. Fluffing separates fibers and restores loft; compaction destroys it. The fluffed, thicker bed keeps insulating under body weight, while the packed bed conducts. Thickness and loft are the evaluation criteria, not packing density.

The correct sequence layers this lesson's priorities: a wind- and rain-blocking shelter, then the ground layer — elevation, a waterproof layer against damp ground, and thick fluffed dry material — then dry sleep. The fire is optional; the bed and the dryness are not.

Low basins collect both water and cold air, and a dry seasonal watercourse can flood without local rain — storms upstream run down the channel. The location decision is the one that cannot be undone, so flood risk and cold-air pooling disqualify the site before anything is built.

Structure choice is matched to climate, materials, labor, and intended stay. A log cabin is durable but heavy in labor; a frame-and-cover is faster, but its cover is the weak point — it wears, UV-degrades, and fails in wind and snow, so it needs a replacement plan and a roof pitched to shed snow.

The stream is a source; the supply is the plan around it — how water is carried or delivered, how much is stored, how it is treated, and what happens in winter when the source freezes or storms cut access. Stored water is a finite, rotated supply, and freeze protection is part of the plan.

Waste and water are planned as one system: the latrine goes downhill and at a distance from the water source and the shelter, with drainage away from both, so contamination never flows toward the supply. Placement between shelter and stream, or above the source, inverts the rule.

NFPA public-safety guidance is consistent: heating equipment stays clear of combustibles (its public guidance for space heaters is a minimum 3 feet, about 1 m, of clearance), combustion needs ventilation, fuel-burning appliances warrant a CO alarm, and fuel is stored separated from the heat source. A smoke alarm alone does not cover carbon monoxide, and nothing about a stove is inherently safe.

Carbon monoxide is produced by combustion and collects in enclosed spaces. The rule is absolute: generators, grills, and camp stoves are never run inside — the shelter needs properly ventilated heating or none. Cold does not change the rule; it raises the stakes.

The weekly check covers the roof and drainage, the chimney and stove pipe, seals and closures, fuel and water storage, and new hazards such as dead branches or erosion after storms. Small problems checked early are cheap; the same failures found late are the ones that end a shelter's season.

Ventilation and sealing must be designed together. Tighter-than-ventilated shelters fill with condensation from breathing and cooking, which wets insulation from the inside and drips on the sleep system. The fix is a controlled vent path, not more sealing.

Roof drainage is the first weatherproofing priority: snow country favors steeper pitches so snow sheds rather than accumulates, and overhang keeps runoff and drip lines off the walls and entry. A flat or shallow roof in snow country trades the structure for the storm.

Winterizing follows the system priorities: the roof and drainage hold the weather out, heating is installed with fire separation, ventilation, and a CO alarm, and stored water is protected from freezing rather than drained (a drained supply is a failed supply). The sleeping area is arranged last, not first.

Any channel that water has shaped is a path water will take again. Flash floods run in dry washes and canyon floors without local rain — storms upstream send water down the channel. The clear sky over your head does not clear the sky upstream, and the sandbar sits in the path.

Fresh talus at the base is evidence that rock has recently come down, which means the slope is still shedding, and water staining marks seepage that loosens rock. The overhang sits in the fall line; the hazard check fails, and the feature is rejected regardless of how dry it is.

Fresh tracks and droppings mean the cave is in use. Blocking the only exit turns the shelterer into the party between the animal and its door, and unventilated fire in an enclosed space is a smoke and CO hazard. Entrance-only use, after inspection, is the rule — and fresh activity is grounds for rejection.

The debris shelter is a frame plus insulation: dry, fluffed material piled thick (a hand's thickness or more) over the ribs, closed end into the wind, entrance away from it, and a raised dry bed beneath the body. Damp ground and thin material do not insulate; orientation and ground layer are part of the build, not afterthoughts.

A snow shelter sealed against the cold is a CO trap: breath moisture and any combustion concentrate in the enclosed space. Ventilation is mandatory, avalanche terrain is disqualifying, and the ceiling is treated as a changing structure checked during storms.

In high-use and sensitive areas, natural shelters are dismantled and the material spread back to restore the ground. Leaving standing structures marks popular sites and concentrates impact; burning is not restoration. In remote areas, natural rot may be acceptable — impact proportional to place is the rule.

Cliff bases sit in the fall line; fresh scars mean the slope is still shedding rock, and even a flat, dry floor does not clear the rockfall check. Sites at the base are rejected regardless of how convenient the ground is.

Storing food with the sleeper turns the shelter into bait: animals investigating the food investigate the sleeper. Food is stored away from the sleeping area and the shelter — the same separation that governs campsites in wildlife country generally.

A debris hut needs a couple of hours of dry gathering to work. With the light nearly gone and dry material thin, the correct decision is the tarp: it is built in minutes and sheds rain immediately. The natural build is chosen when time and material are abundant — not as a religion.

The debris shelter is insulation with a hole in it: the frame only needs to be small enough to cover with the material you can gather. The warmth comes from dry, fluffed cover and the raised bed beneath the body — not from frame size. Small and thick beats large and thin, and a deep pit collects water and cold air.

The grommet is the most common tarp tear point: it concentrates all corner load into a small hole. Distributing the load — a rock or stick balled inside the fabric with the line tied around it — spreads the force across the fabric and saves the corner. Tying to the torn edge just moves the tear.

Natural cordage is fine for light lashings and quick ties, but it degrades when wet, dries and stiffens, and its strength is a fraction of what it appears. A load-bearing ridgeline that must survive the night is the job for carried manufactured line, inspected and padded at bearing points.

Green wood bends under load and springs back — suited to ribs and lashings where flexibility is the point. Dry wood is stiff but snaps without warning under sudden load, and rot weakens it invisibly. The field rule: inspect every member, prefer sound dead wood for structure, and use green wood where flexibility is the job.

Sunlight weakens tarp fabric and coating over time; crease cracks and stiffening are the tell of UV damage. A UV-cracked tarp tears at the fold under load. It is replaced before the trip or used knowing the weak points — never trusted at full strength.

Cordage is a system of line, knot, and bearing point. A sharp edge cuts the line over time and a ridgeline parts at night. Padding the contact point is cheap insurance, and any frayed section is replaced rather than trusted.

Thatch sheds water only when layered thick and sloped, which is hours of gathering — a long-stay material. For a single night, the tarp sheds rain in minutes and beats the hour of thatching. Material choice is matched to the stay, not to a preference.

A stake that goes in easily pulls out easily. In soft ground, the load moves to a deadman — a buried stick tied to the line — which distributes the pull across a wider anchor. Easy stakes, deeper hammering, and sand piles are not anchors.

Natural cordage degrades when wet — it rots and loses strength overnight. The failure mode is known and expected; the lashing is replaced or reinforced with carried line for load-bearing work. Inspection of natural cordage is part of using it at all.

Each material is chosen for the job it actually does: the tarp is the continuous water-shedding cover; the thermal blanket traps air and insulates, but it is not a weather cover for a shelter. Assigning material to function is the whole discipline of shelter materials.

The carried kit wins when it exists: tarp, load-bearing cordage, stakes, and repair tape cover the four shelter jobs in minutes. Natural materials remain the honest backup when the kit does not exist — but planning around the forest's generosity is how single nights become wet ones.

The water W covers drainage and cold-air pooling. A depression collects runoff and night-time cold air — the ground is wetter and the air is colder than the hillside above. The other W's must be checked separately; a valley can also be windy or empty of wood, but that is not what this observation shows.

Washes and dry creek beds are the classic flash-flood sites. Rain that falls far upstream — often out of sight and under your own clear sky — channels down the bed and can arrive suddenly. The water W rejects flood paths outright regardless of how comfortable the ground looks.

Natural windbreaks — terrain, rock, dense vegetation — are the first resource for wind protection, as long as the windbreak itself has no dead limbs or loose rock. Ridges, saddles, and hilltops funnel wind; the lee side of a safe block is the sheltered option.

Dead branches and leaning dead trees are widowmakers — the overhead hazard the checklist exists to catch. Wind, snow, and rain all bring dead limbs down, so a site under a compromised tree fails the overhead check regardless of shade, soft ground, or species.

The overhead check must be repeated when conditions change — a storm can damage a limb that was safe an hour before. Dead material overhead is a hazard at any size. Relocating the sleeping spot is the correct response; there is no reliable way to secure a broken limb.

In a lost scenario, visibility is a rescue asset: a shelter that can be seen from the air or from a trail is a shelter that can be found — the Army survival manual advises making a shelter conspicuous to searchers. Balance visibility against exposure, but don't hide a shelter you want found.

Read the ground: game trails, droppings, scratch marks, and nests reveal regular animal use. Camping off the trail reduces encounters, and food discipline — storing and eating away from the sleeping area — addresses the food-driven nature of most camp wildlife problems.

Wood is a resource check, not a trump card. A wash is a flood path and the steep slope above raises rockfall risk — the water and terrain-hazard checks fail regardless of how much firewood is nearby. When any W fails, walk to the next candidate site.

Public lands commonly require set distances from water sources, trails, and roads — protecting water quality, fragile shorelines, and other users. The rule is to look up the local regulations for the specific area rather than guess, and to combine that with the site checks from this lesson.

A complete site assessment takes about two minutes once you know what to look for, and it must be done before dark — fatigue and darkness are how wrong sites get chosen. Run the checks in order and reject any candidate that fails; do not defer the decision to tomorrow or to assumptions.

The sandbar is a flood path even under a clear sky (storms upstream run down dry beds); the plateau takes the full wind; the dead branch is a widowmaker. The bench combines drainage, wind protection, and a clear overhead.
Wind-driven rain is the tarp's main enemy. The closed or low end takes the wind, and the opening faces away or cross-wind so rain and gusts stay out. A tarp broadside to the wind becomes a sail.

Tension is structural: a taut sheet sheds wind and rain; a flapping sheet tears at its grommets and drips. Center-outward keeps the tension even and the fabric unwrinkled, and finishing at the corners lets you set the final angle.

The tarp blocks wind and rain; it creates no warmth. Heat loss into cold ground can exceed heat loss to the air, and compression destroys the bag's insulation beneath you. The pad — or a built debris bed — is the real warmth system.

The debris bed replaces the missing pad: anything that traps air between body and ground insulates. Thickness matters more than material. Without a ground layer, the compressed bag loses its insulating value exactly where you need it.

A sleeping person exhales roughly half a liter of water per night. Without ventilation, it condenses on the underside of the tarp and drips. The fixes: leave the ends or high edge open, and add drip lines so whatever condenses runs off at the ties instead of into the sleeping area.

Wet clothing inside the shelter evaporates into the air — then condenses on the tarp and on your insulation, making everything damp. It belongs outside the sleeping area or sealed away. A wet jacket spread over a bag wets the bag, not warms it.

Sparks from resinous wood travel farther than the fire looks, and a tarp ignites instantly. The rule is minimum 2 meters separation, fire downwind, cleared perimeter — and never under the low edge. A fire that reaches the tarp turns the shelter into the hazard.

Walking to an existing safe shelter beats a 20-minute cold, exhausted pitch — if you can still move safely. The other options are normal build situations (B, C) or a move-then-build decision (D), not a reason to skip shelter entirely.

The tarp is a wind- and rain-blocking layer. All warmth comes from insulation: the bag, the layers, and especially the ground layer beneath the body. Expecting the sheet to keep you warm is the classic misunderstanding that makes people skip the pad.

Type is a tradeoff, not a ranking. A tunnel tent is lighter and more aerodynamic, but it is only as strong as its stakes; a freestanding dome stands without anchors and is more forgiving of pitching conditions. Match the type to the actual use — wind and soil included.

Site prep beats tent quality. The tent-specific site routine is: level and drained ground, cleared of debris that can puncture the floor, with the full site check from site selection applied — no washes, no standing water, no cold-air pockets.

Weather setup is orientation plus tension: the low, small end faces the wind, the windward corners go in first and hardest, and every guyline is run — guylines are the difference between "stands" and "stays." Tension should be re-checked after gusts.

A taut fly sheds water; a loose one pools, wets out, and drips. The fly should overhang the door so entry does not bring rain in, and water should run off rather than collect. Tension and pitch geometry are the fix, not a new tent.

Every night of sleep releases significant moisture into the tent air. If it cannot escape, it condenses on the coldest surface — the fly, or your bag. Condensation is physics, not a defect: venting, keeping wet gear out of the sleeping space, and brushing frost off in the morning are the management tools.

Fuel-burning stoves, lanterns, and heaters inside a closed tent are a carbon monoxide hazard — the gas has no smell and kills quietly. The rule, consistent with Red Cross preparedness guidance, is that fuel-burning devices belong outside enclosed spaces.

A tent stored wet molds in weeks and its coating degrades — drying it out before storage is the single most important care practice. Seam-sealing and repairs should happen before the trip that needs them, not after.

Poles are the critical failure point of a tent, and the repair kit — a splint or replacement section — is what finishes the trip. Know your pole layout before you need it; the splint is a day-trip fix, and a spare pole set is the real insurance for longer trips.

When grams count — long approaches, fast travel, solo trips — a tarp or tarp-plus-bivy is lighter than the lightest tent. The honest rule: the right shelter is the one you actually carry. Comfort that stays at home protects nobody.

In an emergency you use what is on you — a tent that is too heavy to carry permanently is not a plan. The tarp is the go-bag shelter: lighter, no poles to break, and packable forever. The tent's home is the car or the base camp, not the survival kit.

Wind drives heat loss and wind-driven rain, and it amplifies every other threat. The first adaptation is orientation — closed or low end into the wind, openings away — followed by anchoring and tension. Rain matters too, but wind is what makes a warm wet afternoon dangerous.

Wet plus cold plus wind is the danger combination. The CDC defines hypothermia as a core temperature below 95°F, and it can develop at temperatures well above freezing when wind and wet strip body heat. The 50°F rainy-day scenario is the classic exposure that leads to hypothermia.

Wind shift, building cloud, and temperature drop are the classic signals of weather arriving. They are not a precise prediction — the honest practice is to treat them as a reason to prepare the shelter now, in daylight. The forecast was the baseline; the sky is the live update.

Weather awareness has two layers: the forecast (the baseline, checked before you go — the Forest Service's "Know Before You Go" guidance makes this part of trip planning) and the sky (the live update). Building cloud at sunset is a signal to get the shelter ready in daylight, not a guaranteed prediction.

Orientation first, anchoring second: the closed end faces the wind, windward lines are staked first and hardest, the fly is re-tensioned to shed, and drip lines are cleared so rain runs off rather than in. A shelter facing sideways into wind-driven rain gets its opening soaked.

Rain adaptation includes drainage decided before the rain arrives: high, drained ground so water runs around the shelter rather than under it. Flat, soft ground pools water. The lesson's rule is "shed, don't pool" — and drainage is part of shedding.

Snow is the dual threat: it loads and it insulates. A wet snow load is structural — it bends poles and tears fabric faster than anything else. Steep pitches shed snow, and loading must be checked and cleared during the night, not only at setup.

On frozen ground, stakes alone will not hold: the adaptation is anchoring through the snow to buried anchors (a stake-driven deadman or buried gear). Short stakes in powder pull out; ballast and tree branches are not structural answers.

A sealed shelter is a wet shelter: every night of sleep releases significant moisture from breath and perspiration, and with no escape it condenses on the coldest surface and wets the insulation. Ventilation is the cold-weather rule — and the ground layer does more for warmth than sealing the fly (see [[SHE-tarp-shelters-K01]]).

In heat the shelter's job inverts into a cooling envelope: avoid heat-trap bowls at site selection, shade the sleeping period, and move air through the shelter. Overheating and dehydration are real weather-protection failures — sun is managed by design, not ignored.

The plan is one page with six components: meeting points, out-of-area contact, evacuation rules, communication fallbacks, household specifics, and a review date. A 20-page document will not be read in an emergency — the one-page constraint is a feature, not a shortcut.

The whole point of the external meeting point is to work when the neighborhood is the hazard — fire, flood, evacuation order. A point inside the neighborhood fails exactly when it is needed. Choose a specific named location (relative's house, school, library) outside the zone, hazard-checked.

After a regional disaster, local phone circuits overload while long-distance calls often still connect. One relative or friend outside the region becomes the single relay point: everyone calls them, and they pass messages. Every member carries their number on a printed card.

Call first, then text (which often works when voice circuits are jammed), then the out-of-area contact, then leave a written note at the meeting points stating where you went and when. The chain degrades gracefully as each layer fails.

The rule is written in advance precisely to prevent the midnight debate: leave when the order arrives. Waiting for confirmation, visual proof, or the neighbors burns the time window that evacuation routes need. The worst outcome in most disasters is leaving late, not leaving early.

Shelter-in-place is the opposite action from evacuation: the indoor air is protected by sealing the building, while being outside exposes you to the plume. The plan should state both rules in writing — each trigger maps to one action, decided in advance.

Orders can be delayed or never issued. A visible approaching wildfire is its own trigger — fire moves faster uphill and with the wind, and waiting eats the evacuation window. The plan's evacuation rules exist so this decision is made before the smoke is visible.

Rehearsals (twice a year, walking the actual routes, with children) keep the plan in muscle memory; the fixed annual review date keeps it current — addresses, schools, medications, contacts all change. A plan in a drawer is a souvenir.

Mom is the single point of failure (local, not out-of-area), the mall is neither a home nor an external point, and the absence of cards and a review date guarantees the plan rots. The six-component rewrite fixes the structure, not just the symptoms.

The three legs are the plan (a written, rehearsed household plan), the kit (supplies staged where they will be used), and knowledge (skills that weigh nothing). Food/water/shelter are contents of the kit leg; insurance and savings help recovery but do not cover the first 72 hours.
The standard allowance is 3.8 L (1 gallon) per person per day. Two people × 3 days × 3.8 L ≈ 23 L (6 gallons). Double this in hot climates, and size up to 1–2 weeks for regions with long outages.

Evacuation means movement with two hours of notice, possibly on foot or through debris. One adult cannot carry 28 kg and manage a toddler at the same time. Go-bags are per person: adults carry the weight; children carry a small comfort pack they can actually lift.

Reachability is a design requirement: the bag must be where every household member can grab it, not behind a locked door, in a loft that needs a ladder, or in a garage that may flood or burn first. A bag you cannot reach is not a bag.

A fixed 6-month anchor (the clock change works well) makes rotation a habit: rotate food and water, check medications, test every device, update documents, and walk the plan. Waiting for a forecast leaves no time to fix dead batteries or expired food.

"Later" rarely arrives. The rule is immediate replacement after every use, and the 6-month rotation catches what slips through. A kit that was missing a bandage or a battery in May will still be missing them in November when the power fails.

Preparedness reduces risk and shortens recovery; it cannot guarantee outcomes. Supplies cannot stop a flood, and a plan cannot prevent injury. Recognizing this keeps expectations honest and keeps skill-building (the knowledge leg) as important as buying gear.
An unopened kit is unverified: batteries may be dead, contents unfamiliar. Household B's plan and skills work without any gear at all. The knowledge leg is what makes the kit leg function.

Redundancy beats optimization: two ways to purify water (e.g., filter + tablets), two ways to make light (headlamp + lantern), two ways to get information (radio + phone). Each backup should not depend on the same infrastructure as the primary.

His gaps are the plan (nothing written: no meeting points, no out-of-area contact) and water (4 L is about one person-day against an 11.5 L / 3-day baseline). The generator is a power convenience, not a first-72-hours essential, and his medications are already renewed monthly — a strength he can anchor his rotation to.

Threats act on you at different speeds, and the fastest-acting one leads. Wind and wet drive exposure within hours, while hunger acts slowly. The backpack strap is an inconvenience — improvised. Shelter (getting out of wind and off the cold ground) comes first.

The four needs are the same everywhere; the order is not. The environment dictates which need is pressing — cold pushes shelter and fire to the front, heat pushes water, and food is generally the last of the four to demand action. Memorizing one fixed order ignores the environment.

The survival pattern opens with sizing up the situation — condition, equipment, surroundings — so that action responds to the most important problem rather than the most visible one. It takes minutes and can be done while moving. Hasty action at the most visible task is exactly what the size-up prevents.

In cold conditions the fast-acting threat is exposure, so shelter and warmth lead. Food is the slowest-acting of the four needs — a person can function for a long time without it — so it waits until shelter, fire, and water are handled. Each earlier step buys time and stability for the next.

High-value actions unblock other work: shelter makes fire easier because you are not fighting the wind, and fire makes water easier by enabling boiling and melting. Tasks that make nothing else easier just consume time. Experience and equipment matter, but the sequencing test is whether the task unblocks the rest.

Threats before comfort applies to the shopping list: the items that keep you alive and safe (water, warmth, light, first aid, communication) come first; comfort items wait. A plan that starts with the most expensive or most visible item is not a plan; it is a purchase.

When conditions are closing in, the best use of time is the short, high-value action that buys the next hour — getting out of the wind and wet. When unhurried, the best use of time is preparation: improving shelter, gathering water, arranging signals. Matching the size of the action to the time available is the skill.

In hot, dry conditions, water and shade move to the front of the framework because dehydration acts on judgment and strength quickly in heat. Fire is not the lead need here — it is a warmth and signaling tool for conditions where the pressing problem is the opposite. Food remains the slowest-acting need.

When you are rested, warm, and unhurried, the highest-value use of time is preparation: each improvement — better shelter, more water, arranged signals — makes later tasks easier and raises your margin. Resting, random movement, and large fires all spend time or fuel without unblocking anything.

Preparation reduces the number of decisions you must make under stress. Walking the plan — the meeting point, the communication route, what to grab — converts a document into a practiced sequence the household can execute when thinking is harder. The kit is equipment; the rehearsed plan is the decision-making layer above it.

The starting point is knowing your risks: identify the hazards that could affect your household, then plan for the ones that apply. A hazard that has never been named cannot be planned against. Buying supplies or waiting for a warning skips the naming step, and a generic plan has no priorities.

Risk is the combination of likelihood and consequence. The grease fire is less likely but far more consequential, so it earns preparation (extinguisher, drill, exits) despite low likelihood. The power blip is likely but low-impact, so it is largely accepted. Unlikely is not the same as harmless.

Fast-moving water is a very high consequence hazard, and no amount of rope or early timing changes that realistically. Avoidance is the strongest response and the cheapest: take the crossing off the table. Reduce and prepare are for risks that can be meaningfully shrunk; this one cannot.

Risk assessment is the thinking step that turns vague worry into a short list of actions: identify the hazards that can reach you, judge each one's likelihood and consequence, and choose a response. It does not produce exact numbers, remove risk, or catalog every misfortune — it sets priorities.

At the moment of decision — rain falling, river up, group tired — judgment is under pressure and the instinct to continue is strong. A turn-back condition written in advance ("if the river is up, we go home") is a decision already made, calmly. The exit plan is part of the plan, not a separate topic invented on the spot.

Likelihood and consequence are rated with local information and experience, at the level of high/medium/low. The ranking exists to set planning priorities, not to produce arithmetic precision. The precision of a good assessment lives in the ranking and the actions, not the numbers.

The four responses — avoid, reduce, prepare, accept — are usually mixed. The detector battery and the icy walkway are reduced cheaply and immediately; the car kept ready is preparation. Avoidance is not needed here because the risks are small and reducible, and "accept" is a decision, not a default for everything.

Assessments have a shelf life. A changed environment — forecast, river, temperature, daylight — is an invitation to re-run the same three-step loop with the new facts, and the plan changes with it. Sticking to a stale assessment because it was "already done" is how low-risk plans walk into high-risk days.

The outing assessment checks the forecast and terrain, weighs the group against the day (skill, fitness, gear, daylight, water), and writes the turn-back conditions in advance. A single home check ignores that conditions change at the trailhead, and letting the route decide means deciding under pressure.

Reassessment is part of the method, not a sign of failure. New region means new hazards (different storms, flood or wildfire exposure), and a new member changes who must know the plan, where they meet, and what the household can carry. The loop is re-run with the new facts — it takes minutes and keeps the plan honest.

The guidance to use all your senses means opening the hearing and smell channels, not just watching the path. Sound carries distance and direction (water, wind, thunder), and smell announces smoke or change before sight. A deliberate scan — sight, hearing, smell — is the routine.

Orientation is location, time, and direction, kept current as you move. A person who knows where they are can decide — including choosing to go back the way they came. A person who has lost the picture can only react. Noting landmarks and looking back at them keeps the route known in both directions.

A river turning cloudy, rising, or louder warns of runoff upstream and possible flooding on the way. The cue is read while there is still time: move off the floodline and the crossings. It is not proof the flood is here, and it is not a harmless change — it is an announcement, and announcements are read early.

Awareness is observation plus understanding — gathering with all senses, orienting in place and time, and interpreting what the cues mean with enough margin to act. It is a practiced habit of scanning, not a trait, and not continuous staring at everything.

In a group, attention is divided among conversation, tasks, and the trail, so the environment quietly goes unwatched. A designated, rotated lookout fixes that: one person's job is the sky, the route, and the water while the group works. A quiet group is a group with different pictures of the same day.

Leaving a trip plan with a contact is the standard outdoor safety practice — the person not on the trip watches the other end of the timeline. If the group does not report or return, the contact knows where to point help. Awareness extends beyond the trip itself ([[SUR-preparedness-K01]] frames the same idea for the household).

Smell is one of the earliest channels — it announces things before they are visible. Smoke on the wind is a warning cue: locate the direction and source, keep an exit open, and treat it as real until proven otherwise. "No plume yet" is information about time, not a confirmation of safety.

Losing the picture of where you are is exactly the moment to stop and rebuild orientation — recalled landmarks, the backward view, time and daylight, position on the map. Orientation is the anchor that keeps "go back the way we came" a real option, and it must be rebuilt before darkness removes the evidence.

A darkening sky and a shifting, rising wind are classic early warning cues of building weather. The interpretation step reads them as time — time to change the plan cheaply. Moving the camp to sheltered ground now costs an hour; riding out a storm on an exposed ridge costs much more.

A quiet group is a group with different pictures of the same day. Announcing the change — "the wind is shifting, the river is up" — shares the picture, which is the first step to a shared decision while the margin is still comfortable. Waiting until the changes are obvious to everyone is the definition of reading the cue too late.

The survival manual names fear, anxiety, anger, frustration, loneliness, and boredom as expected reactions. Naming them normalizes them, which is the first step to managing them. The skill is working with the reaction — through routines and small tasks — not pretending it does not exist.

The structured sequence — size up, plan, act — gives the mind one small question at a time instead of the whole situation, which is exactly what stops the looping. It also produces progress, which is the best evidence the mind can receive that the situation is manageable.

When a situation feels overwhelming, the scale of the problem is the enemy. Shrinking the unit of work to finishable steps means steps actually get finished — and each finished step is evidence that action works, rebuilding the sense of control that stress erodes. Momentum is the compounding effect of completed steps.

For decisions under time pressure, a simple rehearsed routine beats analysis: identify the fastest-acting threat, take the action that addresses it and is reversible or cheap if wrong, act, then re-size-up. The routine's value is that it is the same every time — rehearsed in advance, it is available in the moment.

The manual treats the psychological aspect as one part knowledge and one part attitude — and the attitudes (initiative, adaptability, humor, will to live) are behaviors that can be built and practiced. Preparation and rehearsal change how a person responds under stress; it is not a fixed trait.

The manual's list of expected reactions includes boredom and frustration — long, slow situations are part of survival, not an exception. The skill is managing them with purpose: scheduled small tasks, routines, and checkpoints give the wait a structure and keep momentum alive.

Fear has less room in a mind that is doing a defined job. Assigning small, clear tasks to each member converts a stressed, arguing group into a working group with a shared purpose. Named reactions plus defined tasks is the whole skill in one sentence.

The mental side is prepared deliberately in advance: scenario talk-throughs, rehearsed routines, and named expectations. The household that knows what to expect reacts better than the household that is surprised by its own feelings. A rehearsed decision is a decision already made ([[SUR-preparedness-K01]] frames the planning side).

The sequence starts with the size-up — you are physically fine, the gear is usable, and the fast-acting threat is the cold night, not the lost-ness itself. That produces the best next action: shelter, off the cold ground, before dark. The size-up is what stops the loop and points at the one thing that matters now.

This material is practical skill guidance, not medicine: structured thinking and small tasks support good decisions, but they are not treatment. If you are concerned about your own or another person's mental health — before, during, or after an emergency — professional care outranks everything else when it is available.

Boiling kills or inactivates all biological pathogens — no other single field method matches this guarantee. It is NOT the fastest method (filtration is instant), does NOT improve taste (it makes water taste flat), and does NOT remove chemical contaminants.

The CDC and WHO recommend 1 minute of rolling boil at sea level. The older 5–10 minute recommendations are no longer supported by evidence and waste fuel. What matters is a full rolling boil — not just bubbles appearing — maintained for the full minute.

At 2,500 m, water boils at approximately 92°C (198°F) instead of 100°C. Pathogens still die at this temperature, but the kill rate is slightly slower. The WHO and CDC recommend extending the boil to 3 minutes above 2,000 m. Boiling still works at altitude — it just needs slightly more time.

Double-wall insulated bottles have an air gap between the inner and outer walls. When heated, the air in this gap expands, and the sealed construction can cause the bottle to explode. Single-wall metal bottles (cap off), clean metal cans, and camping pots are all safe for boiling. The critical rule: always leave the cap off when heating any container.

A pot lid prevents heat loss through evaporation and can reduce fuel consumption by 30–40%. Boiling without a lid wastes fuel. Boiling extra water "just in case" wastes fuel you may need later. Extended boiling beyond the guideline (1 minute at sea level) wastes fuel without providing additional safety.

Boiling only addresses biological pathogens. It does nothing to remove heavy metals, chemical contaminants, or salt. In fact, if water containing dissolved contaminants is boiled, evaporation can concentrate those contaminants, making the water more hazardous. For chemical or heavy metal contamination, distillation is the appropriate method. Boiling longer changes nothing — the contaminants remain and concentrate.

A sealed container heated over fire will build steam pressure and can explode violently. The cap must be off. The bottle should be supported above the flames, not placed directly in coals where thin metal can burn through. Filling the bottle is fine — the water absorbs the heat and prevents the metal from overheating, as long as steam can escape.

Boiled water has no residual disinfectant protection. Unlike chlorinated water, it can be recontaminated after cooling if stored improperly. Use a clean container, keep it covered, and avoid introducing contamination through dirty hands or utensils. Ice may be made from untreated water and can recontaminate the boiled water.

Chemical disinfection is a chemical reaction, not an instantaneous process. Chlorine and iodine need time to oxidize and destroy the cellular structures of pathogens. Drinking immediately after adding chemicals means drinking untreated water. The 30-minute minimum is not a suggestion — it's the time required for the reaction to complete at room temperature.

The EPA-recommended dose is 2 drops of 5–6% bleach per liter of clear water at room temperature. Note that 5 drops per liter is the dose for 2% iodine tincture — a different chemical. Using 10 drops is unnecessary and makes the water unpleasant. Using only 1 drop may be insufficient.

Cloudy water contains sediment that consumes disinfectant and shields pathogens from contact with the chemical. Pre-filtering removes sediment, and doubling the dose (from 2 to 4 drops per liter for 5–6% bleach) compensates for the remaining organic material. Iodine does not solve the turbidity problem — it has the same limitation.

Iodine crosses the placenta and can affect fetal thyroid development. It is specifically contraindicated during pregnancy. It is also not recommended for people with thyroid conditions or for prolonged daily use beyond 3–4 weeks. For general family emergency kits, chlorine-based treatment is preferred because it has fewer contraindications.

Cryptosporidium oocysts have a tough, environmentally resistant outer shell that prevents chemical disinfectants from penetrating effectively. Even at higher doses and longer contact times, chemical treatment alone cannot guarantee inactivation. The recommended approach in Crypto-risk areas is to combine filtration (which physically removes the oocysts) with chemical treatment (which kills viruses).

NaDCC tablets have a 5+ year shelf life when foil-sealed, are pre-dosed (no measuring), produce minimal taste, and are safe for all family members. Liquid bleach degrades after ~6 months. Iodine has more health contraindications. Pool chlorine products contain stabilizers and higher concentrations not safe for drinking water.

Cold temperatures slow chemical reactions. The correct response is to extend contact time, not increase dosage. Wait at least 60 minutes instead of 30. The dose stays the same — 2 drops per liter for clear water. Cold water is not naturally sterile and still requires treatment. Adding hot water from an unknown source could introduce new contamination.

Filtration removes Cryptosporidium oocysts (3–5 microns, easily captured by 0.2-micron filter) plus bacteria. Chlorine kills viruses that pass through the filter. The order matters: filter first to remove sediment and protozoa, then chemically treat. This combination provides the broadest biological protection. Neither method alone covers everything.

Distillation is for salt, chemicals, and heavy metals — not routine biological treatment. For a clear mountain stream where the only concern is pathogens, boiling or filtration is faster, uses less fuel, and produces more water. Distillation requires ~5× more energy for the same result. Clear water is not safe untreated — it can contain invisible pathogens.

Both methods kill pathogens, so distillation's extra step buys you nothing here — and the phase change is expensive. Turning water into steam consumes roughly 7× more energy than heating it to boiling. The decision rule: if your only concern is pathogens, boil. Reserve distillation for salt, heavy metals, and chemical contamination.

A well-constructed solar still in optimal conditions produces 0.5–1.0 liters per day. Minimum daily water requirement is 2–3 liters. A single still cannot sustain one person — multiple stills are needed. This is the critical reality check: solar distillation is a supplement, not a primary water strategy.

Some volatile organic compounds — certain solvents, some petroleum components — have boiling points lower than water. They can evaporate alongside water vapor and condense with it. Distillation does not guarantee 100% removal of all VOCs. Heavy metals, salts, and pathogens all stay behind — they don't evaporate at distillation temperatures.

Salt is dissolved in seawater at the molecular level. Boiling kills pathogens but leaves the salt behind — drinking boiled seawater accelerates dehydration. Filters cannot remove dissolved salt (reverse osmosis can, but standard field filters cannot). Chemical treatment only addresses pathogens. Distillation — boiling water and condensing the steam — is the only practical field method that separates salt from water. The salt stays behind; the condensate is fresh.

Distilled water lacks minerals, but this is a long-term concern — relevant for months or years of exclusive consumption. In a survival situation lasting days or weeks, dehydration from insufficient water intake is the immediate threat. Drink the water. The mineral issue can be addressed through diet or remineralization if this becomes a long-term situation.

A filter's effectiveness is entirely determined by its absolute pore size — the largest opening in the filter medium. Everything larger than the pore size gets trapped; everything smaller passes through. Brand, age, and color are irrelevant to what the filter can and cannot remove.

Bacteria range from 0.2–10 microns and protozoa from 1–15 microns — both are larger than 0.2 microns and are captured. Viruses range from 0.02–0.2 microns — smaller than the pore size — and can pass through. This is the "virus gap."

Hollow fiber membrane filters are the lightest (60–100 g), have fast flow rates, and are used in most modern backpacking filters. Ceramic filters are heavier. Activated carbon is an add-on, not a standalone filter. Slow sand filters are field-constructed, not carried.

In areas with human fecal contamination, viruses are a significant concern, and 0.2-micron filters do not remove them. Filter first (removes protozoa and bacteria, clarifies water for better chemical effectiveness), then chemically treat (kills viruses). The combination provides the broadest biological protection.

When water inside hollow fiber membranes freezes, the expanding ice crystals rupture the microscopic tubes. The damage cannot be seen, and the filter may appear to function normally while allowing pathogens through the cracks. A frozen hollow fiber filter must be replaced. This is the single most important maintenance rule for this filter type.

Body heat is the most reliable freeze protection in the field. An inside pocket during the day and your sleeping bag at night keep the filter above freezing. A towel provides some insulation but won't prevent freezing in sustained cold. A filter that has frozen is ruined — you can't "pre-freeze" it.

In low-use North American wilderness streams, the primary pathogens of concern are protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) — and a 0.2-micron filter handles both plus bacteria. Viral risk is minimal because there is little human fecal contamination. Adding chemical treatment in this scenario is unnecessary. The key is matching your method to the actual threat level of your water source.

Improvised filtration (cloth, sand, charcoal) reduces turbidity and may remove some larger organisms, but it does not reliably remove bacteria, viruses, or protozoa. It is pre-treatment — it makes subsequent boiling or chemical treatment more effective by removing sediment. Boiling after pre-filtration ensures the water is safe. Running water is not inherently safe — it can be contaminated upstream.

The priority order is a risk ladder: stored water was treated and sealed in calm conditions, home sources are enclosed and mostly predictable, and natural sources are open to contamination. Skipping safer steps in favor of convenience trades safety for effort.

Water runs downhill and concentrates in valleys, ravines, and drainage bottoms, so walking downstream along a dry streambed often leads to water. Animal trails can point to water but guarantee nothing about its safety, and digging where the soil is dry is a guess, not a reading.

The water heater tank is the largest single reserve in most homes. Shut off the inlet valve (and power or gas) before draining so contaminated water cannot refill it and the unit cannot run dry and overheat. The toilet bowl is never a source — only the tank reserve, with the inlet shut off.

Groundwater that emerges as a spring or seep is generally less exposed to surface contamination than open water, making it the lowest-risk natural option. It still requires treatment, and stagnant water is the highest-risk option, not the cleanest.

Contamination is invisible: clarity and speed say nothing about pathogens. Odor, dead animals or algae, and upstream context (farms, settlements, mines) are the real signals, and any natural source still gets treated. Tasting suspicious water risks illness for no information.

Treated water is only as safe as its storage: clean, covered containers keep contamination out, and keeping it physically separate from untreated water prevents the wrong batch being drunk. Cold and freezing do not sterilize, and mixing untreated water recontaminates the whole batch.

In dry country, a band of green vegetation often marks moisture near the surface — a clue to investigate, not a guarantee. The source still has to be found, ranked by risk, and treated like any other natural water. Greenness never substitutes for treatment.

Flood water collects sewage, chemicals, and debris from everything it touched on the way through. It sits at the top of the risk ranking — a source of last resort to avoid entirely, not a first choice with the sediment settled.

A sheen and chemical smell indicate chemical contamination, which boiling does not remove (it can concentrate some chemicals through evaporation). This source fails the contamination check and is rejected; the search moves upstream or to another source.

The toilet tank reserve (never the bowl) holds clean water before use. Shutting the inlet valve prevents contaminated supply water from refilling the tank as you draw. The water heater also needs its inlet shut off — and power or gas off — before draining.

Boiling kills or inactivates all bacteria, viruses, and protozoa — it is the single most reliable purification method. A 0.2 micron filter may not remove all viruses. Chlorine is less effective against Cryptosporidium. SODIS is less reliable against protozoan cysts and depends on weather conditions.

At higher altitudes, water boils at a lower temperature (roughly 1°C less per 300m elevation gain). While pathogens still die at these temperatures, the reduced heat means you should extend the boiling time to 3 minutes to ensure complete disinfection. The old 10-minute recommendation is no longer considered necessary by WHO and CDC.

For clear water, the EPA-recommended dose is 2 drops of 5–6% bleach per liter, with a minimum 30-minute contact time. The water should have a faint chlorine smell afterward — if not, repeat the dose. 5 drops per liter is the dose for 2% iodine tincture (a different chemical). Using too much bleach (10 drops) is unnecessary and makes the water unpleasant.

Viruses range from approximately 0.02 to 0.2 microns — smaller than the 0.2 micron pore size of most backpacking filters. A 0.2 micron filter will reliably remove bacteria and protozoa but may not remove all viruses. In areas with potential human fecal contamination (high-use areas, developing countries, flood zones), you should combine filtration with chemical treatment or boiling.

Chemical disinfection reactions are temperature-dependent. In cold water (below 10°C / 50°F), the reaction rate decreases significantly. You should double the contact time — wait at least 60 minutes instead of 30. If possible, let the water warm up before treating. Iodine is also temperature-dependent — switching chemicals does not solve the cold-water problem.

Iodine has specific health contraindications. It is not recommended for pregnant women, people with thyroid conditions, or for continuous use beyond a few weeks due to potential cumulative effects on thyroid function. It is also not effective against Cryptosporidium. Chlorine-based methods (or filtration) are generally preferred for regular use.

Filtration removes protozoa (which chemicals struggle with) and most bacteria, while chemical treatment kills viruses (which most filters miss). Using both in sequence provides broader protection than either method alone. This is the recommended approach for questionable water sources or when someone in the group is immunocompromised.

Boiled water can be recontaminated if stored improperly. Use a clean container (rinse it with a small amount of the boiled water first if unsure), keep it covered to prevent insects and debris from entering, and avoid introducing contamination through dirty hands, cups, or ladles. Boiled water does not have residual disinfectant protection (unlike chlorinated water), so container hygiene is critical.

A rain barrel system is three parts: the roof that catches the rain, the gutters and downspout that convey it, and the barrel that stores it. Pumps, filters, and wells belong to other kinds of systems.

A barrel is useful when it delivers water where it is used. Placing it near the garden means the water gets used; a barrel whose water must be carried long distances quietly becomes a decoration. Height does not add useful pressure to a gravity barrel, and shade cools water but does not clean it.

Every opening in a barrel is an entry point. Uncovered and unscreened, standing water breeds mosquitoes — which are disease vectors — while debris and animal waste contaminate the harvest. Screening is a design requirement, not an option.

The first flush washes the roof: dust, leaf litter, bird droppings, and roof-material chemicals accumulated since the last rain. Diverting that first runoff away from the barrel means the stored water comes from the cleaner rain that follows.

The EPA flags that rain flowing over a roof can pick up bacteria from birds and animals and chemicals from roof materials. For food crops that contact edible tissue, that is a real consideration — treat the water as suspect and consider testing, rather than assuming rain is clean.

Rainwater meant for drinking becomes a raw-water source and gets the full treat-before-drink rule: boiling, chemical treatment, or filtration (the methods live in [[Water Purification]]), followed by clean storage. Cloth straining removes debris, not pathogens, and settling removes sediment, not pathogens.

A barrel on the ground puts its spigot at ground level — no watering can fits. Elevating the barrel on a stable base lets gravity deliver the water. Full barrels are heavy, so the base must be level and stable.

Harvesting is weather-dependent and every liter carries a treatment requirement before drinking. The stored emergency supply (at least 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days, per FEMA/CDC guidance) was made in calm conditions and remains the primary plan. The barrel supplements — it never replaces.

Stored water goes stale and grows biofilm and sediment when it sits unused. The fix is the same discipline as stored water everywhere: empty, clean the container, and rotate the water through actual use ([[WAT-storage-K01]]).

Water expands when it freezes, and expansion inside a sealed, full barrel cracks containers and fittings. The freezing guidance that applies to all water storage ([[WAT-storage-K01]]) applies here: leave headspace where freezing is possible, or drain the barrel for the season.

SODIS works through UV-A radiation (320–400 nm) reacting with dissolved oxygen in water. This produces reactive oxygen species — hydrogen peroxide and free radicals — that damage pathogen DNA and cell membranes. Heat enhances the effect, but UV-A is the primary mechanism. The bottle does not release chemicals or filter the water. SODIS does not boil water (though on very hot days, water can reach pasteurization temperatures above 50°C).

Glass effectively blocks UV-A radiation — the wavelength that drives the disinfection reaction. Without UV-A reaching the water, SODIS cannot work. Cost and weight are practical considerations, but the fundamental reason is UV transmission. PET (recycling code #1) transmits UV-A while being food-safe and widely available.

The standard SODIS protocol requires 6 hours of direct sunlight on a sunny day. One hour is only sufficient when water temperature exceeds 50°C (122°F) — a combined UV + thermal effect. Twelve hours is not the protocol — 6 hours on a sunny day is the standard.

Cloud cover dramatically reduces UV reaching ground level. The SODIS protocol specifies 2 full days of exposure in overcast conditions. SODIS does still work with cloud cover — just much more slowly. It's not that SODIS "doesn't work at all" in overcast conditions, but rather that it requires much longer. If you need water within the next day, choose another method.

SODIS has two main limitations compared to boiling: (1) it is less reliable against Cryptosporidium oocysts, which are UV-resistant at typical exposure levels, and (2) it requires direct sunlight — it doesn't work at night, in heavy overcast, or in poor weather. SODIS is actually cheaper than boiling (free), requires no special equipment (just a PET bottle), and produces water with no chemical taste.

This scenario is ideal for SODIS — sunny, near the equator (maximum UV), stationary camp. The slightly cloudy water needs pre-filtering through cloth first — if you can't read text through the filled bottle, UV can't treat it effectively. Six hours is the standard sunny-day exposure. Horizontal placement maximizes surface area. One hour is insufficient unless water temperature exceeds 50°C.

FEMA and CDC recommend storing at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day for drinking and basic hygiene. This is the minimum — hot climates, pregnant or nursing individuals, and additional needs like cooking require more. The minimum storage period is 3 days, with 2 weeks recommended.

One person × 2 weeks = 14 gallons. Family of 4 = 56 gallons (224 liters). This is approximately sixteen 3.5-gallon containers or one 55-gallon drum. It's achievable in a basement, garage, or dedicated closet — but requires planning. Start with 3 days and build up.

Food-grade HDPE (#2) is the standard material for long-term water storage — durable, designed for food contact, and widely available. Milk jugs are HDPE but too thin for long-term use and impossible to fully clean of milk residue. Containers that held non-food substances cannot be made safe by cleaning. Cardboard is not watertight for long-term storage.

The residual chlorine film left after pouring out the sanitizing solution provides ongoing protection against microbial growth. Rinsing removes this protective layer. The trace amount of chlorine remaining is safe and beneficial. Fill the container immediately after sanitizing.

Water itself does not expire. Municipal tap water with residual chlorine, stored in sanitized containers in cool/dark conditions, is likely safe even beyond the 6–12 month guideline. But you should inspect it: open one container, check clarity and odor. If fine, use it (rotate the batch) and establish a regular inspection schedule. Boiling is unnecessary if the water was properly stored and shows no signs of contamination.

A standard water heater tank holds 40–80 liters of clean water. Drain from the bottom valve (sediment settles there — let it run clear). The toilet tank (not bowl) holds ~10 L of clean water if no chemical cleaners are used. Toilet bowl water is contaminated. Vase water has been stagnant and may contain bacteria. Pool water contains stabilizers, algaecides, and higher chlorine levels than drinking water standards — it's a last resort, not a planned alternative.

The chain runs source, conveyance, storage, distribution, and point of use. WHO drinking-water guidance protects the whole chain because quality can be lost at every link — testing only the final water finds problems after the chain has already delivered them.

In a gravity system, pressure at the tap depends on the height of the water surface above it, not the volume in the tank. The tall tank's elevation delivers usable flow; the large flat tank holds more water but cannot push it.

An electric pump without a backup is a single point of failure: when power stops, the system stops. Pumping to elevated storage (or keeping a manual pump) means the tank becomes the reserve and the pump only refills it — the resilient pairing.

The submerged hose is a cross-connection. When pressure drops, the system can draw the bucket's contents backward through the hose into the drinking line — backflow carrying whatever the hose was touching. The fix is separation (never submerge hoses) or a backflow-prevention device.

The tank is one link of the chain. It protects storage, but the source, conveyance, distribution pipes, and cross-connections remain entry points — including the backflow paths a clean tank does nothing about.
Most pumps must not run dry: without water for lubrication and cooling, seals and motors fail. Knowing whether a pump needs priming and what dry running does is part of operating it safely.

Water expands when it freezes, and expansion inside pipes, pumps, and tanks cracks them. Winterization is a design decision: drain what can drain, protect what must stay live, and document the sequence ([[WAT-storage-K01]] covers the same expansion principle for stored water).

A contamination event like floodwater entry means the system is suspect until proven otherwise: disinfect or treat the water (EPA emergency disinfection guidance, see [[Water Purification]]), sanitize the affected components, and treat any system water as contaminated in the meantime. Clarity and flushing do not remove pathogens or chemicals.

The pasture is part of the conveyance link: the pipe carries water through an area where animal waste can contaminate it before storage. The fix is protecting the conveyance (secure, leak-proof, clean intake) and inspecting where the pipe actually runs — the chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

A former chemical or fuel container is excluded from drinking-water storage entirely — residues persist in the material and can leach into the water over time (the container-selection rule of [[WAT-storage-K01]]). Rinsing and filtering do not undo a container's history; it belongs in non-potable service or nowhere.
The most dangerous contaminants do not change how water looks, tastes, or smells. That is why testing exists: observation can reject a source, but it can never approve one.

Odor is a rejection signal: a chemical or fuel smell disqualifies the source regardless of how clear it looks. The inverse is also true — a clean smell is not approval. Boiling inactivates pathogens but does not remove chemical contaminants.

Testing for every possible pathogen is impractical. The indicator approach — coliform bacteria, especially E. coli — detects the marker of fecal contamination, which is the common route for the diseases that matter.

Flood water carries sewage and chemicals, and a supply touched by flooding is suspect until treated and verified. Testing after flood events is an obligation, not an option — clarity returning does not undo the exposure.

A sample should represent the water as it is actually used — the tap, after running the line briefly. Sampling the tank answers a different question (tank condition) and misses what the drinker actually receives.

A negative field result means "not detected within the test's limits, at this moment, in this sample." Water quality changes with weather and season, and field kits have lower sensitivity than a laboratory — so the result is evidence, not a certification.

A positive indicator result means the water is unsafe: treat it, find where the contamination enters (wellhead, tank, pipes), and fix the path before re-testing. A one-pot boil covers one meal, not a supply.

A sample that is held warm for days grows or dies its own biology — the lab then reports on the car, not the well. Samples must be sealed, labeled, kept cool, and delivered promptly to report on the water being tested.
Testing the source means sampling before any treatment step; verifying that treatment works means sampling after it. Mixing the two questions produces results that answer neither.

While results are pending, people drink regardless — make it treated water (boiling or chemical treatment per [[WAT-purification-K01]]). Treatment and testing are partners: the test decides the long-term plan; treatment protects the people in the meantime.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
sections.content:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- LO1: Explain the biology of decomposition — who does the work and what they need
- LO2: Classify organic materials as greens or browns by what each contributes to a pile
- LO3: Build a working pile by managing location, material mix, moisture, and air
- LO4: Troubleshoot common pile problems by observing smell, heat, and pests
- LO5: Judge when compost is finished and use it safely on food crops
- LO6: Connect composting to soil health and food production in a preparedness context
