source_fields.description: Turning waste into soil: the biology of decomposition, greens and browns, building and turning a pile, troubleshooting common compost problems, and using finished compost safely in the garden.
The calendar and the map: planting calendars, succession schedules, crop rotation, companion and interplanting decisions, yield estimation, and the record-keeping that makes next year's plan.

The preparedness view of growing food: prioritizing reliable crops, planning around water, time, and labor, realistic harvest expectations, and building resilience through a garden that supplements — not replaces — your stored food supply.

Choosing and laying out a growing area: sunlight, water access, soil, crop selection, spacing, seasons, and the realistic constraints that make the difference between a plan on paper and food on the table.
Extending the season under cover: how greenhouses work, structure choices from cold frames to full greenhouses, temperature and ventilation management, and the honest costs of growing under glass.
Delivering water well: how much plants need and when, deep versus shallow watering, drip versus sprinkler versus hand, mulching, and stretching a limited water supply across a productive garden.

Defending the garden without a chemical war: observation and identification first, cultural controls, barriers, beneficial insects, and the integrated pest management ladder from prevention to the last resort.

Saving seed from your own garden: choosing suitable plants, knowing when seeds are mature, harvesting, cleaning, drying, storage, labeling, viability, and the crops where it is genuinely easy — and where it is not.

What soil is, how it holds water and air, why organic matter matters, basic fertility concepts, and how to observe your own soil — plus how to grow when the soil is poor, using raised beds and containers.
Cooking over open fire safely: pot placement and heat control, grill and support methods, fuel economy, food safety at the fire, and the boundaries between cooking fire and wildfire risk.
The material progression from tinder to fuel: what burns hot, what burns long, reading wood by species and condition, finding dry fuel in wet conditions, and fuel preparation.
The science behind every fire: the fire triangle, heat transfer, combustion stages, and why fires die — knowledge that makes every later fire skill easier to learn and troubleshoot.
Building a fire that lights and burns: teepee, log cabin, lean-to, and platform lays; when each structure fits the fuel and purpose; and the airflow logic that decides success.
Keeping a fire alive and useful: feeding on schedule, managing airflow and coals, banking a fire overnight, rescuing a dying fire, and extinguishing completely when the fire is done.
Prevent wildfires, extinguish fires completely, and recognize fire danger conditions. Learn site preparation, the Drown-Stir-Feel method, and what to do if you encounter a wildfire.
Master the fire triangle, material progression, and ignition methods from lighters to bow drills. Learn to find dry tinder in wet conditions and build a fire that lights every time.
Home canning done safely: high-acid versus low-acid foods, boiling water versus pressure canning, the botulism boundary, tested recipes and processing times, and the signs of a failed jar.

The principles and workflow of food dehydration: why drying preserves, preparation and slicing, temperature and airflow, storage after drying, signs of inadequate drying, and the safety limits that separate drying from cooking and sterilization.
The short-term emergency food supply: what to keep ready to eat without power, calorie and water pairing, special needs and dietary constraints, and keeping a 72-hour supply that actually gets eaten.

Preservation by fermentation: how salt and beneficial microbes preserve food, safe vegetable fermenting practice, signs of success and failure, and the difference between controlled fermentation and spoilage.

The four pillars — Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill — applied under emergency conditions: safe cooking temperatures, cross-contamination control, hand hygiene without running water, and when food must be discarded rather than risked.
The fundamentals of safe food storage: temperature, moisture, oxygen, and light; the danger zone; packaging by timeline; FIFO labeling and rotation; signs of spoilage; and emergency food planning.

Preparedness-oriented long-term food storage: selecting foods, shelf-life conditions, packaging with oxygen control, storage environment, rotation and inventory, realistic limitations, and common failure modes.
Eating to keep working in an emergency: energy needs, protein and micronutrients in stored food, hydration's role in nutrition, special needs, and building a stored diet that covers the essentials.
Cooking when grid-dependent appliances are unavailable: fuel planning, efficient cooking, stove and fire methods, carbon monoxide safety, fire boundaries, weather adjustments, and backup methods.

Smoking for flavor and preservation: hot versus cold smoking, safe temperatures and curing boundaries, equipment, wood selection, and the food-safety rules that separate smoked food from food poisoning.
Toxic plants: ingestion and dermal exposure, toxic parts, documented signs of poisoning, prevention around children and pets, and the response — Poison Control and emergency escalation.
The safety framework for wild food: positive identification before consumption, edible parts and growth stages, preparation, contamination, and why universal edibility tests are not a safe method.
Foraging that leaves the land as found: selective harvest, population health, protected areas, threatened species, private property, local rules, and leave-no-trace principles.
The practical craft of foraging: planning, tools and containers, one-species separation, hygiene and transport, photo documentation, post-harvest confirmation, and when to abandon a collection.
Wild fruits and berries: whole-plant identification, ripeness requirements, seeds and pulp, documented preparation such as cooking elderberries, storage, and the confusion risks with toxic berries.
Wild greens with documented preparation: identification, seasonality, washing and cooking requirements, contamination avoidance, preservation, and the species that must never be eaten raw.

Differential identification between similar species: diagnostic features that truly separate them, documented dangerous pairs, the confirmation process, and the rule — when any feature fails to match, treat the plant as the dangerous option.

Fungal safety education: the limits of visual identification, dangerous groups and look-alikes, why cooking does not make certain species safe, delayed-onset poisoning, and when to call Poison Control.

The discipline of identifying plants: leaf, stem, flower, fruit, and seed characters, growth patterns, multi-character positive identification, documentation and photography, and the limits of identification.
Underground foods: roots, tubers, rhizomes, and bulbs; aboveground identification before digging, documented preparation, contaminated-soil rules, storage, and rejection decisions.

Controlling life-threatening external bleeding: recognition, direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquet principles, shock recognition, reassessment, and knowing when emergency medical care is required.
Burns and thermal injuries at a first-aid level: classification, cooling, covering and protection, chemical and electrical considerations, and the red flags that demand emergency care.

Emergency assessment and triage: scene safety, the primary assessment of responsiveness, breathing, and circulation, activating emergency services, prioritization, and reassessment until help arrives.

Building an emergency medical kit: essential first-aid and wound-care supplies, PPE, organization, inspection and expiration management, field portability, and adapting the kit to realistic scenarios.

Fractures, sprains, and immobilization: recognizing a possible fracture, splinting principles, avoiding unnecessary movement, circulation and sensation checks, and when to escalate to emergency services.
Heat and cold emergencies: heat exhaustion, heat stroke, hypothermia, and frostbite — recognition, immediate first aid, environmental exposure, and emergency escalation.
Wound care and infection prevention: assessing a wound, cleaning and dressing it properly, recognizing contamination, monitoring for infection, and the red flags that require professional care.
The compass as a navigation instrument: components, magnetic versus true north, taking and following bearings, back bearings, declination, common compass errors, and practical field navigation.
Latitude/longitude, UTM and MGRS concepts, reading grid references, plotting positions, datum mistakes, communicating a location, and emergency location reporting.

Getting found: communicating position with coordinates or descriptions, emergency signaling, PLBs and satellite messengers conceptually, battery conservation, and the information rescuers actually need.

GPS and smartphones as navigation tools — and why they stay secondary: GPS fundamentals, GNSS, smartphone limitations, offline maps, downloaded areas, battery management, accuracy, and electronic failure.
Reading a map like a navigator: map types, legends and symbols, scale, grid systems, contour lines, elevation interpretation, terrain features, and extracting usable information.

What goes wrong and how to recover: disorientation, wrong turns, missed landmarks, parallel terrain, drift, confirmation bias, the stop-think-observe-plan procedure, backtracking, and deciding when to stop moving.
What navigation actually is: position, direction, distance, and destination; route versus bearing, the navigation workflow, staying oriented, common mistakes, and choosing a navigation method.

Navigating when the light is gone: reduced visibility, route simplification, pacing, bearings at night, terrain hazards, light discipline, group cohesion, and the decision rules for when NOT to continue.

Planning a route that survives contact with terrain: objective, route selection, distance and elevation, difficulty, water and resupply, alternates, turnaround points, contingencies, and realistic time estimates.

Reading the land itself: ridgelines, valleys, saddles, spurs, draws, and waterways; matching map terrain to real terrain, handrails and catching features, and navigating when map and compass disagree.
Water on the map and on the ground: identifying waterways, rivers as handrails and their traps, selecting safe crossing points, water hazards, bridges, flood conditions, and when NOT to cross.

Navigating when weather erases the landscape: fog, rain, snow, and smoke; visibility degradation, weather effects on terrain and route choice, stop-versus-continue decisions, and emergency fallback procedures.
Staying warm in a shelter: how the body loses heat, insulation principles, ground versus overhead losses, improvised insulation materials, and the moisture rules that undo them.
Shelters meant to last weeks or longer: location, structure choices, weatherproofing, repair and maintenance, and the fire, water, and sanitation systems a long-term shelter must include.

Using what the landscape already provides: rock overhangs, caves, windbreaks, and tree features — with the hazard checks (water, rockfall, wildlife) that decide whether a natural shelter is a refuge or a trap.
The materials a shelter is made from: natural materials, tarps, cordage, and fasteners; strengths and failure modes of each; and matching materials to the shelter job and expected weather.
Choosing where to shelter: the five W's — wind, water, widowmakers, wildlife, and wood — plus drainage, visibility, and the site checks that prevent midnight relocations.
Pitching and living under a tarp: site selection, A-frame/lean-to/plow point configurations, ground insulation, moisture management, fire separation, and when not to build.
Choosing, pitching, and living in tents: tent types and tradeoffs, site preparation, weather setup, condensation and ventilation, care and repair, and when a tent is the wrong shelter.
Shelter against wind, rain, snow, and sun: the principles of shedding water and blocking wind, reading approaching weather, and adapting a shelter to what the sky is about to do.
The one-page household emergency plan: meeting points, out-of-area contact, evacuation decision rules, communication fallbacks, rehearsal.
The three legs of household preparedness — plan, kit, knowledge — with 72-hour sizing, go-bag assembly, and maintenance routines.
The hierarchy of survival needs and how to spend effort in order: immediate threats first, then exposure, water, signaling, food — and how tunnel vision breaks the sequence when it matters most.
Evaluating hazards before they happen: likelihood, severity, and exposure; risk matrices for the household; mitigation versus acceptance; and reassessment as conditions change.
Paying attention on purpose: observation loops, baselines and anomalies, scanning habits, distraction and stress effects, and turning awareness into action without paranoia.
The mental side of emergencies: stress responses, panic and freezing, decision-making under pressure, staying task-focused, and the practical routines that keep a mind — and a group — working.
The most reliable single purification method. Learn the correct boiling procedure, how altitude affects boiling time, which containers are safe, and how to conserve fuel.
Treat water with chlorine or iodine when you cannot boil or filter. Learn correct dosages, contact times, iodine safety limits, and the Cryptosporidium problem.
The most thorough purification method — removes salt, heavy metals, and chemicals that boiling and filtration cannot. Build a solar still and understand when distillation is truly necessary.
How physical filters remove pathogens from water. Understand pore sizes, filter types, the virus gap, proper maintenance, and why freezing destroys hollow fiber filters.

Locating water in the field: landscape reading, where water collects, seasonal sources, animal and insect indicators, and the judgment calls between natural sources, standing water, and what must be treated.
An overview of all major water purification methods — boiling, filtration, chemical treatment, SODIS, and distillation. Learn how each method works, when to use it, and what it cannot remove.
Harvesting rain from roofs: catchment basics, barrels and cisterns, first-flush diversion, screening, storage hygiene, and the limits of collected water for drinking versus irrigation.
Purify water using nothing but sunlight and a PET plastic bottle. A zero-cost, zero-fuel method promoted by the WHO. Learn when it works and when to use something else.
Store emergency water that stays safe for months or years. Learn how much to store, which containers are food-safe, how to sanitize and fill them, and when to rotate.
Small-scale water systems for preparedness: gravity-fed storage and distribution, pumps, plumbing basics, backflow and contamination protection, and what fails when the power does.

Judging whether water is safe: what contamination looks like, taste and odor indicators, what field observations can and cannot tell you, when laboratory testing matters, and how testing fits the treatment decision.

options.text: Heat released as the dry browns reabsorb moisture
options.label: C

options.text: Fermentation of stored kitchen waste in the lower layers
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have a bucket of fresh grass clippings and a bag of dry leaves. Which is a "green," and what does it contribute to the pile?

options.text: The dry leaves — they add structure and hold air
options.label: A

options.text: The grass clippings — they are fresh and nitrogen-rich, feeding the organisms and driving heating
options.label: B

options.text: The grass clippings — they are dry and fibrous, adding bulk
options.label: C

options.text: The dry leaves — they are moist and nitrogen-rich
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your pile smells like rotten eggs, and the center is dark and soggy. What is the correct read and response?

options.text: The pile is too dry — add water and wet greens
options.label: A

options.text: The pile has too many browns — remove half of them
options.label: B

options.text: The pile is finished — screen it and spread it on the beds
options.label: C

options.text: The pile is too wet and dense — turn it and work in dry browns to restore air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does turning a compost pile matter, and what is the honest result of never turning it?

options.text: Turning is purely cosmetic — it makes the pile look managed but does nothing else
options.label: A

options.text: Turning kills all weed seeds, so turned piles are always safe to spread
options.label: B

options.text: Turning restores oxygen and mixes cool outer material into the center — it speeds decomposition, but an unturned pile still breaks down, just more slowly
options.label: C

options.text: Turning compacts the pile, which is the only way it holds heat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Four months after starting, your pile is dark, crumbly, smells like good earth, and no longer warms when you turn it. What does this tell you?

options.text: The pile is finished — the material is stable and ready to use as a soil amendment
options.label: A

options.text: The pile has failed — it never heated, so it cannot be used
options.label: B

options.text: The pile needs more greens immediately to restart it
options.label: C

options.text: The pile is too wet and needs aeration for another season
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor wants to work a load of fresh chicken manure into the vegetable beds two weeks before planting tomatoes. What do you advise?

options.text: Fresh manure is fine — more nitrogen means faster growth
options.label: A

options.text: Do not use fresh manure on food crops — it can carry pathogens; only aged or composted manure is safe
options.label: B

options.text: Fresh manure is fine only if it is mixed with lime first
options.label: C

options.text: Fresh manure is fine if it is spread on top rather than worked in
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Rodents start visiting your open compost bin. Which change is most likely to solve the problem?

options.text: Add more kitchen scraps — the volume will bury the smell
options.label: A

options.text: Water the pile daily so rodents cannot burrow
options.label: B

options.text: Stop adding meat, dairy, and fats, and use a closed bin with no entry gaps
options.label: C

options.text: Move the bin into full sun, which repels rodents
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a household that wants to reduce its dependence on purchased garden inputs, why is a compost pile valuable?

options.text: It is cheaper than buying bags of potting mix for containers
options.label: A

options.text: It replaces the need for any watering in the garden
options.label: B

options.text: It is a decorative garden feature that attracts pollinators
options.label: C

options.text: It manufactures organic matter from household waste — building soil water-holding and structure without a trip to the store
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A small pile you built three weeks ago is dry on the outside, cool in the middle, and has barely shrunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: The pile is too small, too dry, or short on greens — it lacks the conditions for active decomposition
options.label: A

options.text: The pile has too much nitrogen — it has gone anaerobic
options.label: B

options.text: The pile is finished and should be spread now
options.label: C

options.text: The pile is infested with harmless fungi and needs to be abandoned
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your finished compost is dark and crumbly, and you are about to plant seedlings. What is the correct way to use it?

options.text: Fill the planting holes with pure compost so the roots get maximum nutrition
options.label: A

options.text: Spread fresh manure over the top and let the compost absorb it
options.label: B

options.text: Use the compost only as a fuel source for the winter cold frame
options.label: C

options.text: Blend it into the bed soil as an amendment rather than planting directly in pure compost
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor says the USDA hardiness zone for the area says "plant tomatoes in mid-May." What is the accurate response?

options.text: The zone is the only calendar you need — follow it exactly
options.label: A

options.text: The zone describes winter minimums, not planting dates — the calendar comes from local frost dates and days to maturity
options.label: B

options.text: The zone only applies to cool-season crops
options.label: C

options.text: The zone is correct for tomatoes but not for other crops
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener sows an entire lettuce bed in one go and gets a three-week glut, then empty beds until fall. What is the crop-planning fix?

options.text: Sow the whole bed a month later, so the glut arrives with better weather
options.label: A

options.text: Plant nothing but slow crops, which never glut
options.label: B

options.text: Stagger the sowings into short rows spaced by weeks, and mark the replant date the moment a row finishes
options.label: C

options.text: Double the bed size so the glut feeds more people
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A tomato plant develops a soil-borne disease in a bed, and the gardener plans to plant peppers there next season. Why is this a crop-planning problem?

options.text: Peppers prefer full shade, which the tomato bed cannot provide
options.label: A

options.text: Peppers are heavier feeders and will exhaust the soil
options.label: B

options.text: Peppers take twice as long to mature as tomatoes
options.label: C

options.text: Tomatoes and peppers are both nightshades — the same family, so shared diseases and pests can build up in that ground
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which interplanting arrangement relies on a mechanism with real, reliable evidence?

options.text: Sowing radishes with carrots, so the fast radishes are harvested before the slow carrots need the space
options.label: A

options.text: Planting marigolds everywhere, on the promise that they repel every insect
options.label: B

options.text: Pairing crops by their colors, so the bed "looks balanced" to pests
options.label: C

options.text: Planting the same crop in every bed, so the garden is uniform
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A seed catalog claims a variety will produce a huge yield per plant. How should you treat that number when planning the season?

options.text: As the planning number — catalogs are tested in real gardens
options.label: A

options.text: As a conversation starter — the honest estimate comes from what your garden actually harvested per bed in previous seasons
options.label: B

options.text: As the minimum, since gardens outperform catalogs
options.label: C

options.text: As irrelevant — yields cannot be estimated at all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardening website says that planting herb X next to crop Y "repels the pest for certain." What is the evidence-honest approach?

options.text: Build the whole season's plan around the pairing — the website tested it
options.label: A

options.text: Assume it works in reverse and plant them far apart
options.label: B

options.text: Treat it as folklore: rarely harmful, occasionally useful, mostly untested — try it as an experiment without staking the plan on it
options.label: C

options.text: Report the pairing to the extension office as a proven fact
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fall garden plan needs lettuce that matures before the first frost. How do you set the sowing date?

options.text: Sow whenever the seed packet arrives — fall planting is flexible
options.label: A

options.text: Water the lettuce more, so it matures faster
options.label: B

options.text: Sow the whole fall bed at the last frost date
options.label: C

options.text: Count back from the first fall frost date using days to maturity plus a margin, and sow then
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A bed just produced its spring pea crop, which has finished. What does a succession plan say about this bed?

options.text: Replant it the same week with a warm-season or fall crop — empty bed days are lost production
options.label: A

options.text: Leave it fallow until fall — empty beds rest the soil
options.label: B

options.text: Double-crop only by accident, if spare seeds happen to exist
options.label: C

options.text: Move the bed's soil to another location, then replant
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener swears by memory: "I know what I planted." What does the crop-planning discipline say?

options.text: Memory is fine — the garden itself is the record
options.label: A

options.text: Write it down: dates, varieties, harvests, and problems — reviewed at season's end, because memory drifts
options.label: B

options.text: Only record failures, so successes are not second-guessed
options.label: C

options.text: Record everything in the seed catalog margins, never the journal
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener's rotation plan is getting complicated and perfectionist. What is the honest, workable standard?

options.text: Perfect rotation is required — one mistake ruins the soil forever
options.label: A

options.text: Rotation only matters for organic gardens, not others
options.label: B

options.text: A simple bed-by-bed rotation that keeps families moving and spaces out their returns is enough — the plan just needs to keep families on the move
options.label: C

options.text: Rotation applies only to the cabbage family
options.label: D

source_fields.title: Basic Food Production for Preparedness Quiz

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the honest role of a garden in a household preparedness plan?

options.text: It replaces stored food entirely once established
options.label: A

options.text: It is decorative morale value only
options.label: B

options.text: It supplements stored food with fresh produce, practices a production skill while stakes are low, and can close the grow-keep-replant loop
options.label: C

options.text: It matters only if the household owns farmland
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A plan describes a backyard garden that will make a household of four "fully self-sufficient." What is the accurate assessment?

options.text: Overclaim — a home garden can supplement meaningfully but cannot honestly replace the household's staple supply; the stored-food base and the garden strengthen each other
options.label: A

options.text: Achievable in one season with the right seed catalog
options.label: B

options.text: Accurate, provided the garden is at least 200 square meters
options.label: C

options.text: Impossible only in cold climates
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What are the three crop filters for a preparedness garden, in the correct order?

options.text: Novelty, appearance, and catalog popularity
options.label: A

options.text: Reliability in your conditions, productive use of space, and storability
options.label: B

options.text: Storability, cost of seed, and speed of germination
options.label: C

options.text: Taste, yield, and rarity
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which crop set matches extension guidance for dependable, high-yield, productive home gardens?

options.text: Ornamental gourds, exotic greens, and rare heirloom melons
options.label: A

options.text: Only fast-growing salad crops
options.label: B

options.text: A single crop grown in bulk — specialization maximizes yield
options.label: C

options.text: Pole beans, tomatoes, cabbage and other brassicas, root crops, and leafy greens
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the working rule of thumb for how much water vegetables need?

options.text: About an inch per week from rain plus irrigation, and more in heat
options.label: A

options.text: Nothing beyond normal rainfall — vegetables manage themselves
options.label: B

options.text: Daily flooding until the surface stays wet
options.label: C

options.text: A fixed liter per plant per day, regardless of weather
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your preparedness garden plan lists "the municipal tap" as the water source. Why is the plan incomplete?

options.text: Municipal water always contains chlorine, which kills vegetables
options.label: A

options.text: The tap is fine — water never fails in disruptions
options.label: B

options.text: In a disruption, municipal water or the power for pumps may be unavailable — the plan needs a stated source for a dry disruption month (stored, captured, or carried) and the demand it must meet
options.label: C

options.text: Gardens do not need a water plan — only a rain plan
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the most common garden failure, and which planning discipline prevents it?

options.text: Frost damage — prevented by planting later
options.label: A

options.text: Poor seed quality — prevented by buying premium seed
options.label: B

options.text: Soil exhaustion — prevented by heavy fertilization
options.label: C

options.text: Neglect — prevented by sizing the garden to the smallest realistic week and designing chores out
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your whole bean crop ripens in the same week. What does harvest planning say this is, and what should have been decided in spring?

options.text: A windfall — harvest it all and celebrate
options.label: A

options.text: A preservation emergency — the storage path (what dries, what gets eaten fresh, where it all goes) should have been designed before planting
options.label: B

options.text: Normal — every crop ripens at once, and it always works out
options.label: C

options.text: A sign to plant more beans next year
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A summer drought is forecast. Which design response best matches failure-scenario thinking?

options.text: Plant more of everything now, before the drought hits
options.label: A

options.text: Do nothing — droughts are unpredictable and unmanageable
options.label: B

options.text: Apply the pre-planned responses: drought-tolerant crops, mulch, deep infrequent watering, and a garden sized to the available supply
options.label: C

options.text: Move the garden indoors for the season
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why must the preparedness garden exist before the emergency?

options.text: A garden is a practiced system — site, soil, water, seeds, and skills take seasons to establish; the garden that matters is the one already running
options.label: A

options.text: Because seeds cannot be purchased during an emergency
options.label: B

options.text: It does not — a garden can be started any time and produces in weeks
options.label: C

options.text: Only for legal reasons — garden registration takes months
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have picked a sunny, flat spot for a vegetable garden, but it sits 40 meters from the nearest tap with no hose that reaches. Why is this a weak site plan despite the sun?

options.text: Water access is a fixed constraint — if watering is impractical, it will be skipped, and yields collapse in dry spells
options.label: A

options.text: Vegetables do not actually need supplemental water
options.label: B

options.text: Distance from the house only matters for harvesting convenience
options.label: C

options.text: A long walk to water makes plants grow deeper roots, which is good
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are assessing a candidate garden site in spring. The spot is sunny all day in April, but large deciduous trees on the south side will leaf out by June. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Count the April sunlight and proceed — spring is the standard assessment season
options.label: A

options.text: Assume the trees will reduce light and give up on the site
options.label: B

options.text: Assess the site across the growing season, not just spring — count direct sun after the trees leaf out, and match crops to what the light allows
options.label: C

options.text: Choose only root crops, since they grow underground and ignore light
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor asks whether your USDA hardiness zone tells you when to plant tomatoes. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: Yes — the zone gives planting dates by crop
options.label: A

options.text: No — the zone describes average winter minimum temperatures; planting dates come from local frost dates
options.label: B

options.text: Yes — the zone is the same thing as the frost calendar
options.label: C

options.text: No — the zone only applies to houseplants
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household that eats rice, beans, greens, and tomatoes wants to start a first garden. Which crop list follows the planning rule "grow what you eat, and start small"?

options.text: A catalog-driven mix of 20 interesting varieties, including several nobody in the house cooks
options.label: A

options.text: Only the most expensive crops, whether or not the household eats them
options.label: B

options.text: Only fast crops, so the garden can be re-planned monthly
options.label: C

options.text: A short list led by greens, beans, and tomatoes — crops the household actually eats — expanded later from what works
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a bed that runs north–south, where should you place staked tomatoes so they do not shade shorter crops?

options.text: South side — they get the most sun there
options.label: A

options.text: East side — morning sun matters most
options.label: B

options.text: North side — tall crops on the north edge throw shade away from the bed
options.label: C

options.text: Center — surrounded by shorter crops on all sides
options.label: D

questions.question_text: As a general rule, how deep should you plant a seed?

options.text: About 2–3 times the seed's diameter — fine seeds pressed shallow, large seeds deeper
options.label: A

options.text: At least 10 cm for all seeds — depth protects them
options.label: B

options.text: Just under the surface — depth robs seeds of warmth
options.label: C

options.text: As deep as the seed packet's spacing recommendation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is succession planting described as "the cheapest yield increase in gardening"?

options.text: It requires buying new land each season
options.label: A

options.text: It replaces fertilizer, so inputs drop to zero
options.label: B

options.text: It removes the need for weeding
options.label: C

options.text: Staggered sowings and replanting finished space cost only seeds and minutes, but turn one bed into a continuous harvest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning a preparedness garden that currently relies on municipal water for the hose. Which addition best matches the preparedness water rule?

options.text: A larger hose and a longer planting list
options.label: A

options.text: A written water budget plus a stored or captured supply (rain barrels, stored water) for dry periods and disruptions
options.label: B

options.text: Only drought-tolerant crops, with no water plan needed
options.label: C

options.text: Watering only at night, when supply pressure is highest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A yard receives only about 4 hours of direct sun per day. Which crop list is realistic for this site?

options.text: Tomatoes, peppers, and corn — fruit needs the most sun
options.label: A

options.text: Any crop, provided the soil is fertilized well
options.label: B

options.text: Leafy greens, herbs, and some root crops — the shade-tolerant end of the catalog
options.label: C

options.text: Squash and melons, which prefer cool shade
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is three weeks before your area's average last spring frost date. Which crops can safely go into the garden now?

options.text: Cool-season crops like peas, lettuce, and spinach — they tolerate light frost
options.label: A

options.text: Warm-season crops like tomatoes and peppers — they need the full head start
options.label: B

options.text: All crops — frost dates are only advisory
options.label: C

options.text: Only perennials
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a sunny February afternoon, you walk into a closed, unvented greenhouse and it is far too hot to work in comfortably. What is happening, and what is the response?

options.text: The solar trap is working — shortwave sunlight enters and the enclosure holds the re-emitted heat, so the interior overheats on any sunny day; vent early and open the top
options.label: A

options.text: The heater is malfunctioning — turn it off and call for service
options.label: B

options.text: The plants are generating the heat through rapid growth — remove some plants
options.label: C

options.text: The glazing is dirty — clean it to reflect the sunlight
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener wants winter greens for a small household and has a small budget. Which structure decision is most honest?

options.text: A large heated greenhouse — more space means more production, regardless of cost
options.label: A

options.text: A cold frame or small unheated tunnel matched to the winter-greens job — the rung that fits the need and budget
options.label: B

options.text: A walk-in tunnel twice the needed size, in case the crop list grows
options.label: C

options.text: No structure — winter greens cannot be grown under cover at all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An unheated walk-in tunnel is planted with cold-hardy greens in January. What is the honest expectation for overnight temperatures inside?

options.text: The tunnel holds the day's warmth, so the interior stays mild all night
options.label: A

options.text: The plants' respiration keeps the interior above freezing
options.label: B

options.text: Without heat input, the interior drifts toward the outside temperature overnight — thermal mass can shrink, but not remove, the swing
options.label: C

options.text: The soil alone keeps the interior tropical at night
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Where should ventilation be placed, and why?

options.text: Low on the walls — cool air should enter at the bottom only
options.label: A

options.text: Only in the door — opening it while working is enough
options.label: B

options.text: Randomly — vent placement does not matter as long as it is open
options.label: C

options.text: Near the top (ridge) with intakes at the base — hot air rises, so the hottest air escapes from the top and draws cooler air through
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You notice condensation streaming down the inside of the glazing and a patch of mold on a leaf cluster. What is the honest diagnosis and response?

options.text: Enclosed air holds moisture, so humidity builds and damp foliage favors disease — water at the base, keep air moving, and vent to exchange air
options.label: A

options.text: The glazing is leaking — replace the structure's covering immediately
options.label: B

options.text: The plants are diseased beyond recovery — remove the entire crop
options.label: C

options.text: Condensation is harmless — ignore it and continue as normal
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor bought an inexpensive greenhouse kit and now complains it cost far more than the price tag. Which costs are most likely the surprise?

options.text: The paint and finishes need annual touch-up
options.label: A

options.text: Recurring costs: covering replacement as glazing degrades, heating or power, water, and the gardener's ongoing time
options.label: B

options.text: The soil inside needs to be imported and replaced monthly
options.label: C

options.text: Property taxes on garden structures
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The first big storm of winter collapses the film tunnel that was never anchored. What is the correct analysis?

options.text: Film structures always collapse in storms — there is nothing to be done
options.label: A

options.text: The storm was a one-in-a-century event — rebuilding the same way is fine
options.label: B

options.text: Wind failure is a known failure mode — film and lightweight frames act as sails, so anchoring is part of the build, not an optional extra
options.label: C

options.text: The plants pulled the structure down — remove the plants
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A heated greenhouse in December grows lettuce nicely, but the same greenhouse cannot produce ripe tomatoes until mid-summer. What is the honest explanation?

options.text: The heater is undersized — buy a larger one
options.label: A

options.text: The tomatoes are a bad variety — switch to a "winter" tomato
options.label: B

options.text: The greenhouse is too humid for tomatoes in winter
options.label: C

options.text: In winter, light — not warmth — is the limiting factor; short, low winter sun limits photosynthesis even in a warm structure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener in a cold-winter zone wants a structure that will reliably protect overwintering crops. What role does the hardiness zone play in the choice?

options.text: The zone tells what winter cold the structure must buffer against — the choice of structure and its winter routine follow from it
options.label: A

options.text: The zone is irrelevant — all structures perform identically in winter
options.label: B

options.text: The zone only matters for outdoor plants, never for covered ones
options.label: C

options.text: The zone decides which crops grow — structure choice is purely aesthetic
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household is deciding whether to buy any structure at all this year. Which framing is the most honest test of the purchase?

options.text: The bigger the structure, the more food security it provides
options.label: A

options.text: Define the job the structure must do each season, match the rung to it, and put the harvest in the crop and storage plan — a structure without a planned job is a hobby expense
options.label: B

options.text: Buy the cheapest structure and decide what to grow after it arrives
options.label: C

options.text: Structures only pay for themselves in tropical climates
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning irrigation for a new vegetable garden in a dry climate. What is the honest starting estimate for weekly water need?

options.text: Exactly the same amount every week, regardless of weather or soil
options.label: A

options.text: Water until the surface looks dark, twice daily
options.label: B

options.text: One fixed gallon per plant, forever
options.label: C

options.text: Roughly an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, adjusted for heat, wind, soil, and crop stage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener waters the beds every evening with a light sprinkle "so the plants never go thirsty." After the first dry spell, the plants collapse. What happened?

options.text: The plants died from overwatering — the opposite problem
options.label: A

options.text: Frequent shallow watering trained the roots shallow and near the surface, where they failed when the topsoil dried
options.label: B

options.text: Evening watering always kills plants
options.label: C

options.text: The dry spell was unusually severe — no watering pattern could have helped
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a hot, windy day in midsummer. Which watering choice minimizes waste?

options.text: Water early in the day at the base of the plants, so water soaks in and foliage dries before evening
options.label: A

options.text: Run the sprinkler at noon so the sun evaporates the water quickly
options.label: B

options.text: Water in the evening over the leaves so the plants "drink overnight"
options.label: C

options.text: Skip watering entirely on windy days
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement honestly describes the trade-off between sprinklers and drip irrigation?

options.text: Sprinklers are always superior because they cover more ground
options.label: A

options.text: Sprinklers wet foliage and lose water to wind and evaporation, while drip and soaker lines deliver slowly at the base with little waste
options.label: B

options.text: Drip systems require daily dismantling and cleaning
options.label: C

options.text: Sprinklers never wet the foliage — that is a myth
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener has a small garden, a tight water supply, and limited time. Which irrigation setup is the most honest fit?

options.text: A large sprinkler run twice a week — set and forget
options.label: A

options.text: Daily hand watering of every plant with the hose
options.label: B

options.text: Soaker or drip lines on the beds, delivering slowly at the base, matched to the low-pressure supply
options.label: C

options.text: No irrigation — hand water only when plants visibly wilt
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener mulches the beds with straw. Why does this count as part of the watering plan?

options.text: Straw repels rain, so less water enters the soil
options.label: A

options.text: Mulch makes plants need more water by shading them
options.label: B

options.text: Mulch attracts moisture from the air
options.label: C

options.text: Mulch shades the soil, slows evaporation, keeps the root zone cooler, and suppresses weeds that compete for water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household installs a rain barrel under the downspout to water the garden. What is the honest expectation?

options.text: The barrel replaces the municipal supply entirely — garden watering is now free
options.label: A

options.text: The barrel is a finite supplement between storms — sealed or screened against mosquitoes and debris, with the main supply still planned
options.label: B

options.text: Rain barrel water is unsafe for any plant
options.label: C

options.text: Barrels only work in winter climates
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a disruption, municipal water may be unavailable for the garden. What is the correct planning posture?

options.text: The garden's demand is a line in the household's stored-water budget — source, demand, and backup are planned in advance
options.label: A

options.text: The garden can simply go without water during the disruption
options.label: B

options.text: The garden will capture all its own water from dew
options.label: C

options.text: Only ornamental plants need water in an emergency
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At 2 PM on a hot day, the tomato plants' leaves droop. The gardener is about to water them. What is the correct step first?

options.text: Water immediately — drooping always means thirst
options.label: A

options.text: Spray the leaves with cold water to revive them
options.label: B

options.text: Check the soil a few inches down first — some plants wilt in midday heat and recover overnight, so the soil is the judge
options.label: C

options.text: Mulch over the plants entirely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Water supply is cut to a trickle for two weeks. The garden has fruiting tomatoes, a bean bed, and a lettuce row already bolting in the heat. What is the honest prioritization?

options.text: Water the lettuce first — greens are the healthiest crop
options.label: A

options.text: Spread the water evenly and thinly across everything every day
options.label: B

options.text: Water only at night so nobody sees the garden
options.label: C

options.text: Water the fruiting tomatoes first — their yield collapses fastest when the supply is short — then the beans, with the bolting lettuce lowest priority
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an unfamiliar insect on a vegetable leaf. What is the first step of the IPM decision process?

options.text: Identify the organism — what it is, what it is doing, and whether it is a pest at all
options.label: A

options.text: Apply a general-purpose spray immediately to be safe
options.label: B

options.text: Remove all the plants the insect has touched
options.label: C

options.text: Check the weather forecast for the next treatment window
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener wants to prevent pest problems before they start. Which option is a cultural control?

options.text: Spraying the whole garden weekly as insurance
options.label: A

options.text: Building soil health, rotating plant families, and timing plantings to avoid pest peaks
options.label: B

options.text: Buying more seeds in case the crop fails
options.label: C

options.text: Planting the same crop every year, since repetition builds resistance
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener covers the squash bed with a row cover to exclude pests. The plants flower but set no fruit. What is the likely explanation?

options.text: The row cover killed the flowers
options.label: A

options.text: The squash variety is defective
options.label: B

options.text: The cover was left in place during bloom — squash needs insect pollination, so the cover must be removed or opened when the plants flower
options.label: C

options.text: The plants need more fertilizer, not more pollination
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A cluster of aphids covers the tip of one broccoli plant out of twenty, and the garden is far from harvest. What does the tolerance step of IPM say?

options.text: Destroy the entire row — aphids always spread
options.label: A

options.text: Spray the whole garden so no aphid survives
options.label: B

options.text: Treat the garden as an emergency and act instantly
options.label: C

options.text: Some damage is tolerable — observe whether the population is growing, and act only if the damage threatens the crop's value
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener's aphid population is out of control on the beans, and a neighbor suggests releasing lady beetles. What is the honest expectation?

options.text: Lady beetles and lacewings are aphid predators — but beneficials prevent and regulate; they are a season-long strategy with habitat support, not a rescue for an established outbreak
options.label: A

options.text: Lady beetles will eliminate every aphid within hours
options.label: B

options.text: Lady beetles only eat pollen, so they are useless
options.label: C

options.text: Beneficial insects can only survive in greenhouses
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The IPM ladder has been climbed, and a least-toxic contact product is justified for an aphid outbreak on one plant. What are the disciplines of its use?

options.text: Broadcast it across the whole garden for maximum coverage
options.label: A

options.text: Target the infested plant, apply per the label, avoid open flowers, and apply when pollinators are not active
options.label: B

options.text: Apply it on a rainy day so the rain spreads it
options.label: C

options.text: Mix it stronger than the label says, so it works faster
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener decides to start a scouting routine. What does a proper scouting visit actually involve?

options.text: Waiting for the plants to look visibly damaged before looking
options.label: A

options.text: Spraying everything preemptively every visit
options.label: B

options.text: Walking the garden on a schedule, checking leaf undersides and new growth, reading the damage and the insect together, and noting what was found
options.label: C

options.text: Counting only the insects that fly
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two gardens face the same beetle pressure. One grows in poor, compacted soil; the other in healthy, organically managed soil. Which difference matters for pest management?

options.text: None — pest damage is identical regardless of soil
options.label: A

options.text: Poor soil plants have thicker leaves, so they resist better
options.label: B

options.text: The healthy garden will always have more pests
options.label: C

options.text: Healthy soil grows plants that are less susceptible to pest damage — plant health is the first defense
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A product label says an insecticidal soap "must contact the pest to work." What does that tell you about using it?

options.text: It is a contact product — coverage of the actual insects and their susceptible stages matters, and repeat applications are usually needed
options.label: A

options.text: It is systemic, so one watering of the roots is enough
options.label: B

options.text: It works on contact with the soil surface only
options.label: C

options.text: It is a repellent that works before pests arrive
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The plants in one bed are repeatedly attacked, season after season, despite your best spray schedule. What is the most likely durable answer?

options.text: A stronger, more frequent spray schedule next season
options.label: A

options.text: Abandoning that bed entirely
options.label: B

options.text: The lower rungs of the ladder — soil health, rotation, barriers, and beneficial habitat — because no intervention fixes a plant-health problem
options.label: C

options.text: Switching to a different pesticide brand
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You grew an outstanding hybrid (F1) tomato and want that exact plant next year. What happens if you save and plant its seed?

options.text: The offspring will be identical to the parent plant
options.label: A

options.text: The offspring will be even more vigorous than the parent
options.label: B

options.text: The offspring will only be edible if crossed again
options.label: C

options.text: The offspring will be a variable mix unlike the parent — hybrids do not come true from seed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener wants the easiest possible first seed saves. Which set of crops should they choose?

options.text: Corn, squash, and cabbage
options.label: A

options.text: Tomatoes, peppers, peas, and beans — self-pollinating crops that rarely cross
options.label: B

options.text: Carrots, onions, and parsnips — they flower quickly
options.label: C

options.text: Any crop, since all vegetables save equally well
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You want to save seed from two different varieties of broccoli flowering in the same garden. What do you need to know first?

options.text: That both belong to the same species, *Brassica oleracea* — so they will cross unless isolated
options.label: A

options.text: That broccoli cannot flower in a garden
options.label: B

options.text: That different vegetable names always mean different species, so crossing is impossible
options.label: C

options.text: That bees avoid broccoli, so isolation is unnecessary
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your pole beans are at the fresh-eating stage — green, tender, and delicious. What must you do to save seed from them?

options.text: Pick the green pods and dry the seeds from them — pod age does not matter
options.label: A

options.text: Pick the green pods and boil them briefly to stop spoilage before saving
options.label: B

options.text: Leave selected pods on the plant until they are brown, dry, and brittle, with rock-hard seeds inside
options.label: C

options.text: Pick the pods now and freeze them — freezing matures the seed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: When should you harvest tomatoes that you intend to save seed from?

options.text: When they are green — the seed is fully formed first
options.label: A

options.text: When they are fully ripe or even overripe — seed matures well past the table stage
options.label: B

options.text: When they are at perfect eating ripeness, the same day you would eat them
options.label: C

options.text: Only after the first frost
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the most common beginner mistake in seed saving?

options.text: Saving from the best plants instead of the worst
options.label: A

options.text: Labeling the seed too thoroughly
options.label: B

options.text: Drying seed in open air instead of in an oven
options.label: C

options.text: Sealing seed away while it is still damp, so it molds or germinates in storage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Dried seed is going into a glass jar for long-term storage in a refrigerator. Which storage practice is correct?

options.text: Leave the jar open so the seed can breathe
options.label: A

options.text: Add water to keep the seed plump and alive
options.label: B

options.text: Keep the jar airtight and add a desiccant; let a cold jar reach room temperature before opening to avoid condensation
options.label: C

options.text: Store in bright light so the seed stays warm and dry
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an unlabeled envelope of seed from two seasons ago. What is the honest assessment?

options.text: It is not seed stock, it is confetti — without a label you cannot know the variety or year, so it cannot be planned or trusted
options.label: A

options.text: It will be fine — old seed is always viable
options.label: B

options.text: Plant it anyway and it will come true regardless of age
options.label: C

options.text: Discard it — all seed dies after one year
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have stored bean seed from two years ago and want to know if it is still worth planting. What do you do?

options.text: Soak all of it — soaking revives old seed
options.label: A

options.text: Plant it thickly and hope
options.label: B

options.text: Assume it is dead after two years and throw it out
options.label: C

options.text: Run a germination test: 10 seeds on a damp paper towel in a sealed bag, warm, and count what sprouts in the expected window
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why are carrots a poor choice for a beginner's first seed save?

options.text: Carrot seed must be boiled before storage
options.label: A

options.text: Carrots are biennials — they flower in their second year, so the plants must survive the winter before any seed exists
options.label: B

options.text: Carrots are self-pollinating and therefore too easy to be educational
options.label: C

options.text: Carrot seed never stores longer than a few weeks
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the four jobs soil performs for a plant?

options.text: Warmth, shade, wind protection, and pest control
options.label: A

options.text: Support, water, air, and nutrients — and almost every soil problem is one of these jobs failing
options.label: B

options.text: Color, texture, depth, and moisture
options.label: C

options.text: Seeding, rooting, flowering, and fruiting
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A moistened handful of soil squeezes into a shiny, sticky ribbon. What does this tell you, and what follows from it?

options.text: The soil is sandy and will hold water well
options.label: A

options.text: The soil is silty and needs lime
options.label: B

options.text: The soil is high in clay — texture is permanent, so plan around it and work on structure instead
options.label: C

options.text: The soil is contaminated and cannot be gardened
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does organic matter improve BOTH sandy and clay soils?

options.text: In sand it holds water and nutrients like a sponge; in clay it feeds organisms that glue particles into aggregates, opening pores — it fixes structure and biology, not particle size
options.label: A

options.text: It chemically converts sand into clay
options.label: B

options.text: It only helps sandy soil; clay cannot be improved
options.label: C

options.text: It replaces the need for water entirely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After every rain, water stands on your garden plot for hours. What is the diagnosis, and what is the honest fix?

options.text: The soil needs more water, applied more often — the puddles show it is thirsty
options.label: A

options.text: Mix sand into the clay — adding sand fixes slow drainage
options.label: B

options.text: The plot is waterlogged at root level from slow infiltration; the honest fix is structure work — organic matter every season, permanent beds, no traffic on wet soil
options.label: C

options.text: The plot drains too fast, so water less deeply and re-check
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which practice most directly causes soil compaction in a garden?

options.text: Mulching the surface
options.label: A

options.text: Walking on wet beds and repeated tilling
options.label: B

options.text: Adding compost every season
options.label: C

options.text: Deep, infrequent watering
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tomatoes are pale and weak, and you are tempted to apply a heavy all-purpose fertilizer. What is the correct sequence instead?

options.text: Soil test first — then amend only what the test shows is missing, at the recommended rate
options.label: A

options.text: Apply the fertilizer at double strength to catch up
options.label: B

options.text: Apply lime — pale tomatoes always mean acidity
options.label: C

options.text: Buy a different brand of all-purpose fertilizer and compare
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What pH range do most vegetables prefer, and why does it matter?

options.text: Any pH — vegetables ignore acidity
options.label: A

options.text: Strongly acidic, below 5.0, for best nutrient release
options.label: B

options.text: Roughly 6.0–7.0 (slightly acidic to neutral), where nutrients are most available to plants
options.label: C

options.text: Strongly alkaline, above 8.5
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You fill a balcony container with soil dug from the yard. A month later the plant is stunted. What went wrong?

options.text: Balcony plants never grow well
options.label: A

options.text: The pot is too big
options.label: B

options.text: The plant was over-fertilized
options.label: C

options.text: Garden soil compacts in a pot and suffocates roots — containers need potting mix, drainage holes, and an attentive feeding/watering schedule
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A soil test near an old painted fence line shows elevated lead. What is the honest growing strategy for that strip?

options.text: Plant deep-rooted vegetables to draw the lead out
options.label: A

options.text: Lime heavily and plant anyway — lime neutralizes lead
options.label: B

options.text: Lead only affects grass, so vegetables are safe
options.label: C

options.text: Grow in raised beds with brought-in soil, or keep food crops out of that strip entirely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You dig into a struggling patch and find the plant roots twisted, shallow, and blackened. What story do the roots tell?

options.text: Compaction and/or waterlogging — the roots could not penetrate or breathe
options.label: A

options.text: The plant needs more sun
options.label: B

options.text: The soil is too rich in organic matter
options.label: C

options.text: The variety is simply slow-growing
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are choosing a spot for a cooking fire near camp. Which location satisfies the cooking-site rules?

options.text: Level ground cleared to mineral soil, well away from tents, tarps, and overhanging branches, with water and a shovel within reach
options.label: A

options.text: The edge of a tarp — it provides shelter from the rain
options.label: B

options.text: The driest patch of tall grass — it will not catch
options.label: C

options.text: Between two tents — the walls block the wind
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The group is hungry and wants to throw food on the fire immediately, while it is still in the flame stage. Why must you wait for the coal bed?

options.text: Flames are not hot enough to cook
options.label: A

options.text: Flames scorch the outside while leaving the middle raw; a coal bed provides the even, steady heat that cooks food through
options.label: B

options.text: The coal bed is the only source of light
options.label: C

options.text: Food only cooks when the fire is completely out
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cooking potatoes wrapped in foil. Where does the packet go — and why?

options.text: Held directly in the tall flames — it cooks fastest there
options.label: A

options.text: Suspended above the fire on a dry stick
options.label: B

options.text: Into the coal bed — the coal heat cooks it evenly, and the foil protects the food from ash
options.label: C

options.text: On the ground beside the fire — radiant heat will reach it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your chicken stew looks bubbling hot, but you have no thermometer. What is the correct statement about this meal?

options.text: It is safe — visible bubbling means it has boiled
options.label: A

options.text: It is safe — the smell confirms it
options.label: B

options.text: It is safe — it has cooked for twenty minutes
options.label: C

options.text: It is not verified — poultry must reach 165 °F (74 °C) internally, and the only reliable check is a probe thermometer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Rain arrives mid-meal and someone suggests moving the cooking fire inside the tent "just until the stew finishes." What is the correct response?

options.text: No — wood fires produce carbon monoxide, which is colorless and odorless, and an enclosed space can trap lethal concentrations; cooking fires are outdoor-only, always
options.label: A

options.text: It is fine if the tent door stays open
options.label: B

options.text: It is fine for the last few minutes of cooking
options.label: C

options.text: It is fine if the stew is already boiling
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are setting up the cooking site and the only flat spot is directly under a low-hanging tarp, near a dry grass patch. What do you do?

options.text: Build the fire under the tarp — it is the only dry cover
options.label: A

options.text: Move the kitchen to a spot clear of the tarp and the grass, even if it means cooking in a little rain — sparks and radiant heat reach farther than they look
options.label: B

options.text: Trim the grass and build under the tarp anyway
options.label: C

options.text: Build the fire and hold the tarp up with poles
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The stew needs forty minutes of even heat. Your coal bed is glowing nicely. How do you keep the heat even for the whole cook?

options.text: Add a thick log directly under the pot every ten minutes
options.label: A

options.text: Keep piling fine tinder under the pot to restart flames
options.label: B

options.text: Feed new wood at the edge of the bed and rake the coals back under the pot as the bed burns down
options.label: C

options.text: Let the bed burn out and restart the fire halfway through
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After the meal, the fire still glows. The group wants to leave the coals "to finish dying" and go to sleep. What is the correct ending?

options.text: Leave them — coals always die on their own
options.label: A

options.text: Cover the coals with dry sand and walk away
options.label: B

options.text: Leave them if the wind is calm
options.label: C

options.text: Extinguish completely — drown, stir, and verify the ash is cool to the touch; coals stay hot enough to ignite fuel for hours
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Wood is limited and you must produce two hot meals for four people. Which plan stretches the fuel the farthest?

options.text: Cook both meals in one batch on a coal bed, keep lids on, and use a retained-heat box to finish — then boil water while the fire is already burning
options.label: A

options.text: Build a fresh large fire for each meal
options.label: B

options.text: Cook each component separately over tall flames
options.label: C

options.text: Skip cooking and eat everything cold
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While the stew finishes over the coals, you need water from the creek fifty meters away. What is the correct action regarding the fire?

options.text: Run fast — the walk will take less than a minute
options.label: A

options.text: Never leave a cooking fire unattended, even briefly — have someone stay with it, or take the fire through its ending sequence first
options.label: B

options.text: Lower the fire to coals first — coals cannot escape
options.label: C

options.text: Ask a child to watch it — they enjoy fires
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need a fire that will hold a coal bed through the night for warmth. Which fuel choice serves the job?

options.text: Hardwood — dense and slow-burning, it produces long-lasting coals with few sparks
options.label: A

options.text: Softwood — it burns brightest and hottest
options.label: B

options.text: Green wood — it holds moisture for a longer burn
options.label: C

options.text: Bark strips — they burn slowest of all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are splitting firewood and two logs of the same size feel very different — one is noticeably heavier and thuds when struck. What does that tell you?

options.text: The heavy one is denser hardwood — the better fuel for all jobs
options.label: A

options.text: The heavy, dull-sounding log is green or waterlogged — dry wood is lighter and rings when struck
options.label: B

options.text: The heavy log is frozen solid
options.label: C

options.text: Weight and sound are unrelated to dryness
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It has rained all day and every piece of wood on the ground is soaked. Where do you start looking for dry fuel?

options.text: The largest ground logs — their mass keeps them dry
options.label: A

options.text: Any wood under a thick tree canopy — rain never reaches it
options.label: B

options.text: Standing dead wood and upper branches — dead standing material sheds rain, while ground wood soaks it up
options.label: C

options.text: The wettest-looking ground wood — the rain has washed it clean
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tinder has caught and you are ready to build the fire upward. Which size of material comes next?

options.text: Wrist-thickness logs — they burn longest
options.label: A

options.text: The largest fuel you have — bigger catches faster
options.label: B

options.text: Matchstick-sized twigs right after ignition
options.label: C

options.text: Kindling — pencil to finger thickness, the bridge that carries the flame from tinder to fuel
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a cold night, wood is limited, and you only need to keep one person warm. What is the fuel-economy answer?

options.text: The smallest right fire — a modest hardwood coal bed that radiates enough warmth for one
options.label: A

options.text: The largest fire you can build — warmth in reserve
options.label: B

options.text: A fresh softwood teepee every hour
options.label: C

options.text: One log, lit end to end
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to boil water in a hurry and only have one species to choose from. What is the best pick for speed?

options.text: Oak — it burns slowly and evenly
options.label: A

options.text: Softwood — it catches easily and burns fast and hot, producing the fast flame boiling needs
options.label: B

options.text: Hickory — it is the densest fuel
options.label: C

options.text: Any wood boils water at the same speed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend insists green wood is fine because "it just burns slower." What is the accurate explanation of why green wood fails?

options.text: Green wood is too dense to ignite under any conditions
options.label: A

options.text: Green wood produces no smoke
options.label: B

options.text: Green wood must evaporate its water before it can burn — that water absorbs the fire's heat and steals it from the fire itself
options.label: C

options.text: Green wood burns fine; only bark is the problem
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At a campsite you find an old painted pallet and a pile of clean split hardwood. A camper wants to burn the pallet "because it's free." What is the correct response?

options.text: Burn the pallet only if it is broken apart into small pieces
options.label: A

options.text: Burn the pallet — painted wood lights easier
options.label: B

options.text: Mix the pallet with the hardwood so it burns hotter
options.label: C

options.text: Decline — treated or painted wood of unknown origin can release hazardous fumes when burned; burn only clean, identifiable, untreated wood
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are feeding an established cooking fire with a good coal bed. Your fuel staging ran out of kindling-sized pieces. What is the correct processing decision?

options.text: Split some fuel-sized wood down to kindling size — processing fuel for the stage keeps the fire fed at the size it can use
options.label: A

options.text: Feed the largest logs you have — the coal bed will handle anything
options.label: B

options.text: Let the fire die and restart later
options.label: C

options.text: Use green branches — the coal bed will dry them
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are gathering firewood and find a piece of wood you cannot identify, plus a plastic crate. What is the never-burn rule applied?

options.text: Burn the crate only if the plastic is thin
options.label: A

options.text: Burn the unknown wood only if it smells like pine
options.label: B

options.text: Burn both — the fire is hot enough to make anything safe
options.label: C

options.text: Leave both out of the fire — plastics and anything you cannot identify have no place in a fire, and unknown plant material can produce irritating smoke
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tinder has caught, but the fire dies as soon as you lay a flat, tight layer of damp leaves over the flame. Which element of the fire triangle did you remove?

options.text: Oxygen — the tight layer smothered the flame, and removing any one element ends combustion
options.label: A

options.text: Fuel — leaves are not a real fuel
options.label: B

options.text: Heat — the leaves cooled the tinder permanently
options.label: C

options.text: Nothing — the fire died on its own for no reason
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You sit two meters from a campfire and feel strong warmth on your face, while the air between you and the fire stays cool. Which heat-transfer mechanism is delivering that heat?

options.text: Conduction — the ground is conducting heat to you
options.label: A

options.text: Convection — warm air is flowing sideways at face height
options.label: B

options.text: Radiation — heat traveling as waves through the air warms whatever it faces, without touching it
options.label: C

options.text: Convection — the smoke is carrying heat to you
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does a match flame catch fine dry grass almost instantly but do nothing to a thick log?

options.text: Grass contains a special chemical that logs lack
options.label: A

options.text: The grass presents far more surface area per gram to the air, so it reaches ignition temperature quickly; the log's bulk conducts the heat away
options.label: B

options.text: Logs are always too damp to ignite
options.label: C

options.text: A match flame is too small to touch a log's surface
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a damp evening, your kindling was gathered from the ground. The fire now produces thick white smoke and sputters instead of growing. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The kindling is burning too fast and exhausting the oxygen
options.label: A

options.text: The fire lay is too open and the heat escapes
options.label: B

options.text: The tinder was too fine
options.label: C

options.text: The kindling is carrying moisture — the water absorbs the fire's heat and evaporates, leaving little heat for the wood itself
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to cook a meal evenly over your fire without scorching it. Which heat source is the right tool?

options.text: The tallest flame you can build
options.label: A

options.text: A fresh burst of kindling added continuously
options.label: B

options.text: The coal bed — solid fuel burning slowly with steady, radiant heat
options.label: C

options.text: Directly in the rising flame gases
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A fire is smoldering with heavy gray smoke and clearly burning, but it will not grow. Which diagnostic sequence best applies the fire triangle?

options.text: Check airflow into the lay (oxygen), check the newest fuel for moisture (heat stolen), then check whether the fuel size exceeds what the current heat can ignite (fuel)
options.label: A

options.text: Add more fuel immediately — burning fires only fail from lack of fuel
options.label: B

options.text: Blow harder from every direction until the smoke clears
options.label: C

options.text: Let it smolder — heavy smoke means it is about to catch
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to boil two pots of water and keep the group warm for an hour. Why is a deliberately modest fire the better choice than "the biggest fire you can build"?

options.text: Big fires are illegal everywhere
options.label: A

options.text: A fire sized to the job wastes less fuel, is easier to control, and launches fewer embers — oversize fires are the classic path to an escaped fire
options.label: B

options.text: Big fires produce no coals at all
options.label: C

options.text: Small fires burn hotter than large ones
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your metal pot handle grows hot minutes before the water inside boils, even though the handle never touches the flame. Which mechanism explains this?

options.text: Radiation from the flame
options.label: A

options.text: Convection through the steam
options.label: B

options.text: The handle is burning
options.label: C

options.text: Conduction — heat moves through the solid metal of the pot by contact
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tinder burns brilliantly, but every time you add fuel-sized logs directly, the flame dies. What does surface area tell you about the missing step?

options.text: The logs are too coarse to be ignited by tinder's brief heat — you skipped kindling, the fine-to-coarse bridge that carries the flame upward
options.label: A

options.text: Tinder produces too much heat for logs
options.label: B

options.text: Logs must be soaked in water before adding
options.label: C

options.text: The tinder was too dry
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gust of wind has repeatedly blown out your young fire on an exposed ridge. You still need a hot meal. What is the most scientifically sound plan?

options.text: Build the fire three times larger so the wind cannot win
options.label: A

options.text: Shield your face and keep relighting — persistence defeats wind
options.label: B

options.text: Move the fire to a sheltered spot, build it small and protected, and add fuel only as the flame establishes — then cook over the coal bed
