options.label: C

options.text: Give up on cooking until the wind dies completely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tinder ignites, but the fire dies out even though you fed it plenty of fuel. A friend says the pile was "arranged wrong." What does a fire lay actually control?

options.text: Airflow to the burning zone and how heat transfers from fine to coarse fuel
options.label: A

options.text: The color and height of the flame only
options.label: B

options.text: How much smoke the fire produces
options.label: C

options.text: The temperature of the surrounding air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have fifteen minutes to establish a fire and boil water. Which lay is the right choice?

options.text: Log cabin — it burns longest
options.label: A

options.text: Teepee — the cone drafts strongly, producing fast flame that boils water quickly
options.label: B

options.text: Star — it uses the least fuel
options.label: C

options.text: Dakota fire hole — it burns hottest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need a cooking fire for a two-hour meal. Which lay is chosen for the fire it becomes, not the fire it starts?

options.text: Teepee — it burns brightest
options.label: A

options.text: Lean-to — it reflects heat
options.label: B

options.text: Log cabin — the walls collapse inward into a contained, long-lasting coal bed
options.label: C

options.text: Star — the spokes stay cool
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A steady wind keeps blowing out your young fire on an open site. Which lay is designed to survive exactly this?

options.text: Teepee — the cone cuts the wind
options.label: A

options.text: Log cabin — the walls block gusts
options.label: B

options.text: Star — the low profile hides from wind
options.label: C

options.text: Lean-to — the angled backstick and leaning kindling shelter the flame while the open side still draws air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is winter and you must build a fire on packed snow. What do you do before laying any fuel?

options.text: Build a platform of green logs so the fire sits above the snow instead of melting down into it
options.label: A

options.text: Clear the snow to bare ground
options.label: B

options.text: Build the fire directly — snow is a fine base
options.label: C

options.text: Use only liquid fuel, which melts its own platform
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your group needs sustained warmth through a long evening, and you have plenty of wood. Which lay delivers long-lasting radiant heat from a coal bed?

options.text: Teepee — it burns the hottest
options.label: A

options.text: Log cabin — it collapses into a contained coal bed that radiates steadily
options.label: B

options.text: Lean-to — it reflects heat one direction only
options.label: C

options.text: Dakota fire hole — it hides the heat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Wood is scarce and you need a fire that burns for a long time without consuming your whole pile. Which lay is the economy answer?

options.text: Teepee — it drafts efficiently
options.label: A

options.text: Log cabin — it uses small sticks
options.label: B

options.text: Lean-to — it burns one leaner at a time
options.label: C

options.text: Star — only the inner ends burn, and you feed it one log at a time
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your teepee fire catches, but as it grows the whole cone topples into a smoking heap. What is the standard failure you just experienced — and the fix?

options.text: The tinder was damp — replace it with dry material
options.label: A

options.text: The cone was unstable and you waited too long to add the next fuel stage — add fuel before the inner sticks burn through
options.label: B

options.text: The wind was too strong — rebuild with twice the sticks
options.label: C

options.text: The logs were too dry — use greener wood
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You built a log cabin for an evening meal. The walls have burned down into a glowing bed of coals. What is the correct understanding of what just happened?

options.text: The fire failed — you should rebuild the cabin
options.label: A

options.text: The structure was wrong — it should have stayed standing
options.label: B

options.text: The lay did its job — the coal bed is the cooking surface you built the cabin for
options.label: C

options.text: The coal bed means the fire is going out — add logs immediately
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You must cook a meal on a wind-whipped site where digging is permitted and the soil is free of roots. Which lay combines wind-proofing with a low profile?

options.text: Teepee — its height clears the wind
options.label: A

options.text: Star fire — its spokes anchor it
options.label: B

options.text: Lean-to — its backstick faces the wind
options.label: C

options.text: Dakota fire hole — the pit shelters the flame and the side air shaft feeds it, with a low profile
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fire has progressed past the flame stage: the kindling is consumed, the structure has collapsed, and a bed of glowing coals is radiating heat. Which stage is the fire in — and what is the management job?

options.text: Coal bed stage — rake and consolidate the coals, then feed the bed rather than the flames
options.label: A

options.text: Burn-down stage — stop feeding and let it die
options.label: B

options.text: Ignition stage — start over with fresh tinder
options.label: C

options.text: Establishment stage — add the largest logs you have
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Ten minutes after you dropped a thick log across the flame, the fire is barely smoldering. What most likely happened — and what is the correct response?

options.text: The log was too dry — remove it and use greener wood
options.label: A

options.text: The log was too large and placed flat across the flame, smothering it — remove it, add fuel the fire can ignite, and push it into the bed
options.label: B

options.text: The fire is fine — smoldering is normal for ten minutes after feeding
options.label: C

options.text: The oxygen supply is exhausted — seal the fire with ash
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are about to cook on your fire and want even heat under the pot without scorching. What is the correct coal-bed move?

options.text: Pile all the coals into one tall mound under the pot
options.label: A

options.text: Let the flame stage return by adding fine tinder under the pot
options.label: B

options.text: Spread the coals into a thin, even layer beneath the pot, and feed new wood at the edge of the bed
options.label: C

options.text: Remove all coals and cook over direct flame
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fire is roaring far hotter than the job needs, and you still have two hours of cooking ahead. What is the fastest way to bring the burn under control?

options.text: Add the largest logs you have — big wood burns slow
options.label: A

options.text: Pour a small amount of water onto the flame
options.label: B

options.text: Blow on it until the extra fuel is consumed
options.label: C

options.text: Adjust the airflow — feed smaller fuel, pack it more compactly, and let the flame stage die back toward a coal bed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fire burns steadily but refuses to grow, even though the fuel is dry and well-sized. The lay looks dense. Which triangle element is most likely missing — and what is the fix?

options.text: Oxygen — the packed lay is starving the burn; separate the fuel and create a draft into the base
options.label: A

options.text: Heat — the fire needs a larger ignition source
options.label: B

options.text: Fuel — add more wood in any arrangement
options.label: C

options.text: Nothing — this is normal; fires stop growing by themselves
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are tending a cooking fire. The flames have died back and the coals glow. When is the right moment to add the next piece of fuel?

options.text: Only when the fire is completely out
options.label: A

options.text: When the fire shows it is ready — flames beginning to die back, coals glowing — and the added piece is sized to what the stage can ignite
options.label: B

options.text: On a strict 10-minute schedule regardless of what the fire is doing
options.label: C

options.text: Only at ignition, never during the coal bed stage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The wind picks up and you must keep your coal bed alive for a meal still cooking. Which maintenance move protects the working heat?

options.text: Add a tall teepee over the bed to ride out the gust
options.label: A

options.text: Let the bed scatter — it will come back
options.label: B

options.text: Shield the bed from the wind and keep it consolidated; a windbreak and a compact bed survive gusts that scatter loose embers
options.label: C

options.text: Abandon the bed and restart after the wind passes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The evening is over and the group is going to sleep. The flames are gone and the coals look dark. What is the correct ending sequence?

options.text: Leave it — dark coals are harmless by morning
options.label: A

options.text: Cover the coals with a layer of dirt and walk away
options.label: B

options.text: Stop feeding, wait for the fire to die, then simply let it sit
options.label: C

options.text: Burn it down, drown the coals slowly from the edges inward, stir the wet ash, and verify the bed is cool to the touch before leaving
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fire suddenly produces thick white smoke and sputters after you fed it wood you gathered from the ground. What does the symptom report — and what is the fix?

options.text: The fire is about to catch — feed it more of the same wood
options.label: A

options.text: The fire has too much heat — remove some coals
options.label: B

options.text: The fuel is carrying moisture — water is absorbing the fire's heat and evaporating; switch to dry fuel and open the lay for airflow
options.label: C

options.text: The fire is out of fuel — add the largest logs available
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have drowned and stirred the fire and the ash looks flat and dark. Before you leave the site, what is the only test that proves the fire is out?

options.text: The absence of visible flame for five minutes
options.label: A

options.text: The absence of smoke for ten minutes
options.label: B

options.text: The passage of one hour since the last feeding
options.label: C

options.text: The ash bed is cool to the touch — not warm — after drowning, stirring, and re-wetting
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before igniting any outdoor fire, what is the minimum clearance radius you should establish around the fire site?

options.text: 1 meter (3 feet)
options.label: A

options.text: 3 meters (10 feet) down to mineral soil
options.label: B

options.text: 5 meters (16 feet) of mowed grass
options.label: C

options.text: No clearance is needed if you use a fire ring
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What are the three steps of the standard method for extinguishing a campfire?

options.text: Pour, pat, leave
options.label: A

options.text: Bury, cover, mark
options.label: B

options.text: Drown, stir, feel
options.label: C

options.text: Spray, dig, cover
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The fire danger rating for your area is "High" (Yellow). What does this mean for your campfire plans?

options.text: No restrictions — build your fire as usual
options.label: A

options.text: Fires are discouraged; expect rapid spread if one starts; use a contained stove instead if possible
options.label: B

options.text: Total fire ban — no fires of any kind
options.label: C

options.text: Only gas stoves are permitted — no solid fuel
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is using gasoline to start a campfire extremely dangerous?

options.text: Gasoline burns so fast the fire is too brief to light kindling
options.label: A

options.text: Gasoline produces toxic smoke that contaminates food
options.label: B

options.text: Gasoline vapors are explosive — the vapor trail can carry flame back to the container, causing severe burns or death
options.label: C

options.text: Gasoline soaks into wood and prevents it from igniting
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You encounter a wildfire moving uphill toward your position. Which direction should you move?

options.text: Uphill — you need the high ground to see the fire's path
options.label: A

options.text: Directly away from the fire in a straight line
options.label: B

options.text: Downhill, downwind, or perpendicular to the wind direction — fire moves faster uphill and with the wind
options.label: C

options.text: Toward the fire to find the burned area
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You've poured water on your campfire and the flames have stopped. The ashes are steaming but you can hold your hand 10 cm above them without discomfort. Is the fire out?

options.text: Yes — no flames means the fire is out
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — steam indicates the coals are cooling
options.label: B

options.text: No — you must stir the ashes and check again; steam means there is still heat, and buried coals can retain enough heat to reignite
options.label: C

options.text: Yes — as long as you bury the ashes before leaving
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The three elements of the fire triangle are:

options.text: Wood, air, and spark
options.label: A

options.text: Heat, fuel, and oxygen
options.label: B

options.text: Tinder, kindling, and fuel
options.label: C

options.text: Fuel, ignition source, and sparks
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the correct order of the material progression for building a fire?

options.text: Fuel → kindling → tinder
options.label: A

options.text: Kindling → fuel → tinder
options.label: B

options.text: Tinder → kindling → fuel
options.label: C

options.text: Tinder → fuel → kindling
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are trying to start a fire with a ferrocerium (ferro) rod on a rainy day. The rod produces sparks reliably, but the sparks are not igniting your tinder. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Ferro rods don't work in the rain
options.label: A

options.text: Your tinder is not fine enough or is damp — ferro rod sparks require very fine, dry tinder
options.label: B

options.text: You need to strike the rod harder
options.label: C

options.text: You should switch to matches — ferro rods are unreliable in wet conditions
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A beginner builds a teepee fire lay, lights the tinder successfully, sees flames rising through the kindling, and immediately adds several wrist-thick logs. The fire dies within a minute. What went wrong?

options.text: The teepee lay doesn't work — they should have used a log cabin lay
options.label: A

options.text: The logs smothered the fire by blocking airflow and were too large to ignite from the small kindling flames
options.label: B

options.text: The wood was the wrong species
options.label: C

options.text: The tinder was inadequate
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are preparing materials to start a fire in damp conditions after a night of rain. Where is the most reliable place to find dry kindling?

options.text: Dead branches lying on the forest floor
options.label: A

options.text: Standing dead wood — dead branches still attached to trees, or dead standing saplings
options.label: B

options.text: Green branches cut from living trees
options.label: C

options.text: Moss growing on tree trunks
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your fire site is a dry clearing with grass and dead leaves within arm's reach and low branches about 2 meters overhead. Which preparation is most important before you strike the first spark?

options.text: Clear a 3-meter (10-foot) perimeter down to bare earth and check for overhead hazards
options.label: A

options.text: Arrange the tinder bundle in the fire lay before clearing anything
options.label: B

options.text: Dampen the surrounding grass so the fire burns hotter
options.label: C

options.text: Position the fire lay close to the nearest tree for a windbreak
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You want to can a batch of beef-vegetable soup. Which canner does the recipe require?

options.text: A pressure canner — soups with meat and low-acid vegetables are low-acid and must be pressure processed
options.label: A

options.text: A boiling water canner — soup is cooked before canning, so it is already safe
options.label: B

options.text: Either canner works, since the jars will seal either way
options.label: C

options.text: No canner is needed — hot liquid poured into jars and sealed makes safe soup
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor insists that boiling green beans for 3 hours in a boiling water canner must be as safe as pressure canning. What is the accurate response?

options.text: Agree — longer boiling compensates for the lower temperature
options.label: A

options.text: Agree, as long as the lids sealed afterwards
options.label: B

options.text: Disagree — boiling water reaches about 212 °F (100 °C), which does not destroy botulism spores; low-acid foods need pressure-canner temperatures, so time cannot substitute for temperature
options.label: C

options.text: Disagree, but only because the processing time was too short — 6 hours would be fine
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the research-based dividing line that decides whether a food can be boiling-water canned or must be pressure canned?

options.text: Whether the food looks acidic or not
options.label: A

options.text: The pH boundary of 4.6 — high-acid foods (pH ≤ 4.6) may be boiling-water canned; low-acid foods must be pressure canned
options.label: B

options.text: The recipe's cook time before canning
options.label: C

options.text: Whether the food is fresh or stored
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are canning bread-and-butter pickles — cucumbers preserved in a vinegar brine per a tested recipe. Which method is correct?

options.text: Pressure canner — cucumbers are vegetables, and all vegetables are low-acid
options.label: A

options.text: No processing — the vinegar preserves them on its own
options.label: B

options.text: Freezer only — cucumbers cannot be canned
options.label: C

options.text: Boiling water canner — the vinegar makes the product high-acid, so it is processed like a high-acid food per the tested recipe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have canned successfully at sea level and now move to a home at 5,000 feet. What must change about your canning?

options.text: Processing must be adjusted per the USDA altitude tables — longer times for boiling water canning and adjusted pressure settings for the pressure canner
options.label: A

options.text: Nothing changes — processing is the same at any altitude
options.label: B

options.text: You must add more acid to every recipe
options.label: C

options.text: You can stop adjusting once the lids seal
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A tested recipe says to process pint jars for 35 minutes. A friend wants to process the same food in the same canner "for 20 minutes — the jars are smaller, so it must be fine." What should you advise?

options.text: It is fine — smaller jars always process faster by the same ratio
options.label: A

options.text: Use a tested processing time for the exact jar size being processed — never shorten or estimate; heat penetration is research-derived
options.label: B

options.text: It is fine if the water is at a rolling boil the whole time
options.label: C

options.text: It is fine as long as the jar sizes are the same brand
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After processing green beans in a boiling water canner "for extra long," all the jars sealed — lids are depressed and do not move when pressed. Is the batch safe?

options.text: Yes — sealed lids are the accepted proof of safe canning
options.label: A

options.text: Yes, but only if stored in the refrigerator
options.label: B

options.text: Only if the beans look and smell fresh when opened
options.label: C

options.text: No — green beans are low-acid and needed pressure processing; a seal only proves a vacuum formed, not that the food was processed safely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You open a jar of home-canned corn and liquid spurts out with a foul odor. What is the correct action?

options.text: Discard the jar and contents immediately — never taste, and keep it away from pets
options.label: A

options.text: Taste a small spoonful — a bad smell always means detectable bad taste
options.label: B

options.text: Rinse the corn, boil it, and serve it
options.label: C

options.text: Set it aside and taste it cold later when you have time
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is "taste to test" a dangerous habit with canned food, even when the jar looks normal?

options.text: Because tasting ruins the jar for storage
options.label: A

options.text: Because old canned food always tastes bad
options.label: B

options.text: Because botulism toxin has no taste, smell, or color — contaminated food can look and taste normal, so taste cannot reveal danger
options.label: C

options.text: Because the acid in canned food masks toxins
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are adding canning to a household preparedness food plan. Which planning approach best matches the tested-recipe discipline?

options.text: Can everything you can get your hands on — volume is the goal
options.label: A

options.text: Process what the household actually eats, using tested recipes and correct canners, then label, store cool/dark/dry, and rotate like any stored food
options.label: B

options.text: Rely on canning alone and stop maintaining the pantry rotation
options.label: C

options.text: Skip the pressure canner to save money — the boiling water canner works for everything
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does removing water preserve food?

options.text: Water is the food that microbes eat
options.label: A

options.text: Microorganisms need available water to grow — remove enough and they cannot multiply
options.label: B

options.text: Drying kills all bacteria by dehydration
options.label: C

options.text: Water causes oxidation, so removing it stops rancidity
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement about dried food is correct?

options.text: Dried food is sterile because the drying process kills microbes
options.label: A

options.text: Drying stops microbial growth but does not reliably kill pathogens — dried food is not sterile
options.label: B

options.text: Dried food cannot be re-contaminated once sealed
options.label: C

options.text: Drying and cooking are the same process at different temperatures
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does uniform slicing matter so much in drying?

options.text: Uniform pieces dry at the same rate — uneven pieces create over-dried edges with wet centers that mold in storage
options.label: A

options.text: Uniform pieces fit more food on each tray
options.label: B

options.text: Uniform pieces dry faster than thick ones
options.label: C

options.text: It only matters for appearance
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why must most vegetables be blanched before drying?

options.text: Blanching inactivates enzymes that otherwise degrade flavor, color, and nutrients during storage
options.label: A

options.text: Blanching sterilizes the vegetables
options.label: B

options.text: Blanching removes all moisture so drying is faster
options.label: C

options.text: Blanching is only for killing insect eggs
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your dried carrots have been in the dehydrator for 10 hours. How do you test whether they are done?

options.text: Check the timer — the recipe time is the test
options.label: A

options.text: Cut a piece: they are done when crisp and brittle, with no soft or moist interior
options.label: B

options.text: They are done when the dehydrator reaches temperature
options.label: C

options.text: Squeeze the batch — if most of it feels dry, it is done
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You run a loaded dehydrator with the vent closed to "keep the heat in." What happens?

options.text: Drying is faster — more heat, more evaporation
options.label: A

options.text: Drying stalls — moisture-laden air stays around the food, and the risk of under-drying rises
options.label: B

options.text: Nothing — the vent position does not matter
options.label: C

options.text: The food cooks instead of drying
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What does the "conditioning" step accomplish after drying?

options.text: It cooks the food to a safe internal temperature
options.label: A

options.text: It redistributes residual moisture so the batch dries evenly and wet spots are revealed before sealing
options.label: B

options.text: It adds moisture back for better texture
options.label: C

options.text: It removes oxygen from the storage jar
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two weeks after packing, you see condensation droplets inside the jar of dried apples. What is the correct response?

options.text: Shake the jar and put it back — condensation is harmless
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the batch — condensation means moisture was still inside, and mold can follow; diagnose the drying process for next time
options.label: B

options.text: Open the jar and "finish drying" the apples in the dehydrator
options.label: C

options.text: Move the jar to the refrigerator
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are making jerky from ground beef in a 140 °F (60 °C) dehydrator. What is the critical requirement?

options.text: Ground meat is safe after dehydration alone — the dry surface protects it
options.label: A

options.text: The meat must reach 160 °F (71 °C) internally — via a pre-heat step or a drying temperature that achieves it
options.label: B

options.text: Add extra salt to ensure safety
options.label: C

options.text: Dry it for twice as long to be safe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You plan to rehydrate dried soup mix with water collected from a stream. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Add the water straight from the stream — it will boil with the soup anyway
options.label: A

options.text: Purify the water first — treat water of unknown quality before use, and remember that rehydrated food is perishable
options.label: B

options.text: Use more dried mix — it has preservatives
options.label: C

options.text: Rehydrate the mix cold and serve it chilled
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor shows you a garage shelf of sealed buckets filled with rice and beans, labeled for "long-term emergencies," and calls it the household emergency food. What is the accurate classification?

options.text: Long-term storage — rice and beans need water and cooking to become meals, so they do not serve as ready-to-eat food for the disruption itself
options.label: A

options.text: Emergency food — any stored food counts, regardless of preparation needs
options.label: B

options.text: Both — the categories are interchangeable in planning
options.label: C

options.text: Neither — only survival rations count as emergency food
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The power is out, the stove will not light, and water is available only from the household's stored supply. Which list is a usable emergency food supply for these conditions?

options.text: Dry pasta, dried beans, flour, and yeast — the staples of a normal pantry
options.label: A

options.text: Frozen vegetables, refrigerated milk, and leftover cooked rice
options.label: B

options.text: Canned beans and soup (edible cold), nut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk
options.label: C

options.text: Instant coffee, spices, and condiments — the "extras" of the kitchen
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are packing a go-bag for evacuation. Which approach matches the no-cook, no-power rule for carried food?

options.text: A bag of dry rice — it stores best and is the most economical calorie
options.label: A

options.text: Compact ready-to-eat items — energy bars, nut butter, canned fruit or fish — with a manual can opener, sized to what one person can carry
options.label: B

options.text: Canned soups and a camp stove, since cooking will be possible
options.label: C

options.text: Whatever is on sale, so the bag stays cheap
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have planned 2 weeks of ready-to-eat food per person. Why is that plan incomplete until the water plan is sized alongside it?

options.text: Because canned food must be boiled before eating
options.label: A

options.text: Because food and water are separate systems and never interact
options.label: B

options.text: Because stored water is only for hygiene, never for meals
options.label: C

options.text: Because stored food is eaten with stored water — for drinking with meals and for reconstituting or mixing — so both are sized for the same days
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household plans 2 weeks of stored meals for two adults and an infant. Where does the infant's formula-mixing water appear in the plan?

options.text: Nowhere — formula is mixed with juice to save water
options.label: A

options.text: Nowhere — infants drink the same amount as adults
options.label: B

options.text: As a separate line item: formula takes clean stored water beyond the adult drinking allowance, so it is counted explicitly in the water math
options.label: C

options.text: As a shared line with the dog, since both drink from bowls
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A single adult wants a home food supply sized "bigger than 72 hours, smaller than a year." Which target matches preparedness guidance for home supplies?

options.text: About 2 weeks per household member — the planning target where outages commonly cut utilities
options.label: A

options.text: Exactly 72 hours, no more — anything more is wasted money
options.label: B

options.text: One year minimum — anything less is not real preparedness
options.label: C

options.text: As much as the budget allows, with no sizing logic
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household of four wants a 2-week food supply. Which planning step is the correct way to size it?

options.text: Buy one extra large box of mixed rations for "the family"
options.label: A

options.text: Plan per person — roughly 2,000 calories per person per day, multiplied by four people and 14 days — then add separate lines for any special needs
options.label: B

options.text: Triple the family's weekly grocery bill and call it done
options.label: C

options.text: Size it to the largest kitchen shelf that is empty
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your household loves canned chili, so you built the emergency supply around it. The store has a new shipment; you buy a case. Where do the new cans go, and why?

options.text: In front of the old cans, so they are easy to grab
options.label: A

options.text: In a separate closet, so the emergency supply stays untouched
options.label: B

options.text: At the back of the shelf, mixed into normal rotation
options.label: C

options.text: Behind the old cans — First In, First Out — so the oldest is always eaten first and replaced
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend plans to build a 2-week emergency supply entirely from 25-year shelf-life ration buckets sold online — food the household has never tasted. What is the risk in this plan?

options.text: No risk — longer shelf life is the only thing that matters
options.label: A

options.text: Minor — the buckets are sealed, so taste does not matter
options.label: B

options.text: The supply will not rotate: food nobody eats is never consumed and replaced, so it will be stale or unappealing at the exact moment it is needed
options.label: C

options.text: The risk is only financial, since the food will still be safe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household with an infant, an adult with a peanut allergy, and a dog is writing its food plan. Which plan covers all three?

options.text: One standard menu for everyone, since quantities are what differ
options.label: A

options.text: Separate line items: infant formula and baby food with clean water for mixing, peanut-free foods for the allergy, and pet food and water sized to the same days
options.label: B

options.text: The standard menu plus a jar of peanut butter, which everyone can eat
options.label: C

options.text: The standard menu only, and improvise at the emergency
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does salt play a central role in vegetable fermentation?

options.text: Salt kills every microbe, so the vegetables cannot spoil at all
options.label: A

options.text: Salt suppresses many spoilage organisms while lactic acid bacteria tolerate it, letting the good microbes win the competition
options.label: B

options.text: Salt is only for flavor — it has no effect on microbial growth
options.label: C

options.text: Salt keeps the vegetables crunchy by removing all their water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two jars of cabbage sit side by side. One becomes sauerkraut; the other rots. What decides the difference?

options.text: The variety of cabbage
options.label: A

options.text: Whether the cabbage was organic
options.label: B

options.text: The conditions steered by the fermenter — salt per a tested recipe, submersion, cleanliness, temperature, and time — decide which microbes win
options.label: C

options.text: How much cabbage was in each jar
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a patch of fuzzy mold growing on the surface of your fermenting pickles. What is the correct action?

options.text: Discard the batch — mold is a failure signal; scraping it off does not make the rest safe
options.label: A

options.text: Scrape off the mold carefully and continue fermenting — the mold is only on the surface
options.label: B

options.text: Stir the mold into the brine so it spreads out
options.label: C

options.text: Wait a few days — the acid will kill the mold on its own
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why must vegetables be kept fully submerged under the brine during fermentation?

options.text: Submersion makes the vegetables ferment faster
options.label: A

options.text: Submersion replaces the need for salt
options.label: B

options.text: Submersion keeps the vegetables from floating into the lid
options.label: C

options.text: Submersion excludes oxygen — which favors lactic acid bacteria and prevents surface mold that needs air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A week into fermenting sauerkraut, the brine is cloudy and the smell is pleasantly sour, and the cabbage stays submerged. What do these signals mean?

options.text: The batch has failed and should be discarded
options.label: A

options.text: The fermentation is on track — cloudy brine and a sour smell are signs of normal acid development
options.label: B

options.text: The salt was wrong, and the batch must be re-salted
options.label: C

options.text: The ferment is done and must be canned immediately
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend wants to double the salt in a fermented vegetable recipe "because more salt is always safer." What should you advise?

options.text: Follow the tested recipe's salt level — salt levels are recipe-specific, and too much can stop or slow the fermentation and unbalance the product
options.label: A

options.text: Double the salt — extra salt always improves safety
options.label: B

options.text: Half the salt — less salt always ferments faster
options.label: C

options.text: Salt does not matter as long as the vegetables are submerged
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your recipe says to ferment at a cool, stable temperature for the stated time. Your neighbor says the ferment "will be faster and stronger in the warm closet." What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use the warm closet — speed is always better
options.label: A

options.text: Use the warm closet, but check it twice as often
options.label: B

options.text: Follow the recipe's temperature and time guidance — speed and flavor follow temperature, and extremes favor spoilage
options.label: C

options.text: Temperature is irrelevant once the brine is cloudy
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You open a fermenting jar and are hit by a strong putrid, rotten smell. The brine is still cloudy. What is the correct response?

options.text: Taste a small amount — if it tastes sour it is fine
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the batch — a putrid, rotten smell is a failure signal, and tasting is never a valid test
options.label: B

options.text: Re-salt the batch and continue fermenting
options.label: C

options.text: Boil the contents and keep them as cooked food
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is fermentation genuinely useful in a preparedness household despite being a low-tech method?

options.text: It preserves surplus without power — just salt, containers, and time — turning a harvest glut into food that keeps for weeks to months in cold storage
options.label: A

options.text: It makes any food permanently shelf-stable at room temperature
options.label: B

options.text: It requires no salt, no containers, and no temperature control
options.label: C

options.text: It preserves meat and fish safely without any special knowledge
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your sauerkraut is finished per the recipe — sour, crisp, and fragrant. How should you store it?

options.text: In the pantry at room temperature — the acid preserves it indefinitely
options.label: A

options.text: In a warm cupboard — warmth improves the flavor
options.label: B

options.text: Sealed in jars without refrigeration — fermentation is sterilization
options.label: C

options.text: In the refrigerator or a cool cellar — fermentation is not sterilization, and the finished product remains perishable
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household is cooking its first emergency meal with no running water and limited fuel. Which framework organizes their food-safety decisions?

options.text: Expiration dates, odor checks, and taste tests
options.label: A

options.text: Storing everything frozen so bacteria cannot grow
options.label: B

options.text: The four pillars: Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill
options.label: C

options.text: Cooking everything twice, since double cooking is the only rule
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cooking chicken on a camp stove after a power outage. The meat looks brown and steaming. What is the correct way to decide it is done?

options.text: Brown color and clear juices are proof of doneness
options.label: A

options.text: A food thermometer must read 165 °F in the thickest part — appearance is not a reliable check
options.label: B

options.text: Two minutes of boiling in water is sufficient for any meat
options.label: C

options.text: The meat is done when the juices run clear
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Ground beef is cooking for burgers during a camping trip. What internal temperature must it reach?

options.text: 145 °F, the same as whole steaks
options.label: A

options.text: 130 °F, since burgers are eaten immediately
options.label: B

options.text: 165 °F, the same as poultry
options.label: C

options.text: 160 °F — ground meat has a higher safe temperature than whole cuts because grinding moves surface bacteria throughout the meat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Yesterday's stew was refrigerated overnight, and today the power is out. You have heat for one meal. What is the reheating rule?

options.text: Reheat leftovers to 165 °F, verified with a thermometer — the reheating standard is the same as the cooking standard for leftovers
options.label: A

options.text: Reheat until steaming — visible steam is the official check
options.label: B

options.text: Reheat to the original cooking temperature of the stew's main ingredient, whatever that was
options.label: C

options.text: Do not reheat — leftovers are always unsafe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The tap is dry, and you must prepare food. There is a small bottle of hand sanitizer in the supply. What makes it an acceptable fallback for hand hygiene?

options.text: Any hand sanitizer works, regardless of alcohol content
options.label: A

options.text: Hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, applied until dry — the CDC's fallback when soap and water are unavailable
options.label: B

options.text: Sanitizer is never acceptable; food preparation must be skipped
options.label: C

options.text: Sanitizer replaces hand washing entirely, including when water exists
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Water is limited to the household's stored supply, and you are cooking raw chicken, then a ready-to-eat salad, in the same session. How do you sequence your hygiene water?

options.text: Wash hands once at the start of cooking and reuse the water for everything after
options.label: A

options.text: Save the water for drinking only — hygiene water is optional
options.label: B

options.text: Budget water so hands are washed with soap and water at the highest-risk moments — after handling raw meat and before ready-to-eat food — using sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol when water must be conserved
options.label: C

options.text: Use sanitizer only, and spend all water on cleaning the chicken
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You cooked ground beef on the only cutting board and need to slice the tomato for the salad on the same board. What is the correct move?

options.text: Wash the board with soap and water (or the best available substitute) before the tomato touches it — raw meat and ready-to-eat food never share a surface without cleaning between
options.label: A

options.text: Slice the tomato on top of the cooked beef — the juice is sterile
options.label: B

options.text: Wipe the board with a dry towel and proceed
options.label: C

options.text: Skip the tomato — produce cannot be served raw in an emergency
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A cooler holds raw chicken on the bottom and ready-to-eat cheese on a shelf above it. Why is this arrangement correct?

options.text: It is wrong — raw meat should always be above ready-to-eat food
options.label: A

options.text: It makes no difference in a cooler, since everything is the same temperature
options.label: B

options.text: It is correct only if the chicken is double-wrapped
options.label: C

options.text: It is correct — raw meat stored below ready-to-eat food keeps drips from reaching food that will not be cooked again
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The power has been out for six hours. The refrigerator thermometer reads 9 °C (48 °F), and the milk inside looks and smells fine. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the milk — it smells fine, so it must be safe
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the milk — it has been above 4 °C (40 °F) past the danger-zone limit, and appearance and smell cannot overrule the thermometer
options.label: B

options.text: Freeze the milk immediately to kill the bacteria
options.label: C

options.text: Boil the milk and continue using it for everything
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While unpacking stored food, you find a canned soup with a bulging lid. It was bought at the same time as identical cans that look fine. What is the correct action?

options.text: Taste a small spoonful — if it tastes fine, serve it
options.label: A

options.text: Open it carefully and re-cook the soup, since boiling kills anything in it
options.label: B

options.text: Discard it — never taste — because bulging cans are a botulism warning sign, and the toxin is odorless, tasteless, and not destroyed by cooking
options.label: C

options.text: Serve it only to the adults, not the children
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You cook chicken at 4:00 PM and it sits on the counter until 6:15 PM, when you refrigerate it. The kitchen is 24 °C (75 °F). What should you do?

options.text: Refrigerate it — the total time is under 3 hours, which is acceptable
options.label: A

options.text: Discard it — it spent more than 2 cumulative hours in the danger zone
options.label: B

options.text: Refrigerate it — it smells fine, so it is safe
options.label: C

options.text: Reheat it thoroughly and refrigerate — reheating resets the clock
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A sealed jar of dried beans develops mold in your pantry. Which storage factor failed?

options.text: Light — mold grows in darkness
options.label: A

options.text: Moisture — mold needs available water to grow
options.label: B

options.text: Oxygen — mold requires pure oxygen
options.label: C

options.text: Time — mold appears automatically with age
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is an attic a poor place for a food pantry in summer?

options.text: Attics are always too dark for stored food
options.label: A

options.text: Heat accelerates every spoilage process — microbial growth, rancidity, vitamin loss
options.label: B

options.text: Food needs light to stay fresh
options.label: C

options.text: Attics lack enough oxygen for sealed food
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You buy 2 kg of flour to store for up to six months. What is the best packaging choice?

options.text: Leave it in the original paper bag — it breathes
options.label: A

options.text: A sealed, food-grade container (glass jar or food-grade plastic with a tight lid)
options.label: B

options.text: A cardboard box with a plastic liner
options.label: C

options.text: A plastic grocery bag tied shut
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You restock the pantry with a new 12-pack of canned beans, and the old cans have been there for months. Following FIFO, what do you do?

options.text: Put the new pack on top of the old cans — they are identical, so it does not matter
options.label: A

options.text: Put the new pack behind the old cans and use the old ones first
options.label: B

options.text: Discard the old cans immediately
options.label: C

options.text: Move the old cans to the top shelf where they are easier to reach
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a can of soup with a visibly bulging lid. What is the correct action?

options.text: Open it and smell the contents — smell will tell you if it is safe
options.label: A

options.text: Discard it without tasting — bulging cans are a botulism warning sign
options.label: B

options.text: Boil the soup thoroughly — boiling destroys the toxin
options.label: C

options.text: Refrigerate it and use it within a week
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A loaf of bread shows a small patch of green mold. What should you do?

options.text: Cut the moldy slice off and eat the rest — mold does not penetrate bread
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the loaf — mold can penetrate deeper than the visible patch
options.label: B

options.text: Toast the bread — heat kills the mold
options.label: C

options.text: Wash the mold off the surface
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The power is out. Your freezer was full when it failed, and it has been closed for 40 hours. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Everything is safe — a full freezer holds food for 48 hours, and you are inside that window
options.label: A

options.text: Discard everything — any thawing means spoilage
options.label: B

options.text: Start cooking everything immediately to preserve it
options.label: C

options.text: Refreeze whatever is still cold enough to hold ice crystals
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household of 4 wants to build its first emergency food supply. Which is the strongest first step?

options.text: Buy a large "survival food" bucket that no one plans to eat
options.label: A

options.text: Build and rotate a 2-week supply of non-perishable foods the household actually eats
options.label: B

options.text: Store one month of fresh vegetables in the pantry
options.label: C

options.text: Buy extra food only when a storm is forecast
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your refrigerator thermometer reads 7 °C (45 °F). What should you do?

options.text: Nothing — it is close enough to the target
options.label: A

options.text: Adjust the refrigerator so it holds 4 °C (40 °F) or below, and verify with the thermometer
options.label: B

options.text: Lower it to −7 °C (20 °F) to be safe
options.label: C

options.text: Remove the thermometer — it is causing the problem
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two identical bags of white rice: one in a sealed Mylar bag in a cool pantry, one in its original paper bag in a humid garage. The label says the rice "lasts years." What is the correct reading of the label?

options.text: Both batches will last equally long — the food determines the shelf life
options.label: A

options.text: Shelf life depends on packaging and storage conditions — the pantry batch can store for years; the garage batch will fail much sooner
options.label: B

options.text: The paper bag actually preserves rice better because it breathes
options.label: C

options.text: The label is a safety guarantee under any conditions
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A commercially canned low-acid vegetable passes its "best by" date while stored cool and dry in your pantry. What does the date mean?

options.text: The food is now unsafe and must be discarded
options.label: A

options.text: The date is a quality guideline — properly stored canned food is safe beyond it, but quality declines
options.label: B

options.text: The can is guaranteed fresh forever
options.label: C

options.text: The food must be frozen immediately
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which item in your long-term pantry has the shortest practical storage horizon and needs the most frequent rotation?

options.text: White rice in a sealed container
options.label: A

options.text: Honey in a sealed jar
options.label: B

options.text: Walnuts in a sealed jar
options.label: C

options.text: Salt in a sealed container
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are building a long-term food selection. Which choice stores the worst over years?

options.text: White rice
options.label: A

options.text: Brown rice
options.label: B

options.text: Dried white beans
options.label: C

options.text: Rolled oats in sealed packaging
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You sealed dry goods in Mylar bags with oxygen absorbers, yet mold appears months later. What went wrong?

options.text: The oxygen absorber was the wrong size for the bag
options.label: A

options.text: Oxygen absorbers remove oxygen, not moisture — the food was stored too damp or moisture got in
options.label: B

options.text: Mylar bags are not a moisture barrier
options.label: C

options.text: Mold grows from oxygen, so the absorbers caused it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before packaging bulk flour and beans for long-term storage, you freeze them for several days. What does this accomplish?

options.text: It removes moisture from the food
options.label: A

options.text: It kills insect eggs and larvae that may be present in the bulk food
options.label: B

options.text: It sterilizes the food
options.label: C

options.text: It extends the food's shelf life by pre-cooking it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your storage room swings from 15 °C in winter to 30 °C in summer. Why is this a food-storage problem even inside sealed containers?

options.text: Temperature swings make food taste worse but never cause safety issues
options.label: A

options.text: Warm air holds more moisture, and when it cools inside a package it condenses — moisture migrates into the food
options.label: B

options.text: Temperature swings cause cans to rust from the inside
options.label: C

options.text: It is not a problem — sealed containers are immune to temperature changes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During your annual pantry inspection, you find a food-grade bucket with no label. What is the correct response?

options.text: Leave it — unlabeled containers are fine if the food looks normal
options.label: A

options.text: Add it to a written inventory, label it with contents and date, and inspect the rest of the pantry the same way
options.label: B

options.text: Discard the whole pantry — one unlabeled bucket means the system failed
options.label: C

options.text: Move it to the front of the shelf so it is used first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In your long-term stock, you find a can that is bulging at both ends. What is the correct action?

options.text: Open it and check the food's color before deciding
options.label: A

options.text: Discard it without tasting — bulging cans are a botulism warning sign
options.label: B

options.text: Cook the contents thoroughly — cooking makes it safe
options.label: C

options.text: Move it to the fridge and use it first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two years in, your long-term pantry is full but you have never eaten from it. What is the most likely outcome, and what fixes it?

options.text: The food is protected by age and will last indefinitely
options.label: A

options.text: It becomes a "museum pantry" — stored food quietly degrades, and rotation was never exercised; the fix is to eat what you store and replace it
options.label: B

options.text: The food will be safer than fresh food because it aged in a sealed environment
options.label: C

options.text: The fix is to buy larger containers so the food lasts longer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor shows off an emergency supply of rice, pasta, crackers, and canned corn — "plenty of calories." What is the gap in this diet?

options.text: None — calories are the only requirement for stored food
options.label: A

options.text: Protein and micronutrients are missing: the supply covers energy but not the rest of what a diet must provide
options.label: B

options.text: The only gap is flavor variety
options.label: C

options.text: The only gap is water temperature for cooking
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are sizing a 2-week emergency food supply for a household of two adults. Which use of the ~2,000-calorie planning figure is correct?

options.text: As a medical requirement that every person must meet exactly
options.label: A

options.text: As a daily menu that each person must eat in full, every day
options.label: B

options.text: As a sizing anchor — roughly 2,000 calories per person per day, multiplied by people and days to plan quantity, while accepting that real appetites vary
options.label: C

options.text: As a storage requirement — food must be at least 2,000 calories per package
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household of four plans a 2-week supply. Which is the correct first sizing step?

options.text: Apply the anchor per person — about 2,000 calories per person per day — then multiply by four people and fourteen days, and add special-needs lines
options.label: A

options.text: Buy four identical family-sized kits and split them evenly
options.label: B

options.text: Double the normal weekly grocery bill and stop there
options.label: C

options.text: Size to the largest shelf that is empty
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A stored supply has plenty of crackers, rice, and energy bars but no canned beans, canned fish, nut butter, or shelf-stable dairy. What is the specific gap, and why does it grow with time?

options.text: There is no gap — starches cover all dietary needs
options.label: A

options.text: The gap is only texture; crackers and bars satisfy the same need
options.label: B

options.text: The gap is water — starches need more water to eat
options.label: C

options.text: Protein sources are missing — and the longer the disruption, the more protein matters beyond energy
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which stored items add micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — to a pantry diet?

options.text: Crackers, rice, and dry cereal only
options.label: A

options.text: Canned and dried fruits and vegetables, canned tomato products, and vegetable soups
options.label: B

options.text: Energy bars and granola bars exclusively
options.label: C

options.text: Any sealed package, regardless of contents
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is a 2-week food plan incomplete without the water plan sized beside it?

options.text: Because stored water is only needed for cooking, and emergency food is not cooked
options.label: A

options.text: Because water and food are entirely separate systems
options.label: B

options.text: Because water is part of the diet — for drinking with meals and for preparation — so both are sized for the same days, at about 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day
options.label: C

options.text: Because water is only for hygiene, which is optional in the short term
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household stores powdered milk and dried oatmeal for a 2-week emergency menu. Which water consideration must be in the plan?

options.text: Reconstituting the milk takes water beyond the drinking allowance — the preparation water is counted in the same water math as the drinking water
options.label: A

options.text: Powdered milk and oatmeal are eaten dry, so no water is needed
options.label: B

options.text: The oatmeal absorbs water from the air, so none needs to be stored
options.label: C

options.text: Only the drinking water matters; preparation water is optional
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household includes an infant, a school-age child, and an older adult. Which approach to the emergency menu is correct?

options.text: One standard menu for everyone — quantities are the only difference
options.label: A

options.text: The standard menu, plus a jar of baby food "just in case"
options.label: B

options.text: The standard menu only, with improvisation at the emergency
options.label: C

options.text: Planned lines per person: formula and baby food with clean mixing water for the infant, foods the child normally eats, and easy-to-eat, low-preparation foods for the older adult
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household member follows a prescribed diet for a medical condition. The generic emergency menu cannot cover it. What is the correct planning response?

options.text: Substitute the closest generic food at the emergency and hope for the best
options.label: A

options.text: Plan the household's actual prescribed diet into the stored menu, and flag any gap for medical review rather than improvising
options.label: B

options.text: Exclude that person from the food plan
options.label: C

options.text: Replace all stored food with vitamin supplements
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household wants its stored supply to function as a real diet. Which method produces meals rather than a pile of items?

options.text: Buy one of every shelf-stable food on sale and sort it later
options.label: A

options.text: Store only the longest-lasting items, since taste is secondary
options.label: B

options.text: Write the normal weekly menu, translate each meal to shelf-stable versions, check coverage (energy, protein, produce, water) per day, and rotate
options.label: C

options.text: Stock duplicate products in bulk so variety is guaranteed by volume
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The power is out and it is cold. Someone suggests firing up the charcoal grill in the garage "with the door open" to cook and warm the room. What do you do?

options.text: Agree — an open garage door provides enough ventilation
options.label: A

options.text: Refuse — charcoal produces lethal carbon monoxide with little or no visible smoke; it never burns indoors, garage door open or not
options.label: B

options.text: Agree, but move the grill closer to the door
options.label: C

options.text: Agree, but only grill meat, not vegetables
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After cooking with a camp stove under a carport, a family member complains of headache, dizziness, and nausea. What should you do?

options.text: Have them lie down and rest — it is probably the flu
options.label: A

options.text: Get everyone into fresh air immediately and seek medical help — these are carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms
options.label: B

options.text: Give them water and wait an hour
options.label: C

options.text: Close the doors and windows so the room stays warm
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During a winter outage, is it acceptable to use a propane camp stove inside the kitchen "just like the gas range"?

options.text: Yes — a flame is a flame, and the kitchen was designed for cooking
options.label: A

options.text: No — a permanently installed range is vented for indoor use; a camp stove is not, and indoor use causes CO buildup
options.label: B

options.text: Yes, but only for boiling water
options.label: C

options.text: Yes, if you open one window
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household of 4 plans for 5 days of cooking with two hot meals a day on a propane camp stove. What is the correct fuel-planning step?

options.text: Estimate the fuel needed for roughly 40 hot meals before the outage and verify the tank can cover them
options.label: A

options.text: Buy a bigger stove — fuel efficiency is about equipment, not planning
options.label: B

options.text: Assume one tank covers any household of any size
options.label: C

options.text: Plan fuel only when the outage actually starts
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which describes retained-heat ("haybox") cooking correctly?

options.text: Cooking food entirely with a box of hay and no heat source
options.label: A

options.text: Bringing food to a full boil, then finishing it in a well-insulated container without further fuel
options.label: B

options.text: Cooking slowly over a very low flame for many hours
options.label: C

options.text: Wrapping food in hay and burying it for storage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your camp stove flames keep blowing sideways in the wind and meals take twice as long. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Crank the stove to maximum and accept the fuel cost
options.label: A

options.text: Set up a wind screen around the stove, placed far enough to avoid overheating the device and not blocking its ventilation
options.label: B

options.text: Move the stove indoors where there is no wind
options.label: C

options.text: Use a larger pot so the flame cannot be blown out
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You plan dinner for 6:00 PM using a solar cooker, but the day is overcast. What should you expect?

options.text: The solar cooker works fine — it only needs daylight
options.label: A

options.text: The solar cooker will be too slow or ineffective — plan a fuel-based method for overcast days and evenings
options.label: B

options.text: The solar cooker works faster when it is cloudy
options.label: C

options.text: Add more reflectors to double the speed on any day
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You set up a cooking fire 3 meters from your tarp shelter. Which additional fire-safety measure is required?

options.text: None — the distance alone is sufficient
options.label: A

options.text: Cleared perimeter, water or an extinguisher within reach, and never leaving the fire unattended
options.label: B

options.text: Move the fire directly under the tarp's low edge for smoke protection
options.label: C

options.text: Build the fire larger so it burns down quickly
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cooking chicken over a campfire off-grid. What internal temperature must it reach?

options.text: 145 °F (63 °C) — the same as whole cuts
options.label: A

options.text: 165 °F (74 °C) — the poultry standard
options.label: B

options.text: 140 °F (60 °C) — the danger-zone boundary
options.label: C

options.text: Just until the outside looks browned
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your alcohol stove ran out mid-meal and you want to refuel it while it is still hot. What is the correct action?

options.text: Refuel immediately so dinner is not delayed
options.label: A

options.text: Never add liquid fuel to a lit or hot device — wait for it to cool fully, then refuel away from flame
options.label: B

options.text: Pour fuel around the burner and let it pre-warm
options.label: C

options.text: Refuel it outside so any flash fire is contained
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the fundamental difference between hot smoking and cold smoking?

options.text: Hot smoking cooks the food to safe internal temperatures; cold smoking does not cook the food at all
options.label: A

options.text: Hot smoking uses smoke; cold smoking does not
options.label: B

options.text: Cold smoking cooks faster at a higher temperature
options.label: C

options.text: Hot smoking is only for fish; cold smoking is only for meat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a proper cold smoke, the meat leaves the smoker raw. What does that mean for its safety?

options.text: The smoke has made it safe to keep at room temperature
options.label: A

options.text: The smoke has cured the interior of the meat
options.label: B

options.text: The product's safety depends on the prior cure and on careful cold-chain handling afterwards — it is not a cooked product
options.label: C

options.text: Cold-smoked food is sterile because smoke kills pathogens
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor claims that "smoked meat keeps without refrigeration — that's the whole point of smoking." What is the accurate response?

options.text: Agree — smoke is a proven preservation method on its own
options.label: A

options.text: Disagree — smoking alone does not preserve perishable meat, poultry, or fish; smoked food must be refrigerated promptly and used within days
options.label: B

options.text: Agree, but only for fish
options.label: C

options.text: Agree, as long as the smoke was at least 12 hours
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You plan to hot smoke a brisket over many hours at low heat. What food-safety reality must you plan around?

options.text: Low heat eliminates the danger zone entirely
options.label: A

options.text: The smoke kills bacteria during the first hour
options.label: B

options.text: Slow smoking is always safer than fast cooking
options.label: C

options.text: Long low-temperature smokes can hold the meat in the 4–140 °F danger zone, where bacteria multiply — the 2-hour rule governs the process, and the meat must reach its safe internal temperature
options.label: D

questions.question_text: According to the USDA FSIS Safe Temperature Chart, what internal temperature must smoked poultry reach to be safe?
A friend pulls smoked chicken off the smoker and declares it done "because it has a nice smoke ring and brown color." What is the correct response?

options.text: Color and smoke ring are not doneness tests — verify the internal temperature with a thermometer against the FSIS chart
options.label: A

options.text: The smoke ring is the USDA-accepted doneness test
options.label: B

options.text: Brown color always means the center is safe
options.label: C

options.text: Agree, then check only the outside temperature
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is cold-smoked fish considered a higher-risk product than hot-smoked fish?

options.text: Fish is always unsafe to smoke
options.label: A

options.text: Cold-smoked fish contains more salt by law
options.label: B

options.text: It is not cooked, and the CDC documents botulism and listeria associated with cold-smoked fish when the cure or cold chain slips
options.label: C

options.text: Cold smoke attracts insects
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend cold-smokes salmon with no cure at all — "the smoke preserves it, that's how it was done for centuries." What should you advise?

options.text: Nothing — this traditional method is universally safe
options.label: A

options.text: Add more smoke time and it will be safe
options.label: B

options.text: It is safe if it tastes and smells okay
options.label: C

options.text: Cold smoking without a tested cure skips the safety system — the fish is raw and perishable; this is not a safe practice, and the product should not be eaten
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are choosing wood for smoking a batch of chicken. Which selection is correct?

options.text: Clean, dry hardwoods like hickory, oak, or apple — avoid softwoods and any treated, painted, moldy, or unknown wood
options.label: A

options.text: Pine or fir — they are cheap and burn hot
options.label: B

options.text: Pressure-treated scraps — they burn slowly and evenly
options.label: C

options.text: Any wood from the yard, including painted fence boards
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your hot-smoked pork shoulder has come off the smoker at a verified 145 °F internal temperature and rested properly. What is the correct storage plan?

options.text: Hang it in the pantry — smoking makes it shelf-stable
options.label: A

options.text: Refrigerate promptly at or below 40 °F and use within days — or freeze, can via a tested recipe, or make proper jerky for longer storage
options.label: B

options.text: Leave it on the counter overnight to develop flavor
options.label: C

options.text: Wrap it and store it at room temperature — the smoke ring protects it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You brushed against poison ivy an hour and a half ago while hiking and are now worried about exposure. What is the best response?

options.text: Wash the skin now with soap and water, and wash clothing separately — but note that washing this late may not remove all the sap
options.label: A

options.text: Wait for the rash to appear, then treat it with heat to draw out the oil
options.label: B

options.text: Scrub the skin hard with hot water to open the pores and flush the oil out
options.label: C

options.text: Apply a thick layer of petroleum jelly to trap the oil before it absorbs
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A toddler chews on a houseplant leaf and immediately starts crying, drooling, and rubbing her mouth. You have removed the leaf pieces from her mouth. What should you do next?

options.text: Give her milk to neutralize the plant toxins
options.label: A

options.text: Rinse her mouth with water and have her spit, then call Poison Control
options.label: B

options.text: Make her vomit to remove any plant material she swallowed
options.label: C

options.text: Have her swallow some vinegar to kill the toxins on the way down
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement about water hemlock matches what the sources document?

options.text: The leaves are the most toxic part, and the roots become safe once the plant matures
options.label: A

options.text: Every part of the plant is equally toxic at every stage of growth
options.label: B

options.text: The underground portions, especially the tuberous roots, are the most toxic, while leaves and stems lose most of their toxicity as they mature
options.label: C

options.text: The plant is toxic to livestock but has no documented effect on humans
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While clearing brush, you get giant hogweed sap on your forearm and notice it a few minutes later. The sun is out. What is the correct sequence of actions?

options.text: Apply sunscreen first to protect the skin, then wash at camp
options.label: A

options.text: Let the sap dry on the skin, then peel it off with a cloth
options.label: B

options.text: Wait until evening to wash, since light is what activates the reaction
options.label: C

options.text: Wash the area thoroughly with soap and water right away, then cover it and avoid sunlight for 1–2 days
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hiker reports that her child ate a few berries from an unidentified plant twenty minutes ago and shows no symptoms yet. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Call Poison Control now — you do not need to wait for symptoms to develop
options.label: A

options.text: Wait two hours; if nothing happens, the plant was safe
options.label: B

options.text: Give the child a small amount of food to dilute any toxins
options.label: C

options.text: Induce vomiting immediately to remove the berries before symptoms begin
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which combination of signs after a suspected plant exposure requires calling the local emergency number immediately, without waiting for Poison Control advice?

options.text: Mild itching and a few small red bumps on the forearm
options.label: A

options.text: Difficulty breathing, severe mouth swelling, or the person cannot be awakened
options.label: B

options.text: A stomachache that comes and goes for an hour
options.label: C

options.text: A small rash on the ankle that appeared two days ago
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend tells you a plant gave her "sunburn-like blisters" on her arm, but only on the side that faced the sun — the skin under her sleeve is fine. She touched the plant earlier that day. Which documented class of toxicity does this match?

options.text: GI irritant — the plant caused an allergic reaction in her stomach
options.label: A

options.text: Calcium oxalate crystals — the needle-like crystals burned her skin on contact
options.label: B

options.text: Phototoxic compounds — the sap made her skin react to sunlight, causing the blisters only where light reached
options.label: C

options.text: Urushiol — the oil reacts with air, not light, to cause blistering
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your dog chews on a plant in the yard and starts drooling and vomiting. You do not know the plant's name. What is the best first step for a pet exposure?

options.text: Give the dog milk and wait to see if symptoms pass
options.label: A

options.text: Make the dog vomit immediately with salt water
options.label: B

options.text: Do nothing — pets are rarely affected by plant material
options.label: C

options.text: Call the ASPCA Animal Poison Control hotline (888) 426-4435 or your veterinarian, and try to identify the plant
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Ninety minutes after a hiker ate a root she mistook for a wild parsnip, she begins twitching and trembling, then has a violent convulsion. Which documented plant class does this pattern match, and what does it require?

options.text: A nervous-system convulsant such as water hemlock — this is a 911-level emergency
options.label: A

options.text: A mild GI irritant — these signs are a normal stomach reaction and will pass
options.label: B

options.text: An oxalate reaction — the crystals are causing muscle spasms
options.label: C

options.text: A phototoxic reaction — she needs to get out of the sun
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At a campsite, a child is found unresponsive next to a plant with white flower clusters. She has bits of the plant in her mouth. What is the correct sequence?

options.text: Remove the plant bits, then phone Poison Control and wait on hold for guidance
options.label: A

options.text: Call the local emergency number immediately — an unresponsive child is a 911 situation — and start the emergency assessment while help is dispatched
options.label: B

options.text: Give her water to wash the plant down, then monitor her breathing
options.label: C

options.text: Carry her to the trailhead yourself before calling anyone
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which combination of measures best reduces accidental plant exposure for a family with young children and a dog?

options.text: Teach children to identify poison ivy by sight, and keep the dog leashed only on city walks
options.label: A

options.text: Remove all plants from the yard so no exposure is possible
options.label: B

options.text: Teach children to never taste unknown plants, supervise them outdoors, check yard and household plants against the ASPCA list for the dog, and never burn unidentified plants
options.label: C

options.text: Rely on the children's natural caution after one warning, and let the dog roam to build tolerance
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During a hike you find a plant whose leaves look like a garden vegetable you know well, but you are not certain of the species. A friend says the smell seems right and suggests trying a leaf. What must happen BEFORE any consumption?

options.text: Positive identification of the exact species with multiple authoritative sources — certainty, not resemblance or smell
options.label: A

options.text: A small taste test — a bite reveals whether it is safe
options.label: B

options.text: Boiling it first — thorough cooking removes the risk
options.label: C

options.text: Checking whether animals nearby are eating it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have studied a plant all afternoon and narrowed it to two possibilities: a known edible and a poisonous look-alike. The distinguishing feature is tiny and you cannot get a clear view. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Eat a small amount and watch for symptoms — a little bit is a reasonable test
options.label: A

options.text: Cook it thoroughly first — heat resolves the uncertainty
options.label: B

options.text: Do not consume — when in doubt, leave it out
options.label: C

options.text: Taste it and spit it out if it is bitter — bitterness is a reliable warning
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are preparing a rhubarb plant you found in an abandoned farm garden. Poison Control lists "Rhubarb (leaves)" among poisonous plants. Which part of the plant may be used as food?

options.text: The large leaf blades — they are the most nutritious part
options.label: A

options.text: The stalks only; the leaves are discarded and never eaten
options.label: B

options.text: Both parts, after a thorough boil in changed water
options.label: C

options.text: The roots — they are the safest part of the plant
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early spring you find pokeweed shoots just emerging from the ground. You remember that pokeweed shoots are traditionally eaten. Which of the following is the complete and correct statement about eating them?

options.text: Any part of a young pokeweed is safe to eat raw in small amounts
options.label: A

options.text: Mature leaves can be eaten once the plant flowers, since flowering signals ripeness
options.label: B

options.text: The berries can be eaten once they are dark purple, when fully ripe
options.label: C

options.text: Only very young shoots, harvested in early spring, are eaten — and only after thorough cooking in at least 2–3 changes of water; roots, berries, and mature plants are never eaten
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A survival video recommends the "universal edibility test": rub a plant on your skin, press it to your lips, and chew a little before eating. A plant produces no reaction in any of these steps. Why is the plant still not proven safe to eat?
