options.text: Many dangerous plants cause no immediate local reaction, and toxicity can be delayed by hours or days — a clear skin or lip test says nothing about systemic harm
options.label: A

options.text: Because the skin test only works in dry climates
options.label: B

options.text: Because the test is too quick — it needs to be repeated five times to count
options.label: C

options.text: Because no plant is ever safe, regardless of identification
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Someone argues: "The universal edibility test is a survival skill — it's better than nothing when you're hungry." What is the accurate assessment of that claim?

options.text: It is correct — any attempt at food is better than none
options.label: A

options.text: It is only correct for berries, which are lower risk
options.label: B

options.text: It is incorrect — the test is not a reliable safety method; misidentification kills regardless of any test result, and the safe path is positive identification with multiple authoritative sources
options.label: C

options.text: It is correct only when the plant has already been cooked
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have positively identified a common wild green that you know how to prepare correctly. You find a large patch growing along the edge of a busy county road near an industrial zone. Should you harvest it there?

options.text: Yes — the identification and preparation are correct, and that is what matters
options.label: A

options.text: No — roadsides, power line right-of-way areas, and industrial zones are named contamination hazards, because plants can absorb pollutants from the soil, water, and air
options.label: B

options.text: Yes, but only the young leaves — maturity is the only factor
options.label: C

options.text: No, but only because the road makes the patch hard to reach
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A forager says: "I never worry about plant toxins — I always boil everything twice, so cooking takes care of it." What is the accurate general principle?

options.text: Correct — double boiling neutralizes every plant toxin
options.label: A

options.text: Correct only for roots; leaves keep their toxins no matter what
options.label: B

options.text: Mostly correct — cooking is the only step that matters for edibility
options.label: C

options.text: Incorrect as stated — cooking destroys some toxins but not all: young pokeweed shoots become edible only after thorough cooking in at least 2–3 changes of water, yet the roots and berries remain highly toxic and rhubarb leaves are never made safe by cooking
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an abundant, easily identified edible on a stretch of state land you have never visited, with no posted signs. What must you do before harvesting?

options.text: Check the regulations — most public lands prohibit foraging or require a permit, and harvesting is legal only where allowed
options.label: A

options.text: Harvest freely — abundant plants on public land are open to everyone
options.label: B

options.text: Harvest, but take the roots instead of the leaves to be sustainable
options.label: C

options.text: Harvest only at night, so nobody questions you
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have positively identified a well-known edible species and have eaten it before without any problem. Today you pick a larger batch from the same patch and plan to serve it to the whole group, including a friend who has never eaten it. What is the right approach?

options.text: Serve it freely — positive identification means the food is safe for everyone
options.label: A

options.text: Start with a small amount and observe — even edible plants should be eaten in moderation due to personal sensitivities, and first-time eaters get a small, alone, observed taste
options.label: B

options.text: Serve it to everyone but skip the washing — wild food does not need it
options.label: C

options.text: Double the portion size to build tolerance quickly
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You return from a clean harvest site with positively identified greens, ready to cook them for a meal. Which handling practice applies to the harvest, just as it does to store-bought produce?

options.text: Skip rinsing — washing removes nutrients from wild food
options.label: A

options.text: Store them unwashed in a sealed bag for a week before eating
options.label: B

options.text: Wash hands and the greens, and keep the food clean and separated from anything contaminated — the same food-safety disciplines that govern all produce
options.label: C

options.text: Sample a leaf raw in the field before deciding to cook the rest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are hiking in a national park where the posted rules state that plants are protected by law and may not be disturbed or collected. A hillside is covered in ripe, edible berries. What should you do?

options.text: Pick a small handful — the amount is trivial compared to the hillside
options.label: A

options.text: Pick as many as fit in your bag, since leaving them to rot wastes food
options.label: B

options.text: Pick nothing — plants in the park are protected by law, and the rules are the answer
options.label: C

options.text: Pick only berries that have already fallen to the ground, which no one can object to
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a patch of a wild root crop that appears in your field guide as a regional special concern — a slow-growing plant listed as rare in this state. The stand is small, about twenty plants. What is the sustainable decision?

options.text: Do not harvest — rare, threatened, or otherwise protected species are off-limits, and an unconfirmed status means treat it as protected
options.label: A

options.text: Harvest the roots of the five largest plants, since a quarter of a small stand is a small take
options.label: B

options.text: Harvest only the roots and replant the tops, which balances taking with giving back
options.label: C

options.text: Harvest the roots this year but skip next year, which spaces the impact out over time
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend points out a small stand of wild leeks — the leaves are abundant, the bulbs are prized. You want enough for one meal. Which harvest leaves the population able to keep growing?

options.text: Dig up the bulbs of the most crowded plants — thinning a patch helps it
options.label: A

options.text: Cut a few leaves from each of several plants and leave every bulb and root in the ground
options.label: B

options.text: Pull whole plants and take every part — leaves, bulbs, and roots — so nothing is wasted
options.label: C

options.text: Dig up one large bulb and call it a meal — one plant cannot matter to the stand
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The only berry patch you know is in a wet meadow, and reaching the berries means walking across saturated soil and young plants. What is the low-impact choice?

options.text: Walk quickly so your boots spend less time on the ground, then harvest as planned
options.label: A

options.text: Harvest anyway — berries are food, and meadow plants grow back within a season
options.label: B

options.text: Pick only from the plants nearest the trail to keep the damage concentrated in one spot
options.label: C

options.text: Skip the harvest — wet soil compacts and trampling damages neighboring plants, so a sensitive site stays untouched
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A video you watched shows people freely collecting edible mushrooms in a forest, and says the same is legal "anywhere on public land." How should you treat that claim?

options.text: Accept it — rules for public land are consistent nationwide, so the video is good guidance
options.label: A

options.text: Verify the rules for the specific place — collection rules vary by jurisdiction, land manager, and site, and unknown rules mean no harvest
options.label: B

options.text: Follow it only on state land, where rules are uniform within a state
options.label: C

options.text: Follow it only in national forests, which always allow free personal-use harvest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a hillside you find the only patch of ripe berries for a kilometer — birds are visibly feeding there, and the stand is small. You would like enough for a pie. What is the sustainable choice?

options.text: Take half the berries — the birds can share what is left
options.label: A

options.text: Take a full bag — a single visit cannot harm a berry crop
options.label: B

options.text: Leave the stand entirely — the last of a stand belongs to the population and to the wildlife that depends on it
options.label: C

options.text: Take only the berries within arm's reach — the birds keep the higher ones
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which harvest technique best matches low-impact foraging practice?

options.text: Cut cleanly with a sharp knife or pruners and carry finds in a mesh sack that spreads spores and seeds as you travel
options.label: A

options.text: Pull plants by the roots for a complete harvest, since clean stems leave nothing to regrow from
options.label: B

options.text: Use a plastic bag and seal it tightly so no seeds spill along the trail
options.label: C

options.text: Harvest on the wettest days, when plants are easiest to pull and soil damage is hidden
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is harvesting an abundant or invasive species a better choice than harvesting a rare native one, all else being equal?

options.text: Invasive plants contain more nutrients than native plants
options.label: A

options.text: Abundant plants are always easier to identify safely
options.label: B

options.text: Rare species taste better, so they are worth a smaller harvest
options.label: C

options.text: Harvesting abundant and invasive species spares pressure on rare and slow-reproducing natives, and can even help native flora thrive
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You love a certain wild herb and want to use it every week. The local wild stands are small and slow-growing. What is the better long-term choice?

options.text: Cultivate the species in a garden at home, where you control the harvest and leave wild populations untouched
options.label: A

options.text: Keep wild-harvesting — weekly small takes are sustainable by definition
options.label: B

options.text: Harvest only in spring, when the plants are most plentiful
options.label: C

options.text: Ask other foragers to share their favorite patches so the pressure is spread
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a harvest, what is the leave-no-trace standard for the site?

options.text: Leave any trash you generated in a pile at the trailhead, where it is easy to find
options.label: A

options.text: Break down plants you did not take, so the stand looks intentionally managed
options.label: B

options.text: Leave the site as you found it — all waste packed out, holes refilled, no trampled vegetation, so the next person and the wildlife would never know you were there
options.label: C

options.text: Mark your best spots with small stone cairns so other foragers can find the abundance too
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A farmer's woodlot is loaded with the exact mushrooms you want, and the farmer is not home. The property has no posted signs. What is the correct action?

options.text: Harvest quickly and quietly — no posted signs means no stated rule against it
options.label: A

options.text: Do not collect — private land requires the owner's permission, and harvesting without it is trespass, regardless of posted signs
options.label: B

options.text: Collect only a small amount, which stays within the spirit of fair use
options.label: C

options.text: Return after dark, when the owner is less likely to notice the harvest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You want to collect a wild green that is at its best only when young, in early spring. You plan the outing for late summer instead, because your calendar is free. What has the planning loop failed to do?

options.text: Match the outing to the species' growth stage — collecting out of season means collecting the wrong stage of the wrong thing
options.label: A

options.text: Confirm the collection rules for the land you are using
options.label: B

options.text: Leave some material behind for wildlife and future growth
options.label: C

options.text: Choose a location away from roadsides and treated land
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You found a patch of mushrooms you plan to keep separate for study later. Which container belongs in your kit for them?

options.text: A sealed plastic bag — it keeps the specimens clean and contained
options.label: A

options.text: A single large cloth bag shared with the greens you will cut later
options.label: B

options.text: A paper bag — paper lets moisture escape, where plastic traps it and spoils the material
options.label: C

options.text: A bare hands carry — the shorter the time out of a container, the better
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Mid-outing, your bag of confirmed lamb's-quarters is half full, and you spot a second green you are fairly confident about. Your bag is the only container you brought. What should you do?

options.text: Add the second species on top — you can separate them carefully when you get home
options.label: A

options.text: Collect the second species only after emptying the bag — the first species must be secured, and the new material needs its own container
options.label: B

options.text: Fold the new leaves into the middle of the bag so they stay clean on the way home
options.label: C

options.text: Gather both species together and photograph them in the bag for later sorting
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The day is hot, the ride home is an hour, and your harvest is in breathable bags in the back of the truck bed, in full sun. What is the correct transport adjustment?

options.text: Leave the bags open so the wind dries the harvest on the drive
options.label: A

options.text: Roll the bags closed tightly so nothing spills during the ride
options.label: B

options.text: Keep the harvest in the sun — warmth speeds up the drying you want anyway
options.label: C

options.text: Move the harvest into a cooler or the shaded cab — heat in transit is spoilage, and cool, un-crushed transport is part of hygiene
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are documenting a plant in the field so you can confirm it later at home. Which photo set makes confirmation actually possible?

options.text: Whole plant in habitat, close-ups of leaves and flowers filling the frame, and a coin or ruler for scale — checked in focus before you leave
options.label: A

options.text: One wide shot of the whole patch from across the trail
options.label: B

options.text: Close-ups of the most attractive leaves only, with the camera on portrait mode
options.label: C

options.text: Photos of the container after you fill it, so the harvest is recorded
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At home, with your field guide open, you re-verify your collected species leaf by leaf — and one specimen matches on every feature except the stem, which you cannot reconcile. What does post-harvest confirmation require?

options.text: Keep it, but cook it longer — heat settles the question
options.label: A

options.text: Compare it to your previous year's harvest photos — same plant family, good enough
options.label: B

options.text: Discard it — when confirmation fails, the material is discarded, and cooking or drying does not destroy toxins anyway
options.label: C

options.text: Freeze it for a second opinion in a few weeks
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cleaning your harvest at home when you notice one unfamiliar leaf mixed in among the confirmed greens. The leaf has touched the rest of the batch. What is the correct call?

options.text: Pick out the unfamiliar leaf and continue with the rest — one leaf cannot ruin a whole bag
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the entire batch — unknown material touching identified material makes the batch unknown, and the mixing rule does not bend for a single leaf
options.label: B

options.text: Wash the whole batch thoroughly — a good rinse restores the batch to known status
options.label: C

options.text: Keep the batch but eat only the greens on top, which never touched the leaf
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Back from the outing, you wash the wild greens you collected. Which washing practice follows the hygiene guidance for wild-gathered plants?

options.text: A quick shake over the trail before packing — most debris falls off naturally
options.label: A

options.text: A light rinse in the stream you crossed on the way out — it is cold and clear
options.label: B

options.text: No washing at all — washing removes the flavor
options.label: C

options.text: Careful inspection and thorough washing with two or more changes of clean water, to remove grass, insects, and debris
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are packing your day-kit for a foraging outing: knife, labels, paper bags, and camera are in. What else belongs in the kit for the outing itself, in the spirit of a preparedness day-kit?

options.text: Nothing — a foraging trip is short, and the harvest is the priority
options.label: A

options.text: A second, larger harvest bag, in case the yield exceeds expectations
options.label: B

options.text: Water, sun protection, and a way to communicate — the same day-kit logic that makes any outing self-sufficient
options.label: C

options.text: A field guide only — everything else can be improvised
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After the trip, you learn the field you collected greens from had been treated with herbicide the previous week. Your harvest looks clean, and nothing is mixed. What does the abandonment guidance say?

options.text: The harvest is fine — the treatment was on the ground, not the plants
options.label: A

options.text: Discard the affected containers — contamination discovered after harvest is an abandonment trigger, and the batch is not worth the risk
options.label: B

options.text: Wash the harvest twice as thoroughly and proceed — extra washing compensates
options.label: C

options.text: Cook the harvest well — heat neutralizes residues and toxins alike
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your outing targets two species, and you brought two containers. What makes the separation rule work in the field, rather than just in principle?

options.text: Each container is labeled with its species before you fill it, and no container is ever refilled with a second species
options.label: A

options.text: Both containers stay empty until you return, so everything is sorted into them at home
options.label: B

options.text: The larger container holds the first species and the smaller one holds anything that is left over
options.label: C

options.text: Containers are labeled after filling, once you see what is inside
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In an old field you find a low plant with shiny purple-black berries that look exactly like blueberries. You have never positively identified this plant. What is the correct action?

options.text: Taste one berry — if it is sweet, the plant is safe
options.label: A

options.text: Pick a small handful to examine at home before deciding
options.label: B

options.text: Reject the berries until the whole plant is positively identified against authoritative sources — nightshade berries are documented poisonous, with immature berries particularly toxic
options.label: C

options.text: Pick them, since a berry that looks like a market berry must be edible
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You pick a dark berry from a bramble and it comes off with a cup-shaped hollow cavity in its center, and the core is left behind on the plant. What did you pick?

options.text: A raspberry — the receptacle is left behind, which is why the picked fruit is hollow
options.label: A

options.text: A blackberry — the spongy white core stays in the fruit
options.label: B

options.text: A nightshade berry — hollow fruits are always toxic
options.label: C

options.text: An unripe blackberry — blackberries are hollow while red
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An elderberry cluster has turned deep purple, almost black. You have confirmed the whole plant against two extension sources. Can you eat the berries raw from the bush?

options.text: Yes — deep purple means fully ripe and safe to eat raw
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — cooking is optional and only improves flavor
options.label: B

options.text: No — cook ripe elderberries before consumption, and unripe elderberries are never consumed
options.label: C

options.text: No — elderberries are toxic at every stage, ripe or cooked
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find persimmon fruit on a tree in early October. The fruit is orange, firm, and still attached to the branch. What is the documented situation?

options.text: Frost will make it safe — persimmons must experience a frost before they are edible
options.label: A

options.text: Unripe persimmons are intensely astringent from tannins; collectors wait for the fruit to become soft and fall from the tree — frost is not required
options.label: B

options.text: Firm fruit is perfectly ripe — soft fruit has spoiled
options.label: C

options.text: The fruit is safe at any stage as long as you peel it first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In June you find a small native tree with white five-petalled flowers and small round fruit darkening to deep reddish-purple. Which combination confirms it as serviceberry rather than a guess by fruit color?

options.text: The whole plant: small tree or shrub, five-petalled white flowers emerging before or with the leaves, and small pome fruit darkening when ripe — then confirm against a second source
options.label: A

options.text: The fruit is purple, and purple fruit on a tree is always serviceberry
options.label: B

options.text: The fruit is blueberry-sized, and size alone identifies the species
options.label: C

options.text: The season is June, and any fruit ripening in June is a serviceberry
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend shows you a plant in an abandoned lot with green berries and says, "The ripe ones are fine — people make jam from them in some places." You cannot positively identify the plant. What does the documentation say, and what do you do?

options.text: The friend is right — ripeness always removes toxicity, so pick only the darkest berries
options.label: A

options.text: The plant is fine because nightshade berries are never poisonous
options.label: B

options.text: Green berries are always safe because they are unripe
options.label: C

options.text: Nightshade berries and foliage are documented poisonous with immature berries particularly toxic, and toxicity varies greatly — without positive identification the correct action is rejection
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A blackberry patch along a busy road is loaded with ripe fruit and looks perfect. Per the site evaluation rule, what is the correct decision?

options.text: Harvest freely — the fruit looks identical to fruit from a clean site
options.label: A

options.text: Reject the site — brambles favor disturbed habitat, and roadsides carry documented contamination risks from traffic, spraying, and runoff
options.label: B

options.text: Harvest only the berries above head height, which are safe
options.label: C

options.text: Wash the berries twice at home, which removes all site contamination
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While snacking on apples from a wild tree, someone chews and swallows a handful of apple seeds. What does Poison Control document about the risk?

options.text: A single seed is deadly, so call 911 immediately
options.label: A

options.text: Apple seeds are harmless in any amount
options.label: B

options.text: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, a compound the body converts into cyanide; you would need to chew or grind hundreds of seeds to reach a toxic dose — but seeds should not be chewed or eaten
options.label: C

options.text: Only the peel is safe — the entire core is toxic
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a meadow you find a low creeping plant with three coarsely toothed leaflets and small red fruit. Its flowers are yellow. Which statement best fits the documentation?

options.text: It is the wild strawberry — yellow flowers are the normal color for the edible species
options.label: A

options.text: The edible wild strawberry (*Fragaria virginiana*) has five round white petals; a similar plant with yellow flowers is the mock or Indian strawberry (*Potentilla indica*), a documented confusion partner
options.label: B

options.text: Flower color is irrelevant to identification — the fruit decides
options.label: C

options.text: Yellow-flowered strawberries are a rare edible variety, so harvest freely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hiking partner argues, "Birds are eating these berries, so they are safe for people." Which response follows documented principles?

options.text: Wildlife feeding is not a documented safety rule — birds compete for serviceberries while nightshade berries are documented poisonous to humans, so only positive identification of the whole plant counts
options.label: A

options.text: Birds are a reliable proxy — they avoid every toxic plant
options.label: B

options.text: The argument is sound, since birds and humans share identical digestive chemistry
options.label: C

options.text: The argument is sound only for dark-colored berries, which birds prefer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In July you find a bramble with red berries on some canes and near-black berries on others. You know blackberries are red when unripe, and black raspberries are easily confused with blackberries. How do you decide what you are actually looking at?

options.text: The red berries are raspberries and the black ones are blackberries — color settles it
options.label: A

options.text: Pick only the black berries; any black bramble berry is a blackberry
options.label: B

options.text: All bramble berries are edible regardless of species, so identification is optional
options.label: C

options.text: Use the core test and cane characters on each cane: hollow core with the receptacle left behind means raspberry; spongy white core and purplish-red thorny canes mean blackberry
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is the first week of May and you are walking a riverbank. Which green's documented harvest window is now — and closes soon?

options.text: Dandelion — young leaves are harvested in early spring, before the plant flowers
options.label: A

options.text: Purslane — the summer garden weed is coming into season
options.label: B

options.text: Fiddleheads — the documented window is late April through May
options.label: C

options.text: Lamb's-quarters — summer young shoots are a few inches high
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have positively confirmed a plant's leaf shape and its papery scale covering, but you have not yet confirmed the stem character (smooth versus fuzzy) or the groove shape inside the stem. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Harvest the leaves only — the leaf character is the one that matters
options.label: A

options.text: Confirm every documented character before harvesting, and reject the plant while any character is unconfirmed
options.label: B

options.text: Harvest, but cook longer — longer cooking compensates for an unconfirmed identification
options.label: C

options.text: Compare the plant to a photo and harvest if it resembles the picture
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find two dandelion patches: one in a garden you know has not been sprayed or fertilized, and one along a roadside shoulder. Which is the documented acceptable harvest site?

options.text: The roadside patch — roadsides get more sun and grow healthier greens
options.label: A

options.text: Both patches, after thorough washing — washing removes any contamination
options.label: B

options.text: The untreated garden patch — harvest only from areas you know have not been treated with chemicals, fertilizers, or herbicides
options.label: C

options.text: Neither — dandelions are never safe to eat in any location
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You positively identify ostrich fern fiddleheads at a clean, untreated site. Which preparation sequence matches the documented method?

options.text: Rinse them quickly and eat them raw — they are a spring vegetable
options.label: A

options.text: Remove the brown papery scales, wash them in a colander several times in potable water, then boil at a full rolling boil for at least 15 minutes, or steam for 10–12 minutes
options.label: B

options.text: Sauté them lightly for 3 minutes until bright green
options.label: C

options.text: Parboil them for 2 minutes, then chill and serve cold
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have harvested young stinging nettle shoots with gloves, as documented. What must happen before they are food?

options.text: Soak them in warm water to remove dirt and debris, then boil them in salted water for five minutes — the stinging quality disappears after cooking
options.label: A

options.text: Rinse them in cold water — the sting washes off the hairs
options.label: B

options.text: Dry them in the sun for an afternoon before eating
options.label: C

options.text: Freeze them overnight — cold neutralizes the stinging hairs
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend insists raw fiddleheads are fine because they are "just spring vegetables," and lightly sautéing them makes them even better. What does the extension record say?

options.text: Raw fiddleheads simply taste unpleasant — cooking is only for flavor
options.label: A

options.text: Raw fiddleheads are safe if they were washed in potable water
options.label: B

options.text: Only fiddleheads harvested late in the season are unsafe raw
options.label: C

options.text: Several foodborne illness outbreaks have occurred from consuming raw or undercooked fiddleheads — cooking is a documented safety step
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Stinging nettle leaves carry hollow hairs that cause an intense burning and itching sensation. Which statement about making them edible is correct?

options.text: The sting is only a skin issue — cooked or raw, the plant is equally safe to eat
options.label: A

options.text: Cooking neutralizes the stinging hairs; the documented step is boiling the shoots
options.label: B

options.text: Only the oldest leaves sting — young shoots are safe to eat raw
options.label: C

options.text: Washing with dish detergent removes the sting from the leaves
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a leafy green you suspect is lamb's-quarters, but you cannot confirm the identification, and no reliable source tells you the documented preparation for this stage of this plant. What do you do?

options.text: Reject it — a plant whose identification or preparation requirement is unknown has no documented path to safety
options.label: A

options.text: Eat a small bite raw to test it — a little taste proves safety
options.label: B

options.text: Cook it the way you would cook spinach — similar greens prepare the same way
options.label: C

options.text: Harvest it and decide after you get home, when you have time to check
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which dandelion part and stage does the extension guidance document as the food to harvest?

options.text: Fully open flowers — the flowering plant is the most nutritious stage
options.label: A

options.text: Mature leaves in summer — older leaves are sweeter
options.label: B

options.text: Young leaves in early spring, before the plant flowers — older leaves are bitter
options.label: C

options.text: The flower stems — they are the tenderest part
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have harvested more fiddleheads than tonight's meal can use. What is the documented preservation path?

options.text: Freeze or pickle them using extension-tested recipes — and frozen fiddleheads still require the full documented cooking before serving
options.label: A

options.text: Dry them in the open air on a tarp — air-drying is the documented method for fiddleheads
options.label: B

options.text: Seal them in a plastic bag and keep them at room temperature for up to a week
options.label: C

options.text: Salt them heavily and serve the preserved batch raw
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After washing and preparing fresh greens, you will not use all of them today. What is the documented handling step, and what general principle applies?

options.text: Leave them out at room temperature — fresh greens keep fine for a day
options.label: A

options.text: Pack them airtight and store them in a cool, dark place indefinitely
options.label: B

options.text: Freeze them without any preparation — freezing any green is safe
options.label: C

options.text: Refrigerate unused greens promptly — documented for dandelion leaves — and follow storage principles of labeling, dating, and rotating
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an umbel-flowered plant in an open field and suspect it might be wild carrot. Which sequence correctly applies the differential identification method?

options.text: Write down the features you can observe, compare each one against a documented source for the candidate species, and check every diagnostic feature before confirming
options.label: A

options.text: Confirm from the single feature you are most confident about — feature lists are only for beginners
options.label: B

options.text: Match the overall silhouette to a photo you remember, and harvest if the outline looks right
options.label: C

options.text: Ask a companion whether it looks edible and proceed on their answer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are checking an umbel plant against a source that says wild carrot has hairy stems while poison hemlock is hairless with purplish blotches. The plant in front of you has hairless, blotched stems, but its height, leaf shape, and flower shape all match wild carrot. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Harvest it — the height, leaves, and flowers all matched, and the stem difference seems minor
options.label: A

options.text: Harvest only the flowers, since that is the part you verified
options.label: B

options.text: Abandon the identification and treat the plant as poison hemlock — one failing diagnostic feature means the identification is not confirmed
options.label: C

options.text: Crush the leaves; if the plant smells like carrot it is safe regardless of the stem
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is "it looks 90% right, so it is probably fine" a dangerous rule for wild-plant identification?

options.text: Because 90% of the time it is safe, and those odds justify eating
options.label: A

options.text: Because identification requires every diagnostic feature to match — the toxic look-alike matches most features by design and differs on the ones that matter, such as hairless purple-blotched stems
options.label: B

options.text: Because plants change appearance every few hours, so nothing can ever be identified
options.label: C

options.text: Because a 10% risk is only unacceptable for children, not for adults
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early summer you find a tall umbel plant with white flowers. The stem is smooth and hairless with small purplish blotches, the crushed leaves have no carrot smell, and the plant stands about 5 feet tall. Which identification does the evidence support?

options.text: Wild carrot, because the flowers are white and arranged in umbels
options.label: A

options.text: Wild carrot, because it is the more common of the two plants in open fields
options.label: B

options.text: Poison hemlock, because it lacks a carrot smell — the smell test alone settles it
options.label: C

options.text: Poison hemlock, because hairless stems, purplish blotches, height over two feet, and no carrot scent all match the documented features of poison hemlock
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early spring you dig up a bulb with grass-like leaves. Crushed, neither the bulb nor the leaves smell of onion. The leaves are thickened and V-creased in cross-section. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it as death camas: an onion-shaped bulb with no onion odor and V-creased grass-like leaves matches documented death camas features, so do not consume it
options.label: A

options.text: Eat it — an onion-shaped bulb of this size is safe by shape alone
options.label: B

options.text: Boil it thoroughly first, since cooking removes the risk from plant bulbs
options.label: C

options.text: Replant it and wait for flowers, then decide using only the flower color
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You slice a spring mushroom top-to-bottom. The cap is pitted like a honeycomb and attached to the stem at its base, but the interior of the stem is filled with solid material rather than hollow. What does the evidence indicate?

options.text: A true morel — the pits and the cap attachment are the only features that matter
options.label: A

options.text: A true morel — the mushroom is hollow where it counts
options.label: B

options.text: Not a confirmed true morel: documented true morels have a stem that is hollow along its length, and a filled stem matches the false-morel group, so the identification fails and you should not eat it
options.label: C

options.text: A safe mushroom, because false morels only appear in the fall
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why must each feature be compared against a documented source rather than trusted to memory or folklore?

options.text: Because features described from memory are always wrong in every detail
options.label: A

options.text: Because each diagnostic feature must be traceable to a documented description — memory and folklore can blend features of different plants, and a blended "feature" can hide a mismatch with the species you are checking
options.label: B

options.text: Because comparing against a source is legally required before any harvest
options.label: C

options.text: Because comparing against a source is only needed for mushrooms, not for plants
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A plant grows in the same wet patch as a plant you know is edible and looks nearly identical to it. Why is this similarity alone not enough to identify it as safe?

options.text: Resemblance is not identification: toxic look-alikes are documented to share the habitat and general appearance of harmless species — death camas bulbs resemble onions, and water hemlock grows beside water parsnip — so safety depends on checking diagnostic features, not similarity
options.label: A

options.text: Because plants growing in the same patch always become toxic from competition
options.label: B

options.text: Because similarity is only a problem during spring growth
options.label: C

options.text: Because harmless plants transform into toxic ones when crowded
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a wet meadow you are checking an umbel plant against a source for water parsnip, which says water parsnip leaves end at the leaf tips and its flowers have bracts. The plant's leaf veins end in the bottom of the serrations, and the flowers lack bracts. What is the correct action?

options.text: Harvest it anyway — water parsnip is a common plant and wet meadows are its habitat
options.label: A

options.text: Assume the source is describing a different region and proceed
options.label: B

options.text: Eat only the leaves, which is the part you were able to verify
options.label: C

options.text: Abandon the identification: veins ending in the serration bottoms and flowers without bracts match the documented water hemlock description, so treat the plant as water hemlock and do not consume it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Everyone in the area calls a certain plant "wild onion," and it grows where onions are known to grow. Why is the common name an unsafe basis for eating it?

options.text: Common names are always factually wrong
options.label: A

options.text: Common names are not diagnostic features — they vary by region and can be attached to different plants, so identification must come from documented features such as onion odor and bulb structure, not from what the plant is called
options.label: B

options.text: Because plants with common names are always toxic
options.label: C

options.text: Because common names are only unsafe for mushrooms
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Early spring: you find a cluster of grass-like plants with small bulbs and record your feature list — scaly onion-shaped bulbs, V-creased leaves, and no onion odor when crushed. Your source documents that death camas has onion-shaped bulbs, lacks onion odor, has V-creased grass-like leaves, and is poisonous at all growth stages. Which decision follows from the method?

options.text: Eat one bulb — the onion shape proves it is an onion
options.label: A

options.text: Eat only after frying, since heat removes the danger from plant bulbs
options.label: B

options.text: Do not consume it: every observed feature matches the documented death camas description, and death camas is poisonous at all growth stages
options.label: C

options.text: Eat the leaves but not the bulbs
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend says they can reliably tell edible wild mushrooms from poisonous ones "by sight," and offers to pick dinner for the group. Which statement best describes what is documented about visual identification?

options.text: Visual identification alone is error-prone — there is no test or characteristic that separates edible from poisonous mushrooms, and even experienced identifiers can be fooled by look-alikes
options.label: A

options.text: Visual identification is reliable once a person has correctly identified a few common species in their own region
options.label: B

options.text: Visual identification is reliable only for mushrooms that grow on wood
options.label: C

options.text: Visual identification is reliable if the mushroom is photographed first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hiker takes a clear photo of a mushroom, runs it through an identification app, and the app says "edible." What is the documented status of this decision?

options.text: An app match is a valid edibility decision if the photo is well lit
options.label: A

options.text: An app match is valid if the mushroom grows in a familiar habitat
options.label: B

options.text: A photo or app match is not sufficient for an edibility decision — expert-level examination of the actual mushroom is required
options.label: C

options.text: An app match is valid if a second person agrees with it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A family ate wild mushrooms at lunch. At 9 p.m., everyone feels completely fine. The most experienced member says, "See — they were safe, since no one got sick." What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: Nothing — poisonous mushrooms always cause symptoms within the first hour
options.label: A

options.text: Amatoxin symptoms are typically delayed 6–24 hours after ingestion, and by the time symptoms appear the toxins have already been absorbed — feeling fine now proves nothing
options.label: B

options.text: It is correct, because GI symptoms appearing 6–24 hours after a mushroom meal rule out amatoxin poisoning
options.label: C

options.text: It is correct, because symptoms can only appear while the mushroom is still being digested
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Someone argues, "If I boil it long enough, any mushroom becomes safe to eat." Which documented statement applies?

options.text: Boiling for 30 minutes destroys all known mushroom toxins
options.label: A

options.text: Cooking does not make a poisonous mushroom safe, and parboiling, drying, or pickling to remove toxins is a documented myth
options.label: B

options.text: Boiling is effective for amatoxins but not for other toxins
options.label: C

options.text: Boiling is effective only when combined with drying
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early spring you find mushrooms with wrinkled, brain-like caps that a companion insists are morels. Which statement about this look-alike situation is documented?

options.text: False morels grow at the same time as true morels, are commonly mistaken for them, must be regarded as poisonous, and can have deadly results
options.label: A

options.text: Wrinkled caps are the classic sign of a safe, fully grown true morel
options.label: B

options.text: False morels are safe once they are older and dry
options.label: C

options.text: False morels only cause mild stomach upset in children
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A child ate a mushroom from the yard two hours ago and shows no symptoms. What is the documented best response?

options.text: Wait until symptoms appear, since there is nothing to do until then
options.label: A

options.text: Make the child vomit and watch for two hours
options.label: B

options.text: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away, even without symptoms, and preserve a sample of the mushroom
options.label: C

options.text: Serve a bland meal and watch overnight
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A forager recommends using household "tests" — tarnishing silver, whether the mushroom grows on wood, and whether animals eat it — to check whether a wild mushroom is safe. What is the documented status of these tests?

options.text: A silver spoon that tarnishes over a mushroom proves the mushroom is poisonous
options.label: A

options.text: Mushrooms that grow on wood are always safe to eat
options.label: B

options.text: Mushrooms that animals eat are safe for people to eat
options.label: C

options.text: All of the above are documented myths — none is a reliable identification method
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A companion claims, "Any poisonous mushroom makes you sick within the hour — that's how you can always tell." Which documented response is accurate?

options.text: True — symptom timing is identical across all toxic species
options.label: A

options.text: Partly true — only large mushrooms have delayed symptoms
options.label: B

options.text: True — delayed symptoms only occur with mushrooms eaten in large quantities
options.label: C

options.text: False — amatoxin-containing mushrooms typically produce symptoms 6–24 hours after ingestion, and *Amanita* species may take 6–36 hours
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At a group gathering, a forager offers a dish made from mushrooms only they have identified, and says, "Just try a little — if it's toxic, it will be obvious." You cannot confirm the identification. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Refuse the dish — no mushroom should be eaten unless edibility is absolutely certain, and unidentified mushrooms belong out of the shared meal entirely
options.label: A

options.text: Eat a small amount, since a small portion of a toxic mushroom never causes serious illness
options.label: B

options.text: Eat a small amount after it is cooked, since cooking eliminates the risk
options.label: C

options.text: Accept it if the forager has picked mushrooms in their home region for years
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Someone says, "Only big, showy mushrooms can kill you — small brown ones are too small to be dangerous." Which documented statement is accurate?

options.text: Small brown mushrooms are never toxic
options.label: A

options.text: Only bright or colorful mushrooms contain amatoxins
options.label: B

options.text: The amatoxin group includes small brown species such as *Galerina marginata*, *Pholiotina (Conocybe) filaris*, and small *Lepiota* species, which require expert identification
options.label: C

options.text: Small brown mushrooms only cause skin irritation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You wake at 2 a.m. with vomiting and stomach cramps about 9 hours after a dinner that included wild mushrooms. No one else is sick yet. What is the documented best action?

options.text: Wait until someone else gets symptoms, to confirm it was the mushrooms
options.label: A

options.text: Call Poison Control immediately and seek medical evaluation — GI symptoms beginning 6–24 hours after a mushroom meal raise the amatoxin possibility, and a sample of the mushroom should be preserved
options.label: B

options.text: Treat it as ordinary food poisoning and return to sleep
options.label: C

options.text: Induce vomiting at home, then wait for the cramps to pass
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You examine a stem and find exactly two leaves attached directly across from each other at the same point on the stem, and the same pattern at the next node up. How do you record this arrangement?

options.text: Alternate — one leaf per node, staggered along the stem
options.label: A

options.text: Opposite — two leaves directly across from each other at the same node
options.label: B

options.text: Whorled — three or more leaves at the same point
options.label: C

options.text: Basal — all leaves gathered at ground level
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A leaf blade appears divided into several distinct leaflets arranged along a central stalk. How should you record this structure?

options.text: As a whorled leaf — the leaflets radiate from one point
options.label: A

options.text: As a simple leaf — one continuous blade with a wavy margin
options.label: B

options.text: As a compound leaf — leaflets arranged pinnately along a central stalk
options.label: C

options.text: As an entire-margined leaf — a smooth-edged single blade
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A plant's flowers match the photo in your field guide perfectly, but the leaves on your specimen are opposite where the guide shows alternate leaves. What does this tell you?

options.text: The plant is not identified — a key character disagrees with the reference, and the mismatch must be resolved
options.label: A

options.text: The plant is confirmed — the flower is the most visible and therefore the decisive character
options.label: B

options.text: The guide is wrong, since your specimen was found in the field
options.label: C

options.text: The plant must be a hybrid, which means it cannot be identified at all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have narrowed a plant to two similar species. The flowers look identical in both references, but the margin of the leaf differs slightly — entire in one, finely toothed in the other. To reach a positive identification, you should:

options.text: Choose the species with the more familiar common name
options.label: A

options.text: Verify the margin character — and all other key characters — against multiple authoritative sources before concluding
options.label: B

options.text: Decide by tasting a small piece of the leaf
options.label: C

options.text: Accept either species, since they are clearly close relatives
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an unknown plant and want to document it so an identification can be confirmed later. Which photo set best records the evidence?

options.text: A single close-up of the flower in bright light
options.label: A

options.text: Two photos of the leaves from above only
options.label: B

options.text: Whole plant in habitat, leaves top and underside, flowers and/or fruit, stem with buds, and a coin or ruler for scale
options.label: C

options.text: A photo of the location alone, with no plant close-ups
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are recording a leaf's characters and notice the blade edge is smooth with no teeth and no indentations. How do you record the margin?

options.text: Entire — the margin is smooth and unbroken
options.label: A

options.text: Lobed — the margin is deeply indented
options.label: B

options.text: Toothed — the margin has saw-like teeth
options.label: C

options.text: Compound — the margin divides into leaflets
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your photo app matches an unknown plant to an edible species with high confidence, but the plant is out of flower and you have never verified it in person against a reference. For a consumption decision, you should:

options.text: Eat a small piece — the app's match is a reliable identification
options.label: A

options.text: Consume only the parts visible in the app's photo
options.label: B

options.text: Proceed, but cook the plant thoroughly to be safe
options.label: C

options.text: Not consume it — a photo match is not positive identification, and without in-person verification against multiple authoritative sources the plant is unidentified
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A plant germinates in spring, grows, flowers, sets seed, and dies all within a single growing season. How do you classify its life cycle?

options.text: Annual — the whole life cycle completes in one season
options.label: A

options.text: Biennial — it takes two seasons to flower
options.label: B

options.text: Perennial — it lives for many seasons
options.label: C

options.text: Evergreen — it keeps its leaves through winter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early spring you find an unfamiliar plant with only juvenile leaves — no flowers, no fruit, and no seed heads. A quick look through your guide finds nothing that matches well. What does this mean for identification?

options.text: The plant is a new species no reference covers
options.label: A

options.text: Juvenile leaves are identical to mature leaves, so the match should still be possible with more effort
options.label: B

options.text: Identification is limited — without reproductive parts and with juvenile leaves, the plant may not be identifiable right now; document it and return in another season
options.label: C

options.text: The season has no effect — characters like margin are the same at every stage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an evergreen shrub with no flowers and no fruit. Which set of characters can still carry identification evidence?

options.text: The color of the leaves and the height of the shrub
options.label: A

options.text: Leaf arrangement, leaf shape and margin, underside surface, plus bark, buds, and stem features
options.label: B

options.text: Only the soil type it grows in
options.label: C

options.text: The direction the branches lean toward the sun
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You encounter a plant you cannot identify in the field, with time and light available. What is the best next action?

options.text: Dig it up so a specialist can examine the roots later
options.label: A

options.text: Walk on and trust that you will remember the leaf shape
options.label: B

options.text: Pick a leaf to confirm the identification later by taste
options.label: C

options.text: Photograph it fully — whole plant in habitat, leaves from both sides, stem, and any flowers or fruit with a scale reference — and note location and habitat before leaving
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A forager digs a smooth, white, onion-shaped bulb from the edge of a meadow. It looks and smells exactly like a domestic onion. What is the correct decision, and why?

options.text: Taste a small piece — the onion appearance and smell are enough confirmation
options.label: A

options.text: Do not eat it — underground parts cannot be identified from the dug-up part itself; positive aboveground identification comes first
options.label: B

options.text: Cook it thoroughly — heat makes any bulb safe to eat
options.label: C

options.text: Eat only the outer layer — toxins are said to concentrate in the skin
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which pairing of an underground structure with a documented example is correct?

options.text: Taproot — sunchoke, whose deep, slender roots grow to 3 feet in its second year
options.label: A

options.text: Bulb — burdock, whose storage organ is built from overlapping leaf scales
options.label: B

options.text: Rhizome — cattail, which the USDA plant guide describes as an "underground stem"
options.label: C

options.text: Tuber — ramps, whose spring bulbs are technically swollen stems
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A drainage ditch beside an actively sprayed agricultural field holds dense cattails. Why should you NOT harvest the rhizomes there?

options.text: The ground may carry spray runoff — contaminated soil rules out harvesting underground parts
options.label: A

options.text: Cattail rhizomes are never edible at any stage of growth
options.label: B

options.text: Rhizomes can only be harvested in spring, and it is autumn
options.label: C

options.text: The water is fine; only the green shoots are a problem, and they are toxic
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have positively identified cattails in a clean wetland and want the starchy rhizomes. Which preparation is documented in the USDA plant guide?

options.text: Rhizomes must be leached in running water for several days before use
options.label: A

options.text: Only the pollen, never the rhizomes, is food
options.label: B

options.text: Rhizomes are safe only after fermentation
options.label: C

options.text: Rhizomes can be eaten raw, baked, roasted, or broiled, and the core can be ground into flour
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A ramp patch holds roughly 100 plants. Per NC State Extension guidance for wild populations, harvests should be limited to:

options.text: Half the patch — ramps regrow quickly from their roots
options.label: A

options.text: 5% to 10% of the plants in each plot — ramps are slow-growing and intensive harvesting is seriously damaging wild populations
options.label: B

options.text: Every plant with a flower stalk — those are the largest and most robust
options.label: C

options.text: All the leaves and bulbs — the leaves regrow within a week
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find an underground food you cannot positively identify: the aboveground parts match nothing you know, and you have no field guide. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Reject it — no identification, no digging, no tasting
options.label: A

options.text: Dig a small sample and carry it home to compare with pictures later
options.label: B

options.text: Taste a tiny bit — small amounts of most roots are harmless
options.label: C

options.text: Cook and eat a small portion, then wait a day to see if you feel ill
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend plans to dig every sunchoke (Jerusalem artichoke) tuber from a patch, arguing that the plant is perennial and will grow back. What does the documented evidence say?

options.text: Sunchokes die after a single harvest, so nothing grows back regardless
options.label: A

options.text: Digging everything is harmless because sunchoke tubers are annual structures
options.label: B

options.text: Sunchokes spread by rhizomes, and any tiny piece of the plant left in the soil will sprout new plants — full excavation is wasteful and unnecessary
options.label: C

options.text: The patch regrows faster the more thoroughly it is dug
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After harvesting arrowhead tubers, how did documented practice keep them for winter use?

options.text: Stored raw in water until spring — water keeps them crisp
options.label: A

options.text: Buried in wetland mud — mud and ice preserve them
options.label: B

options.text: Kept in a warm, brightly lit room to cure
options.label: C

options.text: Roasted tubers were dried and stored; the Chippewa strung them and hung them overhead to dry, boiling them later for use
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In late autumn you find a burdock plant whose second-year root is long and fibrous. What is the documented guidance for this stage?

options.text: The fibrous second-year root is the most nutritious — harvest it first
options.label: A

options.text: First-year roots are harvested by late autumn before becoming too fibrous; young leaves and immature flower stalks are edible before flowers appear
options.label: B

options.text: Only the flower stalks are edible, and only in winter
options.label: C

options.text: The root becomes edible only after the plant has flowered
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In early spring you see a patch of broad green leaves with a strong garlic-onion smell in rich, moist hardwood forest, and you believe these are ramps. What must happen before any digging?

options.text: Positive aboveground identification using documented characteristics — habitat, season, leaf shape, and odor — before the bulbs are touched
options.label: A

options.text: Dig one bulb and compare it with a store-bought onion
options.label: B

options.text: Smell the dug bulb — the odor alone is conclusive
options.label: C

options.text: Taste a leaf; the flavor confirms the species
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does the structure of the underground part matter for harvest sustainability?

options.text: Structure affects only flavor, not regrowth
options.label: A

options.text: Tubers always regrow faster than bulbs, so collection limits are unnecessary
options.label: B

options.text: Structures regrow differently — rhizomes left in the ground resprout, while digging out every storage organ removes the plant's regrowth source, which is why documented limits exist (no more than 1/4 of the plants in an area; 5–10% for ramps)
options.label: C

options.text: Structure matters only for choosing raw versus cooked preparation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A worker falls onto a broken bottle and cuts their thigh. Blood is flowing continuously and the pant leg is soaked through within a minute. Which observation makes this bleeding life-threatening?

options.text: The blood is flowing continuously and the volume is high — the pant leg is soaked through
options.label: A

options.text: The wound is bleeding at all, so any bleeding is life-threatening
options.label: B

options.text: The cut is on the leg, and leg wounds are always life-threatening
options.label: C

options.text: The worker is standing, and standing increases blood pressure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are applying a tourniquet to a person bleeding heavily from a forearm wound. Where do you place it?

options.text: Directly on top of the wound, to press on it as hard as possible
options.label: A

options.text: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart, avoiding the elbow joint
options.label: B

options.text: As high as possible on the arm, at the armpit, because "high and tight" is the rule
options.label: C

options.text: On the elbow joint, because joints are the strongest part of the limb
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are pressing firmly on a wound and the gauze you are pressing on is soaked through with blood. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the soaked gauze and place a fresh one directly on the wound
options.label: A

options.text: Stop pressing and look at the wound to check how fast it is bleeding
options.label: B

options.text: Add another dressing on top of the soaked one and keep pressing firmly
options.label: C

options.text: Replace the soaked gauze with a tourniquet, even though the wound is on the torso
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person is impaled in the thigh by a thin metal rod that is still in place. Which action is correct?

options.text: Pull the rod out quickly — the wound will bleed more cleanly and clot faster
options.label: A

options.text: Leave the rod in place, press firmly around it, and pad and bandage around the object
options.label: B

options.text: Remove the rod, then apply a tourniquet above the wound
options.label: C

options.text: Leave the rod and apply direct pressure directly on top of the rod
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person has life-threatening bleeding from a deep wound in the groin. Direct pressure is not slowing it. There is no tourniquet that can help. What is the correct intervention?

options.text: Wound packing with gauze plus direct pressure — if you have been trained to pack wounds
options.label: A

options.text: Apply the tourniquet around the waist, as close to the wound as possible
options.label: B

options.text: Elevate the leg and wait — elevation alone will stop the bleeding
options.label: C

options.text: Cover the wound loosely with a shirt and continue asking questions to keep the person awake
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which situation requires calling emergency services immediately, rather than continuing first aid alone?

options.text: A shallow scraped knee that has stopped bleeding after two minutes of pressure
options.label: A

options.text: Bleeding that cannot be controlled, a tourniquet applied, or signs of shock
options.label: B

options.text: A minor cut that is still oozing slightly after the bleeding stopped
options.label: C

options.text: A person who is tired but otherwise comfortable after a fall
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After heavy bleeding from a leg wound, the person's skin is pale, cool, and clammy; their pulse is rapid and weak; and they seem confused. What does this mean, and what should you do?

options.text: They are simply tired from the accident; let them rest and check again in ten minutes
options.label: A

options.text: They are having an allergic reaction; give them water to drink and watch closely
options.label: B

options.text: This is shock — a life-threatening emergency; keep them warm and flat with feet raised, and ensure emergency services are on the way
options.label: C

options.text: This is normal blood loss; elevate the injured leg and continue pressure without further action
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have tightened a windlass tourniquet on an arm and twisted the rod. The person is crying out in pain and the bleeding has not fully stopped yet. What should you do?

options.text: Loosen the tourniquet slightly to reduce the pain, then re-tighten
options.label: A

options.text: Remove the tourniquet and resume direct pressure only
options.label: B

options.text: Stop tightening and hold the current tension — pain means it is working
options.label: C

options.text: Keep twisting until the bleeding stops or the rod cannot twist further, then secure it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person has life-threatening bleeding from an arm wound, and no tourniquet is available anywhere nearby. Direct pressure alone is not controlling it. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Tie a thin shoelace tightly around the arm above the wound
options.label: A

options.text: Keep the arm raised and apply cold water to slow the flow
options.label: B

options.text: Continue direct pressure only — nothing else can be done without a tourniquet
options.label: C

options.text: Pack the wound with gauze (if trained) and keep direct pressure on top of it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You applied a tourniquet 12 minutes ago and the bleeding has stopped. EMS has not yet arrived, and the person asks you to loosen it because it hurts. What is the correct response?

options.text: Do not loosen or remove it — only a medical professional removes a tourniquet; reassure the person and keep it in place
options.label: A

options.text: Loosen it just a little — the bleeding has stopped, so the pressure is no longer needed
options.label: B

options.text: Remove it now and switch to direct pressure, since the wound has stopped bleeding
options.label: C

options.text: Loosen it and re-tighten every five minutes to protect the limb
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person's sleeve caught fire and is out, but the burned forearm still feels hot under the fabric. What is the first first-aid action?

options.text: Apply butter to the burn to soothe the pain
options.label: A

options.text: Move the person away from the heat source and start cooling the burn with cool running water
options.label: B

options.text: Break any blisters that formed so the fluid can drain
options.label: C

options.text: Wrap the arm tightly with an airtight dressing to keep out air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A burn is red, dry, and painful, with no blisters. At first-aid level, how is it best classified?

options.text: Full-thickness (third-degree) — it will turn leathery soon
options.label: A

options.text: Partial-thickness (second-degree) — the moist layer is exposed
options.label: B

options.text: Superficial (first-degree) — only the outer layer of skin is damaged
options.label: C

options.text: Chemical — the color indicates an acid exposure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cooling a scald on an adult's forearm. What is the correct cooling step?

options.text: Run cool (not ice-cold) water over the burn for at least 5–30 minutes, stopping early if the person becomes chilled
options.label: A

options.text: Hold the arm under ice-cold water for two minutes to numb it
options.label: B

options.text: Press a bag of ice directly on the burn for 15 minutes
options.label: C

options.text: Rinse for less than a minute, then apply an ointment to protect the skin
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A partial-thickness burn has blisters. Which action must be avoided?

options.text: Leaving the blisters intact
options.label: A

options.text: Covering the burn loosely with a clean, dry dressing
options.label: B

options.text: Removing rings and watches before swelling sets in
options.label: C

options.text: Popping the blisters to drain the fluid
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Dry chemical powder is on a person's arm. What is the correct first-aid response?

options.text: Brush off excess dry chemical, remove contaminated clothing, then flush the skin with cool running water for at least 15 minutes
options.label: A

options.text: Add water immediately before removing the powder so it dissolves
options.label: B

options.text: Neutralize the chemical with vinegar or baking soda before flushing
options.label: C

options.text: Wipe the powder away with a cloth, then apply oil to protect the skin
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person is in contact with an electrical source. What is the first thing to do?

options.text: Pull the person away from the source with your bare hands
options.label: A

options.text: Safely turn off the power — unplug the device or trip the breaker — before touching the person
options.label: B

options.text: Pour water on the wire or appliance to cool it
options.label: C

options.text: Cover the person with a wet blanket to insulate them
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a fire, which set of signs should make you suspect inhalation injury and seek emergency care?

options.text: A single small blister on the forearm with mild pain
options.label: A

options.text: Red, dry skin that looks sunburned
options.label: B

options.text: Sooty nose or mouth, coughing, a hoarse voice, and difficulty breathing
options.label: C

options.text: A painless, waxy patch that seems to be healing
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does a full-thickness burn that is waxy or leathery require emergency medical care even if its center does not hurt?

options.text: It will heal by itself once the pain stops
options.label: A

options.text: The lack of pain proves the burn is only superficial
options.label: B

options.text: It only needs the same home care as a minor burn
options.label: C

options.text: Deep damage may have destroyed nerve endings, and full-thickness burns are severe regardless of size
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Several days after a minor burn, which finding means you should seek medical care?

options.text: Increasing pain, redness spreading outward from the burn, pus, or fever
options.label: A

options.text: Mild itching around the healing edge
options.label: B

options.text: Slight tenderness when the dressing is changed
options.label: C

options.text: The scabbed area flaking off as it heals
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which situation requires calling emergency services rather than first aid alone?

options.text: A 1-inch superficial burn on the forearm that is red and painful
options.label: A

options.text: A small partial-thickness blister on the shin
options.label: B

options.text: A full-thickness burn on the hand after a household electrical shock
options.label: C

options.text: Mild sunburn across the shoulders
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You come upon a car crash. A power line has fallen across the car, and the driver is slumped over the wheel. A bystander is about to run to the car. What should you do?

options.text: Run to the car with the bystander — every second counts for the driver
options.label: A

options.text: Push the power line off the car with a long wooden branch
options.label: B

options.text: Do not approach: stay at least 20 feet (6 meters) away and keep others back until the power is off, and call the emergency number
options.label: C

options.text: Open the driver's door and pull them out while the wire is still on the car
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have confirmed a scene is safe and reach a person lying motionless on the ground. What is the first step of the primary assessment?

options.text: Shout-tap-shout: tap the shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?" to check responsiveness
options.label: A

options.text: Roll the person into the recovery position to protect the airway
options.label: B

options.text: Start chest compressions immediately
options.label: C

options.text: Give the person a sip of water to see if they wake up
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person collapses in a crowded park, and you have confirmed they are unresponsive and not breathing normally. There are bystanders nearby. What is the best way to get emergency help called?

options.text: Begin compressions and hope someone in the crowd calls on their own
options.label: A

options.text: Point to one specific bystander and say, "You — call the local emergency number, now," then begin hands-only CPR
options.label: B

options.text: Stop and shout to the whole crowd, "Someone call an ambulance!"
options.label: C

options.text: Call the number yourself only after checking the rest of the person for injuries
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An unresponsive person makes occasional gasping sounds. How should you treat this breathing?

options.text: As normal breathing — gasping means air is getting in
options.label: A

options.text: As normal breathing only if the gasps come in a steady rhythm
options.label: B

options.text: Wait 30 seconds to see whether the gasping becomes regular before deciding
options.label: C

options.text: As not breathing normally — gasping is not normal breathing, so act and begin hands-only CPR after calling for help
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person is unresponsive but breathing normally, and you do not suspect a spine injury. Help has been called and is on the way. What should you do while waiting?

options.text: Place the person in the recovery position and keep checking breathing until help arrives
options.label: A

options.text: Leave the person lying flat on their back and do not touch them
options.label: B

options.text: Begin chest compressions — unresponsiveness means CPR
options.label: C

options.text: Sit the person up to make breathing easier
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a person unresponsive and not breathing normally. You have sent someone to call the emergency number. What is your next action?

options.text: Wait for the emergency responders to arrive — compressions by untrained helpers can cause harm
options.label: A

options.text: Place the person in the recovery position until help arrives
options.label: B

options.text: Begin hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 2 inches deep, minimizing interruptions
options.label: C

options.text: Splash water on the face and shout to try to wake the person
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two people are injured in the same incident. One is shouting and calling for help; the other is silent and unresponsive on the ground. Who should you check first?

options.text: The person shouting — responsive casualties can tell you what happened
options.label: A

options.text: The unresponsive person — quiet casualties can be the sickest, so check the unresponsive one first
options.label: B

options.text: Whichever person is closest to you
options.label: C

options.text: The person shouting — they are in pain and need the most help
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You placed an unresponsive person who was breathing normally into the recovery position, and the emergency call has been made. What do you do now?

options.text: Your part is done — the call is what matters now
options.label: A

options.text: Check breathing once more after five minutes, then stop
options.label: B

options.text: Leave them once they look stable, to avoid disturbing them
options.label: C

options.text: Keep rechecking breathing and bleeding — the reassessment loop runs until responders arrive, and if breathing stops, roll them onto their back and begin CPR
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A person fell from a ladder, is conscious, and says their neck hurts. The scene is safe. What is the right action?

options.text: Keep them still, support the head and neck, and do not move them — move only if the scene becomes unsafe
options.label: A

options.text: Help them sit up so they can breathe more easily
options.label: B

options.text: Walk them to the shade while supporting one arm
options.label: C

options.text: Ask them to turn their head from side to side to check if it is just a strain
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before an emergency happens, which household practice most directly supports in-the-moment emergency assessment?

options.text: Memorizing the exact words of this quiz — recall under stress is guaranteed
options.label: A

options.text: Knowing the local emergency number, planning who calls for help, and practicing the plan as a household
options.label: B

options.text: Buying the largest first aid kit available — the equipment does the thinking
options.label: C

options.text: Waiting to read about first aid only when an emergency happens, to keep it fresh
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are stocking a new household first-aid kit and want to start with the wound-care layer. Which set of supplies belongs in that layer?

options.text: Matches, candles, and a fire extinguisher — fire safety gear doubles as wound care
options.label: A

options.text: Antibiotic ointment, pain reliever, antihistamine, and hydrocortisone cream — medications are the wound-care layer
options.label: B

options.text: Sterile gauze, adhesive tape, and antiseptic wipes — bandages are optional if you have gauze
options.label: C
