options.text: Sterile gauze pads, adhesive bandages in assorted sizes, adhesive tape, and antiseptic wipes — the core wound-care set
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Guidance lists consistently specify non-latex gloves for first-aid kits. Why?

options.text: Non-latex gloves protect the responder while avoiding allergic reactions for people with latex sensitivity
options.label: A

options.text: Latex gloves tear too easily to be useful for bleeding control
options.label: B

options.text: Non-latex gloves keep hands completely sterile
options.label: C

options.text: Latex gloves are banned for any first-aid use
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A member of your household takes a daily prescription medication. Which practice is correct for the household kit?

options.text: Skip prescription medications — over-the-counter pain relievers cover most emergencies
options.label: A

options.text: Include a 7-day supply of personal prescription medications, stored with original labels, following label instructions, and replaced before expiration
options.label: B

options.text: Add a supply of prescription antibiotics so the kit can treat infections without a doctor
options.label: C

options.text: Store a 30-day extra supply with instructions to share among household members
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend shows you her kit: instant cold packs and a thermometer sit on top, while bandages, tape, and antiseptic wipes are buried at the bottom of an unlabeled pouch. What organizational principle does this violate?

options.text: Kit contents should always be stored in strict alphabetical order
options.label: A

options.text: All items belong in one unlabeled pouch to save space
options.label: B

options.text: Most-used items should be on top and grouped in transparent, labeled pouches so a responder can find them fast
options.label: C

options.text: Items should only be reorganized after an emergency has occurred
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are setting a maintenance schedule for the household kit. Which cadence best matches preparedness guidance?

options.text: Check every six months (clock-change days work well), restock after any use, and check again before trips
options.label: A

options.text: Check once at purchase — sealed supplies never expire
options.label: B

options.text: Check only after a major emergency
options.label: C

options.text: Check every day to catch any single expired item
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are building a small kit to keep in your vehicle. Compared with the home kit, the vehicle kit should be:

options.text: Identical to the home kit so you never lack options
options.label: A

options.text: Sized to hold the entire household water supply
options.label: B

options.text: Focused on comfort items, since emergencies at home are covered
options.label: C

options.text: A compact version covering the basics — wound care, medications, gloves, and a blanket — since it travels with you
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household includes a 4-year-old, a grandparent with a daily prescription, and a dog. When adapting the kit, which step is the most appropriate?

options.text: Keep one generic kit sized for the largest adult — one kit fits all
options.label: A

options.text: Add child-appropriate bandage sizes, include the grandparent's personal medications (7-day supply), and add a small pet section — stock for medical history, ages, and the household itself
options.label: B

options.text: Buy a second identical generic kit so each person gets their own
options.label: C

options.text: Remove all medications from the kit so the child cannot reach them
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement about the limits of a first-aid kit is true?

options.text: A complete kit removes the need for first-aid training
options.label: A

options.text: A kit with a manual inside is the same as taking a first-aid course
options.label: B

options.text: A kit is equipment — knowing how to use it, and knowing when to call emergency services, matters as much as owning it
options.label: C

options.text: Only trained professionals should keep a kit at home
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your household's emergency supplies include stored water alongside the first-aid kit. Which practice is correct for the water?

options.text: Rotate or replace stored water on a schedule, just like medications, so it stays usable
options.label: A

options.text: Stored water does not expire, so it never needs checking
options.label: B

options.text: Water only needs checking after the kit has been used
options.label: C

options.text: Replace the water only when it visibly changes color
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor says, "We have a great kit, so we are prepared." Which response reflects the correct relationship between the kit and the household plan?

options.text: A well-stocked kit makes a written household plan unnecessary
options.label: A

options.text: The plan only matters during evacuation drills
options.label: B

options.text: The kit replaces the need to call emergency services for severe bleeding
options.label: C

options.text: The kit is equipment — the plan (where the kit lives, who knows it, when to call for help) is what makes it usable in an emergency
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are first on the scene after a hiker falls onto an outstretched hand. Her wrist is bent at an odd angle, swollen, and she heard a "snap" at the moment of impact. What is the best first response?

options.text: Treat it as a possible fracture: keep the limb still, support it, and prepare to splint it in the position found
options.label: A

options.text: Ask her to flex and rotate the wrist to test whether the bone is actually broken
options.label: B

options.text: Gently pull the wrist back into a straight position so it can be wrapped
options.label: C

options.text: Let her rest a few minutes — if the pain eases, she can continue hiking
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend insists her twisted ankle is "just a sprain" and wants to walk it off. Which statement best reflects what a first aider should do?

options.text: Agree — sprains are always less serious than fractures and heal on their own
options.label: A

options.text: Explain that a sprain cannot be reliably distinguished from a fracture without imaging, so treat it as a possible fracture: immobilize, don't walk on it, and get it evaluated
options.label: B

options.text: Walk with her while checking whether the limp worsens over the next hour
options.label: C

options.text: Wrap it in a tight bandage and have her jog briefly to confirm it is only a strain
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are splinting a mid-forearm injury. Which splint placement follows the joints-above-and-below principle?

options.text: Only across the injured area itself, to keep the splint compact
options.label: A

options.text: Just beyond the injury on each end, leaving the joints free to move
options.label: B

options.text: Long enough to immobilize both the joint below the injury (the wrist) and the joint above it (the elbow)
options.label: C

options.text: From the elbow to the shoulder, to stabilize the whole upper arm
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After applying a splint to a leg injury, what is the correct way to check that circulation and function are intact?

options.text: Nothing is needed — a correctly tied splint never affects circulation
options.label: A

options.text: Ask the person to rate the pain on a scale of 1 to 10
options.label: B

options.text: Compare both limbs for equal swelling
options.label: C

options.text: Check the color, warmth, and feeling in the toes beyond the splint, and note whether the person can move them
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A fallen climber has a lower leg that is bent at an unusual angle. Before splinting, what should you do about the deformity?

options.text: Splint the leg in the position it was found — do not try to straighten or realign it
options.label: A

options.text: Straighten the leg gently so the splint can sit flat against it
options.label: B

options.text: Pull firmly on the foot to align the bone before immobilizing
options.label: C

options.text: Apply a tight bandage above the deformity to relieve pressure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A mountain biker crashes and cannot move his leg; the foot below the injury is pale and cold. What action is required first?

options.text: Have him wiggle his toes every few minutes to restore warmth
options.label: A

options.text: Elevate the leg on a pack and wait an hour to see if color returns
options.label: B

options.text: Call for emergency medical services immediately — pale, cold, or blue below an injury signals a limb-threatening problem
options.label: C

options.text: Rub the foot vigorously to restore circulation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An older hiker slips on wet rock and lands hard on her side; she now has pain in her hip and cannot stand. What should you do?

options.text: Help her to her feet to check whether the hip will bear weight
options.label: A

options.text: Keep her still and supported, do not move her, and wait for emergency medical services
options.label: B

options.text: Carry her to the trailhead so she can see a doctor sooner
options.label: C

options.text: Have her take a few steps while you support her weight
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You must improvise a splint for a wrist injury at a campsite. Which combination of materials and placement works best?

options.text: A thin metal rod tied tightly directly over the injured area
options.label: A

options.text: A folded shirt wrapped loosely around the wrist, with no rigid support
options.label: B

options.text: Two pens taped only to the hand, leaving the wrist free to bend
options.label: C

options.text: A rolled newspaper padded with a folded cloth, extending from the wrist to above the elbow, tied above and below the injury
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While waiting for transport, you apply a cold pack to a swollen ankle. Which application is correct?

options.text: Wrap the cold pack in a thin, dry towel and apply it for no more than 20 minutes at a stretch, with breaks between applications
options.label: A

options.text: Place the cold pack directly on the skin and leave it for 45 minutes
options.label: B

options.text: Apply the cold pack over the top of the splint continuously until transport arrives
options.label: C

options.text: Skip the cold pack — cold always makes swelling worse
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A boy says he is fine because "I can still move my wrist, so it can't be broken." What should you tell him?

options.text: He is right — being able to move the joint rules out a fracture
options.label: A

options.text: He is probably right, but he should still ice it as a precaution
options.label: B

options.text: A fracture can still be present even when the limb can be moved — an X-ray is usually required to diagnose a broken bone
options.label: C

options.text: He should move it repeatedly to prove it is uninjured
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a hot afternoon, a hiker shows heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, and nausea. Her skin feels cool and moist, her breathing is rapid, and her pulse is fast and weak — but she answers questions clearly. What is the best assessment and action?

options.text: Heat stroke — call emergency services immediately and begin aggressive cooling
options.label: A

options.text: Heat cramps — rest a few minutes in place, then continue the hike
options.label: B

options.text: Heat exhaustion — move to a cool place, loosen clothing, have her sip cool water, cool her down, and monitor closely
options.label: C

options.text: Dehydration with no illness — normal trail symptoms that resolve with food
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hiker collapses on a 98°F day. His skin is hot and sweaty, and he is confused, slurring his words, and does not recognize the trail. Which set of actions is correct?

options.text: Call emergency services immediately; move him to shade, remove excess clothing, and cool aggressively — cold water immersion if possible, and cold packs on the neck, armpits, and groin — while waiting
options.label: A

options.text: Give him a cold sports drink, let him rest in place for an hour, and reassess; no call needed unless he worsens
options.label: B

options.text: Walk him slowly back to the car with your arm supporting him, then decide what to do
options.label: C

options.text: Fan him gently but keep him in the sun, since the heat is familiar to him and movement speeds cooling
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a friend outside on a cold evening. She is confused and drowsy, her breathing has slowed, and she has stopped shivering even though she is cold and wet. What is the situation?

options.text: She is recovering — the shivering stopping means her body has warmed itself
options.label: A

options.text: She has frostbite of the extremities and needs her hands and feet warmed first
options.label: B

options.text: She is simply tired from the cold and needs rest and food before going inside
options.label: C

options.text: Severe hypothermia — an emergency. Handle her gently, keep her still, warm her gradually, and call EMS
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gardener has been working through the afternoon heat and now has heavy sweating, dizziness, and nausea, but is thinking clearly. Which first-aid sequence is correct for heat exhaustion?

options.text: Keep working but drink a caffeinated beverage to restore energy
options.label: A

options.text: Stop, move to a cool or shaded place, loosen or remove excess clothing, sip cool water, cool the body with compresses or a cool shower, and monitor closely
options.label: B

options.text: Lie flat in the sun to warm the muscles, then resume work slowly
options.label: C

options.text: Take fever-reducing medication and continue with the workday
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a freezing day, your friend's fingertips have turned white and feel numb and waxy. You are indoors, and there is no risk of refreezing. What is the correct rewarming approach?

options.text: Rub the fingers briskly with your hands until color returns
options.label: A

options.text: Hold them near a hot stove or radiator to speed the thaw
options.label: B

options.text: Immerse them in warm — not hot — water for about 20–30 minutes, or use body heat such as an armpit
options.label: C

options.text: Blow warm breath on them while massaging firmly
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are helping a person with severe hypothermia who is confused and barely responsive. Which actions are correct?

options.text: Handle her gently and keep her still, warm the center of the body first with dry blankets, and call EMS — no alcohol or caffeine, and nothing by mouth unless she is fully alert
options.label: A

options.text: Get her moving briskly to generate body heat, then give her a warm alcoholic drink
options.label: B

options.text: Put her in a hot shower immediately and rub her arms and legs vigorously
options.label: C

options.text: Warm her hands and feet first with a heating pad, since the extremities are coldest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A heat wave is forecast, and you are planning a weekend of outdoor work. Which arrangement follows heat-illness prevention guidance?

options.text: Do all the heavy work at midday when the crew is fully awake, and hydrate only when thirsty
options.label: A

options.text: Skip rest breaks in the shade so the work finishes before the heat peaks
options.label: B

options.text: Leave a child in a parked car for ten minutes with the windows cracked while you load equipment
options.label: C

options.text: Schedule exertion for the cooler hours, take rest breaks in the shade, drink fluids throughout, and never leave anyone — especially children — in a parked car
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a winter hike, your partner starts tripping over roots, mumbling answers that do not match the questions, fumbling with the map, and grumbling about small frustrations — he is shivering, and his skin is cold. What do these "umbles" tell you?

options.text: He is just having a bad day and needs the pace picked up to warm him
options.label: A

options.text: These are early signs of hypothermia — cooling is affecting his coordination and thinking, so stop, get him out of the wind, remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground, and warm him
options.label: B

options.text: He is dehydrated and needs only water before continuing
options.label: C

options.text: He is developing frostbite and only his hands and feet need attention
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hunter returns to camp with a frostbitten foot — the toes are white, waxy, and hard. It is a 20-minute walk to a heated cabin, and the temperature outside is below freezing. What should be done?

options.text: Soak the foot in warm water at the campfire site before walking anywhere
options.label: A

options.text: Rub the toes with snow to restore circulation, then walk to the cabin
options.label: B

options.text: Do not walk on the frozen foot; protect the area from injury and rewarm only once in a warm place where the tissue can stay thawed — and seek professional care for deep frostbite
options.label: C

options.text: Pop any blisters that form and apply a heating pad to the toes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before a cold-weather outing, which preparation best follows the prevention principles that reduce the risk of hypothermia and frostbite?

options.text: Check the forecast and plan the route and exit options, pack dry layers and wind protection, cover hands, feet, ears, nose, and cheeks, and arrange to check each other for shivering and behavior changes during the outing
options.label: A

options.text: Pack one heavy cotton sweatshirt, rely on the car heater if it gets cold, and skip the forecast since the season is predictable
options.label: B

options.text: Plan to keep moving at full pace all day so no one has time to get cold, and leave extra clothing behind to lighten the pack
options.label: C

options.text: Rely on experience alone — people who have hiked for years can judge cold without planning
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend cuts her palm on a broken jar at a picnic. The cut is deep and gaping, roughly the size of your thumbnail, and the edges do not meet. Bleeding is steady but slowing under pressure. Based on your assessment, what should you do?

options.text: Rinse it at the picnic table, cover it, and tell her to check it in a week — minor wounds usually heal on their own
options.label: A

options.text: Call 911 immediately — any wound that bleeds at all is an emergency
options.label: B

options.text: Apply direct pressure, then take her to urgent care — a deep, gaping wound of this size may need stitches
options.label: C

options.text: Press the edges together and tape them shut with first-aid tape so it can heal closed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are the first person to reach someone who slipped and cut their forearm on a sharp rock. The wound is bleeding heavily. What is the FIRST priority?

options.text: Steady direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze, with the arm raised, until the bleeding is controlled
options.label: A

options.text: Rinse the wound with clean water immediately so dirt does not dry into it
options.label: B

options.text: Apply antibiotic ointment before dressing, so infection cannot get in
options.label: C

options.text: Remove any visible debris with tweezers before blood covers it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cleaning a shallow scrape on your own knee. Which cleaning approach matches current first-aid guidance?

options.text: Douse it with hydrogen peroxide and let it bubble — bubbles mean it is working
options.label: A

options.text: Scrub the wound itself hard with soap and a washcloth to be thorough
options.label: B

options.text: Rinse the wound with clean running water, then wash the surrounding skin with mild soap — never hydrogen peroxide or rubbing alcohol
options.label: C

options.text: Wipe it dry with a paper towel and bandage it without cleaning, since it looks clean
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After dressing a minor cut with a sterile non-stick pad, when should the dressing be changed?

options.text: Never, until it falls off — removing it disturbs the healing wound
options.label: A

options.text: Only after a full week, to give the wound time to close
options.label: B

options.text: Every hour, so the wound is checked constantly
options.label: C

options.text: At least once a day — and sooner if it becomes wet, dirty, or blood-soaked
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You cut yourself on rusty fence wire while hiking. The wound is shallow and looks clean, but you cannot remember when you last had a tetanus shot. What should you do?

options.text: Nothing — the wound is shallow and clean, so the risk is negligible
options.label: A

options.text: Seek professional care promptly to have your tetanus vaccination status evaluated
options.label: B

options.text: Give yourself a tetanus booster from your first-aid kit to be safe
options.label: C

options.text: Clean it and wait two weeks; if nothing changes, assume you are fine
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While cleaning a gravel scrape, you notice a small piece of gravel stuck in the skin. Per first-aid guidance, what should you do?

options.text: Dig it out with your fingernail so the wound can close cleanly
options.label: A

options.text: Leave all debris permanently — nothing embedded should ever be touched
options.label: B

options.text: Pour hydrogen peroxide over it to flush the gravel out
options.label: C

options.text: Remove small, loose debris gently with tweezers cleaned with alcohol; if it is embedded and will not come out easily, do not dig — seek professional care
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Three days after cleaning and dressing a small wound, the area around it is noticeably redder than before, feels warm, and a red streak is extending from the wound toward your body. What do these signs indicate?

options.text: Normal healing — redness and warmth always mean the wound is repairing
options.label: A

options.text: The wound needs to be left open to the air so it can dry out
options.label: B

options.text: The bandage was applied too tightly and should be loosened
options.label: C

options.text: A possible infection — seek professional care promptly
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your cousin proposes stitching a deep cut closed with fishing line to avoid a trip to urgent care. Why is wound closure outside the first-aid scope?

options.text: It is not outside the scope — anyone can close a wound with clean tools and steady hands
options.label: A

options.text: Because stitches are never needed for any wound
options.label: B

options.text: Closure is a professional medical procedure — improper closure risks infection and poor healing; first aid covers cleaning, dressing, and escalating instead
options.label: C

options.text: Because fishing line is too expensive to waste on a wound
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following wounds should be treated as high-risk and evaluated by a professional rather than managed as self-care?

options.text: A shallow scrape on the forearm that stopped bleeding within a minute
options.label: A

options.text: A small cut on the finger from an animal bite while feeding a stray dog
options.label: B

options.text: A minor scratch on the back that has no visible debris
options.label: C

options.text: A thin paper cut on the fingertip
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You cleaned and dressed a wound two days ago and are now changing the dressing. Which observation should trigger a call to a doctor?

options.text: The wound is draining pus-like fluid and you feel feverish
options.label: A

options.text: The dressing stayed clean and dry for a full day
options.label: B

options.text: The wound's edges look pink and slightly tender, and the redness is not spreading
options.label: C

options.text: The wound stopped bleeding within five minutes of pressure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are teaching a new crew member to identify the parts of a baseplate compass. Which description correctly matches a component to its function?

options.text: The magnetic needle points to true north, so the bezel must be zeroed before any reading
options.label: A

options.text: The direction-of-travel arrow is used only when navigating at night
options.label: B

options.text: The orienting arrow on the bezel floor is aligned with the needle to box it, so the dial can be read at the index line
options.label: C

options.text: The bezel dial is a fixed scale that cannot rotate, so readings never change
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your compass needle comes to rest pointing slightly west of the map's true-north arrow. A teammate says the compass is broken. What is the correct read of the situation?

options.text: The needle is pointing at magnetic north; the angle between it and true north is the magnetic declination, which varies by location
options.label: A

options.text: The needle must be re-magnetized before it will point at true north
options.label: B

options.text: The compass is fine, but the map's north arrow was printed incorrectly
options.label: C

options.text: Magnetic north and true north are identical everywhere except in the southern hemisphere
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are at a trail junction and need the bearing to a radio tower on a hilltop. Which is the correct order of operations for taking the bearing?

options.text: Rotate the bezel to your estimated bearing first, then point the direction-of-travel arrow at the tower
options.label: A

options.text: Point the direction-of-travel arrow at the tower, rotate the bezel until the needle is boxed, then read the dial at the index line
options.label: B

options.text: Align the orienting lines with the tower, then read the angle off the baseplate ruler
options.label: C

options.text: Lay the compass flat, wait for the needle to settle, and read the degrees printed on the baseplate edge
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have boxed the needle on a 70° bearing and must walk a long leg across open woods. What is the correct way to follow the bearing?

options.text: Walk with your eyes fixed on the needle, keeping it centered in the box the entire way
options.label: A

options.text: Rotate the bezel every few minutes so the dial matches your walking pace
options.label: B

options.text: Trust the single reading and stop checking the compass until you judge you have gone far enough
options.label: C

options.text: Pick a distinctive object ahead that sits on the bearing line, walk to it, then pick the next object
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You followed a 55° bearing out to a cache. You must now return to your start point along the exact same line. What bearing do you walk back on?

options.text: 235 degrees
options.label: A

options.text: 125 degrees
options.label: B

options.text: 305 degrees
options.label: C

options.text: 55 degrees
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your map shows the trail junction lies on a true bearing of 290° from your position. Local declination is 10° east. What magnetic bearing do you set on your compass?

options.text: 300 degrees
options.label: A

options.text: 290 degrees
options.label: B

options.text: 280 degrees
options.label: C

options.text: 270 degrees
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a 20-year-old topographic map with "declination 8° east" printed on the collar. Before setting your compass for a long cross-country leg, what should you do?

options.text: Use the printed 8° east — the map's collar value is the official figure for the area
options.label: A

options.text: Look up the current declination for your location, because declination changes over time and the collar value is a snapshot for the year the map was made
options.label: B

options.text: Treat the declination as zero — old maps are already corrected
options.label: C

options.text: Double the printed value, because declination increases by the same amount every decade
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are taking a bearing on a mountain summit, but the readings jump by 20 to 30 degrees between attempts. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: The needle needs re-magnetizing by tapping the compass against your hand
options.label: A

options.text: The sun's position is shifting the magnetic field
options.label: B

options.text: The target is too steep to sight reliably
options.label: C

options.text: Nearby metal or an electronic device — a phone, a vehicle, or a knife — is deflecting the needle
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You set out on a 100° bearing, but after walking 300 meters you realize you are heading roughly 280° — back the way you came. Which error most likely happened?

options.text: The bezel slipped because it was not locked
options.label: A

options.text: The bearing was taken with the wrong end of the needle boxed, producing a 180-degree error
options.label: B

options.text: Declination was ignored, shifting the reading by about 10 degrees
options.label: C

options.text: The map was oriented to grid north instead of true north
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your group hiked out on a 15° bearing and camped. At dawn you must return to the vehicle along the same line, with the vehicle behind you. What bearing do you set?

options.text: 195 degrees
options.label: A

options.text: 165 degrees
options.label: B

options.text: 345 degrees
options.label: C

options.text: 15 degrees
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your phone's navigation app shows the position 44.976331, -110.700936. A friend asks you to read it in degrees-minutes-seconds so she can find it on a paper map. Which is the correct DMS reading?
You are explaining map lines to a hiking partner. Which statement about latitude and longitude is correct?

options.text: Parallels run pole to pole and measure east–west distance; meridians run east–west and measure north–south distance
options.label: A

options.text: Parallels run east–west and measure distance north or south of the equator; meridians run pole to pole and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian
options.label: B

options.text: Parallels are farthest apart at the equator and converge to nothing at the poles
options.label: C

options.text: Latitude is measured east and west of the equator in degrees up to 360
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are inside a grid square on a topographic map. The vertical line to the left is labeled 16 and the horizontal line below is labeled 23. What is the correct order for building a grid reference?

options.text: Read the horizontal line first, then the vertical line — "up, then right"
options.label: A

options.text: Read the largest label in the map margin and round to the nearest kilometer
options.label: B

options.text: Read the vertical line (easting) first, then the horizontal line (northing) — "read right, then up"
options.label: C

options.text: Average the four corner labels of the square to find its center
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A radio caller gives you a UTM coordinate: "Easting 523580, northing 4980364." What is missing that would make this location usable?

options.text: Nothing — easting and northing are all a UTM coordinate needs
options.label: A

options.text: The zone — the world is divided into 60 UTM zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide, and the same easting and northing exist in every zone
options.label: B

options.text: The latitude and longitude — UTM values cannot be used on their own at all
options.label: C

options.text: The scale — without the map's scale the meters cannot be converted to grid lines
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You read the coordinate 45° 12' 30" N, 68° 55' 10" W from a 1970s topographic map and enter it into your GPS, which you have never configured. Your plotted position ends up tens to hundreds of meters from the map feature you were aiming for. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The map is too old to be accurate — terrain and landmarks have moved
options.label: A

options.text: The GPS needs recalibration — reset it to factory settings
options.label: B

options.text: GPS satellites drift over time, and five decades of drift explains the gap
options.label: C

options.text: The map is on the NAD 27 datum while your GPS defaults to WGS 84 — the same printed coordinate falls on a different ground point under each datum
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are on a 1:24,000 map whose grid lines are 1,000 meters apart. You want to report a position that a rescuer can find to within about 100 meters. What do you do?

options.text: Estimate the point's position in tenths of the square from the western and southern grid lines and build a six-digit reference — easting first, northing second
options.label: A

options.text: Read only the four-digit square — finer references are not legitimate on this map
options.label: B

options.text: Count the contour lines between the grid lines and convert them to digits
options.label: C

options.text: Use the nearest labeled map corner as the reference and add the scale in meters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You must radio your position to a rescue team from a place with no repeaters and a weak signal. Which report gives them the best chance of finding you?

options.text: Read the coordinate once, quickly, so the search can start sooner
options.label: A

options.text: Give only a nearby landmark name — names are easier than numbers to write down
options.label: B

options.text: State the coordinate digit by digit with its format and datum, then add a short description of your surroundings
options.label: C

options.text: Give only the grid zone and your elevation to keep the report short
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement about grid reference digits and precision is correct?

options.text: A four-digit grid reference places you within about 1 meter
options.label: A

options.text: An eight-digit grid reference identifies a 1,000-meter square
options.label: B

options.text: Every digit you add halves the size of the square
options.label: C

options.text: A six-digit grid reference locates you within about 100 meters, and an eight-digit within about 10 meters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A GPS screen shows 37.7749, -122.4194. What format is the device displaying?

options.text: Decimal degrees — one number per axis, with a decimal point
options.label: A

options.text: Degrees-minutes-seconds — phone apps always display DMS
options.label: B

options.text: UTM coordinates — they are always written with a comma
options.label: C

options.text: MGRS — the letters were simply omitted by the app
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A search-and-rescue team member reads you a location in MGRS. Why would a ground unit use MGRS instead of a full latitude/longitude statement?

options.text: MGRS is a separate system unrelated to UTM, used only on nautical charts
options.label: A

options.text: MGRS is the military's implementation of the UTM system — it adds zone and 100,000-meter square identifiers so a short string pinpoints a location without ambiguity
options.label: B

options.text: MGRS works only with GPS and cannot be read from paper maps
options.label: C

options.text: MGRS uses miles and feet instead of meters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your GPS device shows a position of 38.8977, -77.0365. You are about to read it to a dispatcher. What must you include for the position to be usable?

options.text: The format and datum the device displays, the numbers spoken slowly digit by digit, and a confirmation read-back
options.label: A

options.text: Only the numbers themselves, read as fast as possible so the call is short
options.label: B

options.text: A nearby town name instead, since dispatchers know local areas better than coordinates
options.label: C

options.text: The elevation only, since latitude and longitude are assumed to be the same everywhere
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You get through to a dispatcher with a weak signal. Which message gives rescuers the most usable information in the shortest time?

options.text: "I'm lost, please send help as soon as possible."
options.label: A

options.text: Who you are, what happened, where you are, your injuries, your resources, and your plan — spoken slowly and repeated for confirmation
options.label: B

options.text: A detailed account of everything that went wrong since you left home that morning
options.label: C

options.text: Your name and your GPS coordinates, then hang up to save battery
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before your hike, you left a trip plan with a trusted contact: the trail, the planned route, your return time, and the number of people in your group. How does this help the search if you do not return?

options.text: It does not help — rescue crews have to confirm the plan before they can start searching
options.label: A

options.text: It only helps if the contact is standing at the trailhead when you fail to return
options.label: B

options.text: It tells rescuers the corridor you intended to travel, so the search can begin along your planned route instead of at a guess
options.label: C

options.text: It replaces the need for any signaling or message from you once the search starts
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is 23:00, you are lost in dense forest, and you hear what might be searchers in the distance. Which signal is the best choice right now?

options.text: Whistle three sharp blasts, pause, and repeat — sound carries at night, and the pattern is what rescuers recognize
options.label: A

options.text: Shout continuously until someone answers, since your voice is always the clearest signal
options.label: B

options.text: Build a large signal fire immediately so the flame is visible over the trees
options.label: C

options.text: Flash your light in a steady, unbroken beam toward the sound
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend says, "My phone and a PLB are basically the same thing — both call for help." How would you correct them?

options.text: "True — the only difference is the battery life."
options.label: A

options.text: "False — a PLB costs more, so a phone is always the better choice."
options.label: B

options.text: "False — a phone can text friends, which a PLB can also do if you hold it right."
options.label: C

options.text: "Not quite — a phone needs cell coverage, while a 406 MHz PLB alerts the satellite-based rescue system from anywhere, but it is a one-way alert, not a call."
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You became lost at 14:00 on a ridge trail. It is now 16:30, you are tired but uninjured, and you think you remember roughly which way the trailhead lies. What should you do?

options.text: Walk toward the trailhead now, while there is daylight to travel
options.label: A

options.text: Stay put, keep warm, and signal — movement makes you harder to find, and you move only if there is an immediate threat to your life
options.label: B

options.text: Walk downhill until you find any watercourse, then follow it, since water always leads to people
options.label: C

options.text: Hike back the way you came for exactly one hour, then decide
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your phone is dead and your device shows no position. Which statement is the best descriptive fallback for your location?

options.text: "Somewhere in the mountains, maybe two hours from the car."
options.label: A

options.text: "I can see trees and rocks all around me."
options.label: B

options.text: "On the north shore of the lake below the east face of the granite ridge, at the junction where the creek crosses the trail."
options.label: C

options.text: "About halfway up whatever hill I was climbing."
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are lost with a phone at 40% battery and no signal. Which battery plan keeps the device most useful for the hours ahead?

options.text: Put it in airplane mode, power it on only at scheduled check-in times to attempt one short message, then power it off
options.label: A

options.text: Leave it on and check for signal every few minutes — the screen activity alerts rescuers to your position
options.label: B

options.text: Use it as a flashlight until the battery drains, since the light is more visible than a call
options.label: C

options.text: Turn the screen brightness to maximum in case a satellite passes overhead
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a clear, sunny afternoon and you can hear an aircraft searching the valley. Which signal are you best positioned to give?

options.text: Three whistle blasts, since sound always carries best in daylight
options.label: A

options.text: A small signal fire, even though it is dry season and fire risk is high
options.label: B

options.text: Repeated SOS text messages to your family, hoping they reach a tower
options.label: C

options.text: A mirror flash aimed slowly toward the aircraft, plus a bright shape laid out in the open
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have a twisted ankle that slows you to a crawl, but you are not bleeding and can still bear weight. You finally reach a dispatcher. Why is it important to report the injury accurately even though you feel it is minor?

options.text: It is not important — reporting injuries would delay the rescue
options.label: A

options.text: Because your condition determines what the rescue crew brings and how fast they move — an understated injury produces an under-resourced rescue
options.label: B

options.text: Because dispatchers are required to refuse help for unreported injuries
options.label: C

options.text: Because the rescue crew will judge your competence by the accuracy of your report
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are in a canyon with no cell service but a clear sky overhead. Your phone shows a position fix. How did it get that position?

options.text: It triangulated your position against nearby cell towers — which is why service matters
options.label: A

options.text: It measured one-way signals broadcast from satellites and computed a three-dimensional position and time — no cell service required
options.label: B

options.text: It downloaded your location from a data server the last time it had a connection
options.label: C

options.text: It estimated your position from stored Wi-Fi networks you passed on the way in
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend's phone is labeled "GNSS-capable," and in a deep valley it holds a fix where yours struggles. What explains the difference?

options.text: GNSS is a paid subscription that unlocks extra satellites
options.label: A

options.text: GNSS is the brand name of a competing system that replaces GPS
options.label: B

options.text: GNSS is the umbrella term for satellite constellations providing positioning, navigation, and timing — GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou are the four global ones, and multi-constellation receivers use several at once
options.label: C

options.text: GNSS only operates in urban areas where GPS cannot reach
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At the trailhead, there are no bars. A hiker announces, "We can't navigate — the phone has no service." What is the flaw in that statement?

options.text: GPS needs no cell signal — the phone can still compute its position from satellites; what it cannot do without a connection is download map data, which should have been done at home
options.label: A

options.text: The hiker is right — without service, the GPS receiver shuts down automatically
options.label: B

options.text: Service is only needed for the first fix; afterwards the phone caches the entire route on its own
options.label: C

options.text: You can simply call for help anyway, so service is not needed for navigation at all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your trip starts tomorrow morning. You have Wi-Fi at home and unknown coverage at the trailhead. How do you prepare the phone tonight?

options.text: Nothing — GPS works without data, so the maps will appear when you arrive
options.label: A

options.text: Download the map area at the trailhead tomorrow using cell data, so it is as fresh as possible
options.label: B

options.text: Download offline map areas covering the full route plus its surroundings tonight, over Wi-Fi, and verify they render with service off
options.label: C

options.text: Take a screenshot of the route tonight and zoom into it during the hike
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a two-day route with no charging available, your phone is at 70%. Which battery strategy keeps navigation available the longest?

options.text: Keep the screen at full brightness — visibility matters more than battery
options.label: A

options.text: Turn on airplane mode and re-enable location; keep the screen dim and off between checks, and close background apps
options.label: B

options.text: Leave the tracking app recording the entire route so the track is complete
options.label: C

options.text: Turn the phone fully off and power it on only at night to plan the next day
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a 5°F winter day, and your phone's battery dropped from 80% to 40% in two hours of light use. What is the most likely cause, and the correct countermeasure?

options.text: GPS satellites transmit stronger signals in winter, forcing the receiver to draw more power — nothing can be done
options.label: A

options.text: Cold weather triggers a software bug that drains the battery — a restart fixes it
options.label: B

options.text: Batteries actually last longer in the cold, so the drop must be a display error
options.label: C

options.text: Cold drains battery charge — keep the phone in an inside pocket near body heat, and carry a battery backup kept warm as well
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your map app draws a circle around your position and labels it "the area you are likely in." A partner insists you are exactly at the center. What is true, and how should you proceed?

options.text: The center is your true position — the circle is drawn around it
options.label: A

options.text: The circle is only the map's zoom indicator, not a statement about accuracy
options.label: B

options.text: The circle means the phone has lost its fix entirely and you should stop using it
options.label: C

options.text: The circle is an estimate, not a guarantee — typical smartphone accuracy is within about 4.9 m (16 ft) under open sky and worse near buildings and trees, so verify against terrain and the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Walking between tall buildings downtown, your position marker jumps from one street to the next. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Multipath — satellite signals reflected off buildings and walls degrade the fix, and blockage by buildings reduces accuracy
options.label: A

options.text: The satellites' orbital paths changed within the last hour
options.label: B

options.text: The battery is low, so the phone computes only a rough position
options.label: C

options.text: Civilian GPS is intentionally degraded in urban areas
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Mid-route, your phone slips into a stream crossing and will not turn on. Your paper map and compass are in your pack. What is the correct sequence of actions?

options.text: Wait for the phone to dry and then continue relying on it — it usually comes back
options.label: A

options.text: Mark your last known position, switch to paper map and compass, and keep the phone off unless an emergency call is needed
options.label: B

options.text: Walk toward the direction of the last fix to help the phone reacquire its map
options.label: C

options.text: Turn around and walk straight back the way you came, without checking the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are assembling the navigation kit for a multi-day route. Which setup reflects the correct relationship between GPS and map-and-compass skills?

options.text: A phone with offline maps only — lighter than a paper map and accurate to a few meters
options.label: A

options.text: A phone plus a second fully charged power bank — redundancy is the plan
options.label: B

options.text: Paper map and compass as the primary system, practiced and carried, with the phone as a convenience layered on top
options.label: C

options.text: A paper map alone — GPS adds nothing once you know the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning a two-day trip through mountainous country with no maintained trails, and you need to judge cliffs, saddles, and valleys before choosing a route. Which map serves this purpose best?

options.text: A 1:24,000 topographic map showing contour lines, water, and vegetation
options.label: A

options.text: A road map showing highways and towns
options.label: B

options.text: A recreation overview map of the region showing campgrounds
options.label: C

options.text: A satellite photo printed from a phone app at whatever zoom you chose
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a 1:24,000 topographic map you measure a straight trail section at 2.5 inches. How far is that on the ground?

options.text: 2,500 feet
options.label: A

options.text: 5,000 feet
options.label: B

options.text: 2,400 feet
options.label: C

options.text: 24,000 feet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You open a topographic map and find a symbol you have never seen before, near the edge of the map. What is the correct way to learn what it means?

options.text: Guess from context — most symbols are intuitive
options.label: A

options.text: Ask another hiker what that symbol usually means
options.label: B

options.text: Find the symbol in the map's legend and marginal information
options.label: C

options.text: Ignore it — minor symbols rarely matter to the route
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a topographic map, contour lines form a series of V shapes that point toward higher ground, and a blue stream line runs through the middle of the V's. What terrain feature are you looking at?

options.text: A ridge
options.label: A

options.text: A valley or draw
options.label: B

options.text: A saddle
options.label: C

options.text: A depression
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are comparing two route options on the same map. Along one route the brown contour lines are packed close together; along the other they are spread far apart. What does the map tell you?

options.text: The close-packed route is steeper than the spread-out route
options.label: A

options.text: The close-packed route is higher in elevation than the spread-out route
options.label: B

options.text: The close-packed route is wetter than the spread-out route
options.label: C

options.text: The close-packed route is shorter in distance than the spread-out route
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your map has a contour interval of 20 feet. An index contour is labeled 1,040. Following the pattern of index contours, what elevation does the next index contour uphill show?

options.text: 1,060 feet
options.label: A

options.text: 1,120 feet
options.label: B

options.text: 1,200 feet
options.label: C

options.text: 1,140 feet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two maps cover the same area: one at 1:24,000 and one at 1:250,000. You need to find small streams, foot trails, and individual buildings to plan an off-trail route. Which map should you use, and why?

options.text: The 1:250,000 map, because it covers more area and you will not lose the region
options.label: A

options.text: The 1:250,000 map, because a larger number means a larger scale
options.label: B

options.text: The 1:24,000 map, because the larger scale shows more detail
options.label: C

options.text: Either map, because scale does not change what features are shown
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On your map you see a closed loop of contour lines with short tick marks pointing inward, toward the center. The ground inside the loop is lower than the ring around it. What is this feature?

options.text: A depression — a hole or sink in the ground
options.label: A

options.text: A hilltop — the highest point in the area
options.label: B

options.text: A saddle — the low point between two summits
options.label: C

options.text: A spur — a ridge running downhill
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Along your trail you cross an index contour labeled 2,800 and later an index contour labeled 2,600. Between the crossings, what is the trail doing?

options.text: Climbing 200 feet
options.label: A

options.text: Climbing 2,600 feet
options.label: B

options.text: Staying level — index contours only mark every fifth line
options.label: C

options.text: Descending 200 feet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your map shows a maintained trail along a ridgeline, but on the ground the trail is gone — overgrown and blocked by a recent landslide, and the ground does not match the map. What is the correct action?

options.text: Push on along the mapped route — the map was made by professionals
options.label: A

options.text: Believe the terrain — the map may be outdated, so reassess and adjust the route to the actual ground
options.label: B

options.text: Turn back and abandon the trip entirely
options.label: C

options.text: Re-check the map every few minutes until the ground starts matching it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are hiking a ridge you have walked before. The saddle you expect after forty minutes has not appeared after an hour. The terrain looks plausible — similar slopes, similar treeline. What is the most important first reaction?

options.text: Treat the missing saddle as data: stop and verify your position before the error compounds
options.label: A

options.text: Walk another ten minutes to give the saddle a fair chance to appear
options.label: B

options.text: Trust the terrain — it looks like the right ridge, so it must be
options.label: C

options.text: Turn back immediately in alarm, without checking the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You come to a fork in the trail. The map shows the route should bend west, but both branches look equally used and equally wide. What is the correct move before committing to a branch?

options.text: Choose the branch that looks more worn — use of a trail is evidence of the route
options.label: A

options.text: Check the compass bearing and the terrain against the map before committing
options.label: B

options.text: Follow the branch that keeps the sun on the same side as before
options.label: C

options.text: Take either branch, since forks always rejoin further ahead
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You descend to a stream that "matches" the one on your map — same width, same bend direction. But the map shows your stream should flow into a lake about 2 km south, and there is no lake. What is most likely true?

options.text: The lake simply dried out — map features change over time
options.label: A

options.text: You are at the right stream and are misreading the map scale
options.label: B

options.text: You are on the parallel stream in the next valley — matching one feature without confirming its neighbors is how parallel-terrain errors happen
options.label: C

options.text: The compass is off — reverse your bearing and continue
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You suspect you are lost on a forested slope with light fading. According to the stop–think–observe–plan procedure, what is the FIRST thing you do?

options.text: Take a compass bearing toward the nearest trail you remember
options.label: A

options.text: Stop moving, stay calm, and resist the urge to push on
options.label: B

options.text: Climb to the nearest high point to see the terrain before dark
options.label: C

options.text: Walk back along your tracks for a few minutes to confirm the route
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have stopped and calmed down. Your last confirmed position was the stream crossing at 10:10, you have walked about ninety minutes since, and the saddle the map promised has not appeared. Which sequence best applies the procedure?

options.text: Plan first — decide the fastest route out, then check the map against it
options.label: A

options.text: Move to the nearest ridge to observe the terrain, then think about where you are
options.label: B

options.text: Think about the last known position and the time and distance since, then observe the terrain and map to narrow where you are, then make a plan
options.label: C

options.text: Signal for help immediately and stay put without further assessment
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are fifteen minutes past your last confirmed point on a clear, well-defined trail, with three hours of daylight left. The trail ahead is easy to follow. Which decision best applies the recovery rules?

options.text: Continue forward — an obvious trail will likely reach a junction
options.label: A

options.text: Stop and shelter now — any uncertainty is a reason to stay put
options.label: B

options.text: Leave the trail and cut across the forest to the road shown on the map
options.label: C

options.text: Backtrack to the last known position while the route is clear, then re-plan from a known point
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You cannot safely backtrack — the route behind climbs through cliff bands, and darkness is about two hours away. The map shows a river about 800 m southeast that flows down to a road. What is the sound navigation decision?

options.text: Aim for the river — a catching feature that is hard to miss and leads to a road — rather than guessing a shortcut
options.label: A

options.text: Stay where you are — never move after becoming disoriented, regardless of conditions
options.label: B

options.text: Follow the cliff band westward, since cliff lines are a reliable linear feature
options.label: C

options.text: Pick a random bearing and walk a straight line until you find anything
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is late afternoon, clouds are building, and you do not have a known position — your last confirmed point is over an hour of rough terrain behind you. What do the stop-moving rules say?

options.text: Push on — moving keeps you warm, and someone may find your tracks
options.label: A

options.text: Backtrack quickly while there is still some light
options.label: B

options.text: Walk downhill along the easiest drainage to find a road
options.label: C

options.text: Stop now and prepare shelter — darkness, building weather, and no known position are conditions for stopping, not continuing
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are exhausted and have a twisted ankle, two hours before dark. You know exactly where you are: the correct ridge, with the trailhead about 6 km away over steep ground. What is the right decision?

options.text: Push the 6 km — the trailhead is a guaranteed known position and warmth
options.label: A

options.text: Stop early, treat the injury, and shelter for the night — exhaustion and injury are stop-moving conditions even with a known position
options.label: B

options.text: Descend the steepest slope to shorten the distance before dark
options.label: C

options.text: Blow a whistle continuously until dark in case anyone is near
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before the trip, you left a route plan with a trusted contact: trailhead, route, expected return time, and vehicle description. You are now lost but calm, stopped, and you have signal. What is the correct use of that plan?

options.text: Wait at least 24 hours — calling early wastes rescue resources
options.label: A

options.text: Stay quiet about being lost — describing your location would confirm the mistake
options.label: B

options.text: Call or message your contact, report the last known position and conditions, and let the plan guide the response — it gives searchers your route and expected return time
options.label: C

options.text: Leave the shelter and walk out so you meet the expected return time
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You stop on a rise and realize you can name exactly where you are and where you want to be — but you have no idea how far you have traveled or in which direction you have been walking. Which components of the navigation problem are missing?

options.text: Position and destination
options.label: A

options.text: Direction and distance
options.label: B

options.text: Bearing and route
options.label: C

options.text: Checkpoints and timing
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your map shows a creek crossing that lies on the direct line from your camp to the lake — but the direct line climbs a steep talus slope. You plot a bearing of 240 degrees to the lake. What is the difference between the bearing and the route you will actually walk?

options.text: They are the same thing — a route is just a bearing applied over distance
options.label: A

options.text: The bearing is the path, and the route is the compass direction you use to follow it
options.label: B

options.text: The bearing is a direction to a point; the route is the path you actually walk, chosen for terrain
options.label: C

options.text: The bearing applies only when using GPS, and the route applies only when using a map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are standing at a trailhead with a map of the area, about to start an 8-kilometer walk to a fire lookout. According to the navigation workflow, what is the first step?

options.text: Identify your starting point on the map and fix your position there
options.label: A

options.text: Start walking and take your first bearing after the first hour
options.label: B

options.text: Choose the fastest pace you can sustain for the whole walk
options.label: C

options.text: Wait for the sun to be high enough to check your shadow direction
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are navigating cross-country on a steady bearing and expect to cross a creek near the 3-kilometer mark. You reach a creek. What should you do before crossing?

options.text: Cross immediately — being on schedule is what matters
options.label: A

options.text: Turn around — a checkpoint that arrives on schedule is a warning
options.label: B

options.text: Speed up — momentum is the best verification of a route
options.label: C

options.text: Verify your position: confirm the creek's position, direction of flow, and surrounding terrain against the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are hiking a forested trail with no views, keeping a steady pace. Which practice keeps you oriented without any instruments?

options.text: Walking in a straight line at a constant speed — consistency preserves orientation
options.label: A

options.text: Deliberate observation — noting junctions crossed, streams passed, and the direction slopes trend as you go
options.label: B

options.text: Counting steps and multiplying by stride length every hundred meters
options.label: C

options.text: Waiting for the next break in the canopy to check the sun once
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You followed a ridge for over an hour, expecting it to curve left toward the valley you want — but it keeps trending right, and the ground below looks like nothing on your map. What is the most likely mistake?

options.text: You chose the wrong ridge at the junction — a parallel spur that looked identical
options.label: A

options.text: Your compass is broken, so all bearings are unreliable
options.label: B

options.text: The terrain is featureless, so navigation is impossible today
options.label: C

options.text: The map was published too long ago to trust
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You set out on a bearing of 130 degrees across an open slope. An hour later you re-check and find you have actually been walking 145 degrees. What happened, and what should you do?

options.text: Nothing — drift under 20 degrees is normal over an hour
options.label: A

options.text: The compass is faulty — switch to natural indicators for the rest of the day
options.label: B

options.text: You drifted off bearing — the drift built silently, and it must be corrected now and rechecked regularly
options.label: C

options.text: Keep going — 15 degrees only matters over very long distances
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are in dense forest with short-range visibility, no prominent landmarks, and a poor trail description. You carry a topographic map, a compass, and a charged GPS. Which method should lead?

options.text: Natural indicators — the sun is reliable all day
options.label: A

options.text: GPS alone — it is the most precise tool available
options.label: B

options.text: Terrain association — the map's contours are all the landmarks you need
options.label: C

options.text: Map and compass as primary, with GPS as a cross-check
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are crossing a broad, flat, featureless basin in full daylight, with a map, a compass, and a working GPS. Which statement is most accurate for this terrain?

options.text: With no landmarks to verify against, disciplined direction and distance tracking are your only reliable tools
options.label: A

options.text: Landmark matching is the most reliable method in flat, open terrain
options.label: B

options.text: Natural indicators are fully sufficient in daylight conditions
options.label: C

options.text: GPS is unnecessary here because there is nothing to collide with
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An hour into your planned four-hour hike, low clouds cut visibility to a few meters, your map is saturated, and you have not fixed your position since the trailhead. What is the safest navigation decision?

options.text: Speed up to make up time — daylight is the only limit
options.label: A

options.text: Push ahead until the clouds lift — visibility always returns
options.label: B

options.text: Stop, fix your position as carefully as you can, and be prepared to turn back or wait rather than walk blind
options.label: C

options.text: Follow any stream downhill — streams eventually reach roads
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a moonless, clear night. Which navigation cue is the most likely to still work reliably in the dark?

options.text: Reading the spacing of contour lines to judge how steep a slope is
options.label: A

options.text: A ridgeline silhouetted against the sky
options.label: B

options.text: The color contrast of trail blazes on trees
options.label: C

options.text: Depth perception for judging how far away a drop-off is
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At a night checkpoint you hear a stream running and see a dark gap where the trees open ahead. What does this tell you?

options.text: The sound alone proves the stream is shallow enough to wade safely
options.label: A

options.text: The gap is definitely the correct crossing point, since water sound marks safe ground
options.label: B

options.text: The sound confirms the stream as a usable night cue, but crossing safety still needs light and a pre-selected point
options.label: C

options.text: Sound cues are unreliable at night and should be ignored
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Between the same two points, which route should you choose for night travel?

options.text: The route that follows a road and then a stream to the objective, even if it is slightly longer
options.label: A

options.text: The shortest cross-country route, since less distance means less time in the dark
options.label: B

options.text: The route with the most elevation change, since relief features stay visible at night
options.label: C

options.text: The route you walked in daylight last summer, whatever it crosses
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning tonight's final leg to the trailhead. Which is the best checkpoint to select?

options.text: A small knoll identifiable only by its contour pattern on the map
options.label: A

options.text: A subtle junction where two similar forest paths meet
options.label: B

options.text: A point "about halfway up the hillside" where the trees thin
options.label: C

options.text: A road crossing, followed by the edge of the lake
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your pace count says you should be at the checkpoint, but you are not there yet. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The count is exact — the checkpoint must be in the wrong place on the map
options.label: A

options.text: The count is an estimate and distance error is common; verify position and continue carefully
options.label: B

options.text: Walk faster to make up the missing distance before the count drifts further
options.label: C

options.text: Abandon the map — a calibrated pace count is more reliable than any checkpoint
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At night you must follow a bearing on a 400-meter leg with no visible endpoint. What is the best technique?

options.text: Break the leg into short intermediate points within your light range, walking from one to the next
options.label: A

options.text: Walk the whole leg at a steady speed, trusting the direction set at the start
options.label: B

options.text: Use a bright white light to scan for the endpoint so you can walk straight to it
options.label: C

options.text: Have the group spread out so someone can spot the endpoint
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to read the map at night and your headlamp is currently on white. What is the correct light discipline?

options.text: Use the white light freely — reading the map matters more than preserving night vision
options.label: A

options.text: Keep the white light on for the whole leg so your eyes stay adjusted to it
options.label: B

options.text: Switch to red light for reading; use white only briefly when safe footing or hazard assessment requires it
options.label: C

options.text: Turn off all lights and read by moonlight to save the batteries
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your group is moving at night. At every checkpoint, the standard check before continuing is:

options.text: The fastest member pushes ahead to scout the next leg
options.label: A

options.text: Each member walks at their own pace and regroups at the next checkpoint
options.label: B

options.text: The leader counts only the gear, since the people are always together
options.label: C

options.text: A headcount and position check of every member
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is 0100, the temperature is dropping, and after a wrong fork you are uncertain of your position. The group is warm enough, and both headlamps work. What is the best action?

options.text: Stop, establish shelter, and continue navigation at first light
options.label: A

options.text: Push on — the lights work and the group is warm, so the error is small
options.label: B

options.text: Split the group: two people scout each direction while the rest wait
options.label: C

options.text: Walk downhill in any direction until you hit a road
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which situation most clearly triggers the rule "camp early and navigate at dawn"?

options.text: The moon is bright and the headlamp batteries are at half charge
options.label: A

options.text: The group is shivering, one headlamp has failed, and the route ahead crosses an open hillside
options.label: B

options.text: The checkpoint is ten minutes ahead but the trail is overgrown
options.label: C

options.text: You are tired of walking but otherwise warm and confident of the route
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning a weekend trip and have not yet chosen a route. Per the route-planning sequence, what is the first thing to settle?

options.text: The objective and the destination — what the trip must accomplish and the exact point on the map it ends at
options.label: A

options.text: The gear list, so you know what you can carry before drawing lines
options.label: B

options.text: The starting time, so the route can be planned backward from it
options.label: C

options.text: The trail with the best reputation, then shape the trip around it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two routes reach the same destination: a direct line over a ridge, and a longer trail through the valley. The map shows the ridge line with closely spaced contour lines and the valley trail with widely spaced ones. What does this tell you before you leave?

options.text: The ridge route is shorter and faster because closely spaced contours mean easy, direct travel
options.label: A

options.text: The ridge route climbs steeply — closely spaced contours mean steep ground — so the longer valley trail may be faster in real time despite more miles
options.label: B

options.text: The valley trail is impassable because widely spaced contours mean flood-prone ground
options.label: C

options.text: The contour spacing only matters for water crossings, not for route difficulty
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your route follows a winding stream for three miles on the map. What is the correct way to measure the actual ground distance of that leg?

options.text: Draw a straight line between start and end and measure it with a ruler — streams never add meaningful distance
options.label: A

options.text: Estimate from the representative fraction alone, which gives ground distance directly without the graphic scale
options.label: B

options.text: Lay a piece of string along the route, mark the endpoints, then read the string's length against the graphic (bar) scale printed on the map
options.label: C

options.text: Count the number of bends in the stream and multiply by a fixed factor
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The map margin says the contour interval is 40 feet. Your route crosses 12 contour lines between start and finish, including ups and downs. What is the best estimate of elevation gain for planning purposes?

options.text: 480 feet, treated as exact — contour lines are precise survey data
options.label: A

options.text: 3.3 feet — divide the interval by the number of lines crossed
options.label: B

options.text: Cannot be estimated from contours; only a GPS altimeter can give a number
options.label: C

options.text: 480 feet, treated as a floor — the count covers total gain but real gain includes every up-and-down, so actual climb is likely more
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a map, a ridge crossing shows contour lines packed tightly together, followed by an open area above treeline. Which terrain difficulty factors should your leg table record for that stretch?

options.text: Steepness from the contour spacing, and exposure from the open ridge above treeline
options.label: A

options.text: Water crossings only — ridge terrain has no other hazards
options.label: B

options.text: Vegetation only — tight contours always mean dense forest
options.label: C

options.text: Nothing — map symbols cannot describe terrain difficulty in advance
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your planned leg crosses a river and then runs dry of marked water features for four miles. Before departure, what belongs in the plan for this leg?

options.text: Nothing special — you can find water along the way, and the crossing will be obvious when you get there
options.label: A

options.text: A marked crossing with the hazard questions asked (currents, underwater hazards, cold water), a planned treatment method, and the longer carry reflected in the leg's time estimate
options.label: B

options.text: A detour around every water feature on the map, since all crossings are unsafe
options.label: C

options.text: Extra food instead of water, since the four-mile dry stretch proves water is not needed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You committed to a turnaround rule before departure: "If we are not off the ridge by 1:00 PM, we turn around at the last treeline junction." At 12:45 PM, the party is one hundred feet below that junction, the sky is still clear, and the summit is visible. What do you do?

options.text: Push to the summit — the sky is clear, and the rule was made when you were being overly cautious
options.label: A

options.text: Split the party — the two fastest continue and the slowest two turn back
options.label: B

options.text: Extend the rule by thirty minutes at the junction, then decide again
options.label: C

options.text: Turn around at the junction as committed, even though the summit is close — the calmly made rule is the one you trust on the trail
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The NPS Trip Planning Guide advises choosing a backup activity rather than canceling when conditions change. How does that logic translate into a route plan?

options.text: Every route gets a primary route, an alternate route, and a bail-out — the shortest escape to trailhead, road, or help — chosen before departure
options.label: A

options.text: The backup is chosen at the trailhead once you see the weather
options.label: B

options.text: A backup plan is only needed for multi-day expeditions, not day trips
options.label: C

options.text: The bail-out is the same as the alternate route, so only one fallback is ever needed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The party of four includes one member who is noticeably slower on climbs, and the forecast calls for afternoon storms. Which time estimate best follows conservative planning principles?

options.text: Base the leg times on the fastest member's pace, since that sets the group's potential
options.label: A

options.text: Use a published rule of thumb formula as the authority, since it is based on average hikers
options.label: B

options.text: Fit each leg's estimate to the slowest member, adjust upward for climb and rough going, add margin for rests and weather, and compare actual to plan at every checkpoint
options.label: C

options.text: Plan only the total day time, since leg-level estimates are unnecessary detail
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before departure, you tell a trusted contact where you are going, what you are doing, and when you will be back. What does this accomplish for the route plan?

options.text: It satisfies park rules, which is its only purpose
options.label: A

options.text: It anchors the plan's outer deadline — the contact knows the return time, can alert authorities if you are overdue, and the return time becomes the turnaround rule's final check
options.label: B

options.text: It guarantees rescue, so the rest of the plan can be relaxed
options.label: C

options.text: It replaces the need for an alternate route and bail-out
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a topographic map, contour lines that bend into a sharp V pointing toward higher ground — upstream — mark a:
