options.text: Ridgeline
options.label: A

options.text: Draw or valley
options.label: B

options.text: Saddle
options.label: C

options.text: Bench
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A ridge runs north to south. On the map, the contour lines bulge out from the ridge crest toward lower ground in a U shape whose opening faces downhill. This bulge marks a:

options.text: Valley
options.label: A

options.text: Depression
options.label: B

options.text: Spur
options.label: C

options.text: Saddle
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two closed contour loops sit side by side on a ridge, with the contours between them pinched into a narrow waist. This contour pattern marks a:

options.text: Saddle
options.label: A

options.text: Peak
options.label: B

options.text: Draw
options.label: C

options.text: Bench
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before you look up from the map, the terrain-association habit requires you to:

options.text: Rotate the map so that features ahead on the map match features ahead on the ground
options.label: A

options.text: Predict which features should be visible ahead, left, and right, and roughly how far away each should be
options.label: B

options.text: Fold the map so that only your current leg is visible
options.label: C

options.text: Wait for a trail sign or junction to confirm the route first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You follow a valley floor and reach the stream crossing where the map shows it should be; the ridge sits on your right exactly as mapped. What does the association loop require next?

options.text: Continue without adjusting — a confirmed crossing means the loop is done for the day
options.label: A

options.text: Turn back to the last confirmed point and re-walk the leg to be sure
options.label: B

options.text: Switch to compass bearings for the rest of the trip
options.label: C

options.text: Update your position estimate on the map and schedule the next check at the next decision point
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You plan a leg down a valley to a river crossing two kilometers away. Which pairing uses the handrail and catching feature logic correctly?

options.text: Handrail: the stream in the valley floor; catching feature: the river crossing at the leg's end
options.label: A

options.text: Handrail: the river crossing; catching feature: the stream in the valley floor
options.label: B

options.text: Handrail: the ridge crest above the valley; catching feature: the valley mouth
options.label: C

options.text: Handrail: the compass bearing; catching feature: the edge of the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two candidate handrails cross your intended route: a stream that meanders through the valley and a ridgeline that runs straight toward your objective. What matters most in choosing?

options.text: The stream, because water is always the best handrail
options.label: A

options.text: The ridgeline, because higher ground is always easier to follow
options.label: B

options.text: The one that runs closest to your intended direction and is easy to identify on the map and on the ground
options.label: C

options.text: The one marked with the thickest line on the map
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The map shows a saddle on the ridge ahead. You crest the ridge and see an unbroken crest with no saddle anywhere along it. Your honest response is to:

options.text: Assume the saddle is just around the next bend and keep walking the crest
options.label: A

options.text: Walk to the far end of the ridge to see if the saddle was simply misplaced on the map
options.label: B

options.text: Note that the map is old and ignore the discrepancy
options.label: C

options.text: Stop and re-establish your position before continuing — terrain association is a confirmation skill, not a guessing skill
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During a deliberate observation stop, which action makes what you see usable for navigation?

options.text: Photographing the view for later reference
options.label: A

options.text: Naming each visible feature out loud — ridge, spur, draw, stream — and matching it to the map
options.label: B

options.text: Waiting for a landmark to look familiar before moving on
options.label: C

options.text: Estimating how far you have walked from how tired you feel
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a USGS topographic map, a dashed blue line most likely marks:

options.text: An intermittent or seasonal stream
options.label: A

options.text: A perennial river
options.label: B

options.text: A hiking trail
options.label: C

options.text: A contour line
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On your topographic map, a stream is drawn as a broken blue line crossing your planned route, while another is a solid blue line. Before you reach either, what do the symbols tell you?

options.text: The broken line is an intermittent stream that flows seasonally or after rain — it may be dry, or it may be running high after storms — while the solid line flows year-round
options.label: A

options.text: The broken line is a stream too small to be dangerous, while the solid line is always uncrossable
options.label: B

options.text: The broken line marks a lake outlet, and the solid line marks a marsh
options.label: C

options.text: The broken line means the stream has already flooded this season and should be avoided
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your route crosses a stretch of flat, unwooded ground immediately beside a blue line, and the contour lines are widely spaced there. What should you plan for?

options.text: A reliable ford — flat ground beside a stream always marks a safe crossing
options.label: A

options.text: A lakeshore — flat unwooded ground beside water is a lake bed
options.label: B

options.text: A flood plain — the stream spreads across this ground during high water, so it is off-limits when water is high and camp should be set well away
options.label: C

options.text: A swamp — all flat ground near blue lines is marsh and should be avoided
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have been following a river for two hours as a handrail, and the map shows contour lines pinching tightly toward the stream ahead. What is the risk, and what is the correct move?

options.text: The river is about to widen into a lake — move closer to the water to keep the handrail
options.label: A

options.text: The river is entering a gorge or canyon with no exit — step back from the river and route on the ridge or bench the map shows is passable
options.label: B

options.text: The river is about to rise from snowmelt — cross immediately before the water climbs
options.label: C

options.text: The river is drying up — the handrail is ending, so turn around now
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to cross a river. Two candidates are visible: a narrow channel where the water is pinched between cut banks, and a wide, straight section with braided channels. Per documented crossing guidance, which is the correct choice and why?

options.text: The narrow channel — less water to wade means a faster, safer crossing
options.label: A

options.text: The narrow channel — the pinched banks hold the water shallow
options.label: B

options.text: Either one — crossing sites are interchangeable once the water is under knee depth
options.label: C

options.text: The wide, straight section — as the water disperses it flows slower and becomes shallower, which is the documented safe pattern
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Below your planned crossing line, you see branches and fallen trees piled across the channel — water is flowing through them, but they look dense. What have you identified, and what does it mean for the crossing?

options.text: A strainer — it lets water through but can trap you and your gear against it, so the crossing needs to move, or the hazard becomes a rescue plan before anyone enters
options.label: A

options.text: A beaver dam — it will hold the water back, making the crossing easier
options.label: B

options.text: A natural bridge — you can use the log pile to cross dry
options.label: C

options.text: A sandbar — the pile marks shallow water, so this is the ideal crossing spot
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are unsure where you are on the map. You find a stream and confirm from its current that the water is flowing from your right to your left. How does this orient you?

options.text: It tells you the time of day the stream last rose, nothing more
options.label: A

options.text: It proves you are on the north side of the watershed
options.label: B

options.text: Rivers always run downhill, so the water flows toward lower elevation — the flow direction tells you which way the ground slopes and where you sit in the drainage
options.label: C

options.text: It means the stream has its source on your left and you should walk upstream
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your route reaches a ford symbol where a road dips into a stream — but the map also shows a bridge two miles upstream where the same stream crosses a forest road. The ford looks shallow. Which choice follows sound navigation logic?

options.text: Use the ford — it is on the route, and a shallow-looking crossing saves the two-mile detour
options.label: A

options.text: Walk upstream to the bridge — a mapped bridge is a crossing that keeps you out of the water entirely, while an unknown ford may fail under current conditions
options.label: B

options.text: Cross the ford but only one at a time — speed through the water limits the risk
options.label: C

options.text: Wait at the ford for another party to cross first and show it is safe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It rained hard in the mountains overnight. At your crossing, the stream is running over the trail — brown, fast, and impossible to see through. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Cross quickly before the water rises any further — timing beats depth
options.label: A

options.text: Cross with linked arms — a group crossing is safe in any water
options.label: B

options.text: Wade out a few steps to test the bottom, then decide
options.label: C

options.text: Do not cross — it is never safe to walk into flood waters; turn around, wait it out, or take the detour
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is late afternoon, the stream is cold, you are hiking alone, and the crossing point has water above your knees with a bottom you cannot see. Which decision follows the no-cross rules?

options.text: Walk around or wait — when the bottom is invisible, the water is cold, you are alone, or darkness is near, the default answer is not across
options.label: A

options.text: Cross fast before the cold numbs your legs — speed reduces exposure time
options.label: B

options.text: Cross wearing your pack for ballast — the weight steadies you in the current
options.label: C

options.text: Find a flat pool and wade across — a calm surface guarantees safe water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After scouting, you find a wide, straight stretch with a flat pool at the crossing line, little or no current, and a visible bottom with a clear exit on the far bank. Per the crossing-selection rules, what is this site?

options.text: Unsafe — any deeper wading is prohibited by the rules
options.label: A

options.text: The one acceptable deeper wade — the rules allow wading deeper water only in a flat pool with little or no current, and you have confirmed the exit
options.label: B

options.text: A strainer trap — flat pools always hide undercut banks
options.label: C

options.text: A flood channel — flat, wide water marks where the river rises
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are on a familiar trail when dense fog rolls in. Which cue loss should you treat as the signal that terrain association is no longer reliable?

options.text: The trail underfoot is still visible, so navigation is unaffected
options.label: A

options.text: Distant landmarks and depth perception are gone — you can no longer match the terrain to the map
options.label: B

options.text: Only your sense of distance is affected, and landmarks remain usable
options.label: C

options.text: The fog only removes color, which is unimportant for navigation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Fog has swallowed every landmark in sight. Your last confirmed position is marked on the map. Which navigation method should you switch to now?

options.text: Bearing-and-distance discipline: deliberate compass bearing, short legs, distance tracked by pace or time
options.label: A

options.text: Terrain association, practiced harder — squinting at the map will recover the features
options.label: B

options.text: Walk toward where you remember the destination being, checking only occasionally
options.label: C

options.text: Follow the direction of the wind, which is consistent and verifiable
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Dense fog closes in on a trail you have hiked twenty times. You cannot confirm your position, and visibility is still deteriorating. The decision rule says:

options.text: Continue quickly — familiarity with the trail is a form of position
options.label: A

options.text: Continue slowly — speed up the pace to spend less time exposed
options.label: B

options.text: Stop now and wait or shelter — do not advance on an unconfirmed position in deteriorating visibility
options.label: C

options.text: Reverse course immediately, even though you cannot confirm the way back either
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You crossed a small stream at knee depth this morning. Heavy rain fell all morning, and the stream now runs brown and fast. What changed, and what does it mean for your plan?

options.text: Nothing — the stream returns to morning levels as soon as the rain stops, so cross now
options.label: A

options.text: The stream is only dangerous downstream, so find a wider crossing upstream
options.label: B

options.text: The map will have been updated to show the new crossing, so follow it
options.label: C

options.text: Small streams rise and fall within minutes or hours of rain — the crossing is a new decision, re-evaluated at the water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A snowstorm buries the trail ahead. Which additional cue losses does snow impose beyond covering the path?

options.text: None — a buried trail is the only navigation effect of snow
options.label: A

options.text: Flat light removes depth perception, color contrast fades, and whiteout removes all directional cues
options.label: B

options.text: Snow only removes the sound of streams, which was the last usable cue
options.label: C

options.text: Snow removes landmarks but leaves depth and color intact
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Wildfire smoke has moved over your area, and the air quality index (AQI) is above 100. You had planned a long, strenuous hike. What does the National Park Service guidance recommend?

options.text: Proceed normally — smoke affects views but not exertion
options.label: A

options.text: Proceed only if you hike alone, where pace is easier to control
options.label: B

options.text: Reduce outdoor activity, especially strenuous hikes or prolonged exposure — consider delaying or adjusting plans
options.label: C

options.text: Hike only in the morning, when air quality is always better
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A whiteout hits while you are on an open ridge. Your position is unconfirmed, visibility is zero, and there is no handrail to follow. The correct response is:

options.text: Stop in place, establish shelter, communicate your situation, and wait for the weather window
options.label: A

options.text: Keep moving downhill — gravity will lead you to the valley and the trail
options.label: B

options.text: Spread out your group and walk parallel lines until someone finds the trail
options.label: C

options.text: Advance slowly on your last bearing, since any movement is better than none
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In foggy conditions you must choose between a route along a valley floor and a route along a ridge crest. What is the decision logic?

options.text: Always take the valley floor — it is sheltered and requires less energy
options.label: A

options.text: Always take the ridge — it is always faster and always safer
options.label: B

options.text: Take whichever route is shorter on the map, regardless of visibility
options.label: C

options.text: Choose the line you can verify — the ridge crest is a linear handrail you can stay on, while the fogged valley floor offers no reference; weigh wind and exposure on the ridge
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before a day trip, the forecast calls for afternoon fog and a chance of thunderstorms. Which preparedness step most directly reduces the navigation risk this forecast creates?

options.text: Check the forecast and air quality, plan route and timing around the weather window, and share the trip plan with someone who knows your expected return
options.label: A

options.text: Pack extra snacks so a long wait in fog is comfortable
options.label: B

options.text: Leave earlier than planned so the fog finds you already at the trailhead
options.label: C

options.text: Rely on the phone's GPS, which is unaffected by weather
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are deep on the trail. Smoke has thickened, distant landmarks are gone, the AQI has climbed above 100, and you can smell fire. When is the decision to leave the area correct?

options.text: Never — you are committed to the route once you leave the trailhead
options.label: A

options.text: Now — unhealthy air, collapsed visibility, and a possible fire are grounds to stop the outing and leave, reporting what you saw
options.label: B

options.text: Only when the smoke is so thick you cannot see the person beside you
options.label: C

options.text: Only when park rangers close the trail — closures happen in time to protect you
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You wake at 3 AM in a tarp shelter and find the tarp covered in condensation that is starting to drip onto your sleeping bag. What is the correct response?

options.text: Seal the shelter completely so no more outside moisture can enter
options.label: A

options.text: Ignore it — condensation never reaches the insulation
options.label: B

options.text: Open a small vent to let breath moisture escape, and move anything critical away from the drip line
options.label: C

options.text: Build a fire inside the shelter to dry the air
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have a choice between a quality sleeping bag with no pad, or a basic pad with no bag, on a cold night. Which choice follows the insulation priorities of this lesson?

options.text: The pad alone — the ground layer is the first insulation priority; the bag's loft is crushed under your weight
options.label: A

options.text: The bag alone — bags insulate more than pads
options.label: B

options.text: Neither — you must have both or sleep sitting up
options.label: C

options.text: The bag, but worn instead of slept in
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are building a debris bed from forest material on damp ground. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Pile whatever is handy, wet or dry, as deep as you can
options.label: A

options.text: Lay a pine-bough base to lift the bed, then a hand-thick layer of dry leaves, fluffed, with extra under hips and shoulders
options.label: B

options.text: Sleep directly on the duff — it is already soft
options.label: C

options.text: Use only the thickest logs, regardless of damp
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You sweated heavily while pitching your shelter, and your only sleepwear is now damp. You have one spare set of dry clothing. What is the right move for the night?

options.text: Sleep in the damp clothing — it will dry from body heat in the bag
options.label: A

options.text: Sleep in both sets layered, damp inside
options.label: B

options.text: Air the damp set inside the bag so it dries faster
options.label: C

options.text: Sleep in the dry set and hang the damp set outside the sleeping area, sealed from the sleep system
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a cold night you sleep in a good sleeping bag directly on bare ground, and your back stays cold all night. Why does the bag fail you there?

options.text: The bag's loft is compressed under your weight at the contact point, so the ground conducts heat out through it
options.label: A

options.text: Bags only insulate when suspended
options.label: B

options.text: Cold always rises from the ground regardless of insulation
options.label: C

options.text: The bag is too small for the ground's heat loss
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two candidate sleep spots on a windy, cold night: (A) a flat clearing, calm but fully exposed; (B) a sheltered hollow with a natural windbreak, but slightly damper ground. Which choice best applies this lesson's priorities?

options.text: Spot A — flat ground matters more than wind
options.label: A

options.text: Spot A — exposure is irrelevant at night
options.label: B

options.text: Spot B — block the wind, then manage the ground moisture with elevation or a waterproof layer
options.label: C

options.text: Spot B — windbreaks only matter for fires
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cold and tired and the shelter is half-built. Why is pushing hard to finish it quickly a hidden danger?

options.text: Shelters never need to be finished
options.label: A

options.text: Heavy work makes you sweat, wetting clothing from the inside — wet clothing conducts heat away far faster than dry air does
options.label: B

options.text: Sweating warms the shelter air, which attracts condensation
options.label: C

options.text: Exhaustion makes knots untie
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While collecting debris for your bed, you find an unlimited supply of wet leaves and only a little dry grass. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Use the wet leaves — quantity beats quality
options.label: A

options.text: Mix wet and dry — the wet ones will dry from body heat
options.label: B

options.text: Use only the dry grass, and hunt for more dry material — wet material conducts heat instead of trapping air
options.label: C

options.text: Use the wet leaves, but stomp them flat first so they pack tighter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are comparing two debris beds: one is a thin layer of packed, stomped-down leaves; the other is a loose, fluffed pile twice as thick. Which is warmer and why?

options.text: The stomped bed — compaction improves contact
options.label: A

options.text: The fluffed bed — insulation is trapped air, so loft and thickness beat packing, as long as it stays thick enough under body weight
options.label: B

options.text: The stomped bed — packed leaves block wind better
options.label: C

options.text: They are identical — material matters, not structure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Nightfall approaches: 2°C (36°F), damp duff, no pad, and a tarp, poncho, cord, and sleeping bag in your pack. You have about twenty minutes of daylight. What is the best order of actions?

options.text: Pitch the tarp first, then worry about the bed in the dark
options.label: A

options.text: Build the bed first and skip the tarp — the bed is the priority
options.label: B

options.text: Spend the light collecting firewood instead of bedding
options.label: C

options.text: Pitch the tarp, build the ground layer (bough base, waterproof poncho, fluffed dry debris, extra under hips), vent it, and go to bed dry
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are choosing a site for a shelter you will use through the wet season. The most attractive flat ground sits in a low basin next to a seasonal creek that is dry today. Why is this site disqualified despite the flat, sheltered ground?

options.text: Flat ground is always worse for drainage
options.label: A

options.text: The basin is a flood path and cold-air pool — a watercourse that is dry today can be a torrent after upstream storms
options.label: B

options.text: Seasonal creeks are protected habitat and cannot be built near
options.label: C

options.text: Low ground attracts lightning, which is the only real concern
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are choosing between a heavy log cabin build and a fast frame-and-cover structure for a two-month winter stay in heavy-snow country. What is the honest comparison?

options.text: The cabin is always the right choice because it is stronger
options.label: A

options.text: The frame-and-cover is always right because it is faster
options.label: B

options.text: Match the choice to the stay: the cabin costs far more labor but survives winters with little maintenance; the frame-and-cover is viable only with a cover replacement plan and correct snow pitch
options.label: C

options.text: Structure choice does not matter — only the site matters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your long-term shelter's water plan currently says "collect from the stream by the door." Why is this not a complete water plan for a winter stay?

options.text: Streams are always unsafe to drink from regardless of treatment
options.label: A

options.text: A source is not a supply: the plan must state carry/delivery, storage, treatment, and what happens when the source freezes or cannot be reached
options.label: B

options.text: It is complete — a source is a plan
options.label: C

options.text: The plan needs a backup only in summer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Where should the latrine go at a long-term shelter with a stream as the water source?

options.text: Between the shelter and the stream, so it is easy to reach
options.label: A

options.text: Beside the shelter door for convenience in bad weather
options.label: B

options.text: On the high ground above the water source, so drainage runs away from it
options.label: C

options.text: Downhill and a reasonable distance from the water source and the shelter, with drainage away from both
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are installing a wood stove in the shelter. Which fire-separation requirement is part of the installation, not an option?

options.text: Clearance from anything that can burn, combustion ventilation, a carbon monoxide alarm, and separated fuel storage
options.label: A

options.text: Only a fire extinguisher near the door
options.label: B

options.text: Nothing — stoves are inherently safe if they burn dry wood
options.label: C

options.text: A smoke alarm is sufficient for a fuel-burning appliance
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is freezing, the power is out, and you want to warm the shelter with a camp stove. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Run it briefly indoors — the cold makes the risk worth it
options.label: A

options.text: Never run a camp stove, grill, or generator inside an enclosed space — combustion indoors without proper ventilation is a carbon monoxide hazard
options.label: B

options.text: Run it only at night when everyone is sleeping
options.label: C

options.text: Run it indoors only if the windows are all closed to keep the heat in
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In the weekly inspection of a long-term shelter, which items belong on the list?

options.text: Only the roof — everything else is fine until it is not
options.label: A

options.text: Only the stove — fire risk is the main risk
options.label: B

options.text: Roof and drainage, chimney and stove pipe, seals and closures, fuel and water storage, and new hazards after storms
options.label: C

options.text: The interior only — exterior condition is cosmetic
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have sealed your shelter tightly to keep the cold out, and now you wake to condensation dripping from the roof and damp sleeping bags. What went wrong?

options.text: The insulation is too thin
options.label: A

options.text: The building materials are wrong
options.label: B

options.text: The shelter is not sealed tightly enough — add more sealing
options.label: C

options.text: The shelter was sealed tighter than its ventilation — breath and cooking moisture condensed inside, wetting the insulation from within
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In heavy-snow country, what roof decision matters most for the shelter's survival through the season?

options.text: A pitch steep enough that snow slides rather than loads, with overhang that keeps runoff and drip lines away from walls
options.label: A

options.text: A flat roof that collects snow as insulation
options.label: B

options.text: The lowest possible pitch to reduce material use
options.label: C

options.text: No roof overhang, so snow cannot accumulate on it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before the first hard freeze, you have one afternoon to winterize the shelter. What is the correct sequence?

options.text: Interior comfort first — arrange the sleeping area, then worry about the roof
options.label: A

options.text: Decorate and seal the windows last — appearance is the priority
options.label: B

options.text: Verify the roof and drainage, install and check the heating with separation and CO alarm, protect stored water from freezing, and confirm fuel is dry and separated
options.label: C

options.text: Drain the stored water so it cannot freeze, and skip heating — cold is manageable
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are considering a wide, flat sandbar in a dry wash as a shelter site — it is soft, sheltered, and the sky above you is clear. Why does the hazard check still reject it?

options.text: Sand is always too cold to sleep on
options.label: A

options.text: The wash is a flood path — a flash flood can arrive from an upstream storm you never see, even under a clear sky
options.label: B

options.text: Sandbars are always full of insects at night
options.label: C

options.text: The wash is fine as long as you check the weather before bed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a deep, dry rock overhang at the base of a cliff. Beneath it, the ground is covered with fresh-looking rock fragments, and the overhang's ceiling shows water stains. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Reject it — fresh debris means the cliff is still shedding rock, and water-stained rock marks seepage that loosens the ceiling
options.label: A

options.text: Use it — depth and dryness outweigh any rock concern
options.label: B

options.text: Use it, but only for a daytime rest, never overnight
options.label: C

options.text: Use it, but sleep at the very back where the ceiling is thickest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You inspect a cave mouth and find fresh animal tracks and droppings just inside, and the entrance narrows behind a bend. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Enter fully — caves are stable and safe
options.label: A

options.text: Enter fully, but keep a fire burning for protection
options.label: B

options.text: Do not enter — a den that shows fresh activity is occupied or used; use only the entrance area if at all, and never block the only exit
options.label: C

options.text: Seal the entrance with rocks, then use it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are building a debris lean-to at dusk, with damp ground and a light breeze. Which build order is correct?

options.text: Frame first, then a thin layer of whatever material is nearest — speed matters most
options.label: A

options.text: Frame first, then pile dry material hand-thick over the ribs with the closed end into the wind, and a raised dry bed inside
options.label: B

options.text: Bed first, then frame around it, then orient the entrance into the wind
options.label: C

options.text: Skip the frame and sleep in the open pile — material matters, structure does not
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You finish a snow shelter late in the day. Which of the following is mandatory before you seal yourself in?

options.text: Nothing — sealing keeps the warmth in
options.label: A

options.text: A fire, to raise the temperature quickly
options.label: B

options.text: A flat floor only — airflow is irrelevant in snow
options.label: C

options.text: A ventilation opening, so breath and any combustion cannot concentrate carbon monoxide in the enclosed space
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You built a debris shelter in a popular campsite area and are packing out in the morning. What is the correct impact decision?

options.text: Leave it standing — the next person may need it
options.label: A

options.text: Leave it standing — it will rot anyway
options.label: B

options.text: Dismantle it and spread the material back, restoring the ground — impact is proportional to the place, and high-use areas are restored, not left marked
options.label: C

options.text: Burn it, so nothing is left
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Where should you never place a shelter relative to a cliff, even if the ground is dry and flat?

options.text: In the fall line directly below a cliff face showing fresh scars — rockfall collects at cliff bases
options.label: A

options.text: On the far side of a nearby river, above the bank
options.label: B

options.text: In the middle of a flat meadow, far from the cliff
options.label: C

options.text: Behind a low wall of boulders at the cliff's base
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In wildlife country, where does the food go relative to a natural shelter?

options.text: Inside the shelter, so it stays dry and close
options.label: A

options.text: Under the bedding, where it is hidden
options.label: B

options.text: Next to the entrance, for quick access at night
options.label: C

options.text: Away from the sleeping area and the shelter — a food-free camp is the rule where animals roam
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Conditions: dusk, rain by midnight, light almost gone, and the only dry debris material is a thin layer under the trees — not enough for a proper hut. You have a tarp in your pack. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Build the hut anyway — natural is always better
options.label: A

options.text: Pitch the tarp — when daylight, time, or dry material is short, a tarp beats a half-built debris hut
options.label: B

options.text: Sleep in the open — the rain is light
options.label: C

options.text: Spend the remaining light hiking to find better material
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have one hour of daylight left and a support tree for a lean-to. Which use of the hour produces the warmest shelter?

options.text: Building the tallest, most elaborate frame you can
options.label: A

options.text: Digging a deep pit to sleep in
options.label: B

options.text: Framing small and low, then spending most of the hour gathering dry material for a hand-thick cover and a raised bed inside
options.label: C

options.text: Decorating the entrance with branches for looks
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are tensioning a tarp corner and notice the grommet is starting to pull through the fabric under load. What is the correct response?

options.text: Ball a small rock or stick inside the fabric at that corner and tie around it — load is distributed to the fabric, not the grommet alone
options.label: A

options.text: Pull the grommet harder — it will seat itself
options.label: B

options.text: Remove the grommet entirely and tie to the tarp edge
options.label: C

options.text: Accept the tear — one corner can be lost
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need to tie your tarp's ridgeline for a windy night and have a choice: carried paracord, or fresh inner-bark cordage twisted from a nearby basswood. Which do you use for the ridgeline?

options.text: The natural cordage — it is free and just as strong
options.label: A

options.text: The natural cordage — it stretches less than manufactured line
options.label: B

options.text: The carried paracord — natural cordage dries, stiffens, and rots when wet, and carries far less than it looks like it should
options.label: C

options.text: The natural cordage, but only if it is wet when you tie it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are selecting branches for the ribs of a debris shelter. A green sapling bends easily and springs back; a dry dead branch is stiff and snaps when you flex it hard. Which choice is correct for a shelter rib that must hold its curve?

options.text: The dry branch — stiffness is always better
options.label: A

options.text: The green sapling — it bends under load and springs back, which suits curved ribs, but it must be inspected and expected to move
options.label: B

options.text: Neither — only manufactured poles are acceptable
options.label: C

options.text: The dry branch, but only if it is soaked first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find your tarp in the pack with faint crease cracks across a folded section and stiff fabric in spots. What does this tell you, and what is the correct decision?

options.text: It is fine — folds always leave marks
options.label: A

options.text: It needs to be folded differently
options.label: B

options.text: It needs a waterproofing spray
options.label: C

options.text: UV degradation has weakened the fabric — a cracked tarp tears at the fold exactly when it is needed, so it is replaced or treated as a cover with known weak points, not trusted at full strength
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your shelter ridgeline runs over a sharp rock edge. What does the cordage system require?

options.text: A padding sleeve under the contact point — a line bearing on a sharp edge abrades and parts, and the bearing point is part of the cordage system
options.label: A

options.text: Nothing — rope is abrasion-proof
options.label: B

options.text: A tighter knot at the anchor to compensate
options.label: C

options.text: A longer ridgeline so the rock is not touched
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are deciding how to cover a shelter for a one-night stay, with a tarp in your pack and abundant dry grass nearby. What is the honest material decision?

options.text: Thatch — natural cover is always the right choice
options.label: A

options.text: The tarp — thatch takes hours of gathering to shed water and is a long-stay material, not a tonight material
options.label: B

options.text: Thatch — it takes only a few minutes to layer
options.label: C

options.text: The grass only, since it is free
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are staking a shelter into loose sand. Your regular stakes went in easily and are already leaning. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Hammer them deeper with a rock — depth always holds
options.label: A

options.text: Use a deadman — a buried stick tied to the line distributes the load where stakes will not hold
options.label: B

options.text: Switch to shorter stakes — they catch less wind
options.label: C

options.text: Remove the stakes and pile sand on the tarp edges
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During the night you check the shelter and find your natural-cordage lashing has gone stiff, and one strand is visibly rotted where it was damp. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: It is fine — natural cordage always stiffens
options.label: A

options.text: Stiffness means it is drying and gaining strength
options.label: B

options.text: Wet natural cordage rots and weakens — the lashing is replaced with carried line for anything load-bearing, or reinforced before it is trusted
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A thermal blanket and a tarp are both in your pack. You need a cover that sheds rain and a layer that traps heat under the body. What is the correct assignment?

options.text: Tarp for the cover — continuous, water-shedding; blanket for insulation beneath the body — trapped air is its job
options.label: A

options.text: Tarp under the body and blanket overhead — either way works
options.label: B

options.text: Tarp for both — a cover can do every job
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are packing for a weekend where a tarp-and-cord shelter is the plan. Which kit decision matches the material principles of this lesson?

options.text: Minimal gear — the forest will supply everything
options.label: A

options.text: Only stakes — everything else can be improvised
options.label: B

options.text: Tarp, load-bearing cordage, stakes, and repair tape — carried kit wins where it exists, with natural materials as the backup, not the plan
options.label: C

options.text: Natural materials only — carried gear is a sign of inexperience
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are walking a candidate campsite and running the five W's. You notice the site is in a grassy depression at the bottom of a valley. Which W or W's is this failing?

options.text: Water — depressions pool rainwater and collect dense, cold air at night
options.label: A

options.text: Wood — valley bottoms never have usable material
options.label: B

options.text: Wind — only wind, because valleys block it
options.label: C

options.text: Wildlife — only wildlife, because animals always live in valleys
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A dry creek bed looks flat, soft, and sheltered — perfect for the night. Why should you not camp there?

options.text: Dry creek beds are always on private property
options.label: A

options.text: It is a flood path — storms upstream can send water down a bed that has been dry for months, even under a clear sky
options.label: B

options.text: The soft soil will not hold stakes, so the shelter will collapse
options.label: C

options.text: The soil in creek beds always harbors insect nests
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The evening forecast calls for high winds. Where is the least exposed place to camp?

options.text: On an open saddle between two hills — the wind passes over it
options.label: A

options.text: On a bare hilltop — the wind is thinner at altitude
options.label: B

options.text: In the lee of a rock outcrop or dense vegetation, away from any hazards above
options.label: C

options.text: In the middle of a field, where the wind is uniform
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are about to pitch under a large old tree. Which single observation most strongly argues for a different site?

options.text: The tree's canopy provides shade from the afternoon sun
options.label: A

options.text: The tree is a species that loses its leaves in winter
options.label: B

options.text: The ground under the tree is soft and level
options.label: C

options.text: The tree has several dead branches and one dead limb wedged in the crown
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a windstorm, you re-inspect the overhead above your camp and find a newly cracked dead limb overhanging the sleeping area. What should you do?

options.text: Move the sleeping spot (or the whole camp) so nothing dead is overhead — wind, snow, and rain can bring it down at any time
options.label: A

options.text: Tie the limb up to the tree so it cannot fall
options.label: B

options.text: Wait until morning — limbs only fall in strong storms
options.label: C

options.text: Sleep elsewhere only if the limb is larger than your arm
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A search-and-rescue helicopter may pass over your area tomorrow morning. Which shelter location helps you most?

options.text: The densest thicket you can find, for concealment
options.label: A

options.text: A spot visible from the air — a clearing or open slope — even if it means a bit more wind exposure
options.label: B

options.text: The deepest part of a valley, out of sight of the ridge
options.label: C

options.text: Under a large tree, where the canopy hides the shelter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You notice a well-worn game trail crossing the center of your candidate site, plus droppings near the edge. What is the right read?

options.text: The trail is a sign of healthy local wildlife — a good sign for the site
options.label: A

options.text: Animals never approach campsites that already have tents
options.label: B

options.text: The site sits on a regular animal route — expect traffic through camp; pick a spot off the trail and keep food away from the sleeping area
options.label: C

options.text: Droppings mean the area is clean of predators
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You find a site with abundant firewood and clean ground, but it sits in a rocky wash below a steep slope. How should you decide?

options.text: Take it — wood availability is the most important W in cold weather
options.label: A

options.text: Take it for one night only — it will be fine if it doesn't rain
options.label: B

options.text: Take it, but pitch the shelter higher up the slope
options.label: C

options.text: Reject it — the site fails the water and hazard checks (flood path, potential rockfall), and the fifth W never overrides the other four
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You arrive at a lakeside campsite area on public land and want to pitch near the water. What is the correct first step?

options.text: Look up the local regulations — many public lands specify how far campsites must be from water, trails, and roads
options.label: A

options.text: Pitch as close to the water as possible — water access always wins
options.label: B

options.text: Pitch anywhere the ground is level
options.label: C

options.text: Ask other campers what the custom is
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The light is fading and you must choose a site now. Which sequence matches this lesson's guidance for a fast, correct decision?

options.text: Pick the most comfortable-looking spot quickly, then improve it tomorrow
options.label: A

options.text: Set up wherever the previous campers did — their site passed the checks
options.label: B

options.text: Run the five W's plus drainage, visibility, and regulations in order; if any check fails, move to the next candidate — then pitch in daylight discipline
options.label: C

options.text: Wait for full darkness so the stars can guide the choice
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The forecast is clear and calm. Which candidate site is the safest choice for a tarp shelter?

options.text: A flat sandbar in a dry creek bed — soft and sheltered
options.label: A

options.text: An exposed plateau above the valley — flat with good views
options.label: B

options.text: A bench midway up the slope behind a rock outcrop — clear ground, no dead trees overhead
options.label: C

options.text: Directly under a large tree with one dead branch hanging above
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a steady northwest wind, how should the shelter be oriented?

options.text: The opening faces directly into the northwest wind
options.label: A

options.text: The closed or low end faces the wind; the opening faces away or cross-wind
options.label: B

options.text: The long side faces the wind
options.label: C

options.text: Orientation does not matter for a tarp
options.label: D

questions.question_text: While pitching an A-frame, what does "tension the long edges center-outward" mean, and why does it matter?

options.text: Pull hardest on the corner stakes first — it is faster
options.label: A

options.text: Work from the center of each edge toward the corners, keeping the fabric taut — a flapping tarp shreds and sheds poorly
options.label: B

options.text: Tighten only the windward side
options.label: C

options.text: Leave slack so the tarp can stretch when wet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a cold night, which is more important for staying warm: the tarp or the ground layer under your body?

options.text: The tarp — it traps body heat
options.label: A

options.text: The ground layer — you lose more heat downward, and a sleeping bag compressed under body weight loses its loft exactly where it touches the ground
options.label: B

options.text: They contribute equally
options.label: C

options.text: Neither — only a fire matters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have a sleeping bag but no pad, and the forest floor offers dry leaves and pine boughs. What do you do?

options.text: Sleep directly on the bag — the tarp will keep you warm
options.label: A

options.text: Build a ground bed of leaves and boughs a hand's thickness or more beneath the bag
options.label: B

options.text: Hang the bag from the ridgeline to stay off the ground
options.label: C

options.text: Sleep sitting up to reduce contact with the ground
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a night in a fully closed A-frame, you wake to water dripping from the tarp and a damp sleeping bag. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Rain leaking through the tarp fabric
options.label: A

options.text: Condensation — a night of exhaled breath moisture condensed on the tarp because the shelter had no ventilation
options.label: B

options.text: The ground absorbed water and released it upward
options.label: C

options.text: The ridgeline was too low
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your wet rain jacket is inside the sleeping area. What should you do with it for the night?

options.text: Spread it over the sleeping bag for extra warmth
options.label: A

options.text: Keep it inside — it will dry overnight
options.label: B

options.text: Store it outside the sleeping area or sealed in a waterproof bag
options.label: C

options.text: Use it as the ground layer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You plan a small fire near your lean-to tarp shelter. Which placement is correct?

options.text: Directly under the low edge of the lean-to to trap heat
options.label: A

options.text: At least 2 meters from the tarp, downwind, with a cleared perimeter
options.label: B

options.text: Upwind, 1 meter from the tarp, so smoke blows away
options.label: C

options.text: Inside the lean-to — it is sheltered from wind there
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of these is a situation where building a tarp shelter is the WRONG decision?

options.text: You are cold, exhausted, and a maintained trail shelter is two hours' walk away — you can still walk safely
options.label: A

options.text: Rain starts at dusk and you have a tarp and cordage ready
options.label: B

options.text: The wind is rising and you have already selected a protected site
options.label: C

options.text: You are above treeline and moving to lower, sheltered ground will take twenty minutes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does a tarp shelter provide "almost no insulation on its own"?

options.text: Tarp fabric is too thin to trap any air
options.label: A

options.text: Its job is blocking wind and rain — warmth comes from the sleeping system, clothing layers, and the ground layer, not from the sheet
options.label: B

options.text: Tarps reflect body heat away
options.label: C

options.text: Tarps only insulate in summer
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are choosing between a freestanding dome and a tunnel tent for a trip where you expect strong wind and thin, soft soil. Which consideration should drive the choice?

options.text: The tunnel is lighter and sleeker in wind — but it needs stakes at both ends to stand, and on soft, thin soil its strength depends entirely on anchors that may not hold
options.label: A

options.text: The dome is always stronger than a tunnel in wind, no matter the soil
options.label: B

options.text: Tunnel tents cannot be used on soft ground at all
options.label: C

options.text: Freestanding domes are only for car camping
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You arrive at a flat, grassy spot that looks perfect for the tent. What is the correct first step before pitching?

options.text: Pitch immediately — flat grass is all a tent needs
options.label: A

options.text: Walk the site: check drainage and slope, clear rocks and sticks from the footprint area, and confirm no wash or standing water is nearby
options.label: B

options.text: Set up the fly first, then decide the site from inside
options.label: C

options.text: Stake the corners first and decide the site from the stakes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A gusty wind is forecast overnight. You are pitching your dome tent on exposed ground. What is the correct sequence and emphasis?

options.text: Stake any corner first, then deal with wind after dinner
options.label: A

options.text: Pitch with the door facing the wind so it flutters dry
options.label: B

options.text: Pitch with the lowest, smallest profile into the wind, stake the windward corners first and hardest, and run every guyline the tent has
options.label: C

options.text: Weigh the tent down with a pack on the floor instead of staking
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The fly pools water in a sagging spot every time it rains, and water seeps in near the door. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The tent is defective — pooling means it must be returned
options.label: A

options.text: Rainwater always pools on flys; it is harmless
options.label: B

options.text: The door should face uphill to shed the water
options.label: C

options.text: The fly is not taut and the drip line over the door is wrong — pitch tension and fly positioning, not the tent's quality, decide whether water runs off or runs in
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a clear, cold night you wake to find the inside of the fly wet and your bag damp at the foot. What is the best explanation and the correct fix for the next night?

options.text: It is condensation from your breath and body moisture — vent more (open fly vents and inner mesh), keep wet gear out of the sleeping space, and brush frost off the inner wall in the morning
options.label: A

options.text: The tent is defective — moisture should never form inside
options.label: B

options.text: The ground is wet — move the tent to a dry spot
options.label: C

options.text: The fly should be removed entirely on clear nights
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is a cold, rainy evening and you want to warm up and cook dinner inside the sealed tent. What is the correct call?

options.text: Cook inside with the door slightly open — a crack is enough
options.label: A

options.text: A small stove is fine if the flame is low
options.label: B

options.text: Never run a fuel-burning stove inside a closed tent — carbon monoxide is odorless and deadly; cook outside, or at worst in the open vestibule with the tent fully vented, never in a sealed space
options.label: C

options.text: Cooking inside is fine as long as the tent is ventilated by the mesh window
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You return from a wet weekend and are exhausted. What is the minimum correct after-trip care for the tent?

options.text: Stuff it in the storage bag wet — it will dry at the bottom of the closet
options.label: A

options.text: Set it up or hang it to dry completely before storage, and repair or seam-seal as directed before it is needed again
options.label: B

options.text: Shake it off and store it — the coating is waterproof anyway
options.label: C

options.text: Leave it in the car — the heat will dry it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your tent pole snapped at the elbow joint mid-trip, 20 km from the trailhead. Which combination of preparedness and field response is most honest?

options.text: Abandon the tent and sleep under the stars — poles are irreplaceable
options.label: A

options.text: Tie the broken pole to a tree branch to brace it
options.label: B

options.text: Poles never break in practice
options.label: C

options.text: A pole splint or taped repair can finish the trip, and the real lesson is that poles are the critical failure point — carry the splint before you need it, and know which pole does what
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are planning a solo trip where every gram counts, over rough terrain, with several nights out. Your shelter decision should weigh which honest comparison?

options.text: A tarp or tarp-plus-bivy is lighter than the lightest tent — when weight discipline matters, the tent is often the wrong tool
options.label: A

options.text: A tent is always worth its weight — no other shelter protects as well
options.label: B

options.text: Weight only matters for beginners
options.label: C

options.text: The heaviest tent is always the safest tent
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A friend says, "I keep a tent in my emergency go-bag — that's my shelter plan." What is the most accurate response?

options.text: A tent in the go-bag is a great plan — it is the fastest shelter to deploy
options.label: A

options.text: An emergency uses what you carry — if the tent is too heavy to live permanently in the kit, the go-bag shelter should be a tarp, which is lighter and needs no poles that can break
options.label: B

options.text: The go-bag should always contain both a tent and a tarp
options.label: C

options.text: The tent in the go-bag is fine — poles are optional in emergencies
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A warm, wet, windless afternoon turns into a windy night with rain. Which of the four threats is doing the most damage to your warmth, and what is the first adaptation?

options.text: Wind — it strips body heat and drives rain; orient the shelter with its closed or low end into the wind
options.label: A

options.text: Rain — only rain matters when the air is warm
options.label: B

options.text: Snow — only snow matters at night
options.label: C

options.text: Sun — only sun matters on clear days
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is 50°F, raining steadily, with a stiff breeze. A friend says this is not cold enough to be dangerous. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: Correct — hypothermia only occurs below freezing
options.label: A

options.text: The combination of wet, cold, and wind can drive core temperature down well above freezing — the CDC defines hypothermia as a core temperature below 95°F, and this is exactly the exposure that takes people down
options.label: B

options.text: Correct — rain at 50°F only matters for comfort
options.label: C

options.text: Incorrect — but only because of the wind, not the wet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At camp, you notice the wind shifting to the northwest and strengthening, clouds building on that horizon, and the temperature dropping. What is the right response?

options.text: Ignore it — forecasts are the only reliable source
options.label: A

options.text: Wait until the first raindrop, then prepare
options.label: B

options.text: Treat the signals as "get the shelter ready now" — re-orient, re-tension, and prepare in daylight rather than predicting the hour
options.label: C

options.text: Move camp to the ridge top to watch the weather arrive
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your forecast said clear and calm, but you checked the sky at sunset anyway and saw building cloud to the west. Which combination of actions best follows this lesson's weather-awareness practice?

options.text: Trust the forecast — clear means clear
options.label: A

options.text: The sky at sunset is always deceptive — ignore it
options.label: B

options.text: Pack up and leave immediately whenever clouds build
options.label: C

options.text: Check the forecast before departure and before the trailhead, read the sky at camp, and treat the building cloud as a signal to prepare the shelter early
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Wind-driven rain is forecast overnight. Your tarp A-frame currently faces southeast, away from the current breeze. What is the correct sequence of adjustments?

options.text: Re-orient so the closed end faces the windward side, re-stake the windward lines first and hardest, re-tension the fly, and clear the drip lines
options.label: A

options.text: Face the opening into the wind so rain blows through and out
options.label: B

options.text: Lower the windward end to ground level and leave the rest alone
options.label: C

options.text: No change — A-frames handle all wind directions equally
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Rain begins at 2 AM. The ground around your shelter was flat and soft when you pitched. What was the missed adaptation?

options.text: None — flat ground drains fine in rain
options.label: A

options.text: Drainage — the shelter should have been on high, gently sloping ground so runoff passes around rather than pooling under the sleeping system
options.label: B

options.text: The fly should have been left loose so rain filters through
options.label: C

options.text: A ditch around the shelter is required on all ground
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It begins to snow wet, heavy flakes. Which is the priority concern for the shelter overnight?

options.text: The cold — snow always means the shelter must be sealed tight
options.label: A

options.text: The wet — snowflakes cannot damage a shelter
options.label: B

options.text: Loading — wet snow accumulating on the fly can bend poles and tear fabric, so pitch steeply and knock accumulation off during the night
options.label: C

options.text: The wind — snow has no wind when it falls
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The ground is frozen solid and snow is accumulating. Your tent stakes will not hold. What is the correct anchoring adaptation?

options.text: Skip the anchors — the tent's weight is enough
options.label: A

options.text: Tie the tent to the nearest tree branches
options.label: B

options.text: Pile snow on the floor of the tent for ballast
options.label: C

options.text: Anchor through the snow to buried anchors — a stake-driven "deadman" — rather than trusting a short stake in powder or frozen ground
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a cold, clear night you zip the shelter completely closed "to keep the heat in." What happens, and what is the correct practice?

options.text: The shelter stays warmer and drier — sealing is correct on cold nights
options.label: A

options.text: Breath and perspiration condense on the cold fly and soak the sleeping system — a sealed shelter is a wet shelter; vent anyway, and keep the ground layer beneath you
options.label: B

options.text: Sealing creates condensation only on hot nights
options.label: C

options.text: The fly should be removed entirely on cold nights
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are camped in a heat wave with a forecast of 38°C and no cloud. Which setup best follows the sun-threat adaptations?

options.text: Pitch in a closed heat-trap bowl — it collects the coolest night air
options.label: A

options.text: Seal everything during the day to keep hot air out
options.label: B

options.text: Choose a site that avoids heat-trap bowls, shade the sleeping period, and maximize airflow through the shelter
options.label: C

options.text: Sleep outside the shelter entirely — shelter has no role in heat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following belongs in a one-page household emergency plan?

options.text: A 20-page risk analysis with historical data
options.label: A

options.text: Meeting points, out-of-area contact, evacuation rules, communication fallbacks, household specifics, and a review date
options.label: B

options.text: Only emergency phone numbers
options.label: C

options.text: A list of every emergency in the region for the last 50 years
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household sets its external meeting point at a large oak tree at the end of their street. Why is this a poor choice?

options.text: Trees are harder to find than buildings
options.label: A

options.text: It is still inside the neighborhood — an external point must be outside the likely evacuation area, reachable if the neighborhood itself is the hazard
options.label: B

options.text: The tree might be cut down
options.label: C

options.text: Trees do not provide shelter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the role of the out-of-area contact in the communication plan?

options.text: They store spare keys to the house
options.label: A

options.text: They act as the switchboard: separated household members check in with one person outside the affected region, who relays status and locations
options.label: B

options.text: They call emergency services on behalf of the household
options.label: C

options.text: They are responsible for evacuating the household
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the correct order of the communication fallback chain?

options.text: Written note → text → call → out-of-area contact
options.label: A

options.text: Call → text → out-of-area contact → written note at the meeting points
options.label: B

options.text: Text → call → email → social media
options.label: C

options.text: Out-of-area contact → call → text
options.label: D

questions.question_text: An evacuation order arrives for your neighborhood. What is the written rule?

options.text: Wait for a second confirmation before leaving
options.label: A

options.text: Leave when the order arrives — do not wait
options.label: B

options.text: Stay until you can see the hazard with your own eyes
options.label: C

options.text: Evacuate only if neighbors are leaving too
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A chemical release has occurred upwind of your home and authorities advise sheltering in place. What is the correct action?

options.text: Evacuate immediately on foot
options.label: A

options.text: Stay inside, seal windows and doors, and follow official instructions
options.label: B

options.text: Open windows to air out the house
options.label: C

options.text: Drive toward the chemical plant to see the situation
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A wildfire is visible moving toward your neighborhood, but no evacuation order has been issued. Which written rule applies?

options.text: Wait for the official order — orders always arrive in time
options.label: A

options.text: Leave if you can do so safely — a visible approaching fire justifies evacuating without waiting for an order that may never come
options.label: B

options.text: Shelter in place until the fire passes
options.label: C

options.text: Walk toward the fire to assess it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: How often should the household plan be rehearsed and reviewed?

options.text: Rehearse twice a year; review on one fixed annual date
options.label: A

options.text: Only when a new family member joins
options.label: B

options.text: Every five years
options.label: C

options.text: Never — a written plan does not need updating
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household's plan reads: "If there's an emergency, call Mom. She'll pick up the kids. We'll meet at the mall." No cards, no external point, no review date. Which single change addresses the most weaknesses at once?

options.text: Buy better phones
options.label: A

options.text: Rewrite the plan to the six-component one-page standard — a real external meeting point, an out-of-area contact on printed cards, and a fixed review date
options.label: B

options.text: Memorize Mom's number
options.label: C

options.text: Move closer to the mall
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly names the three legs of household preparedness?

options.text: Food, water, and shelter supplies
options.label: A

options.text: Plan, kit, and knowledge
options.label: B

options.text: Insurance, savings, and supplies
options.label: C

options.text: Threat assessment, evacuation route, and go-bag
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household of two adults wants a 72-hour water supply at the standard allowance. How much water should they store?

options.text: 8 liters (2 gallons)
options.label: A

options.text: 12 liters (3 gallons)
options.label: B

options.text: 23 liters (6 gallons)
options.label: C

options.text: 50 liters (13 gallons)
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is a single 28 kg (62 lb) family go-bag a poor design for a household with children?

options.text: It exceeds airline weight limits
options.label: A

options.text: No single adult can carry it while managing a child — go-bags should be per person, sized so each member can carry their own
options.label: B

options.text: It is too small to hold supplies for everyone
options.label: C

options.text: It is difficult to store in a closet
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Where should a household's go-bag live?

options.text: In the attic, protected from damp
options.label: A

options.text: In the garage, near the car
options.label: B

options.text: Near a main exit, where every household member can reach it
options.label: C

options.text: In a locked storage room, to protect the contents
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the recommended maintenance rhythm for emergency supplies?

options.text: Once a year, after the holiday season
options.label: A

options.text: Every 6 months, anchored to a fixed date like the daylight-saving clock change
options.label: B

options.text: Only when an emergency is forecast
options.label: C

options.text: Whenever something looks expired
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household keeps borrowing items from the go-bag — batteries for a remote, bandages for a scrape — and replacing them "later." What is the actual risk?

options.text: The bag becomes slightly lighter
options.label: A

options.text: The kit quietly stops working — an emergency kit that is used as a storage bin is incomplete exactly when it is needed
options.label: B

options.text: The items lose their resale value
options.label: C

options.text: There is no risk if the items are eventually replaced
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of these is a limitation of preparedness — something it genuinely cannot do?

options.text: Reduce the severity of most household emergencies
options.label: A

options.text: Guarantee the household's safety
options.label: B

options.text: Shorten recovery time
options.label: C

options.text: Make evacuation decisions easier
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two households face the same outage. Household A owns a large sealed emergency kit they have never opened. Household B owns less gear but stores water, rehearses a written plan, and knows how to purify water. Which is better prepared, and why?

options.text: Household A — more gear is always better
options.label: A

options.text: Household B — practiced skills and a rehearsed plan beat untested gear
options.label: B

options.text: They are equally prepared
options.label: C

options.text: Neither — only professional responders are ever prepared
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which critical functions should have redundancy in a preparedness system?

options.text: Water purification, light, and information
options.label: A

options.text: Only water purification
options.label: B

options.text: Only food storage
options.label: C

options.text: None — one reliable method per function is enough
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A single adult in an earthquake-prone city has one case of bottled water (~4 L), no written plan, no stored documents, and a monthly medication renewal. What should be done FIRST this weekend?

options.text: Buy a generator
options.label: A

options.text: Write the one-page plan and expand water storage toward the 72-hour baseline
options.label: B

options.text: Replace the medications
options.label: C

options.text: Move to a lower-risk city
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It is early winter, late afternoon, and you are wet and cold. You have a lighter, a knife, and a small pack. Which problem is the fastest-acting threat, and therefore the first priority?

options.text: Exposure — wind and wet are acting on you right now, so shelter work comes before everything else
options.label: A

options.text: Hunger — you have not eaten in hours and need calories for warmth
options.label: B

options.text: The cold meal — eating something warm would improve morale
options.label: C

options.text: The broken backpack strap — gear must be repaired before it fails completely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two groups teach survival priorities differently: one says "shelter first, always," another says "water first, always." What does the framework actually require?

options.text: Picking one fixed order and sticking to it — consistency beats analysis
options.label: A

options.text: The order depends on the environment — cold leads with shelter and fire; hot, dry conditions lead with water
options.label: B

options.text: Food always comes first, since hunger is the strongest signal
options.label: C

options.text: The order only matters in the first ten minutes, then all needs are equal
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before committing to a course of action in a survival situation, the recommended first step is to:

options.text: Build the largest fire you can — visible effort builds confidence
options.label: A

options.text: Eat and drink first — judgment improves with fuel
options.label: B

options.text: Size up the situation: your physical condition, your equipment, and your surroundings
options.label: C

options.text: Walk in one direction for an hour to gather information
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cold, wet, and in early winter darkness is approaching. Your pack contains food, a lighter, and an emergency blanket. Why does food wait until last in this scenario?

options.text: Food is contaminated and unsafe to eat in cold weather
options.label: A

options.text: Eating raises your metabolism and uses up warmth faster
options.label: B

options.text: There is never enough food to matter in the first hours
options.label: C

options.text: Cold is acting on you within hours, while hunger acts over days — warmth first, food later
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have limited daylight and energy. Which test tells you whether a candidate task is the right next action?

options.text: If I do this first, does it make everything else easier or harder?
options.label: A

options.text: Is this the task I am best at performing?
options.label: B

options.text: Does this task use the most impressive equipment I carry?
options.label: C

options.text: Have I ever done this task before on a trip?
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your household has a small budget for emergency supplies. Which purchase sequence follows the prioritization logic of "threats before comfort"?

options.text: Comfort items first — morale gear, games, and extras — so the kit gets used
options.label: A

options.text: The most expensive single item first, while it is available
options.label: B

options.text: Water, warmth, light, first aid, and communication first — then comfort items
options.label: C

options.text: Whatever is on sale this month, spread across every category
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A storm is forecast to arrive in about twenty minutes, and you are still setting up camp. How should prioritization change versus when you were unhurried?

options.text: Keep the same sequence — the plan does not change because of weather
options.label: A

options.text: Switch to short, high-value actions that buy the next hour — shelter and wind protection now, longer projects later
options.label: B

options.text: Finish the elaborate camp kitchen first, since it is half-built
options.label: C

options.text: Stop all work and wait to see if the forecast is accurate
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a hot, dry environment with a long walk ahead and the sun high, which need leads the framework?

options.text: Fire — it signals rescuers and purifies water
options.label: A

options.text: Food — long walks burn calories quickly
options.label: B

options.text: Shelter from sun and wind — a shelter is the universal first need
options.label: C

options.text: Water and shade — dehydration impairs judgment and strength fastest in the heat
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are unhurried, warm, and dry, with several hours of daylight. What is the best use of the time, according to the prioritization principles?

options.text: Preparation — improving shelter, collecting extra water, arranging signaling options
options.label: A

options.text: Resting completely — conserving energy is always the priority
options.label: B

options.text: Hiking out immediately in a random direction — movement attracts help
options.label: C

options.text: Cooking a full meal with the largest fire you can manage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does a household plan that has been written and rehearsed once outperform a perfect plan that has never been practiced?

options.text: Practicing is only useful for children and pets
options.label: A

options.text: A rehearsed plan is a decision already made — under stress you fall back on what you have walked through, not what you have read
options.label: B

options.text: Written plans become outdated within weeks, so rehearsal is pointless
options.label: C

options.text: Practice is the same as building the kit, and the kit alone is the plan
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A family starts a risk assessment for their home. Which first step follows the planning guidance?

options.text: List the hazards that can actually reach their area — local weather, power loss, flooding, wildfire — before planning against any of them
options.label: A

options.text: Buy a large supply of candles and batteries immediately
options.label: B

options.text: Wait until the next storm warning to decide what to prepare
options.label: C

options.text: Plan for a generic "disaster" with no specific hazard in mind
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household lists "minor power blips" and "kitchen grease fire." Both are possible, but which ranks higher for planning, and why?

options.text: Power blips — they are far more likely, so they matter more
options.label: A

options.text: The grease fire — likelihood is lower but consequence is much higher, so it earns preparation
options.label: B

options.text: Power blips — the fire is too unlikely to deserve any thought
options.label: C

options.text: They are equal — likelihood and consequence do not change planning
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A planned route crosses a river that is running fast and high after rain. Which response best fits this hazard?

options.text: Accept — the crossing is part of the adventure
options.label: A

options.text: Prepare — pack extra rope and attempt it carefully
options.label: B

options.text: Avoid — do not attempt the crossing; choose a different route or a different day
options.label: C

options.text: Reduce — cross earlier in the morning when the water is lower
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement best defines risk assessment?

options.text: A way to prove, with exact numbers, that a plan is safe
options.label: A

options.text: A one-time document that removes all risk
options.label: B

options.text: Imagining every possible misfortune in detail
options.label: C

options.text: Identifying what could go wrong, judging likelihood and consequence, and deciding what to do about it
options.label: D
