questions.question_text: Why must turn-back conditions be written before a trip, rather than decided at the moment?

options.text: A rule made calmly in advance is enforceable at the decision point — the moment the situation appears is the worst time to invent the rule
options.label: A

options.text: Written rules are required by park regulations everywhere
options.label: B

options.text: Deciding at the moment gives you the freshest information
options.label: C

options.text: Turn-back conditions only apply to other members of the group
options.label: D

questions.question_text: "The ratings high, medium, and low are judgment, not arithmetic." What does this mean for the assessment?

options.text: Ratings are meaningless, so the assessment cannot work
options.label: A

options.text: The ratings exist to rank priorities using local information — not to prove a precise number
options.label: B

options.text: Only official agency ratings are usable; personal judgment is not allowed
options.label: C

options.text: Ratings should be replaced by the number of items on the list
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household has a smoke detector that chirps, a walkway that ices over in winter, and a rarely-used car. Which set of responses best mixes the four standard options?

options.text: Ignore all three — none of them has happened yet
options.label: A

options.text: Move house — the only real response is to avoid the problems
options.label: B

options.text: Accept all three — risk cannot be changed anyway
options.label: C

options.text: Replace the detector battery (reduce), sand the walkway (reduce), and keep gas in the car (prepare)
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A trip was assessed on Monday as low-risk. By Friday the forecast has changed to heavy rain and the river gauge is rising. What should happen?

options.text: Nothing — the assessment was already done this week
options.label: A

options.text: Add one extra hour of daylight to the plan to compensate
options.label: B

options.text: Re-run the assessment with the new facts — the forecast change is exactly the trigger that retires or promotes hazards
options.label: C

options.text: Trust that the gauge reading is an instrument error
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Before committing to a hiking route, what is the correct sequence of checks?

options.text: Check the weather once at home, then commit — the forecast is stable enough
options.label: A

options.text: Check the forecast and terrain, weigh the group's skill, fitness, gear, and daylight, and write turn-back conditions before starting
options.label: B

options.text: Start early and let the conditions on the route decide everything
options.label: C

options.text: Ask only the strongest member of the group whether to continue
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A family's home plan was written two years ago. Since then, the family has moved to a new region and gained a new member. Why should the assessment be re-run?

options.text: It should not — plans are meant to stay fixed
options.label: A

options.text: Only because the new member is too young to understand the plan
options.label: B

options.text: The household changed — new home, new local hazards, new members — which is exactly the trigger for re-running the identify–evaluate–decide loop
options.label: C

options.text: Only if a disaster actually occurs first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are walking a canyon trail with your eyes on the path, listening to music. Which change in your behavior best matches the survival guidance to "use all your senses"?

options.text: Stop, lift the music, and deliberately scan with sight, hearing, and smell — the river's sound, the wind, the air — before continuing
options.label: A

options.text: Keep the music on but watch the path more carefully
options.label: B

options.text: Speed up so you spend less time in the canyon
options.label: C

options.text: Ask the group for a second opinion on the weather app
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What does "remember where you are" mean in practice, and why does it anchor decision-making?

options.text: It means recalling your childhood address in an emergency
options.label: A

options.text: Keeping track of your location, the time, and your direction of travel — because knowing where you are is what makes "turn back" a real option
options.label: B

options.text: It means writing your name on your gear in case you are separated from it
options.label: C

options.text: It means staying with the last group member you saw
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The river beside your camp was clear this morning. By afternoon it is cloudy and noticeably louder. What is the correct reading of this cue?

options.text: The river is simply carrying more sediment — a normal, harmless change
options.label: A

options.text: It is too late to do anything — the flood is already here
options.label: B

options.text: Cloudy, rising, faster water can announce flooding upstream — move off the floodline and the crossings while the action is still cheap
options.label: C

options.text: The sound of water always stays the same — you are mishearing it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which statement best defines situational awareness?

options.text: Always knowing the exact weather forecast for the next three days
options.label: A

options.text: A personality trait some people are born with
options.label: B

options.text: Noticing everything around you at every moment, without stopping
options.label: C

options.text: Continuously observing your environment and understanding what the observations mean before they become a problem
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a group outing, why is designating one person as the lookout a better arrangement than everyone "just paying attention"?

options.text: Attention gets shared out in a group — a named lookout ensures the environment is actually watched while the group works, and the duty rotates so no one carries it all day
options.label: A

options.text: It removes the need for everyone else to pay any attention
options.label: B

options.text: It is required by park rules on every trail
options.label: C

options.text: It lets the group move faster with fewer stops
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A trip plan — destination, route, and expected return — is left with a friend who is not going. What part of the awareness system does this serve?

options.text: Nothing — the plan is only useful to the people on the trip
options.label: A

options.text: The person who stays behind becomes part of the system: if the group does not return on time, the absence of the plan is itself information that triggers help
options.label: B

options.text: It replaces the need for any other preparation
options.label: C

options.text: It is only useful for long wilderness expeditions, not day trips
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A hiker smells smoke on the wind but sees no flames or smoke plume. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: No plume means no fire — continue as planned
options.label: A

options.text: The smell is likely from a distant barbeque and can be ignored
options.label: B

options.text: Smell can announce a fire before sight can confirm it — identify direction and source, keep an exit open, and treat it as a warning until proven otherwise
options.label: C

options.text: Smoke smell is only a concern at night
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You realize you are not sure whether you passed the second ridge or the third, and the sun is dropping. What is the correct response?

options.text: Keep walking — motion is always better than stopping
options.label: A

options.text: Wait for darkness to navigate by the stars
options.label: B

options.text: Ask a stranger for directions to the trailhead
options.label: C

options.text: Stop and rebuild orientation: recall the landmarks passed, look back along the route, check the time and daylight left, and relate your position to the map — before the light runs out
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The sky in the west has turned dark and the wind has shifted and risen. Your group planned to camp on an exposed ridge tonight. What does the interpretation step of awareness demand?

options.text: Continue — forecasts are usually wrong in the mountains
options.label: A

options.text: Wait until the first raindrop to decide
options.label: B

options.text: Read the cue as weather building, and change the plan while the action is cheap — move the camp to sheltered ground before the storm arrives
options.label: C

options.text: Pitch the tent faster so you are ready when the rain arrives
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You notice the wind shifting and the river picking up, but the rest of the group is chatting and not looking up. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing — pointing out changes might alarm anyone
options.label: A

options.text: Wait until the changes are obvious to everyone, then act
options.label: B

options.text: Quietly start packing your own gear and walk toward the exit
options.label: C

options.text: Announce the change out loud: spoken changes become shared changes, and the group decides together while the action is still cheap
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Hours after getting lost, you notice your heart is up and your mind keeps replaying every wrong turn. What is the correct way to read this?

options.text: This is a normal stress reaction — fear and anxiety are expected responses that get managed, not signs you are failing
options.label: A

options.text: This proves you are not cut out for survival situations
options.label: B

options.text: The only correct response is to ignore the feelings completely
options.label: C

options.text: A reaction like this means the situation is already hopeless
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your mind is looping — replaying the situation and the worst outcomes — and you are getting nothing done. Which response best counters the loop?

options.text: Wait until you feel calm, then start thinking
options.label: A

options.text: Run the structured sequence: size up (condition, resources, surroundings), choose the single best next action, act — then repeat
options.label: B

options.text: Think harder about every possible outcome before acting
options.label: C

options.text: Change location immediately, since movement always helps
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are cold, wet, and the situation feels enormous. Why does breaking the work into small tasks — drink water, move out of the wind, gather ten pieces of fuel — work better than contemplating the whole problem?

options.text: Small tasks take less energy, so you conserve your reserves
options.label: A

options.text: Small tasks keep you busy, which passes the time
options.label: B

options.text: Each finished step restores a sense of control and produces evidence that action works — momentum builds from completed steps
options.label: C

options.text: Small tasks are easier to abandon if the plan changes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A situation demands a decision in the next minute, and you do not have time for a long analysis. Which routine is the right one?

options.text: List every possible option and evaluate each one carefully
options.label: A

options.text: Defer the decision until the group can vote on it
options.label: B

options.text: Choose the option that feels most familiar
options.label: C

options.text: Ask one question — what is the fastest-acting threat right now? — and take the action that addresses it and is cheap or reversible if wrong
options.label: D

questions.question_text: "Some people are natural survivors and the rest are not." What does the manual's framework say about this?

options.text: The psychological side is trainable — routines, practice, and named reactions shape how a person responds under stress, the same way drills shape physical skills
options.label: A

options.text: It is accurate — survival attitude is fixed at birth
options.label: B

options.text: It is accurate only for fear, not for boredom
options.label: C

options.text: The framework does not address attitude at all
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are three days into a slow situation: nothing is failing, but nothing is happening either, and the waiting is eating at you. How should you read the boredom and frustration?

options.text: They are evidence that your morale is broken and the situation is lost
options.label: A

options.text: They are expected reactions — the manual lists boredom among the normal stress reactions, and long waits are managed with purpose, not endured passively
options.label: B

options.text: They only happen to unprepared people
options.label: C

options.text: They are a signal to stop working and wait for rescue
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your group is stressed and starting to argue. Which action applies the lesson's group version of the small-task skill?

options.text: Leave the group alone until everyone calms down
options.label: A

options.text: Collect everyone's opinions and make a list of all of them
options.label: B

options.text: Assign one small, clear task to each member — one watches the river, one gathers fuel, one works the shelter — turning a scared group into a working group
options.label: C

options.text: Ask the group to stop talking about feelings entirely
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A household has never discussed what they would do in a power outage or an evacuation. What does the psychological preparation principle say about this?

options.text: Discussion is unnecessary — the plan will emerge when the emergency arrives
options.label: A

options.text: Talking about it might scare the household, so it should be avoided
options.label: B

options.text: Only children need to hear the plan
options.label: C

options.text: Talking through scenarios and rehearsing routines at home is the psychological drill — each rehearsal is one fewer decision to make under stress
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are lost at dusk with water, a lighter, and a light jacket. Your first use of the structured sequence should produce what?

options.text: A size-up — condition, resources, surroundings — leading to one best next action, which is getting warm and dry before dark
options.label: A

options.text: A complete map of the area drawn from memory
options.label: B

options.text: A decision to hike in one direction for three hours
options.label: C

options.text: A careful ranking of the ten things you wish you had packed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After an emergency, a family member is struggling and you are worried about their mental health. What is the correct guidance?

options.text: Keep it private — these feelings always pass on their own
options.label: A

options.text: Assign them more small tasks so they stay busy
options.label: B

options.text: Tell them that fear is normal, and the topic is now closed
options.label: C

options.text: Seek professional care when it is available — concern for mental health is a reason to get help, and seeking help is part of the plan, not a sign the plan failed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is boiling considered the single most reliable water purification method?

options.text: It's the fastest method available
options.label: A

options.text: It's the only method that improves the taste of water
options.label: B

options.text: It kills or inactivates all types of biological pathogens — bacteria, viruses, and protozoa
options.label: C

options.text: It removes chemical contaminants along with pathogens
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At sea level, how long should you maintain a rolling boil to ensure water is safe to drink?

options.text: 30 seconds — as soon as it bubbles, it's safe
options.label: A

options.text: 1 minute of rolling boil
options.label: B

options.text: 5 minutes to be safe
options.label: C

options.text: 10 minutes — the old guidelines are the safest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are camping at 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). How does this affect your boiling procedure?

options.text: Water boils faster at altitude, so 30 seconds is sufficient
options.label: A

options.text: No change — 1 minute is always enough
options.label: B

options.text: Extend boiling time to 3 minutes — water boils at a lower temperature at altitude
options.label: C

options.text: Boiling doesn't work at high altitude — use chemical treatment instead
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following containers should you NEVER use to boil water?

options.text: A single-wall stainless steel water bottle with the cap off
options.label: A

options.text: A clean metal food can supported above the fire
options.label: B

options.text: A titanium camping pot with a lid
options.label: C

options.text: A double-wall insulated bottle
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an effective technique for reducing fuel consumption when boiling water?

options.text: Boil water without a lid — evaporation cools the water faster
options.label: A

options.text: Use a lid on the pot — it can reduce fuel consumption by 30–40%
options.label: B

options.text: Boil an extra liter "just in case" to avoid having to boil again later
options.label: C

options.text: Boil for 10 minutes to make sure all pathogens are dead
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A stream near an abandoned mine may contain heavy metals. Will boiling the water make it safe to drink?

options.text: Yes — boiling removes all contaminants, including heavy metals
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — the heat causes heavy metals to evaporate
options.label: B

options.text: No — boiling does not remove heavy metals or chemical contaminants; in fact, evaporation may concentrate them
options.label: C

options.text: No — but boiling longer than 3 minutes will remove them
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are in a survival situation with only a single-wall metal water bottle and a lighter. What is the correct safety precaution when boiling water in the bottle?

options.text: Tighten the cap securely so water doesn't spill
options.label: A

options.text: Leave the cap off — pressure buildup in a sealed container can cause an explosion
options.label: B

options.text: Place the bottle directly in hot coals for maximum heat transfer
options.label: C

options.text: Fill the bottle only halfway so there's room for steam
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You've boiled water and let it cool. What should you do to prevent recontamination?

options.text: Nothing — boiled water stays sterile indefinitely
options.label: A

options.text: Add ice to cool it faster so you can store it sooner
options.label: B

options.text: Store it in a clean, covered container and avoid touching the inside or the water with unwashed hands
options.label: C

options.text: Leave it uncovered so air circulation keeps it fresh
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is the 30-minute wait after adding a chemical disinfectant essential?

options.text: It allows the chemical taste to fade
options.label: A

options.text: It gives the chemical reaction time to inactivate pathogens — it is not instantaneous
options.label: B

options.text: It allows sediment to settle to the bottom
options.label: C

options.text: It lets the water cool to a safe drinking temperature
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are treating clear water at room temperature with standard unscented household bleach (5–6% sodium hypochlorite). What is the correct dosage?

options.text: 1 drop per liter
options.label: A

options.text: 2 drops per liter
options.label: B

options.text: 5 drops per liter
options.label: C

options.text: 10 drops per liter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: When treating cloudy water with bleach, what adjustment should you make?

options.text: Use the same dose but wait twice as long
options.label: A

options.text: Use half the dose — cloudy water needs less chemical
options.label: B

options.text: Pre-filter through cloth and double the dose to 4 drops per liter
options.label: C

options.text: Switch to iodine — bleach doesn't work in cloudy water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following people should NOT use iodine for water purification?

options.text: An adult male backpacker on a weekend trip
options.label: A

options.text: A pregnant woman
options.label: B

options.text: A teenager on a scout camping trip
options.label: C

options.text: A retired hiker in good health
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why is neither chlorine nor iodine considered reliable against Cryptosporidium?

options.text: Crypto is too small for chemicals to detect
options.label: A

options.text: Crypto oocysts have a tough outer shell that resists chemical penetration
options.label: B

options.text: Crypto only occurs in tropical water sources
options.label: C

options.text: Crypto multiplies faster than chemicals can kill it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are building a water treatment kit for long-term storage. Which chemical option is the better choice?

options.text: A bottle of liquid household bleach
options.label: A

options.text: NaDCC chlorine dioxide tablets in foil seals
options.label: B

options.text: A bottle of 2% iodine tincture
options.label: C

options.text: Pool chlorine tablets
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are treating near-freezing water (below 10°C / 50°F) with chlorine. What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Use double the normal dose — more chemical compensates for cold
options.label: A

options.text: Use the same dose but double the contact time to 60 minutes
options.label: B

options.text: Cold water doesn't need chemical treatment — it's naturally sterile
options.label: C

options.text: Warm the water by adding hot water from another source
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are concerned about both Cryptosporidium and viruses in a water source. You have a 0.2-micron filter and chlorine tablets. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use chlorine tablets alone — they handle everything
options.label: A

options.text: Use the filter alone — 0.2 microns catches everything
options.label: B

options.text: Filter first, then chemically treat — the filter removes Crypto, and the chlorine kills viruses
options.label: C

options.text: Chemically treat first, then filter — the chemicals make the filter work better
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are at a clear mountain stream with no known chemical contamination. Which method should you use?

options.text: Distillation — it's the most thorough method available
options.label: A

options.text: Boiling or filtration — distillation is overkill for biological contamination and wastes fuel
options.label: B

options.text: Distillation — it's the only method that works on clear water
options.label: C

options.text: None — clear mountain water is safe to drink untreated
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your water source is a clear mountain stream with no known chemical contamination. Why would distillation be a poor choice here compared to boiling?

options.text: Distillation leaves viruses in the water that boiling kills
options.label: A

options.text: Distillation needs a power source, while boiling works over any fire
options.label: B

options.text: Distillation vaporizes the water — which consumes roughly 7× more fuel than simply boiling — for no added benefit against pathogens
options.label: C

options.text: Distilled water is unsafe to drink for more than a few days
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Under optimal conditions (hot, sunny, moist soil), approximately how much water can a single solar still produce per day?

options.text: 5–10 liters — enough for a family
options.label: A

options.text: 2–3 liters — enough for one person
options.label: B

options.text: 0.5–1.0 liters — survival quantity, not comfort quantity
options.label: C

options.text: 10–20 liters — more than enough for anyone
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which type of contaminant can potentially pass through distillation along with the water vapor?

options.text: Heavy metals like lead and mercury
options.label: A

options.text: Salt from seawater
options.label: B

options.text: Some volatile organic compounds (VOCs) with boiling points lower than water
options.label: C

options.text: Bacteria and protozoa
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are in a coastal survival situation. The only water source is seawater. Which purification method will work?

options.text: Boiling — it kills everything in seawater
options.label: A

options.text: Filtration with a 0.2-micron filter — it removes salt
options.label: B

options.text: Chemical treatment with chlorine — it neutralizes salt
options.label: C

options.text: Distillation — it is the only field method that removes salt
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You've been drinking only distilled water for four days in a survival situation. Is this dangerous?

options.text: Yes — distilled water is toxic and causes immediate organ damage
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — distilled water lacks minerals essential for survival beyond 24 hours
options.label: B

options.text: No — mineral deficiency from distilled water is a concern for months/years, not days; dehydration from not drinking is the immediate threat
options.label: C

options.text: No — distilled water contains more minerals than regular water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What determines what a water filter removes from water?

options.text: The brand of the filter
options.label: A

options.text: The age of the filter
options.label: B

options.text: The absolute pore size of the filter
options.label: C

options.text: The color of the filter cartridge
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A standard 0.2-micron backpacking filter reliably removes which of the following?

options.text: Bacteria, viruses, and protozoa
options.label: A

options.text: Viruses and protozoa only
options.label: B

options.text: Bacteria and protozoa — but NOT viruses
options.label: C

options.text: Protozoa only
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which filter type is the lightest and most common in modern backpacking filters?

options.text: Ceramic candle
options.label: A

options.text: Hollow fiber membrane
options.label: B

options.text: Activated carbon block
options.label: C

options.text: Slow sand
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are traveling in a developing region where tap water is not safe and sanitation infrastructure is limited. You have a 0.2-micron filter. What should you do?

options.text: Use the filter alone — 0.2 microns is sufficient
options.label: A

options.text: Add chemical treatment after filtering — the filter misses viruses, and human fecal contamination means virus risk is high
options.label: B

options.text: Use only chemical treatment — the filter isn't needed
options.label: C

options.text: Skip treatment — the water looks clear
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your hollow fiber filter was left in your pack overnight and the temperature dropped below freezing. In the morning, water still flows through it normally. Is it safe to use?

options.text: Yes — if water flows through, the filter is working
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — hollow fiber filters are freeze-resistant
options.label: B

options.text: No — ice crystals rupture the microscopic tubes, and the damage is invisible; the filter must be replaced
options.label: C

options.text: Maybe — run some clean water through and taste it first
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the correct way to protect a hollow fiber filter from freezing during cold-weather travel?

options.text: Store it in an outside pack pocket so it stays cold and doesn't sweat
options.label: A

options.text: Keep it in an inside pocket close to body heat during the day, and in your sleeping bag at night
options.label: B

options.text: Wrap it in a towel in your pack — the insulation will protect it
options.label: C

options.text: Store it with the water bladder full — full containers freeze slower
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are backpacking in a low-use wilderness area with clear mountain streams. A 0.2-micron hollow fiber filter is your primary method. Is this sufficient on its own?

options.text: No — you should always add chemical treatment regardless of conditions
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — viral risk is minimal in low-use wilderness streams, and the filter handles bacteria and protozoa, which are the main concerns
options.label: B

options.text: No — you should boil instead; filtration isn't reliable
options.label: C

options.text: Yes — any water that looks clear is safe to drink unfiltered
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are stranded without a commercial filter. You have a clean cloth and materials to build a fire. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Filter water through the cloth and drink it — cloth removes bacteria
options.label: A

options.text: Build a sand-charcoal-gravel filter and drink directly — improvised filters are reliable
options.label: B

options.text: Pre-filter through the cloth to remove sediment, then boil the water — improvised filtration is pre-treatment, not treatment
options.label: C

options.text: Drink directly from the stream — running water is safe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The tap is dry and your household needs water. Which sequence follows the correct priority order for emergency water?

options.text: Stored supply first, then home sources like the water heater tank, then natural sources
options.label: A

options.text: Nearest natural source first, because it is unlimited
options.label: B

options.text: Natural sources first, then stored supply, then home sources
options.label: C

options.text: Home sources first, because they are easiest to reach, ignoring the stored supply
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are walking a dry streambed in hilly country and want to find water. Which reading of the landscape is most reliable?

options.text: The highest point on the ridge, because water pools at the top of drainages
options.label: A

options.text: Dig wherever the soil is driest, because dry ground means water is close below
options.label: B

options.text: Follow the widest animal trail, which always leads to a safe spring
options.label: C

options.text: Follow the drainage downstream — water concentrates in valleys, ravines, and low points
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You need the largest reserve of water inside a home with no running supply. Which source do you access, and what is the correct first step?

options.text: The toilet bowl, because it holds more than the tank
options.label: A

options.text: The water heater tank, after shutting off the power or gas and the inlet valve
options.label: B

options.text: The refrigerator's drip tray, because it refills itself
options.label: C

options.text: The hot water pipes only, since they hold the most water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Standing at a stream, you see three options: the fast main flow, a stagnant backwater pool, and a seep emerging from a bank of the stream. Which is the best natural choice, and why?

options.text: The stagnant pool — still water settles contaminants out
options.label: A

options.text: The fast main flow — speed always means safety
options.label: B

options.text: The seep — water emerging from the ground is generally less exposed to contamination than open surface water
options.label: C

options.text: The pool and the flow mixed together, to dilute any problems
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A stream looks clear, cold, and fast. Which combination of checks tells you the most about whether it is safe to use?

options.text: Smell for fuel, sewage, or chemical odors; inspect for dead animals; check what is upstream
options.label: A

options.text: Check that it is moving fast enough to carry away anything bad
options.label: B

options.text: Confirm the water is clear and cold, since both indicate purity
options.label: C

options.text: Taste a small sip — the flavor tells you if it is contaminated
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have treated a batch of stream water and a batch of snow melt. What protects the treated water from becoming dangerous again before it is drunk?

options.text: Leaving both batches uncovered so they stay fresh
options.label: A

options.text: Storing treated water in clean, covered containers, kept separate from untreated water
options.label: B

options.text: Mixing treated and untreated water, since treatment spreads
options.label: C

options.text: Refreezing the treated water, since cold kills pathogens
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In a dry landscape you spot a band of lush green vegetation between two hills. What does this clue tell you — and what does it not tell you?

options.text: It guarantees a clean spring, so no treatment is needed
options.label: A

options.text: It only tells you the soil is rich; water has nothing to do with it
options.label: B

options.text: It suggests moisture near the surface, but the water must still be located, inspected, and treated
options.label: C

options.text: It marks the site of an old mine, which is always a good water source
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After a flood, you are considering flood water as a supply. What is the accurate assessment?

options.text: Flood water is fine once the mud settles out
options.label: A

options.text: Flood water is fine because it is moving water, which dilutes contamination
options.label: B

options.text: Flood water is fine if it does not smell
options.label: C

options.text: Flood water is the highest-risk source — it can carry sewage, chemicals, and debris, and is to be avoided even with treatment
options.label: D

questions.question_text: The water at your collection point has a faint oily sheen and a chemical smell. You have a stove and can boil it. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Reject this source — boiling inactivates pathogens but does not remove chemical contaminants, so this water is not usable
options.label: A

options.text: Boil it longer — extended boiling removes chemicals
options.label: B

options.text: Boil it and add purification tablets for double treatment
options.label: C

options.text: Skim the sheen off the top and boil the rest
options.label: D

questions.question_text: In your home, which water is an acceptable emergency source, and what must you do before drawing it?

options.text: The toilet bowl, as long as you skim from the surface
options.label: A

options.text: The toilet tank reserve, after shutting off the inlet valve so contaminated water cannot refill it
options.label: B

options.text: The toilet tank reserve, with the inlet open so it refills as you draw
options.label: C

options.text: The water heater tank, without shutting anything off
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following water purification methods kills ALL types of biological pathogens — bacteria, viruses, and protozoa?

options.text: Filtration with a 0.2 micron filter
options.label: A

options.text: Chemical treatment with chlorine
options.label: B

options.text: Boiling water at a rolling boil for 1 minute
options.label: C

options.text: Solar disinfection (SODIS)
options.label: D

questions.question_text: At altitudes above 2,000 meters (6,562 feet), how long should you maintain a rolling boil?

options.text: 30 seconds — higher altitude means water boils faster
options.label: A

options.text: 3 minutes — the lower boiling temperature at altitude requires longer contact time
options.label: B

options.text: 1 minute — same as sea level
options.label: C

options.text: 10 minutes — high altitude requires full sterilization
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are treating clear water with standard unscented household bleach (5–6% sodium hypochlorite). How many drops per liter should you use, and how long should you wait?

options.text: 1 drop per liter, wait 5 minutes
options.label: A

options.text: 2 drops per liter, wait at least 30 minutes
options.label: B

options.text: 5 drops per liter, wait at least 30 minutes
options.label: C

options.text: 10 drops per liter, wait 10 minutes
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why might a high-quality backpacking filter with a 0.2 micron pore size NOT be sufficient on its own in some situations?

options.text: 0.2 micron filters don't remove sediment
options.label: A

options.text: 0.2 micron filters can miss viruses, which are smaller than 0.2 microns
options.label: B

options.text: 0.2 micron filters remove beneficial minerals
options.label: C

options.text: 0.2 micron filters only work with clear water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are purifying near-freezing water (below 10°C / 50°F) using chlorine bleach. What adjustment should you make?

options.text: Use half the normal dose — cold water purifies faster
options.label: A

options.text: Use boiling instead — chlorine doesn't work at all in cold water
options.label: B

options.text: Double the contact time — chemical reactions slow down in cold water
options.label: C

options.text: Use iodine instead — iodine works faster in cold water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a valid reason to AVOID using iodine as your primary long-term water purification method?

options.text: Iodine is ineffective against bacteria
options.label: A

options.text: Iodine is only effective in warm climates
options.label: B

options.text: Iodine is not recommended for pregnant women, people with thyroid conditions, or prolonged daily use
options.label: C

options.text: Iodine loses its effectiveness in clear water
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the best approach when you are unsure about the safety of a water source and have both a filter and purification tablets available?

options.text: Use the filter alone — it's faster
options.label: A

options.text: Use the tablets alone — chemicals are more thorough
options.label: B

options.text: Filter first, then chemically treat — the methods complement each other
options.label: C

options.text: Boil instead — combining methods has no advantage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You've boiled water and it's now cool. What should you do to prevent it from becoming recontaminated?

options.text: Nothing — boiled water stays safe indefinitely
options.label: A

options.text: Add a small amount of bleach to preserve it
options.label: B

options.text: Store it in a clean, covered container and avoid touching the inside of the container or the water with unwashed hands
options.label: C

options.text: Keep it in the same pot you boiled it in, uncovered, so air can circulate
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are installing your first rain barrel. What are the three parts of the system you are building?

options.text: Roof catchment, gutters and downspout conveyance, and barrel storage
options.label: A

options.text: A pump, a hose, and a nozzle
options.label: B

options.text: A filter, a faucet, and a drain
options.label: C

options.text: A well, a tank, and a pressure system
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You have two downspouts: one near the vegetable garden, one near the driveway. Which layout choice best serves a rain barrel's practical purpose?

options.text: The driveway downspout, because runoff there is cleaner
options.label: A

options.text: The garden-side downspout, because the water will actually be used there instead of carried
options.label: B

options.text: The highest downspout, because height adds pressure
options.label: C

options.text: The north side, because shade keeps the water cool
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A neighbor's barrel has no screen on the inlet and no lid. What is the most serious consequence, and why?

options.text: The water will evaporate faster, so the barrel will be empty
options.label: A

options.text: The barrel will fill with too much water and overflow
options.label: B

options.text: Mosquitoes will breed in the standing water, and debris and bird waste will enter the stored supply
options.label: C

options.text: The water will freeze more quickly in winter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After three weeks of dry weather, the first storm is about to fill your barrel. What should happen to the first minutes of runoff?

options.text: It should fill the barrel — it is the cleanest rain of the storm
options.label: A

options.text: It should be captured separately and used for drinking, since it is freshest
options.label: B

options.text: It should be boiled before it enters the barrel
options.label: C

options.text: It should be diverted away from the barrel — it carries accumulated dust, droppings, and roof chemicals
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Rain barrel water is fine for the lawn, but you are considering it for your vegetable garden. What is the accurate position?

options.text: It is equally fine — soil filters everything by the time it reaches the roots
options.label: A

options.text: Roof pollutants — bacteria from birds and animals, chemicals from roof materials — are a real consideration for edible plantings
options.label: B

options.text: It is fine only if the garden is raised beds
options.label: C

options.text: It is never acceptable, because any roof runoff kills plants
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You want to drink from your rain barrel. Which chain is required between the downspout and your mouth?

options.text: None — rain is distilled by nature
options.label: A

options.text: Strain through a clean cloth only
options.label: B

options.text: Treat the water like any raw water: boiling, chemical treatment, or filtration, then store it clean
options.label: C

options.text: Let it sit for a week so sediment settles, then drink
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You place a barrel on the ground next to the downspout. What is the most practical consequence?

options.text: A watering can will not fit under the spigot, so you need another container — elevate the barrel so gravity is the pump
options.label: A

options.text: The water will be colder, which makes it unsafe
options.label: B

options.text: The barrel will fill more slowly
options.label: C

options.text: The barrel will need no overflow
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your household's stored emergency water is nearly gone and you are considering the barrel as the replacement supply. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: The barrel is the replacement — rain fills it continuously
options.label: A

options.text: The barrel is better than stored water because it never needs rotation
options.label: B

options.text: The barrel water is already safe because the rain was clean
options.label: C

options.text: The barrel is a raw-water supplement at best — it is weather-dependent, needs treatment for drinking, and does not replace the stored emergency supply
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your barrel has been sitting full for a month and the water smells stagnant. What went wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — stagnation is normal and harmless
options.label: A

options.text: The system lacked turnover and cleaning: empty the barrel, clean out sediment and biofilm, and set a use-and-rotate pattern
options.label: B

options.text: The roof was wrong — change the roof material
options.label: C

options.text: The water is unsafe because the barrel was elevated
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Winter is coming and the barrel is full. What is the correct seasonal move?

options.text: Leave it full — frozen water is still usable in spring
options.label: A

options.text: Top it off so the ice cannot damage it
options.label: B

options.text: Drain the barrel before hard freezes — expanding ice can crack barrels and fittings
options.label: C

options.text: Move it into the sun so it thaws between storms
options.label: D

questions.question_text: What is the active mechanism by which SODIS inactivates pathogens?

options.text: The plastic bottle releases antimicrobial chemicals into the water
options.label: A

options.text: UV-A radiation reacts with dissolved oxygen to produce reactive oxygen species that damage pathogen DNA
options.label: B

options.text: Visible light heats the water to boiling, killing everything
options.label: C

options.text: The bottle filters out pathogens as water passes through the opening
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why must SODIS use PET plastic bottles rather than glass bottles?

options.text: PET is cheaper than glass
options.label: A

options.text: Glass blocks most UV-A radiation, which is the active disinfecting agent
options.label: B

options.text: Glass bottles are too heavy to carry
options.label: C

options.text: PET bottles filter the water as it sits
options.label: D

questions.question_text: On a sunny day with less than 50% cloud cover, what is the standard SODIS exposure time?

options.text: 1 hour
options.label: A

options.text: 3 hours
options.label: B

options.text: 6 hours
options.label: C

options.text: 12 hours
options.label: D

questions.question_text: It has been overcast for two days. According to the SODIS protocol, how long must water be exposed?

options.text: 6 hours — the UV still penetrates clouds
options.label: A

options.text: 1 day — cloud cover halves UV intensity, so half the normal exposure is enough
options.label: B

options.text: 2 full days — cloud cover dramatically reduces UV intensity
options.label: C

options.text: SODIS doesn't work at all in overcast conditions
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key limitation of SODIS compared to boiling?

options.text: SODIS is more expensive than boiling
options.label: A

options.text: SODIS is less effective against Cryptosporidium and does not work in all weather conditions
options.label: B

options.text: SODIS requires special equipment not available to most people
options.label: C

options.text: SODIS makes water taste worse than boiling does
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are at a sunny base camp at low altitude near the equator. The stream water is slightly cloudy. You have clear PET bottles. Is SODIS appropriate, and what should you do?

options.text: No — SODIS only works with perfectly clear water
options.label: A

options.text: Yes — pre-filter the water through a cloth until it's clear enough to read through, then place bottles horizontally in direct sun for 6 hours
options.label: B

options.text: Yes — fill bottles directly from the stream and leave for 1 hour, the sun handles the rest
options.label: C

options.text: No — SODIS doesn't work near the equator because it's too hot
options.label: D

questions.question_text: According to FEMA and CDC guidelines, how much emergency water should you store per person per day?

options.text: 1 liter (0.25 gallons)
options.label: A

options.text: 2 liters (0.5 gallons)
options.label: B

options.text: 3.8 liters (1 gallon)
options.label: C

options.text: 10 liters (2.6 gallons)
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A 2-week water supply for a family of 4 requires approximately how much water?

options.text: 24 liters (6 gallons)
options.label: A

options.text: 56 liters (14 gallons)
options.label: B

options.text: 224 liters (56 gallons)
options.label: C

options.text: 500 liters (132 gallons)
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Which of the following containers is SAFE for long-term emergency water storage?

options.text: An empty milk jug, thoroughly washed
options.label: A

options.text: A food-grade HDPE (#2) jerry can
options.label: B

options.text: A container that previously held laundry detergent, thoroughly rinsed
options.label: C

options.text: A cardboard juice carton
options.label: D

questions.question_text: After sanitizing a water storage container with a bleach solution, what should you do?

options.text: Rinse thoroughly with tap water to remove all bleach residue
options.label: A

options.text: Rinse with distilled water only
options.label: B

options.text: Pour out the sanitizing solution and do NOT rinse — the residual chlorine film continues to protect
options.label: C

options.text: Let the container air-dry completely before filling
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You stored water in sanitized HDPE containers in a cool, dark basement 18 months ago. The water was municipal tap water (pre-chlorinated). You haven't checked it since. What should you do?

options.text: Discard immediately — water expires after 6 months
options.label: A

options.text: Inspect the water for cloudiness, odor, or container damage — if clear and odor-free, it's likely safe; rotate this batch and set a reminder to check every 6 months
options.label: B

options.text: Drink without checking — sealed containers keep water safe indefinitely regardless of conditions
options.label: C

options.text: Boil all of it before drinking — stored water always needs re-treatment
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your stored emergency water has run out during an extended power outage. The tap is dry. Which of the following is a safe alternative water source in your home?

options.text: Water from the toilet bowl
options.label: A

options.text: Water from the water heater tank, drained from the bottom valve
options.label: B

options.text: Water from a decorative vase that's been sitting for weeks
options.label: C

options.text: Swimming pool water — it's chlorinated so it's safe
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are auditing a water system. In what order do the links of the chain run, and why does the order matter?

options.text: Source → conveyance → storage → distribution → tap; contamination can enter at any link, so the whole chain must be protected
options.label: A

options.text: Tap → distribution → storage → conveyance → source; testing the tap covers everything upstream
options.label: B

options.text: Storage → source → tap → conveyance → distribution; the tank is the only link that matters
options.label: C

options.text: Source → tap → storage → conveyance → distribution; only the ends of the chain matter
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You can choose between two tanks for a gravity-fed system: a tall narrow tank on a high stand, or a large flat tank on the ground. Which delivers stronger flow at the tap, and why?

options.text: The large flat tank — volume is what creates pressure
options.label: A

options.text: The tall tank on the high stand — pressure comes from the height of the water surface above the tap
options.label: B

options.text: They are identical — tank shape never affects flow
options.label: C

options.text: Neither — only pumps create pressure
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A cabin relies on an electric pump that lifts water directly to the taps. What is the system's single point of failure, and what pairing fixes it?

options.text: The tank is too small — a bigger tank fixes it
options.label: A

options.text: The pipes are too narrow — larger pipes fix it
options.label: B

options.text: The pump dies when power dies — pair the pump with elevated storage (or a manual pump) so water is held above the taps
options.label: C

options.text: The water is cold — insulation fixes it
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A garden hose rests in a bucket of soapy water. The system loses pressure during a pipe repair. What happens, and what is the danger?

options.text: Nothing — pressure loss only affects the repair point
options.label: A

options.text: The soapy water flows out of the bucket into the yard, which is harmless
options.label: B

options.text: The hose fills with clean water from the system, which rinses the bucket
options.label: C

options.text: The pressure drop siphons the bucket's contents backward into the drinking line — a backflow contamination event
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two statements describe a clean, covered storage tank in a gravity system. Which statement is the more accurate assessment of system safety?

options.text: A clean, covered tank guarantees clean water at every tap
options.label: A

options.text: A clean tank is all that matters; distribution pipes cannot contaminate water
options.label: B

options.text: A clean, covered tank protects that link, but contamination can still enter at the source, the distribution pipes, or a cross-connection
options.label: C

options.text: A covered tank is worse than an open one, because covered tanks cannot be cleaned
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A system's pump has run dry for several minutes during a repair. Which consequences are most likely?

options.text: The water it pumped is contaminated
options.label: A

options.text: The water becomes hotter
options.label: B

options.text: The tank overflowed
options.label: C

options.text: Seals or the motor were damaged — running dry is a common way pumps are destroyed
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Winter is coming and the cabin's system will sit unoccupied. What is the correct winterization approach?

options.text: Drain the lines, pump, and tank; leave valves open; write down the sequence — water expands when it freezes and cracks everything it is inside
options.label: A

options.text: Leave everything full — the ice seals the pipes
options.label: B

options.text: Drain only the tank, since pipes are stronger than tanks
options.label: C

options.text: Keep the water warm by leaving the pump running
options.label: D

questions.question_text: During a flood, floodwater entered the distribution system through an exposed intake. The water looks clear again a week later. What is the correct response before anyone drinks from the system?

options.text: Drink it — clarity proves the contamination is gone
options.label: A

options.text: Treat or disinfect the water (per EPA emergency disinfection guidance) and treat the system as contaminated until proven otherwise
options.label: B

options.text: Boil a single potful for the household and use the rest untreated
options.label: C

options.text: Run the taps for an hour to flush, then drink
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A system draws from a spring-fed cistern whose inlet is a pipe laid through a pasture. Which entry point for contamination is this — and what is the fix?

options.text: A cross-connection — install a vacuum breaker
options.label: A

options.text: A backflow event — drain the cistern
options.label: B

options.text: A conveyance failure — the pipe passes through an area where animal waste can contaminate the water before it reaches storage
options.label: C

options.text: A storage failure — the cistern is too small
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A new tank for a drinking-water system used to hold agricultural chemicals. What is the correct decision, and why?

options.text: Rinse it thoroughly and use it — washing removes everything
options.label: A

options.text: Use it only for the garden line, since chemicals are fine for plants
options.label: B

options.text: Use it with a filter added to the outlet
options.label: C

options.text: Reject it — containers that previously held chemicals or fuel cannot be made safe for drinking-water storage
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A stream looks clear, cold, and tastes fine. Why is this still not enough to certify the water safe?

options.text: Pathogens are invisible — bacteria, viruses, and protozoa leave no sensory trace at harmful levels
options.label: A

options.text: The water is probably too cold to be safe
options.label: B

options.text: Clear water is always contaminated, since sediment indicates safety
options.label: C

options.text: Taste only works for detecting salt
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Water from a new source has a faint chemical smell but looks clear. What is the correct reading of the observation signals?

options.text: The chemical smell is irrelevant — clarity is the deciding signal
options.label: A

options.text: The odor is disqualifying — observation rejects the source, and the absence of smell would have proven nothing
options.label: B

options.text: Smell a second time; if it fades, the water is fine
options.label: C

options.text: Boil it — boiling removes chemical smells permanently
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Why does WHO guidance test for microbial indicators like E. coli rather than trying to detect every possible pathogen?

options.text: E. coli is the only pathogen that causes illness
options.label: A

options.text: Pathogens are easier to count than indicators
options.label: B

options.text: Counting every pathogen is impractical — an indicator organism signals fecal contamination efficiently
options.label: C

options.text: Indicators are cheaper than any other test
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your well casing was submerged during a flood and the water is now clear again. When should you test?

options.text: Next season, when the water settles for good
options.label: A

options.text: Only if someone gets sick
options.label: B

options.text: When you remember to buy a kit
options.label: C

options.text: Immediately — flooding is exactly the event that makes a supply suspect until treated and verified
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You are testing the kitchen tap of a house with a storage tank. Where do you take the sample from, and why?

options.text: The tap a drinker actually uses, after running the line briefly — it represents what a drinker gets
options.label: A

options.text: The top of the tank, because it is the cleanest water
options.label: B

options.text: The bottom of the tank, because it concentrates everything
options.label: C

options.text: Anywhere — sample location never matters
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Your field test returns a negative coliform result. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: The water is certified safe for the next year
options.label: A

options.text: No indicator was detected within the test's limits, at this moment, in this sample — evidence, not a warranty
options.label: B

options.text: The water is safe only if it also tastes good
options.label: C

options.text: The test failed, since clean water always shows positive results
options.label: D

questions.question_text: A lab test for a permanent supply comes back positive for coliform. What is the correct sequence of next steps?

options.text: Drink it anyway, since the water looks fine
options.label: A

options.text: Retest with a field kit and drink if that is negative
options.label: B

options.text: Treat the water (boiling, chemical, or filtration), identify the contamination path, and plan the fix before re-testing
options.label: C

options.text: Boil one potful for the household and leave the rest as-is
options.label: D

questions.question_text: You sample the well for the lab, but the sample sits in a hot car for two days before delivery. What does the result now describe?

options.text: The well's normal water quality, unchanged
options.label: A

options.text: The water's quality only if it stayed cool
options.label: B

options.text: Nothing — heat does not affect samples
options.label: C

options.text: The conditions of the sample during transit, not the well — time and temperature affect microbial results
options.label: D

questions.question_text: Two questions can be asked of the same treatment system: "is the source clean?" and "does the treatment work?" How should the sampling differ?

options.text: Source quality is sampled before treatment; treatment verification is sampled after treatment — two different questions, two different sample points
options.label: A
